problem: The SNIPER 32 GB / 73% result arises from aggregating per-test MCS sets, and the paper's remedy is a joint MaxSAT encoding, not a size cutoff; also 92.3 to 4.5 is for a random measurement strategy (informed sda(ew) is 42.0 without pruning).
fix: On c432 a random strategy needs 92.3 measurements (single fault) without cardinality pruning vs 4.5 with it; MMCS and RS support size cutoffs and Berge can be adapted; separately, SNIPER hit the 32 GB limit on 73% of TCAS programs when aggregating per-test MCSes (not a cutoff result).

fix: ToT's appendix (Game of 24) suggests the bottleneck is thought generation: GPT-4 generating with GPT-3.5 evaluating gets 64% vs 74% with GPT-4 for both.

problem: The Kamoi survey says prompted-LLM feedback succeeds only in exceptionally suited tasks and, separately, that self-correction works with reliable external feedback; the claim merges these into one condition.
fix: A critical survey finds no clear success with prompted-LLM feedback outside tasks exceptionally suited to it; self-correction works where reliable external feedback exists.

problem: Smith (N=94/91/80), Marsh (N=80, .087-.280, 4.4-5.4) and Verma (33-68% vs 2-14%) verified; George & Wiley visual-example originality drop is only in the no-avoid condition (interaction, no main effect); evidence line b01 says 3.5 creatures but paper shows 2.95/3.08 (not in claim).

Numbers verified (53.3 vs 56.1, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0, Chakrabarty no positive correlation, Hivemind misalignment) but Si never says judges are at chance: best judge 53.3% is slightly above the 50% baseline, and Chakrabarty's GPT-4 reached kappa>0.2 on two tests.
fix: LLM judges rank ideas barely above chance and worse than experts: the best LLM evaluator reached 53.3% vs expert inter-reviewer 56.1% (top vs bottom 25% of ideas; GPT-4o pairwise 45.0%); on a Torrance-style story rubric no LLM assessor correlated positively with experts on average (correlations near zero); reward models and LLM judges align worse with humans on open-ended prompts where raters disagree.

Ward 2002 (99/97/91%, N=71; handles 23 vs 73%, mouthpieces 39 vs 1%) and Birdsell 2019 (legs 72%, eyes 88%, n=25 usable) verified; three of four evidence lines are the same Ward paper, and the replication is small (25 creatures).

Ricks et al. 2007 (knowledge x problem type F(1,52)=5.58, WMC no help on misleading items) verified; Purcell & Gero 1996 exists (Design Studies 17:363-383) and the mechanical-engineering result is only confirmed secondhand via Wang et al. 2023 review; Ricks warns baseball demand may have been guessed.

Ma 2024 (crowd more diverse on all topics/metrics), Meincke (.243 vs .255-.432), Anderson (d=.47 group, individual ns) and Hivemind (>0.8) verified; the Meincke human pool is a student group, a high bar.

IDEAFix Fig 5a distances .206-.341 and its shared-semantic-space statement, plus Hivemind cross-model similarity, verified; 'small' distance has no human or within-model baseline in IDEAFix, and it is a preprint.

Deng (slopes 1.013->1.363, categories 18.45->24.84, human slope 1.035 vs 1.035), Ma critique-critique best, IDEAFix +10% to +41%, Verbalized Sampling jokes 1.83->2.93 and Huang 75.8->38.1 all verified; Deng human CoT also lowered category count slightly (26.29->25.36), so 'did nothing' holds for slope only.

Ward 62% vs 66% and Meincke Jobs .368 vs .377 hold, but IDEAFix says the opposite of the last clause: short plain 'think outside the box'/'wild'/'unconventional' prompts did as well as or better than long method prompts, so explicit divergence wording does help LLMs.
fix: A generic 'be creative' instruction did not change human reliance on Earth fruit (66% vs 62%, ns; 'not bound by Earth fruit' cut it to 48%), and 'think like Steve Jobs' barely moved GPT-4 pool similarity (.368 vs .377 baseline); in contrast IDEAFix found short explicit divergence prompts ('wild', 'unconventional', 'think outside the box') matched or beat long creativity-method prompts on LLM novelty, though homogenization stayed.

problem: Wadinambiarachchi (+0.32, BF 124, N=60, lower fluency), Cheng & Zhang (N=204 per study, simple vs complex) and Kumar (1,100 participants, no solo carry-over) verified; Cheng's 'LLM partner' is a scripted pool of ideas delivered by an assistant, and the CI upper bound is .55 in the paper.

MacGyver (35-42% vs 65.1%) and BrainTeaser (ChatGPT 63/53 vs 92%) verified, but CreativityBench's .19 vs .51 compares gold part-level to entity correctness within LLMs and has no human baseline, so it does not support 'fewer than people'.
fix: Default LLMs solve far fewer functional-fixedness style problems than people: MacGyver single-attempt success 35% to 42% vs 65.1% for the average human; BrainTeaser ChatGPT 63% (sentence) and 53% (word) vs 92% human. On CreativityBench (no human baseline) LLMs pick a plausible entity far more often than the right part: gold part-level correctness .19 vs entity correctness .51.

problem: In Wong et al. the highest judged creativity (88.1 vs 69.6) came from random-term context while the flexibility gain (12.4 vs 9.4) came from the unrelated-context type; and in HAICo the associative-prompting diversity gain is an offline GPT-5 ablation run on the 24 participants' prompts, not an outcome of the 24-person user study.
fix: Across four open-weight models (2,880 responses) injecting a short random-term fact raised LLM-judged creativity (88.1 vs 69.6 baseline) and an unrelated-context fact raised flexibility (12.4 vs 9.4); no context type won on all metrics. In the HAICo system paper, an offline GPT-5 ablation using the 24 participants' prompts found associative-thinking prompting gave higher embedding-based idea diversity than non-associative prompting.

problem: Smith Exp 2 (N=91, delay did not significantly diminish conformity; apparent drop was an order effect), Marsh Exp 3 (F(1,73)=4.74, .169 vs .242) and Yun et al. (template tokens cause diversity collapse) verified; Yun clause is unrelated to the delay finding.

mARC-QA (52/50/50/48 vs 66%, p values) and MedEinst (5,383 pairs, 17 LLMs, trap rates 42.98-60.90 and up to 66.1) verified; 43-66% is the span across the models quoted, not all 17.

Rashid & Kellis (Hit@1 0.0% hard; Hit@10 21.0/55.4 hard; 97.6 easy for Gemini, 95.2 for Qwen; 95.2-99.8% misses lexically closer) and BRIGHT (59.0 vs 18.3, BM25 14.5) verified; the 97.6% easy figure is for one embedder only and the Rashid paper is a single-author preprint.

Rashid (5.4-63.3% of gap closed, lexical control hurts math), Barakat & Kochmar (0.557->0.673) and BRIGHT Table 3 (BM25 14.3; GPT-4 17.4/17.0; MiniLM 13.1/8.3) verified; the 14.3 is the un-reranked BM25 baseline, and with the Google retriever GPT-4 depth 100 (22.6) did beat depth 10 (21.5), so 'not reliably' is right.

Table 2 of the graph-retrieval paper (BGE vs ours 27.6/34.3, 40.7/47.1, 66.2/68.8, 72.8/74.4; math_qa worse) and Sultan et al. (o1 52->80, GPT-5 88->96, 50 problems, 3x5 budget) verified; the PDF text extraction mislabels the table rows but the values match.
Minor: BM25 14.5 to 27.0 is 12.5 points, slightly above the stated 12.2 headline; claim wording keeps both.
Gentner Exp 3 comparison alone (no heavy scaffolding) reached 70% unaided, contradicting "only heavy scaffolding reaches 70 to 90%"; sources are two labs.
fix: Even with comparison, most learners do not transfer unaided in most lab conditions (about 40 to 48%), though comparison alone reached 70% in one live negotiation experiment and guided scaffolding (definition, diagrams, guiding questions) reached 90%. Transfer is real but partial.

problem: Comparers linking the cases were 98% (Gentner Exp 2) and 100% (Loewenstein), not 88%; also Gentner Exp 3 found 45% of separate-case learners linked cases (vs 90%), so 16 to 18% holds only for Exp 2 and the teams study.
fix: Comparison helps only when effortful and aligned: separate interpretation gave no benefit, joint interpretation with listed correspondences gave most insight; in two studies only 16 to 18% of separate-case learners linked the cases (vs 98 to 100% of comparers; 45% vs 90% in a third experiment); teams did no better than solo (32% vs 34%); one study found benefit only for learners who disliked maths. Several results come from one research group.

problem: Minor: Stitch is comparable-or-better, and mixed in the list domain.

Numbers are correct, but both re-evaluations (LEGO-Prover and TroVE, plus the single-use paper) share author Berlot-Attwell, so they are one research thread; 'mostly vanish' for LLM library methods rests on two methods.
fix: Two re-evaluations by an overlapping author group (Berlot-Attwell et al.) found that gains of two LLM library methods shrink at matched compute: TroVE on MATH 0.24 (primitive, K=15) vs 0.25 (TroVE), not significant; LEGO-Prover costs 5.84x-14.23x the baseline per attempt and the baseline matched or beat it at equal cost (4o-mini 35.9 vs 25.8 at equal attempts).

problem: Minor: Evo-Memory ExpRAG averages in the paper (0.50/0.64 Gemini) differ slightly from the researcher's note (0.46/0.63); direction holds. CRAFT without abstraction keeps only part of the GQA gain (45.4 to 37.1).

Numbers are right, but 'comparisons published so far are not compute matched' generalises from Dynamic Cheatsheet and ArcMemo; other cited work (TroVE and LEGO-Prover re-evaluations, K14) did compute-match.
fix: The Dynamic Cheatsheet memory-versus-sampling comparison is not compute matched: it beat 3-sample majority vote (50.0 vs 23.3 on AIME 2024 with Claude 3.5 Sonnet) but its footnote gives average output tokens 370 baseline, 494 instruction-only, 1035 DC-RS, 1831 DC-Cu, and the instruction-only arm already reached 36.7. With a verifier, repeated sampling scales log-linearly (SWE-bench Lite 15.9% to 56% from 1 to 250 samples) while voting plateaus around 100 or more samples. ArcMemo reports token use similar to the baseline, with memory-augmented runs tending to use more output tokens.

problem: Minor: ARES token reductions are 'up to' 52.7% on TAU-Bench (35.2% in total reasoning tokens on Retail); R2-Router 4-5x taken from the abstract.
Minor: Falk et al. is only 2 raters on 30 projects, and Chakrabarty's 0.41 is across creativity tests rather than novelty alone.
Kappa .41 is called moderate by the source, not weak; alpha .8-.96 spans two papers with different designs; TTCW listed twice (one source).

Nonexpert raw alpha was .935 (unreliable only after Spearman-Brown standardisation to .575); Clements found creative-expertise self-report lowered ratings while choreographic experience raised them; generalisation from one poetry CAT study.
Claim quotes only the 50-53% judges (GPT-4o pairwise was 45.0%); Si listed three times and TTCW twice, so independent sources are fewer than listed, but all numbers match.
Minor: Tutone judge is Llama-3.3-70B and novelty human p=.293 as stated; all quoted numbers matched; 'rubric plus run history' judge result is a single ML-agent setting.

The 65.25% figure is length bias in human upvote-chosen Reddit stories (LitBench training data), and Buczak reports longer responses get higher human ratings; only Domanti shows an automatic scorer confounded by elaboration.
fix: Automatic originality scorers overrate machine text partly through response elaboration (controlling for elaboration shrank the machine advantage in OCSAI, CLAUS and ChatGPT-4o), and human originality ratings, which supervised scorers learn from, are higher for longer answers; in the LitBench story data 65.25% of the upvote-chosen stories were longer than the rejected ones.

problem: 'Validated' rests on 79% on 100 pairs (NoveltyBench) and kappa .56 comes from a separate 2026 paper's semantic entropy vs human labels on 50 problems; NoveltyBench listed twice.
Si dedup and NoveltyBench numbers match; 'restores diversity' is roughly matched human diversity for three models on 100 curated prompts.
Si r values match; Bhushan impact-vs-creativity correlations are weak (human -0.111), not zero.
The 29% vs 35.3% is overlap with the diverse-beam pick, not a test of creativity-picking against chance, and the authors read it as the self-evaluation not being random (subverting DBS).
fix: In Creative Beam Search the model's self-picked 'most creative' candidate coincided with the diverse-beam-search pick 29% of the time versus 35.3% expected from random selection (the authors read this as the self-evaluation overriding rather than confirming the diversity score), and in Si et al. only 17 of the 49 ideas in the human-reranked condition overlapped with the agent's own ranking.

problem: Poly-encoder r=.74 and GPT-4 zero-shot .2-.67 come from different datasets and studies (and a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-7b also reached .74), so only LitBench is a like-for-like trained-vs-zero-shot comparison.
fix: Trained scorers and reward models match or beat zero-shot LLM judges: on LitBench story preference a trained Bradley-Terry reward model reached 78% vs 73% for the best zero-shot judge, and a small poly-encoder reached r=.74 with human creativity ratings (reported alongside GPT-4 zero-shot r of .2-.67 from other studies, not a head-to-head test).

problem: Gemma-2-9b-it peak at 3 is about 80% for novelty (about 75% for usefulness); TPR paper shows a medium-novelty bias.

In Falk et al. only Prometheus outputs got moderate agreement (k .47/.44) as representative and useful, the others had low agreement (.05-.2 on representativeness), and kappa is rater agreement not a usefulness level; RINoBench supports the rationale-alignment half.
fix: LLM judges' justification text closely mirrors expert rationale in RINoBench (alignment about 78-90 on known and novelty aspects, low hallucination rate) even though their novelty scores diverge from experts; in a hackathon study raters agreed that one judge's (Prometheus) explanations were representative and useful to experts, while other models' outputs had low agreement on representativeness.

problem: Falk, Literature-Grounded and Sternlicht support time/reference dependence and verdict shifts with retrieved sets, but no source varies a per-case date cutoff (Sternlicht uses one fixed retrieval cutoff, 2025-03-01); Falk's time-dependence is a qualitative remark.
fix: Novelty is reference- and time-dependent: a hackathon project can lose novelty as similar ones appear (a qualitative observation), and LLM novelty verdicts depend on which prior papers are retrieved (retrieval ablations in Literature-Grounded Novelty Assessment; retrieval of 5 abstracts moved judge accuracy by up to 16 points or hurt it in Sternlicht et al.). A time-split with a fixed cutoff gives an outcome-based novelty check (HindSight). No study varied the corpus date on the same ideas and measured the drift directly.

problem: Every number comes from the single Sternlicht et al. paper (its two evidence lines are the same paper); the second listed source, RQ-Bench, does not address prompt instability or cheap-vs-dedicated pipelines. Numbers themselves (52.6, 55.8, quarter to a third, 8 to 29 macro-F1) match.
SoundnessBench figures match (74.0%, 64.8%, 65.7% for ScholarEval); 'inflate approval' is for ML proposals judged against ICLR-reviewer proxy labels.
RINI numbers match; RQ-Bench narrowness result and Sternlicht retrieval case study are consistent; fixes being designed after the failure is the authors' own admission-level framing, not checked.

Numbers (3/40, 4/40, 39/40) match, but all listed lines are the same Lehman and Stanley 2011 paper (four times) plus a later paper from the same lab (Pugh, Soros, Stanley), which does not replicate the maze comparison; no independent replication.
Lehman numbers (5/100 vs 2/100) and Conti/GEP-PG numbers match; NSRA-ES merely equals ES (p>0.05) rather than beating it on humanoid, so 'fixed' means closed the gap.
Pugh text says 'two solutions found across all 20 runs', i.e. 2 solutions, not necessarily 2 of 20 runs; Kistemaker figures (63,440 to 27,427; 21 and 29 of 70) match.

ELM and LMX figures match; the 'over 50%' parent-order swing is stated as 'sometimes by over 50%' in LMX; ELM and LMX are by overlapping authors (Lehman/Stanley lab vs Meyerson et al.) but are distinct papers.
QDAIF human QD 0.772 vs 0.767 and quality 3.900 vs 4.133 match; Hivemind drop is on similar-quality and high-disagreement subsets; single human check (one median-QD run per method, three domains).
Rainbow Teaming numbers match; ShinkaEvolve ablation run count is not stated and Rainbow baselines are the authors' own, as the claim notes.
ShinkaEvolve threshold 0.95 and marginal LLM-judge gain match its text (though its figure caption says the judge variant strongly beats no rejection); Si 5% of 4000 at cosine 0.8 matches.

NoveltyBench, Hivemind and DEI numbers match; 'a mix of models is not a source of independent diversity' is the authors' framing and is partly contradicted by DEI's Core War result, which the claim itself flags.
Mind Evolution numbers (95.6/55.6/82.8, 87.5 vs 77.4, 46.1 to 95.6) match; AlphaEvolve database MAP-Elites plus islands confirmed; 'not isolated' is a negative claim about the literature.
Rainbow Teaming filter numbers, ELM 95K/80% vs 280K/50% and QDAIF LMX quality-only 0.650 consistent with sources (Rainbow filter ASR numbers from three runs).
Large Monkeys, Gao et al. and the PRM stress-test figures match; Gao uses a synthetic gold reward model, and the PRM test shows exploitability rather than lowered true quality from optimisation.
Conti and Boldi match (p<0.05, 5 of 12 Atari games with ES stuck); 'the rest were not deceptive' is an inference: the paper only says ES gained nothing from exploration pressure in the other games.

Fast Downward's IPC-4 configuration is built on the causal-graph heuristic (Helmert 2006), not on delete relaxation; FF's AIPS-2000 win, LAMA's IPC-2008 win (built on the FF heuristic plus landmarks) and 24 of 30 domains with no unrecognised dead ends match.
fix: Ignoring what an action undoes (delete relaxation) gives a cheap estimate that guides greedy search well on most planning benchmarks. FF, built on it, won AIPS-2000; LAMA, which combines the FF heuristic with landmarks, won the IPC-2008 sequential satisficing track; Fast Downward won the IPC-4 non-optimizing track using a causal-graph heuristic (later adding the FF heuristic and preferred operators); under ideal h+, 24 of 30 domains have no unrecognised dead ends.

problem: FF Mystery/Mprime failure, randomisation not helping, and 6 of 30 domains match; but in LeanPlan SCP solved more tasks in four of ten IPC 2023 domains without the paper attributing all four to ignored object interactions (only Sokoban's state-expansion gap is so attributed, 'presumably').
fix: The relaxed estimate is blind to trouble caused by the constraint that was dropped. FF fails on Mystery and Mprime (fuel dead ends) and random restarts did not fix it; 6 of 30 domains have unrecognised dead ends (a rover takes a one-off sample, then cannot reach the lander). Gap check 2026-10-26: LeanPlan's generated heuristics were beaten by saturated cost partitioning (SCP) on solved-task count in four of ten IPC 2023 domains (in Sokoban SCP expands fewer states, presumably because its abstractions capture box interactions that LeanPlan's relaxations ignore), and a dead-end test gave LeanPlan its largest single gain (Spanner).

problem: Minor: FF text says 40 to 5 percent of successors on average; the 2% figure is the Schedule example, so '40% down to 2%' merges two numbers.
Minor: the 4 unsolved tasks belong to the FF planner as a whole (with goal ordering), not the bare FF heuristic.
Minor: Tuisov text says SP-10 276 with GPT-4.1 while its Table 2 lists 281 for SP-10 and 234 for first compile; HTN virtual best is over the five main models of nine evaluated.

All numbers check out (LeanPlan 67/51/11, Gestrin 368 vs 352, Rod-Rings 58 vs 59), but all three papers share Jendrik Seipp as author (same research group), so they count as one lab, not independent replication.

Little or no gain was measured only for blocks-world (30 min vs 23 min); for local search, unsolvable and easy instances the sources report only absence of a heavy tail, and Gomes 2000 notes restarts are routinely used in local search.
fix: Restarts help only when the run-time distribution has a falling hazard (heavy tail or mixed easy/hard runs); they are neutral for exponential (Weibull k=1) and harmful for increasing-hazard shapes (k>1). No heavy tail was found for blocks-world planning (where randomisation gave only 30 min to 23 min), for local search (Walksat), for unsolvable instances, or for easy solvable instances.

problem: Numbers match the corrected row mapping, but every usable source is the same Gomes/Selman/Kautz table (AAAI-98 Table 1 reprinted as Table IV in the 2000 JAR paper); Huang 2007 does not cover these instances, so it is one source.
Minor: the 12 to 24 iteration cutoff comes from one LLM study on hot steel rolling and varies with the reward target.
Minor: 'best of seven' includes the no-restart baseline; the LLM-loop figures are simulated from one steel-rolling study.
Minor: the Huang GPT-4 GSM8K 89.0 and CSQA 41.8 figures are after round 2 (5 calls) of intrinsic self-correction; reflection result is from one agent benchmark.

In s1 the 57.6 is GPQA Diamond with no extrapolation; AIME24 is 50.0 without Wait, 53.3 with two Waits in the ablation table, and 56.7 (about 57) in the main result and the appendix 4-Wait row.
fix: Forcing a model to continue ('Wait') gives small gains that flatten (s1-32B AIME24 50.0 to 53.3 with two Waits and 56.7 with the main budget-forcing setting; MATH500 fell from 93.0 to 90.2 when the stop token was ignored with no string) and longer reasoning is not always better (GPT-4o on NaturalPlan peaks at a medium budget; R1 easy items 0.95 with short vs 0.72 with long traces).

problem: Minor: the general-resolution result is from Beame et al. 2004, cited by Huang, not proved there.
Minor: DeepConf 52.8 percent saving is one setting (DeepConf-low, AIME24, budget 512), and the 0.90 accuracy cost there is only 0.26 points.

Katebi et al. ablated only four features (learning, VSIDS, 2WL, restarts) on MiniSat, so learning is the most important of those four, not shown to be the single most important ingredient; Bayardo and Schrag's 100% failure is on two instances (bf1355-075, ssa2670-141).
fix: Among the four CDCL features ablated in MiniSat (learning, VSIDS, 2-watched-literals, restarts), clause learning mattered most: switching learning off cuts solved instances from 9068 to 4837 of 10000, versus 6932 without VSIDS, 8409 without 2WL and 8653 without restarts. Bayardo and Schrag saw plain DP with no look-back fail in 100% of runs on two hard real-world instances, and Elffers et al. found learned clauses essential for going beyond tree-like proofs.

problem: Minor: 'developed separately' is inferred (relsat paper does not cite GRASP); GRASP's 149 instances are the full BF-1355 class and relsat's 13% is a different benchmark.

Minor: the one to two order gain is Chaff versus other solvers, attributed by the authors to optimized BCP (watched literals) and the decision strategy, not isolated per feature; the ablation ranks learning first.

'Every successful solver bounds retention' is wider than the sources, which cover GRASP, relsat and Glucose; the Glucose 176 vs 132 to 153 result is for the whole solver (LBD deletion plus Luby restarts and phase saving), not deletion alone.
fix: Unbounded clause storage is costly, and the solvers examined bound retention. GRASP kept clauses of at most 20 literals. relsat relevance-bounded learning beat size-bounded (hanoi4 fail 13% vs 94% and 92%). Glucose, with LBD-based aggressive deletion plus Luby restarts and phase saving, solved 176 of 234 vs 132 to 153 for older solvers. Elffers et al. add that over-aggressive erasure hurts when memory is tight.

problem: The first-UIP smallest-LBD result is a proved property (Property 1, from Jabbour and Sais) not a correlation, and 'the main evidence' for which no-goods to keep is the claim writer's judgement; the usage statistics are from one paper (Audemard and Simon), with Elffers et al. a co-authored follow-up.
fix: Short clauses spanning few decision levels (low LBD, glue clauses) are used far more than longer ones in propagation and conflict analysis on SAT-Race 06 benchmarks (Audemard and Simon 2009; clauses of LBD 2 used 202 and 1827 times vs 26 and 136 at LBD 4); this usage evidence is empirical and from a single paper. The first-UIP clause having the smallest LBD is a proved property, and Elffers et al. 2018 report that LBD often selects the right clauses to keep.

problem: Katebi Table 2 (checked against column sums) gives sverif 592 solved without VSIDS vs 1006 with full CDCL; the 420 belongs to termrw (full CDCL) and the earlier extraction mixed rows, so sverif is not an example of VSIDS hurting.
fix: Learning is not a universal win. Look-back gave little on random 3SAT. No DP variant solved the 3bit circuits that WSAT solved trivially. ISAMP was about 10x faster than relsat(4) on six scheduling instances. In MiniSat, the ranking of features differs by family: termrw solved 446 with restarts off vs 420 with full CDCL (restarts help overall, 9068 vs 8653), and sverif without VSIDS still solved 592 of 1200 runs, so VSIDS is not what rescues that family (full CDCL 1006). Winners are instances with short, easily derived no-goods.

problem: Gomes et al. (JAR Table IV and text) say randomization improved the 14-team round-robin from 411 s to 250 s; 17 min is the randomized time for 3bit-adder-31, so 'got worse' is wrong.
fix: Restarts help on average but depend on the family. MiniSat without restarts solved 8653 vs 9068. Luby on gave 4533 SAT and 4535 UNSAT vs 4230 and 4423 off. termrw solved more without restarts (446 vs 420). Clique formulas need restarts off. Heavy-tailed run times justify randomised restarts with a tuned cutoff (round-robin 14 improved from 411 s to 250 s).

problem: Minor: the CL-beats-regular result needs a new learning scheme (FirstNewCut) and the 'does not predict real speed' remark is the claim writer's reading of the authors' caveat about nondeterminism.
Minor: HumanEval 91% vs 80% compares to GPT-4 baseline; the Reflexion numbers all come from one paper's own ablations.
TIDE Table 2 (BW, FL, Su, AW, WS): Qwen3-4B has 32.0% loop ratio in FrozenLake but Qwen3-30B-A3B has 37.7% there; the fall to 1.0% and 5.7% is in BlocksWorld (15.8 to 1.0) and WebShop (36.7 to 5.7).
fix: Repeating a step that already failed is a common, measured LLM-agent failure. Step repetition (FM-1.3) is 15.7% of annotated failures (1642 traces, 7 multi-agent systems). In TIDE, Qwen3-4B has a loop ratio of 32.0% in FrozenLake; scaling from Qwen3-4B to Qwen3-30B-A3B cuts it from 15.8% to 1.0% in BlocksWorld and from 36.7% to 5.7% in WebShop, but not in FrozenLake (37.7%). A no-good filter targets exactly this.

problem: Minor: 'strong SAT bias' is the paper's wording for 'nearly every'; the final sentence (store and checks should be code) is a design inference, not a finding, and the DPLL-trace models were trained on 6-15 variables only.

DaSAThco says a well-tuned single solver is a strong baseline in-domain on CoinsGrid but DaSAThco still gets the best results on both datasets, so 'a single tuned solver can still win in-domain' is too strong; AutoSAT and AutoModSAT are the same lab.
fix: LLM-written CDCL heuristics improve solvers on chosen families (AutoSAT beats MiniSat on 9 of 12 datasets and Kissat on 4; AutoModSAT reports about 40% PAR-2 gain over its base ModSAT). Gains rest on scoring by running code and vanish on some families; in-domain, a single well-tuned solver is a strong baseline, though DaSAThco's per-instance selection still beat it.

problem: Two of the three listed items are the same Kambhampati paper; Bayardo and Schrag is a separate source and supports short derived nogoods as the success condition (loosely).

Tyen et al. is a simulation of mistake-location accuracy for backtracking on BIG-Bench Mistake with PaLM 2; it says gains exceed losses at roughly 60-70% for most tasks and losses plateau at 65%; Kamoi gives no threshold, so the general claim for any failure signal is wider than the sources.
fix: In a simulation of mistake-location finders for backtracking on reasoning traces (Tyen et al., BIG-Bench Mistake, PaLM 2), accuracy gains exceeded losses on most tasks once the finder was right about 60 to 70% of the time, and losses on correct traces plateaued near 65%; a trained classifier did not reach that level. The survey of Kamoi et al. gives no numeric threshold.

problem: Numbers check out, but 'across systems only a minority are true, new and used' is wider than the sources: Rabe et al. report 3445 of 3857 assumption theorems and 979 of 3440 equalities used (usage is a low bar), the template example is a single running example, and Lemmanaid's 22.6% is match to human lemmas, not usage.
fix: Machine-proposed lemmas are often not useful in the settings measured: Lemmanaid on HOL-test had 22.6% matching human gold lemmas and 23.6% false; Rabe et al. free-form conjecturing gave 12.7% provable-and-new (uniform data) with 49 of 130 theorems later used (though 3445 of 3857 assumption theorems were used); in the template-conjecturing running example 2 of 10 proved lemmas were used; QuickSpec precision was under 1% on Octonions.

problem: Minor slip: Lemmanaid applies Nitpick/Quickcheck in evaluation and suggests a counterexample checker to the user rather than as a built-in filter stage; MathlibLemma and Hipster figures check out (3427+2591+3130=9148; 4028 = 44%).

The chained-conjecturing 54.5% to 63.8% figure is an idealised evaluation in which good mid-proof lemmas are assumed guessable (a middle way between cheating and honest settings), not an achieved conjecturing system; the other numbers (Vampire 7 to 25, +40 on Prod, IsaPlanner 60% unaided) check out.
fix: Conjecturing helps most when it bridges toward a specific goal the base prover cannot reach. Vampire went from 7 to 25 of 50 TIP problems with QuickSpec lemmas; template conjecturing gave +40 points on Prod; an idealised chained-conjecturing evaluation (assuming good mid-proof lemmas can be guessed) raised HOL Light Q2 from 54.5% to 63.8%. Gains are small where the base prover already solves most (IsaPlanner 60% unaided).

problem: Minor: the 2123 theorems re-proved were generated by the loop under the same context, so the 99% vs 91% comparison is partly circular; numbers match.
Minor: paper says 'about 2-3%' gain at pass@128, which the note renders as points; all other numbers match.

Ritchie and Hanna (via Wikipedia) criticised AM's architecture as not matching Lenat's description and its published rules as vague with discovery hidden in unexplained procedures, not that the descriptions did not match behaviour; also evidence c27 points to the wrong AAAI URL (a Salzberg paper) and duplicates the Lenat-Brown paper.
fix: Early automated discovery (AM, Eurisko, Graffiti, HR) produced real results (refactorable numbers added to OEIS, many graph-theory papers) but AM's success depended on representation: concepts as small Lisp predicates mutate usefully, two-page heuristics mutated into junk. Critics (Ritchie and Hanna) argued AM's published architecture did not match its description, its rules were vague, and much of the discovery work was hidden in unexplained procedures.

problem: Negative literature claims (only Rabe reports per-lemma reuse; no held-out split) cannot be verified from the sources, but the cited numbers match (3 of 6 merged, 24% of 135 problems).

Garivier and Moulines give total regret O(sqrt(T Upsilon_T log T)) for Upsilon_T breakpoints and a sqrt(T) lower bound for a two-breakpoint game, not a cost of order sqrt(T) per change; the own-simulation count-cap effect is at most 0.15 (12.54 vs 12.69), not under 0.15, and cannot be checked against a source.
fix: When the best operator changes, plain stationary bandits lag; sliding-window, discounted or restart variants recover, with total regret of order sqrt(T times the number of breakpoints times log T) (and a sqrt(T) lower bound in a two-breakpoint game), and need a window or discount that depends on the unknown number of changes. Own simulation (not a published source): count caps of 5 to 50 changed regret by at most about 0.15 at 30 to 60 pulls, even after a mid-run switch.

problem: Numbers and the 'beats independent arms when candidates outnumber budget' finding check out, and gains differ between GPT-3.5 and Llama2, but neither source tests how the gain depends on embedding prediction quality; that part is inference.
fix: When candidates outnumber the budget, sharing information across similar candidates (embeddings, clustering) beat independent-arm baselines in TRIPLE (e.g. 21%/28% over BO-EI on GPT-3.5, with different margins on Llama2), and TS that models shared structure beats independent TS in a shortest-path tutorial; the advantage shrinks as budget grows, and it is untested here how much depends on embedding quality.

problem: Minor: the TIDE ablation pattern (w/o UCB best at scale 50, worst at 200) holds on TSP only, and the full TIDE model beats every ablation, so the UCB contribution there is not small at scale 200.

Krishnamurthy et al. found only one satisfactory configuration among GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama2 prompt designs (GPT-4, chain of thought, summarised statistics), but later sources in the same list show other fixes (algorithm-guided values and fine-tuning in EVOLvE, reasoning models in Zhang et al.), so 'only' is too wide.
fix: LLMs used as bandit agents mostly fail to explore in context (in Krishnamurthy et al., GPT-4 with a basic prompt had suffix failure in more than 60% of replicates; only GPT-4 with chain of thought and externally summarised statistics worked among the prompt designs tested), are biased by arm labels (Semantic Bandits), and numeric contextual bandits on text embeddings often match or beat LLM agents (Berdica et al.); other remedies such as reasoning models or algorithm-guided prompts and fine-tuning also improve exploration.

problem: Own paired analysis reproduced from OPTS Table 2 (DE: +1.79, t=2.61, TS higher on 18 of 27); 'weak or author-tuned baselines' is only loosely supported (Meta-Reasoner baselines mixed).
Go-Explore Phase 1 relies on restoring simulator states (stated by the authors), not noted in the claim; numbers 57,439, 57%, 17,500 and 74,500 match.
Pitfall 22-room figure is the no-domain-knowledge Phase 1 result; 640M to 57.6M and 57,439 to 148,220 match.
Score-based rule correlations span 0.27 to 0.44 (Polyglot SICA is 0.274), not 0.29 to 0.44; minor rounding slip.
AB-MCTS paper says repeated sampling on ARC only begins to plateau while AB-MCTS keeps improving between 200 and 500 calls (figure, budget capped at 512); it does not show flat beyond about 500.
fix: Solved-problem coverage keeps rising with independent samples far past 20: roughly log-linear over several orders of magnitude (CodeContests Gemma-2B 0.02% to 7.1% at 10,000 samples; SWE-bench Lite 15.9% to 56% at 250). Plateaus appear later and depend on method and model: repeated sampling on ARC begins to plateau around 200 to 500 calls (budget tested up to 512), the 7B search in SOAR flattens near 5.2k attempts.

problem: SEP attributes 'a candidate worth investigating, not asserted true' to Frankfurt's reading of Peirce (which SEP questions), not to Peirce himself, who calls abduction the process of forming explanatory hypotheses.
fix: SEP presents Peirce's cycle as abduction forming explanatory hypotheses, deduction drawing testable consequences, and induction judging the hypothesis by how many consequences hold; Frankfurt reads abduction as picking hypotheses worth investigating, and Hanson's retroductive schema yields a type of hypothesis worth elaborating. Generate-then-test is the classic frame, and the discovery-machine objection says no rule mechanically outputs good hypotheses. Secondhand via SEP only.

problem: Dellsen paper PDF blocked; checked via abstract only (consolidation, good enough). SEP says catch-all is 'hardly informative'; SEP also says ABD3 avoids the bad-lot objection, so 'unresolved' is a mild gloss.

Half of the 9% false positives are on problems where majority vote would still pick the right output (wording 'lose to majority vote' is compatible); the 'BARC' label refers to the Li et al. ARC induction setup.
Reflexion 91.0 vs 80.1 compares to a no-reflection baseline, not model-only feedback; it supports but is not a direct tool vs no-tool contrast.

Li et al.'s 575K Lean problems are called candidate counterexample problems (hypotheses dropped, only grammar rechecked), not confirmed false statements with known counterexamples; only SymCE has verified witnesses.
fix: Dropping a hypothesis from a proved theorem is a cheap source of candidate false conjectures (exception-barring in reverse). Two groups built corpora: Li et al. made about 575K candidate counterexample problems in Lean from 212,463 seed theorems (candidates, not all confirmed false), and Zouak et al. released SymCE, 4,707 false statements with verified witnesses and a 97.7% accurate verifier.

problem: Drift rates in the roundtrip paper span about 9% to 45% across rows (pooled 16.2% equivalent vs 28.7% non-equivalent), so '15-45%' is a loose range; the Isabelle audit is a single-author case study.
The 34% pilot figure is given as 'about one third' on the DLR page; 34% not seen there.

Klein's studies used semistructured interviews, on-site observations and protocol analysis (including simulations), and the pilot study is a simulator experiment, so not all frequency evidence is retrospective interviews; 'no outcome-quality control' and 'coders from the research team' are not stated in the sources.
fix: Klein's RPD frequency figures come from field studies using semistructured interviews, observation and protocol analysis, coded with a liberal criterion for 'analytical' (any sign of two options contrasted), and report how decisions were made, not whether they were good. A frequency of recognitional strategy describes process, not that the process is better.

problem: In Raab et al. Table 4, -1.14 and 2.32 are the all-positions means of first-move quality under time pressure by Stockfish and expert rating, not tactical vs strategic; the sample is Elo under 2000, not experts.
fix: Under time pressure, first-move quality in chess players with Elo under 2000 was worse in tactical than strategic positions by Stockfish rating (-1.80 vs -0.51, d=0.62), while expert ratings did not differ significantly (2.22 vs 2.41, p=.2).

problem: Both studies come from the same Rotterdam group (Mamede, van Gog) but support different parts of the claim.
Text gives matched-subset LLM accuracy as about 50% (Table 4 may show 49); minor.

WebDreamer paper reports 34.1% relative gain on VisualWebArena (17.6 to 23.6), not 33%; cost $0.4 vs $2.7 and Shopping 20.8 vs 28.1 are from WMA (WebArena), a different benchmark than the VWA figures.
fix: Imagining each candidate action outcome and scoring it beats a reactive agent modestly (WebDreamer on VisualWebArena 17.6 to 23.6, +34.1% relative) and WMA on WebArena costs far less than real tree search ($0.4 vs $2.7 per task, 140 s vs 748 s), but real search is still better in some domains (WebArena Shopping 28.1 vs 20.8).

problem: Minor: AUROC 0.86 is for Gemma-3-4B on MATH500 (not GSM8K specifically); 78.6% is an average over models.
In Koh et al. the 24.5% row is no search at all, not tree search with no value function; the other numbers match.
fix: Check quality drives most of the check-and-revise gain. Sound verifier 88% vs LLM critic 55% vs none 40% (Blocksworld GPT-4); on a VisualWebArena subset, GPT-4o with no search gets 24.5%, tree search with a GPT-4o value function (n=20 consistency) 37.0%, and with the ground-truth reward 43.5%; a critical survey finds no prior work showing successful self-correction with prompted-LLM feedback except in exceptionally suited tasks.

problem: Minor: the two K&K URLs are the same paper; the sources are K&K plus a Gruning and Krueger review, and the claim itself says the basis is conceptual. Phrase a correct first answer is luck is a mild strengthening of K&K.
Minor: K&K say confidence is set by internal consistency of the information; Steyvers and Xiong concern LLM confidence and human reading of it, supporting only indirectly.
Grove 136/63/65/8 verified in K&K text and Kuncel .44 vs .28 verified; the claim is about low-validity tasks while Grove covers mixed clinical and medical domains.

Aegisdottir 48 effects: 25 (52%), 18 (38%), 5 (10%) verified; d+ = .12 verified; job performance and training gain are from Kuncel (selection, not mental health), which is consistent with the claim wording.
The CGES -69.4% calls figure is from arXiv v1 only; the current version reports 58% fewer calls (16.0 to 6.7) at about -0.4 pp; ReASC -71.1% (92.04 vs 92.12) and ASC -62.5% verified.
fix: Agreement among sampled answers is a usable but imperfect trust signal and drives early-exit gating: ReASC -71.1% compute at 92.04 vs 92.12 accuracy (GSM8K, Gemma-3-4B), CGES -58% calls (16.0 to 6.7) at within 0.4 pp (v1 of the paper reported -69.4%). Gain over earlier adaptive self-consistency is smaller (ASC already -62.5%). Same-model samples share errors. Counter-evidence: Kapoor 2024 found sampling-based uncertainty discriminates very weakly on MMLU.

problem: Mind Your Step GPT-4o -23.1 (artificial grammar) and -12.8 (face recognition) verified; Sprague title says mainly math and symbolic reasoning; Illusion of Thinking regimes verified.

Gobet 1998 (macro-structure, pooled comparison with de Groot t-tests all ns, pooled de Groot reinvestigations 2.4+1.2) verified; de Groot 49-protocol figures (n0 4.5, only 2 with none) could not be checked because the book text was not accessible; Gobet 1998 sample is 48 players.

Gobet 1998 finds mean depth does differ with skill (F(3,44)=2.9 p<.05, Master 5.0 vs Class B 2.9; Elo slope significant at .005), so depth is not simply not reliably different; max depth, nodes, node rate and base-move rate are the non-significant ones. De Groot 8.2 vs 5.2 figure not checkable (Gobet Table 1 uses a different quality scale, 4.8 vs 2.6).
fix: On an easy position solvable within about 9 plies, maximum depth, node count, nodes per minute and rate of generating moves do not reliably separate grandmasters from experts or Masters from weaker players, while move quality differs a lot; mean depth shows only a small but significant slope of about 0.6 ply per 200 Elo (Masters 5.0 vs Class B 2.9 plies, only that pair reliably different).

problem: Gobet 1998 17.6% (p<.005), Campitelli and Gobet 2004 10 s results (46.9/36.9/8.2/4.1) and Chassy 44% verified; recall/practice-hours sub-claims not individually re-read.
Huang et al. numbers (CSQA 75.8/38.1/41.8; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5/91.5/89.0; Llama-2 62.0 to 36.5), Kamoi survey statement and ThinkRetrieve 83% to 52% at B=22K verified.
