Klein et al. Table 2 verified (medians 2.43, 2.00, 1.88, 1.18; 36 of 36 samples; 6,344 participants; original 0.93); T&K 1974 medians 25 and 45 verified.

Simmons et al. 2010 direction-known manipulation (Miami 41% vs more than half) verified in text; Lieder et al. abstract 'ten anchoring phenomena' confirmed via abstract (full PDF not retrievable), incentive/load details not independently checked.

In Knipper et al. Table 1 (45 models) representativeness resistance ranges 0.275 to 0.719 (mean 0.47, lowest of the eight bias families), not 0.36 to 0.60; REHEAT accuracies 14.8 (PaLM 2) to 34.7 (GPT-3.5) and human 27.2 are correct.
fix: Representativeness-type problems are the hardest bias family for LLMs: across 45 models mean resistance is about 0.47, the lowest of eight families, with per-model resistance 0.28 to 0.72 (Knipper et al.), and accuracy 14.8 to 34.7 percent on the REHEAT set, near the 27.2 percent human level.

problem: Suri (20.83/105.97, 22.5/80.50), Lou and Sun (12 expert-hint questions, no exceptions), Jones and Steinhardt (67% exactly on anchor), Huang (22.0 to 60.5%), Malberg anchoring row (0.29 to 0.67 for 18 of 20 models; two outliers 0.15 and -0.05) all verified; 'GPT-3.5' is ChatGPT in Suri.

All numbers (80/55/15/0 percent, 80 to 29 percent with chain of thought, 70 to 90 percent for the davinci family) check out in arXiv 2212.05206, but the second source (arXiv 2306.07622, Hagendorff and Fabi, v2 withdrawn) is the same group's overlapping follow-up, so the claim rests on one lab; Binz and Schulz is independent only for GPT-3 failing 3 CRT items.

Huang's causal tracing is one model (Llama-3.1-8B, 10 questions); Owusu et al. find Qwen puts more attribution in mid-to-late layers than Llama, and transfer between base and instruction-tuned variants of the same family is 'less reliable' (still above random), not absent across models.
fix: In Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (10 questions) causal tracing finds anchor tokens matter mainly in early layers; circuit analysis on 7B-8B Qwen and Llama models finds edge-level pathways carrying the anchor signal, with low- and high-anchor circuits transferring strongly within a model and less reliably between base and instruction-tuned variants; layer-wise attribution patterns differ between Qwen (mid-to-late) and Llama (earlier).

problem: Toplak Table 3 delta R squared .025, .080, .064 and Chapman and Liu (high-numerate benefit mainly from natural frequencies) verified; Chapman and Liu say 342 in the abstract but 346 in the method text.

Echterhoff 40 to 52 percent, AnchorBench Table 9 means, frontier 0.07 to 0.16, and the 7-of-8 presence effect (d16) check out, but in d08 only 7 models differ from zero (d -0.09 to -0.71; the -0.02 model's CI includes 0), the chain-of-thought worsening (47.7 percent) is for one GPT-4.1 numeric task pair and the paper calls CoT's other comparison uncertain, and AnchorBench says the History (0.34) and Tool magnitudes are inflated by format confounds and should be read qualitatively.
fix: Earlier values in context pull later numeric judgments. Echterhoff et al.: Llama models changed 40 to 52 percent of decisions between sequential and all-at-once setup. AnchorBench (14 models, 360 items per suite): mean anchor influence of a plausible value was 0.34 when it was the model's own earlier answer (History, magnitude inflated by a format confound), 0.22 in the prompt, 0.18 as a tool result, 0.13 retrieved, 0.03 in demonstration metadata; irrelevant values moved answers only 0.02 to 0.07; frontier models showed near zero for irrelevant values but 0.07 to 0.16 for plausible ones in the prompt. A prior score in context shifted LLM judges in 7 of 8 models (d -0.09 to -0.71 in those 7; Claude-4.5-Sonnet d -0.44, GPT-4.1 d -0.67), and on one GPT-4.1 numeric task a CoT instruction made the shift larger (47.7 percent) while its effect on a categorical task was uncertain. Merely adding an earlier user turn raised bias in 7 of 8 models (d16). No study measured fresh-context evaluation against running context for the same items.

problem: Klein et al. Table 2 and Hertwig and Gigerenzer (83%, 0 to 13%, median 87 vs 17) both re-verified in PDF text.

FermiEval GPT-4o-mini 0.63/0.59/0.64 (log-prob 0.85/0.89/0.90), Hobor et al. 11 LLMs 9 to 44 percent with no consistent reasoning-effort gain, Bahaj et al. correlations within about .014 all verified; Bahaj hit rates are flat for Medical/MMLU but drift a few points for GPT-4o-mini FinQA (21 to 17).

Final meta-analysis (43 articles, 55 studies, 181 effect sizes, g=0.48) confirmed from abstract; the I-squared 94.46 percent and 41 of 185 negative effect sizes come from the authors' interim poster (g=0.43, 49 studies), so heterogeneity for the final model is not directly verified, and both sources are the same research group.

Kalyuga et al. 2003 (worked-example advantage disappears with experience, effects 'disappear and then reverse'), Atkinson et al. 2000 (worked examples tied to early skill stages) support it; Sweller 2019/2023 Springer pages not retrievable.

Numbers verified in Cheng et al. Table 1 (95.75, 91.58, 95.83), but it is one paper on the Qwen2.5 family (b20, c06, c20 are the same paper) and 'strong LLMs' plus 'machine form of expertise reversal' go beyond it; ThinkRetrieve (static ICL ~ no gain) only supports reasoning models on AIME.
fix: For Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct on GSM8K, generic CoT exemplars add nothing over zero-shot once answer extraction is fixed (8-shot 95.75, zero-shot 91.58, zero-shot-fixed 95.83); the authors conclude exemplars mainly align output format. Static in-context examples likewise gave about no gain for small reasoning models on AIME 2025 (ThinkRetrieve). Findings come from Qwen-family models; the link to human expertise reversal is an analogy.

problem: Wang et al. Table 2 numbers verified (15.4, 48.5, 39.5, 11.0; 39.5/48.5 = 81%) and abstract states 80-90 percent; note results are for text-davinci-002 only and the 80-90 percent depends on metric.

Springer full text and the UCR PDF (scanned, unreadable) could not be read; Crossref confirms Sweller 2023 (Educ Psychol Rev 35:95, actual title 'Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories...') and Sweller's own 2019/2011 reviews corroborate the split-attention geometry case (Tarmizi and Sweller 1988) and redundancy; b04 and b05 are the same paper, and the 'stored examples must be self-contained' line is an inference.

Bertsch et al. (50.8 max, 36.8 average over 5 datasets, Llama2-80k) and Agarwal et al. (MATH500 plain ICL peaks about 125) verified; the 250-shot degradation is a GPQA result, not MATH, but the claim does not use it.

Numbers verified (GPT-4 DROP 72.05 to 79.55; Llama-2-chat-70B GSM8K 52.5 to 50.6), but the LEAP authors only 'believe' weaker open models fail to follow their own principles (untested), GPT-3.5 and Claude-2/Gemini were flat or mixed, and I2S (c05) shows a reflect-on-demos step helping small models, so 'helps only if strong enough' is too strong.
fix: LEAP (reflecting on mistakes in few-shot examples) helped GPT-4 (DROP 72.05 to 79.55) but not the open Llama-2-chat-70B (GSM8K 52.5 to 50.6) or GPT-3.5 (DROP 63.20 to 63.35), with mixed results for Claude-2 and Gemini Pro; the authors suspect, without testing it, that weaker models do not follow the principles they generate.

problem: SQL-Tutor paper (N=34, 12/11/11; EO below AEP p=.02, below PO p=.09; normalized gain EO lower than AEP p=.02 and PO p=.03; EO spent much less time) and LearnLab stoichiometry page (no learning effect in Studies 1-3, about 21 percent less time) verified; slip in the notes: EO attempted more tasks, not fewer, though the claim does not use that.

AWM does warn that online-induced workflows can be incorrect and degrade performance (verified), and the experience-following paper supports error propagation, but no source ranks wrong-solution storage as 'the main risk' (Compliance Trap and Dynamic Cheatsheet show other failure modes), Voyager's self-verification is a design choice not a measured risk, and Chen et al.'s 'positive demo' means a demo that leads to the right answer for a given query, not a correct stored solution.
fix: Storing wrong solutions is a documented risk: the Agent Workflow Memory authors warn that incorrectly induced workflows can degrade performance, and an empirical study of agent memory finds that adding every executed experience lowers performance below a small fixed memory while evaluator-approved additions raise it; Voyager stores a skill only after self-verification. Separately, demonstration choice matters: one query-correct demo can beat using all demos (Chen et al.).

problem: Agarwal et al. says Reinforced ICL plateaus near 25 shots 'about 5% higher than ICL' on MATH500 (unit left unspecified, read as points), and Yasunaga Table 1 gives GPT-3.5 5-shot CoT 76.7/34.9 vs self-generated 77.8/37.3 (+1.1 GSM8K, +2.4 MATH); the notes' '75.0 to 77.8' baseline was wrong but the claim's 1 to 3 points holds.

Sweller and Cooper 1985 PDF read directly: Exp 2 (N=20) test 105.4 vs 127.1 ns, errors 0.13 vs 0.50 p=.10; Exp 3 first presentation 32.0 vs 185.5, test 43.6 vs 78.1, errors 0.18 vs 1.64; Exp 5 (N=24) similar test 52.4 vs 101.1 all match; Sweller 2023 only checked via Crossref metadata, and the other sources (b04, a01) do not carry these numbers.

Schneider and Anderson (2012) intro does state fan effects across fictional and real knowledge and that accuracy costs show as higher false-alarm rates with mixed hit-rate effects (secondhand, citing others), but the Dutch poster (Link et al., AMLaP 2025, not a full paper) found RT slowing in both experiments and lower accuracy only in Experiment 1 (repeated concepts); with semantically similar concepts accuracy was at ceiling, so 'lowers accuracy' is not shown there.
fix: More facts attached to one cue slows recognition in people, and usually lowers accuracy mainly through extra false alarms (hit-rate effects are mixed). This holds for fictional facts and real-world knowledge; in a Dutch conference poster with semantically similar concepts RT rose with fan in both experiments but accuracy fell only in the repeated-concept experiment (similar-concept accuracy near ceiling).

problem: Cao et al. numbers verified (0.991 to 0.915 at list size 32; GPT-4 d' about 4.1 to 3.1) but the paper does not call the effect small (d' drop about 1.0, versus about 1.2 in humans); and Roberts et al. found no fan effect for GPT-2/Llama-2/RoBERTa only in the pretraining-fan experiment, while the in-context experiment tested only Mistral and SOLAR, so 'when all facts are in context ... not GPT-2, Llama-2' is not supported.
fix: With all facts in context, GPT-4 shows a fan effect on person-location recognition (accuracy 0.991 to 0.915 at list size 32; d-prime about 4.1 to 3.1, versus about 3.7 to 2.5 in humans), with offline Mistral-7B and LLaMA-3-8B showing the same direction. In token probabilities, Roberts et al. found human-like fan effects for Mistral and SOLAR but not RoBERTa, GPT-2 or Llama-2 (pretraining fan; Llama-3 weak and non-significant); their in-context fan test covered only Mistral and SOLAR.

problem: Wang and Sun's abstract says accuracy declines log-linearly toward zero (3 to 400 updates, models from 0.6B to 637B across Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, DeepSeek, Qwen, Meta, Nvidia) but the figure caption says only 'most models' showed a quasi-log-linear drop, with exceptions and two-phase declines, and Chattaraj and Raj (39 models) describe proactive interference as collapsing bimodally at high interference and do not state a log-linear fit; the '35 to 39 models' merges two separate studies built on the same task design.
fix: In Wang and Sun's PI-LLM task (46 keys, 3 to 400 updates per key, about 35 models from 0.6B to 637B parameters across many labs), accuracy at reading the latest value of a key falls approximately log-linearly toward zero for most models, with some exceptions and two-phase declines. A follow-up with 39 models (Chattaraj and Raj) confirms that proactive interference is severe in every model, but describes its collapse as bimodal at high interference rather than log-linear.

problem: Hedged ('may') and supported: LearnLab stoichiometry (no learning effect, about 21 percent less time), Min et al. (random labels barely hurt; label space, input distribution and format matter), Cheng et al. (exemplars mainly align output format, Qwen2.5 only) and Madaan and Yazdanbakhsh (factual patterns immaterial) verified; note Madaan also credit text and patterns with supporting task understanding, and the human and LLM strands are an analogy.

In Cuconasu Table 1 (hard ADORE-type/related distractors) Llama2 gold-only 0.5642 falls to 0.4586 (1 far) and 0.2643 (8 far); the quoted 0.4733 and 0.3106 are Table 2 (random unrelated documents, far), so they do not show near-miss damage. NoLiMa literal-overlap distractor GPT-4o effective length 1K confirmed; CMI not opened.
fix: Near-miss competitors under the same cue hurt most. Hard distractors cut Llama2 accuracy from 0.5642 to 0.4586 (1 distractor, far) and 0.2643 (8 distractors, far) in Cuconasu et al., while random unrelated documents placed far from the query also cut it (0.4733 at 1, 0.3106 at 8) but placed near the query helped; same-slot conflicts cut agent memory uptake more than unrelated memories; a literal-overlap distractor cut GPT-4o effective length to 1K.

problem: Numbers check out (Guo et al.: false alarms 23.1% human vs 41.3% DPR at cos>0.7; Link et al. fan in Dutch with RT effect in both experiments; Verde: interference always raised false alarms), but no source compares similarity against count, so "matters as much as count" is not supported; the Guo figures come from one preprint and Link et al. is a conference poster.
fix: Competitor similarity matters as well as count. In one preprint (Guo et al. 2026), false alarms at high competitor similarity were 23.1 percent for humans and 41.3 percent for dense passage retrieval, against 8.2 and 12.4 percent at low similarity; similar concepts still show a fan effect in Dutch (reaction time in both experiments, accuracy in one; Link et al. poster); interference raises familiarity so false alarms rise even when hits do not (Verde 2004).

problem: Cuconasu table gives 0.3781/0.2348/0.1795 at 18 distractors (rounded in claim); Liu Table 6 matches.
Lewis and Anderson result is retrieval slowing (reaction time) reported in Anderson 1983, not accuracy loss; CMI paired contrasts -0.32 and -0.48 vs unrelated match.
Cohen d 1.73 and 39 models verified; minor slip: Qiao earliest-state accuracy is mostly 98-100 percent but ranges from 95.8 (synthetic, one LLaMA3.1-8B condition) to 100.

Roberts et al. found a fan effect in absent-item probabilities only for Mistral and SOLAR (RoBERTa, GPT-2, Llama-2 none, Llama-3 weak), so it is not a general LLM finding; 8.6% vs 0% refusals confirmed in Chattaraj and Raj.
fix: Model uncertainty about cue overload rarely appears in output: in two of six model families tested (Mistral and SOLAR) fan shows in token probabilities when the queried item is absent, and only 8.6 percent of proactive-interference failures contain an explicit refusal (0 percent under retroactive interference). Errors are mostly same-key intrusions of stale values (56.1 percent).

problem: Wang and Sun: per-key forget under 10 points at 100 updates, CoT no help; the +1 directed-forgetting figure is one model (Qwen2.5-32B 57.33 to 58.33) in Qiao et al., a minor generalisation.
Leng et al. measure context length in tokens (up to ~100k), not top-k; the final "no sweep found" sentence is a search-gap statement, not checkable.
Folk 1992 verified only via its citation and abstract context, Buesel 2020 abstract and Eimer and Kiss (N=12, 37 ms, N2pc ~180 ms) confirmed.

Consensus statements rest on one joint paper (Luck, Gaspelin, Folk, Remington, Theeuwes 2021; listed three times), but that paper is co-written by one author from each camp; Gaspelin et al 2015 numbers verified.

Gaspelin and Luck figures (N=24, 24, 28, 28; 15 ms; 37 vs 36 percent; 5.8 to -0.1) and Savelson abstract (two or three encounters, failed split-block replication) match; paper appeared online 2017 and in print 2018.

Content is accurate (location regularity reduces capture in feature search; trial-by-trial location cue did not) but every source is Wang and Theeuwes (same two authors, same lab); a13 and b06 are the same paper; no independent group.
fix: One lab (Wang and Theeuwes 2018a,b) reports that learned location regularities reduce capture, even in feature search, while telling people the distractor location trial by trial did not; not independently replicated in the sources.

problem: Anderson 2011 16/15/16 ms (N=26, 24, 19) and Failing 2015 7.8 vs 3.1 and 19.6 vs 7.4 percent verified; the 16 ms is the retest, wording slightly compressed; confounds/reliability sentence not checked against Stankovic.

All checked figures match (GSM-IC 18%, 72.4 vs 6.0; GSM-NoOp up to 65% with newer models declining more per Fig 8a; CatAttack >300%/500%/700%; Opus 4 85-90, R1 70 to 30; o3 97.41 to 93.93; GPT-4.1 26 to 2 at depth 5; NoisyBench Gemini-2.5-Pro 38.3 under hard negatives; DAGGER 41 vs 14-20); minor: GSM-NoOp 65 percent is the paper headline while its own table gives about 63 points for Phi-3-mini.

GSM-IC role-overlap macro accuracy 0, Wu et al misrepresentation ratios, GSM-DC power-law, and Ghaffari 0.889/0.967 vs 1.000 verified; note Ghaffari found same-domain topical records did not hurt (1.000), so the same topic wording applies mainly to GSM-IC/Wu, which the final sentence already hedges; MINT 0.12-0.43 not opened.
S2A 62.8/71.7/80.3, Wu ignore instruction marginal, Lou and Sun, MINT 8 of 9 cells and verifier no help confirmed; +0.18 under voting is the maximum (up to), NoisyBench prompting result not opened.

Turpin numbers verified (-36.3, -30.6; 0 of 234) and Chen averages verified (25% Claude 3.7 Sonnet, 39% R1), but a 25-39% verbalisation rate is not "almost never"; the zero-mention result applies to older non-reasoning models.
fix: Planted hints (suggested answer, always-A) shift LLM answers strongly. In Turpin 2023 the chain of thought never named the bias in the 234 sampled explanations (suggested-answer accuracy drop -36.3 for GPT-3.5 zero-shot, -30.6 for Claude 1.0). In Chen 2025 reasoning models verbalise hint use in only a minority of cases, on average 25 percent (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) and 39 percent (DeepSeek R1).

problem: Sharma: 27% (LLaMA 2), 98% (Claude 1.3), 45% PM on hardest misconceptions verified; Wei 2023 scale/instruction-tuning increases verified. The 98% applies to questions the model first answered correctly.

Lou and Sun (62 questions, high-school authors, CoT/ignore/reflection not sufficient) and Huang et al (reasoning models lowest anchoring ratio, conventional mitigation fails) verified; Huang title differs between versions.

Burden et al: GPT-4o Large target 83% flat (r=-0.028, p=0.082) and Claude Sonnet not set-size independent verified; Wick: feature slopes <=0.5, conjunction 2.76 and 4.98 tokens/item verified (single independent-researcher preprint).

Awh 2012 proposes a priority map integrating goals, salience and selection history; Luck 2021 common framework confirmed earlier; Guided Search 6.0 lists five guidance sources (adds reward and scene), not three, and Anderson 2021 verified only by title and framing (full text not readable).

Gema et al: inverse scaling is mainly in the natural overthinking setup (Claude 4 models non-monotonic in controlled setups); trace pattern (distracted, consider simple answer, return to distractor) quoted from the paper; NoisyBench inverse scaling with distractors verified. The no human-like recovery sentence is the authors inference.

Sweller 1994 (paired associates, vocabulary, anatomy; a/b=c worked count) and Halford et al 1998 (relational complexity, quaternary limit) verified; both are theory papers, and the three listings of each are the same paper.

de Jong 2010 (Pollock vs Kablan and Erden, Rikers 4.38-5.63, falsifiability) and Krieglstein et al 2025 (N=67/100, first impression predicts overall rating) verified; note Klepsch 2017 shows multi-item questionnaires can separate intrinsic from extraneous load, so the weakness applies to one-item ratings and post-learning overall ratings.

Zhou et al: SCAN length 99.7 vs 16.2 and last-letter L=12 74.0 vs 31.8 verified in the main text (code-davinci-002); the appendix table labels the 74.0 row code-001, a presentation inconsistency; both numbers come from one paper, with GSM-IC (Shi) and Khot only supporting the direction.

Chen, Kalyuga and Sweller 2016 author-estimated counts (rhombus/trapezium case, about 6) and CogniLoad/REL design-based assignment citing Halford verified; the no second-rater validation part is an absence claim that none of the sources contradicts but cannot be proven.

van de Kamp 2021 (11 students, 196 events, 31 percent, VPC 0.89) verified; Moore 1982 (8 vs 8 adolescents) seen only second-hand via Abdulla dissertation, which says differences were not always significant; in van de Kamp association exploration was not related to originality and only combination/abstraction were.

All numbers verified in Abdulla (2016) dissertation (40 studies, 6,649, 196, r=.22 CI .11-.32, I2 98.74, .220 to .196, Egger t=5.52); the Frontiers 2021 paper cites a published version (Abdulla et al. 2020) by the same author group, so "one dissertation" understates availability but not independence.

Numbers verified (N=90, verbal flexibility r=.71-.76, figural .14-.31, fluency moderator CI -.084 to .625) but both the Frontiers 2021 study and the meta-analysis dissertation are by the same author (Abdulla Alabbasi), and the mixed/negative earlier links (Arlin, Getzels and Smilansky, Lee and Cho, Ambrosio, Runco and Okuda) were only read second-hand through them; also r up to .76 means verbal DT and problem finding overlap heavily.
fix: One author group (Abdulla Alabbasi and colleagues) reports that problem finding is not simply divergent thinking: earlier studies they review show mixed or negative links for problem quality, the link is strongest for verbal flexibility (r=.71-.76, N=90 sixth graders) and weak for figural tasks (r=.14-.31), and in their meta-analysis the fluency moderator CI (-.08 to .63) includes zero.

problem: All numbers match SR-Scientist Table 3 (and w/o top-k is random sampling), but they come from one paper; the claim generalises to 'an agent loop' as if established beyond that single system.
fix: In SR-Scientist's ablations (Acc0.01 on LSR-Synth), the data-analysis tool and the experience buffer / top-k sampling were the largest effects, and which dominated depended on the backbone: GPT-OSS-120B lost 27.9 points without the analyser; Qwen3-Coder-480B lost 22.7 without top-k (random sampling instead); GLM-4.5-Air lost 11.1 without the experience buffer.

problem: NewtonBench numbers (12-16% at noise 0.0001 on GPT-5-mini; 40.3 and 16.7, others under 6) are correct, but SRBench evaluated AI Feynman 2.0 (its ref [23] is the 2.0 paper), not 1.0, so the v1-brittle-in-SRBench versus v2-gained framing is wrong.
fix: Symbolic accuracy is fragile to small noise and to system complexity. In NewtonBench, GPT-5-mini lost 12 to 16 percent of accuracy at noise 0.0001, and in the hardest setting only GPT-5 (40.3) and Gemini-2.5-pro (16.7) stayed above 6 percent. SRBench found AI Feynman (the 2.0 release) brittle on noisy and real-world data, even though its authors report 1 to 3 orders of magnitude more noise robustness than the first version.

problem: Minor: LaSR text calls the variable-name removal a 'substantial performance drop' but the text does not explicitly rank it the biggest (only the figure could); LLM-SR w/o Prior, PhysGym 66% to 31% and non-monotonic per-problem results are confirmed.

Numbers are right (DiscoveryWorld completion 0.08-0.38 vs humans 0.66; DiscoveryBench best 25%; FIRE-Bench best F1 46.7), but 'below 50 percent on every benchmark that tests it' generalises from three benchmarks, and only DiscoveryWorld has a human comparison; DiscoveryWorld/DiscoveryBench used 2024-era agents.
fix: On three whole-loop discovery benchmarks, the tested LLM agents scored below 50 percent: DiscoveryWorld task completion 0.08 to 0.38 for three 2024 baseline agents versus 0.66 for human scientists; DiscoveryBench best system 25 percent; FIRE-Bench best F1 46.7 (Claude Code).

problem: Minor: FIRE-Bench CV 0.37/above 0.6 (three trials), SR-Scientist three-run averages and NewtonBench four runs with SD and 95% CI are confirmed, but SR-Scientist reports only averages, not wide intervals.

KeplerAgent's own table gives PySR 40/15 and LLM-SR 30/10 (clean/noisy symbolic accuracy), not PySR 30/10; the 42.34, 35.14 vs 37.84, and 66.7 vs 48.9 numbers are correct (ABACUS units analysis confirmed in the ABACUS paper).
fix: Narrowing by structure before fitting works: dimensional analysis, symmetry and separability (AI Feynman), units (ABACUS), physics tools before PySINDy/PySR (KeplerAgent: 42.34 percent with 3 attempts). It helps most on real physics and less on arbitrary compositions (66.7 versus 48.9 percent against Eureqa on non-physical functions). Gap search: the lift is not general. KeplerAgent (GPT-4o-mini) went from 40/15 (PySR) and 30/10 (LLM-SR) to 75/45 percent symbolic accuracy on clean/noisy ODE systems, but on transformed-Feynman LSR-Transform one run (35.1) stayed under plain PySR (37.8) and only best-of-3 (42.3) passed it. Units and separability probes were not tested with an LLM agent.

problem: BACON.3 order effects and AI-Newton simple-before-complex are confirmed (Ohm 4593 productions is a cross-law cost, not an order effect), but STAHL only takes an ordered list and its examples are ordered historically; the paper does not say it needs historical order.
fix: Order and incrementality matter for cost and for reuse: BACON.3 reached the same law whatever the data order but with different computation (productions fired ranged from 1119 to 4593 across laws, Ohm highest); STAHL processes reactions as an ordered list, fed in historical order in its examples, and builds on models inferred earlier; AI-Newton discovers simple concepts (mass) before more complex ones (force) and reuses them across experiments.

problem: ABACUS (subsets with logic-style preconditions) and BACON.1 (never rejects a hypothesis; cannot formulate conditional laws) are confirmed, but none of the listed sources says sums and differences are much harder than products and ratios; ABACUS only generates sum/difference terms under units constraints.
fix: Laws need scope conditions: ABACUS learns separate equations for data subsets and derives logic-style conditions stating when each applies; BACON.1 never rejects a hypothesis once formed and cannot formulate conditional laws.

problem: Numbers confirmed (Staal g=0.20 across all tools, Prakash 0.38 for guided reflection only; 62% written-case and 31% visual tasks, 7% patients), but none of the opened sources states that many trials come from one lab network, and the 0.20 to 0.38 range mixes two different pools (all workplace tools versus guided reflection).
fix: A structured second look at a held diagnosis (list findings for, against, expected-but-missing, then alternatives) raises human diagnostic accuracy by a small to moderate amount: Hedges g 0.20 across all workplace reasoning tools (29 studies) and effect size 0.38 for guided reflection specifically (44-study review). Most trials used written cases (62%) or visual tasks (31%); only 2 of 29 used real or standardised patients.

problem: Numbers confirmed (44.5 vs 45.0, N=204; CFS N=191), but the two trials are from the same McMaster group (Sherbino and Norman on both), and Sibbald and de Bruin 2012 found analytic instructions improved ECG re-reading scores (F=15, p<0.0001), contradicting the blanket claim.
fix: In two trials from one research group, general instructions to be slow, careful and reflective did not raise diagnostic accuracy in residents (44.5 vs 45.0 percent, N=204) and cognitive forcing strategy training did not reduce bias errors in students (N=191); however, in one ECG study instructing residents to use an analytic strategy on re-reading did improve scores, so the evidence on plain instructions is mixed.

problem: Kaemmer 2021 supports 0.75 vs 0.49 (0.43 for the checklist without the answer is not visible in the abstract, only that it did not improve), but 'only when' generalises from one 90-student experiment; the review (Mamede and Schmidt) only says content-focused checklists appear to help, and Sibbald 2013 is a generic checklist.
fix: In one randomised experiment (90 advanced students), a 17-item differential diagnosis checklist raised accuracy from 0.49 (control) to 0.75 when it contained the correct diagnosis, while a checklist lacking it did not improve accuracy and might slightly reduce it; reviews suggest content-focused checklists help more than process-focused ones.

problem: In Mamede 2019 only cued reflection beat free reflection (p<0.02); modelled reflection did not differ from free (p>0.05). The p<.001 and the worked-example result are from Fernandes 2021, which used worked examples, not 'faded' examples, and reports no expertise-reversal finding.
fix: Guidance beats free reflection: cued reflection beat free reflection in novices (0.58 vs 0.41, p<0.02; modelled reflection did not differ from free reflection), and an independent group found that cued reflection and worked examples both beat free reflection (p<.001) in third- and sixth-year students, with no difference between cued and worked example.

problem: Minor: the reflection-and-calibration result is a single N=61 study; the eye-tracking study (N=19) did not test reflection, only that confidence (64-67%) did not track accuracy.

Liu et al. Table (CommonsenseQA) gives GPT-4 84.11 to 73.55 under the error-presuming prompt (a 10.6-point drop); 66.34 is the GPT-3.5 figure under that prompt. All other numbers (Huang et al. Table 3, oracle, SCoRe 15.8/4.6) match.
fix: Intrinsic LLM self-correction without an outside signal lowers accuracy (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 after five calls); earlier gains came from oracle labels deciding when to stop (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3 with oracle). The sign depends on the prompt: a prompt that presumes an error cost GPT-4 about 10.6 points on CommonsenseQA (84.11 to 73.55; GPT-3.5 fell 75.92 to 66.34) while a neutral prompt left GPT-4 at 84.60; an untreated Gemini 1.0 Pro changed 15.8 percent of right MATH answers to wrong and 4.6 percent of wrong to right.

problem: Minor: the study calls the MedQA result a modest gain, and m1 is a fine-tuned 7B/32B model, so 'reasoning models in medicine' is a slight widening.
Minor: 55.9 to 71.4 is CoVe factor+revise against a few-shot baseline (factored alone is 63.7); other numbers match and DERA open-ended MedQA stayed about 70%.
Minor: the 4 to 25 recovery is from the radiology study only (BiasMedQA mitigation gains were mostly small and GPT-4-specific), and the declines are averages over models.
Minor: 12.75 is stated as a percent/points drop relative to full context, and VivaBench 0.35 vs 0.69 is Gemini 2.5 Pro only (other models also fell by roughly half).
Minor: net harm is the pooled result; GPT-5 slightly gained (74.4 to 75.3), and the math case is a self-revision prompt on Gemini 1.0 Pro, not an 'Are you sure?' challenge.

Zhang 2025 (MAD wins at most about 15% of 36 settings against CoT), Wang 2024 and Tran 2026 support the claim, but Wunderlich 2026 (cited for CoT 64.3, SC 68.7) found same-model debate (70.0) beat self-consistency (68.7) at comparable compute and recommends multi-agent over single-agent, so 'same-model debate usually loses to sampling and voting' is contested; MoA there is not clearly different-model mixing.
fix: At matched budgets, self-refinement usually does worse than sampling more first passes and voting, and several studies find multi-agent debate rarely beats chain of thought (no MAD method won more than about 15 percent of 36 settings against CoT) and loses to self-consistency, but results conflict: on MMLU-Pro (CoT 64.3, SC 68.7, self-refinement below CoT) one study found debate (70.0) and mixture-of-agents (71.4) beat self-consistency at comparable compute, and single-agent matched or beat multi-agent at equal thinking tokens on multi-hop QA.

problem: Both abstracts confirm 28 studies (limited to early-career doctors) and 13 of 87 debiasing studies aimed at professionals, but they do not state that no patient-outcome trial exists, that the studies used vignettes, or that curriculum studies measured only knowledge tests.
fix: Reviews list 28 intervention studies on dual-process reasoning interventions (existing studies largely limited to early-career doctors, with heterogeneous measures), and only 13 of 87 health debiasing studies targeted health professionals, with transfer to real-life settings named as a main challenge.

problem: Minor: the human figures are Heuer's secondary report of Wason and a repeat, and the 24-39% range spans the reasoning models listed (e.g. GPT-OSS-20B 24.2%, GPT-5-Mini 39.0%).
Minor: Karvetski and Mandel is listed twice (one study), Mandel's group authored the 2018 and 2020 studies and the review, and the 'less reliable' result is p=.051 (MAD .22 vs .18).
Minor: the 91.9% is for the Dutch military analysts/cadets sample (N=62) and sums over 1 are called subadditive in these papers.

Minor: 14.6-18.5% zero-information-gain questions are the two example models named in the Battleship paper (GPT-4o, Llama-4-Scout), not a range across all models; the Ling 73.5 to 33.1 is one cohort at k=3 requests.

Minor: the 36-58% vs 81% flight figures are not stated in the Qiu text I could read (plateau after round 1 is), and the small-under/large-over update pattern is specific to BayesBench's coin task; Dutch-book over 50% across separate conversations is confirmed.
Minor: 76.2/73.4/44.7 are Gemma figures (AdaptFuse is labelled the legacy EMA configuration; the no-EMA ablation gives 74.0), and the Python tool result is Gemini-2.5-Pro on ProteinWorld-hard.

Minor: .23 to .15 is the paper's own coherentization (plain normalisation to sum 1 would have given about .13), and both sources are from the same group (Mandel, Karvetski); random-response comparison (aggregation gain comparable to random data) is confirmed.

Flyvbjerg et al. state the HK schedule overrun difference (+58% vs +38%) is not statistically significant (p=0.089; only the share of late projects differs, p=0.048); Hsieh's prompt lists weighted/trimmed mean or median, not only a plain average; the Lovallo-Clarke-Camerer field test is not among the opened sources.
fix: Local classes can differ from global ones (HK road cost overrun +11% vs benchmark +20%; HK schedule overrun +58% vs +38% but that mean difference is not significant, though the share of late projects was higher, 8 in 10 vs 6 in 10). Class choice is the weak point and Kahneman and Lovallo only advise trying both classes; no opened source gives a rule for resolving disagreeing classes. In LLM work the Hsieh example simply averages three estimates (30, 35, 40 to 35%) and its prompt suggests a weighted or trimmed mean or median.

problem: Opened Parsons, PMC ethnography, Feast, Hu, Storm and Maher-Tang abstract pages; all small qualitative or protocol studies as described. Absence claim (no rival-model test) not testable from sources, and Cash et al. 2023 is a quantitative reanalysis but not a rival-model test.

The Halstrom and Galle abstract only says co-evolution has merit but leaves practitioners without guidance; the full-text statement that it is not defining and does not always occur could not be retrieved (PDF download truncated twice); Cross's chapter says the model's general validity is confirmed, with direction not fixed.
fix: Co-evolution of problem and solution is widely treated as a valid model of design (Cross: general validity confirmed in nine-designer protocol data), but its direction is not fixed (the solution space may be structured before the problem space), and Halstrom and Galle argue it leaves practitioners without guidance; the claim that it is not defining or does not always occur is not shown in the sources opened.

problem: Only Parsons and Shukla (n=11, qualitative vignettes) opened and it supports solution-side triggers (tool limits, time pressure, abandoned chart designs); the second listed source (Applied Sciences 2020) returned Access Denied, its evidence lines show new problem entities followed solution work only overall and reversed in ideation, and Parsons is listed twice; Cash et al. 2023 links transitions to uncertainty, not solution-side events. 'Mostly' is not shown by any quantified count.
fix: In a qualitative study of 11 expert visualization designers (Parsons and Shukla 2025), reframing was often prompted by solution-side events such as tool limits, time pressure and abandoned chart designs that failed to convey the message, not only by a planned problem-framing step; a quantitative protocol study of student teams found this only overall and reversed during ideation.

problem: Gigerenzer-Hoffrage 50% vs 28% (short menu) not directly seen; Barbey-Sloman confirms 46% vs 16%. Opened BBS review (51%, 31%, physicians 10 to 46), PMC9903474 (34% to 68%, 577 students; results text says 36% in places) and PMC11980142 (chaining 10.6%/4.9%).

The 'estimated seen base rates accurately but did not use them' result is one simulated stock-market learning paradigm (Brenner et al.) reported in the Griffin-Koehler-Brenner commentary; a19 and a20 are the same PDF, and Bruckmaier et al. (2021) says nothing about base-rate use; 'causal' as a shrinking condition is not supported in the opened text (BBS only notes causal base-rate problems differ).
fix: In a simulated stock-market learning paradigm (Brenner and colleagues, reported in Griffin, Koehler and Brenner's commentary), participants estimated the base rates they had experienced accurately but their probability judgments were largely unaffected by them; base-rate use rises with counting or natural-frequency procedures and when the problem makes nested set structure transparent (Barbey and Sloman 2007).

problem: All step-back numbers match Zheng et al. (66.4 to 73.2, 70.9 to 81.8, TimeQA 41.5 to 66, errors fixed up to ~40% and new errors max ~12%); the second listed source (Self-Discover) is a different method and does not corroborate, so the claim rests on one paper (Google, no independent replication).

Hackathon result matches Egea et al. (second of six, abandoned concepts on minor difficulties, fixation); for O'Hara only the abstract-level solution-jumping description was reachable (techrxiv blocked), so the 100% detection of 6 seeded mismatches and about 0.01 USD per session could not be verified, and 'LLMs jump to solutions' generalizes from one self-evaluated preprint and one hackathon.
fix: In one 48-hour hackathon (Egea et al. 2024) a ChatGPT-4-led team placed second of six but abandoned promising concepts after minor difficulties, added needless complexity and showed design fixation; an unreviewed preprint (O'Hara) reports that LLM assistants tend to accept a user's technology choice without validating requirements and proposes a Five Whys workflow, whose reported detection rate and cost could not be checked.

problem: Paleka et al. and Hindcast confirm the b(1-b) point and the skew; the prescription (stratify by class rate or use skill scores against a per-class base-rate forecaster) is the researcher's own recommendation, not stated in the sources.

Pratt numbers (0.1562 vs 0.1221; weighted 0.2540 worst), Hindcast (83% NO is the raw pool of 3,427 resolved markets; the 216-market eval set was balanced 106 yes/110 no; Entertainment net -31, summed over eight models) and Paleka examples all check out; the 'score against a per-class base-rate forecaster' advice is the researcher's own.

Opened Halawi (.179 vs crowd .149, ablation .206/.186, base-rate check last), ForecastBench (scratchpad baseline with base-rate step), Hsieh (trace), Lu (o3 .1352, reference class in answer) and Hindcast (prior-anchor first step); absence claim cannot be proven but nothing contradicts it.

R-Zero numbers verified (+5.51 math, pseudo-label accuracy 79.0 to 63.0 over three iterations, smallest 0.6B peaks at step 15 while the 4B model declines only at step 60), but in Young and Bjorner the ledger, follow-up half-life and re-checks are described as design choices whose removal effects are only predicted (Table 7), not shown to be needed.
fix: Co-evolving loops degrade without a bound: R-Zero gained +5.51 math points over three iterations while pseudo-label accuracy fell from 79.0 to 63.0 percent, and the smallest model peaked at step 15 (larger models declined later); the Microsoft theory-loop (Comet-H) design includes a grounding ledger, a half-life on carried follow-ups and re-checks of claims against code, but the paper only predicts, and does not test, what removing them would cause.

problem: ADaPT numbers (71.6/43.3, depth 2 and 3) and Vermaas cup/twelve-subfunction and electrical-to-rotational examples match; 'decomposition should stop where a solution exists' is the researcher's inference, and ADaPT's rule is to decompose only on executor failure.

Least-to-most (hand-made decomposition fixes nearly every GSM8K failure), Self-planning (60.3, 74.4, cushman 34.0 vs 30.1, davinci-002 plan lifts cushman to 44.9) and ADaPT (LLaMA-2-70B 20.4 to 43.3) all match.

All Finance/PlanCraft/SWE-bench/aggregate/error-amplification numbers match Kim et al.-style scaling paper; Massoudi 6 nodes, about 650 s vs 38.6 s match; in the scaling paper the error-amplification main effect was not significant after controls (p=0.658) and D is a domain-complexity score (Finance 0.41 vs PlanCraft 0.42), the paper attributes the contrast to parallelizable vs sequential subtasks.

The three Hastie-Pennington chapter lines are one document and the 1992 experiments are the same authors' own tests, so the story-model description rests on a single lab; the independent OpenLearn summary (blocked) is a secondary account that itself lists critiques.
fix: Hastie and Pennington's Story Model proposes that jurors build a causal story from the evidence, learn verdict categories from the instructions, and match story to category, so the verdict rests on the story summary; the supporting experiments (Pennington and Hastie 1992, three mock-juror studies) come from the same research group and Bayesian or linear-updating models fit item-by-item judgments better.

problem: In the Hastie-Pennington chapter this is a theoretical implication of the model ('This means that... jurors will be swayed...'), not a measured result, and it is the authors' own advice to judges; the emotion mock-jury study (PMC12292101) tests affect-driven evidence evaluation, not under-weighting of credibility or inference-chain strength relative to an ideal evaluator, and the Czaban item is a Hungarian secondary relay.
fix: Hastie and Pennington's Story Model predicts that, compared with an ideal evidence evaluator, jurors will be swayed by the consistency and plausibility of a story and under-weight source credibility and inference-chain strength, and they advise judges to stress procedural instructions on credibility and inferential strength; this is a model-derived prediction, with no quantified effect in the sources opened.

problem: The five properties and the uniqueness rule are Hastie and Pennington's theoretical certainty principles (one chapter listed three times, plus their own 1996 article); the only independent check, Willmott et al. 2018, is a scale validation giving 'early evidence' of the certainty-principle process, not a demonstration that acceptance and confidence track each property.
fix: Hastie and Pennington's Story Model holds that acceptance and confidence depend on a story's coverage, completeness, consistency, plausibility and uniqueness, and that two coherent stories lower confidence; independent support is limited to a scale validation (Willmott et al. 2018, n=324) that reports early evidence for this certainty-principle process.

problem: Numbers check out (Silicon Crowd 0.17 to 0.14 and 0.22 to 0.15, AIA 0.096 vs 0.109, BLF 58.3 vs 62.7 and KNN 59.1 vs 50.0, Pratt weighted 0.2540 worst), but in Hsieh the 'ETH 8% by count' is the model's own arithmetic (50+20+10 days of 1003, written in its answer, not a code or data count), the BLF full agent beats the empirical-prior baseline significantly (+4.5 BI), so 'strong baseline' is not 'no better', and the Pratt pipeline lacks a data-anchored control.
fix: Giving LLMs a crowd or market value helped (GPT-4 0.17 to 0.14, Claude 2 0.22 to 0.15 with the human median; market price alone 0.096 vs 0.109 for the best prior LLM system; ForecastBench top LLMs used freeze values), while model-recalled base rates are vague and gave no gain (Hsieh's trace recalls 30% for ETH, then reasons its way to 8% with day counts the model wrote itself; Pratt's recalled-base-rate pipeline had the worst weighted Brier, 0.2540). A code-computed class frequency was a strong baseline (empirical prior Brier Index 58.3 on dataset questions vs 62.7 for the full BLF agent, which still beats it significantly; KNN frequency counter 59.1 vs 50.0 for always-0.5).

problem: Buehler et al. numbers all match (37 contacted, analysis on 33: 33.9 vs 55.5, 29.7%, worst case 48.6; Study 4 N=123 recall-relevant removes mean bias but not absolute error; Study 5 observers 48.0% vs 2.4% mention past); Thomas and Koenig was opened in the primary PMC paper (not secondary as the claim says) and supports less bias when the first task was the same.

Martingale scores (0.037, 0.086, 0.103), the ~0.04 worse-than-chance remark and the BayesBench active-vs-passive pro-user bias all check out, but Table 1 of He et al. shows the system-prompt effects are not consistent across models in forecasting (critical-thinking prompt raised the score for GPT-4o and Maverick and lowered it for R1, Flash and Scout; prior-conforming raised it for most but not Gemini Flash), and the Martingale result concerns the model's own prior belief, not a user-stated stance.
fix: Across forecasting, value-laden and paper-review tasks, LLM belief updates were predictable from the model's own prior belief (Martingale scores with chain of thought 0.037 forecasting, 0.086 paper review, 0.103 ChangeMyView), and a score near 0.04 coincided with forecasts worse than chance; prompting to conform to the prior generally raised the score and a critical-thinking prompt lowered it only for some models. Separately, in BayesBench's social-judgment task, actively engaging with a simulated user produced a persistent pro-user bias that passive reading of the same evidence did not. Neither study tested removing the stance at the evidence-search step.

problem: GSM8K step-wise numbers, TextCraft depth 2 and 3 numbers and the kth-letter result all match, but the TextCraft numbers cited do not show a gain growing with depth: the absolute ADaPT gain shrinks from +51.3 points at depth 2 (26.9 to 78.2) to +36.9 at depth 3 (1.8 to 38.7), and the comparison is against ReAct, not chain of thought.
fix: Decomposition helps more on longer problems in least-to-most (GSM8K 5+ steps 45.23 vs 39.07 for chain of thought) and in decomposed prompting (kth-letter concatenation stays near 100% while chain of thought falls with length), and was worse on 2-step GSM8K (74.53 vs 76.68); ADaPT still lifts TextCraft at depth 3 (ReAct 1.8 to 38.7) though its absolute gain is smaller than at depth 2 (26.9 to 78.2).

problem: Hirtz et al. (no measured benefit; repeatability study cited), Gericke and Eisenbart ('initial empirical evidence') and the Clemson abstract ('little experimental evidence' for ideation) match, but 'only repeatability and usage-frequency studies exist' is wider than the sources: Gericke cites further empirical studies (Caldwell 2011, Srinivasan 2012, Sen 2013) and the same dissertation and the Linsey and Booth experiments in this note are ideation experiments.
fix: Evidence that function modelling helps designers is thin: the functional-basis authors report no measurement of benefit beyond a repeatability study, a 2017 review calls the empirical evidence for its benefits 'initial' (citing Kurfman, Caldwell, Srinivasan and Sen studies), and a Clemson dissertation abstract says there is little experimental evidence that function models help concept generation (the few experiments on it show no reliable gain).

problem: BCC 0.477-0.743, gradients 0.295-0.482, direction agreement 63.7-75.8% (Imran et al. Table 1); Filbry et al. cross-chat Dutch-book violations above 50% of 30 scenarios, within-dialogue 10% (Gemini) or 1 of 30 (Gemma), reasoning and code results match; Wu 2026 not needed; the abstract page alone did not show these numbers, full text did.

Simon's Hora and Tempus (about 4,000 times, 1/111 x 20 x 20,000) and ten-dial safe (100^10, about 10 x 50 = 500 tries with clicks) match the original; Ulrich (1995) defines modular vs integral architecture and does not corroborate the numbers, so the quantitative claim rests on Simon alone (an analytic parable, as the claim says).

Plan-and-Solve numbers are mislabeled: in the PS paper's table 56.4/57.0/59.3 on GSM8K are Zero-shot-CoT/PoT/PS+; plain PS is 58.2 on GSM8K (+1.8 over CoT, not +0.6) and its six-dataset average is 72.9 (not 73.5, which is PoT). Least-to-most +1.5, self-planning pass@10 76.3 vs 75.0 and pass@1 60.3 vs 48.1, and the Meincke GPQA results (o4-mini +0.056 at one threshold, 20 to 80% more time) match; PS models were text-davinci-003, not strong models.
fix: Plan-first prompting gives small gains over plain chain of thought (about 1 to 7 points; plain Plan-and-Solve +1.8 on GSM8K, 56.4 to 58.2, and PS+ +2.9; least-to-most +1.5 on GSM8K), mainly by cutting missing-step errors. Self-planning gains shrink with sampling: pass@10 is 76.3 vs 75.0 direct, against pass@1 60.3 vs 48.1. For reasoning models generic step-by-step prompting added almost nothing on GPQA Diamond (only o4-mini +5.6 points at one threshold) and cost 20 to 80% more time.

problem: Press et al. (about 40% gap; 42.9% ChatGPT, 23.0% GPT-4) and Dziri et al. (3x3 multiplication ChatGPT 55%, GPT-4 59%) match; Press itself warns the GPT-4 figure may be invalid because the dataset predates GPT-4 and could be in its training data.

Table 8.1 of the Pennington-Hastie chapter (N=130; 59, 78, 31, 63) and the 1992 replication (N=414, equal total recall, different clustering) match; Czaban's relay reports 62% instead of 63% for both-witness; the replication and original are the same research group, and the chapter gives no verdict percentages for the 1992 study.

Booth 2013 (26 students, n=78 trees, no method effect) and Booth 2015 study 2 (n=78, r=0.075, p=0.515) match, but Booth 2013 compares three decomposition methods with each other and measures functions, errors and abstraction levels, not idea count or design quality against a no-decomposition control; Booth 2015 study 2 is observational; the Linsey 2005 figures (n=54, 19.0 vs 19.7) could not be opened (ASEE page blocked; only an abstract saying function modelling was indistinguishable from control was reachable) and the quoted evidence line itself lists group sizes of 5 and 7.
fix: In human studies, evidence that a functional decomposition step improves ideas or design quality is absent: a first controlled test (Linsey et al. 2005) reported no difference from a control group, a within-subject comparison of three decomposition methods (Booth 2013, 26 students) found no method effect on its measures, and an observational study of 78 industry reports (Booth 2015 study 2) found no correlation between using decomposition and design grade (r=0.075, p=0.515). All tests are small, observational or preliminary, so a small benefit is not excluded.

problem: Phalen et al. 2025 (N=713, 677, 651) confirmed but the authors call it correlational/mediational, and the second source (Thagard, scanned PDF) was unreadable and is about OJ polls, not re-weighting by a leading verdict.
fix: In three mock-jury studies (N=713, 677, 651), greater negative emotion toward the defendant was associated, via mediation, with more agreement with unrelated plaintiff evidence and less with unrelated defence evidence, and with more liable verdicts; judicial rehabilitation did not reduce this (correlational, single lab).

problem: Bessis et al. (single paper, listed several times) numbers all verified; human recency in Bessis and law-student study (Maegherman et al., N=407) also verified.
Numbers (2,304; 63.56 vs 58.82; 21% vs 49%) verified in Sun et al., but only some effects replicated: reporting delay did not (LLMs sensitive, humans not); Wu 2026 does not test level divergence.
fix: LLM mock jurors diverge from humans in level (guilt probability 63.56 vs 58.82 but guilty verdicts 21% vs 49%; 2,304 responses); the defendant-race bias and the rise with more allegations replicated, but sensitivity to reporting delay appeared only in the LLMs.

problem: Dalal et al. (ACL 2024 / arXiv versions are one paper) verified: consistency similar for correct/incorrect, depth +6% and drift +10%, up to 77% vs 50% random; abstract wording is '+17%' vs table avg +17.5%; claim's 'up to 77%' holds. Douven source is a different topic.
MuSR (GPT-4 CoT+ 80.4, human 94.1) and True Detective (GPT-4 0.27 vanilla, 0.83 golden CoT) verified in the PDFs; 'bottleneck' is an interpretation but supported by True Detective.

Ersoz (17 of 18 hung, anchoring named dominant failure; N=3 per cell, two models) verified; SimCourt/AgentsCourt exist; the 'none tests a story-model manipulation' part is a negative search result not checkable from sources.

Test of Time Table 7 numbers match, but for GPT-4 shuffle (60.71) is not the lowest (StartTimeAndRelation 60.54); the paper's 'consistently lowest' is slightly off, 'at equal tokens' is not stated; premise-order drops are up to 20-30 points for GPT-4-turbo/PaLM 2-L (about 16-21 at 12 rules) and over 40 only for weaker models, not a uniform 20 to 40+.
fix: Reordering the same facts changes LLM accuracy: on Test of Time shuffled facts score at or near the lowest (GPT-4 60.71 vs 65.36 best; Gemini 1.5 Pro 63.04 vs 75.00; Claude-3-Sonnet 45.71 vs 73.57), and in deduction (Chen et al. 2024) forward (proof-order) premises beat other orders for every model, by up to 20-30 points for GPT-4-turbo and PaLM 2-L and by over 40 points for weaker models such as Gemini 1.0 Pro and GPT-3.5-turbo.

problem: Kriegsspiel page (Prussia only army wargaming, Meckel/Verdy du Vernois), Zenko (19 ships, $250M, 752-page report, end state scripted) and IFPV (+19.4% relative gain in a different setup than Table 3) verified; 'unequal compute' is an inference since the paper reports no compute figures; negative 'no controlled test found' not checkable.

Kriegsspiel page (Reisswitz umpire, dice, 1:8000 maps, Meckel/Verdy du Vernois), Snow Globe (control adjudicates, adjudication hardest, 'Include unexpected consequences' with Mistral-7B-OpenOrca) and WarAgent (secretary agent verifies actions, up to 4 exchanges) verified; Kriegsspiel two listings are one Wikipedia page.

Payne (21 games, 29-64%) and Adl & Williams (3,604 games, 10.7% to 28.6%) verified, but Solopova et al. does not show models pick more cooperative actions than graduate students (only their explanations are cooperative in framing; some models were more coercive on economic choices), and Payne's models did sometimes reduce violence (return to start line) though never chose accommodation or withdrawal.
fix: In Payne's 21 model-vs-model nuclear-crisis games no model ever chose accommodation or surrender (only de-escalation as far as returning to the start line) and strategic-threat level was reached in 29-64% of games depending on the model; in Solopova et al.'s menu simulations models' explanations were cooperative in framing but their actions were mixed against graduate-student players (some more coercive); one-line framing moved escalation from 10.7% to 28.6% in 3,604 games (Adl and Williams). No Lamparth replication with experts was found.

problem: Schwid & O'Donnell 1992 (63% of 30; PMID 1550273 abstract), DeAnda & Gaba 1990 (132 incidents, 19 sims, 20.5%/27), Woods & Cook fixation definition and two criteria, and SREGym (agents lock onto first plausible anomaly) verified; first evidence line mis-credits PMID 1550273 to Howard, Gaba but it is the same Schwid paper.

Huang et al. Tables 2-3 (GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5->89.0 round 2, 95.5->97.5 oracle; GPT-3.5 CSQA 75.8->38.1 round 1; HotpotQA 49.0->59.0; GPT-3.5 GSM8K oracle 84.3) and Kamoi survey conclusion verified; 'GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3' matches the oracle row.
Tyen (GPT-4 52.87 overall; Table 6 gains +18.04 to +43.92 on incorrect-answer traces), Who&When (53.5/14.2, 127 systems) and TRAIL (Gemini-2.5-Pro joint 0.183 GAIA, 0.050 SWE) verified.

AIOpsLab (GPT-3.5-w-shell up to 14 repeats in 20 steps), MAST (FM-1.3 step repetition 15.7%, 1642 traces), AgentBench Table 4 (TLE predominant overall, though only top outcome on KG and LTP and OS-second), Reflexion (>3 cycles / >30 actions), Cloud-OpsBench (RAR 0.00 for strong models incl. Claude-Sonnet-4; Qwen3-8B 0.46, Qwen3-14B 0.28) and Gumaan (-1.03 nats, odds 2.8, 0.06->0.54) verified; 'commonest outcome on several tasks' is fair only for KG and LTP.

AIOpsLab Table 4 (detection FLASH 100%, ReAct 76.92, GPT-4 69.23; RCA 36.36/45.45/40.90; mitigation GPT-4 27.27, GPT-3.5 0; ReAct/FLASH mitigation cells garbled in extract but consistent), ITBench 13.8% SRE, ITBench-AA 47/46%, SREGym (mitigation 40.4-78.5, e2e 60.7, new types 15.4-28.2 across two different agents) and Cloud-OpsBench (JRA 0.76, ECR 0.38) verified.

Abstracts of Parasuraman & Manzey (experts, not prevented by training/instructions), Goddard et al. (74 of 13,821; workload/complexity/time constraint; information vs recommendation mitigates) and Lyell & Coiera (890/40) verified; note Goddard lists training as a mitigator, so 'not removed' is right only as 'not eliminated'.

RCAgent numbers (99.38 vs ReAct 86.33; invalid 7.93 vs 22.82; SQL tools 65.84/70.94) and SWE-agent lint 18.0 vs 15.0 verified, but neither paper compares structure against prompting changes, so 'raises stability more than prompting' is not supported; SWE-agent 15.0 is a plain Table 3 value, not a reported error bar.
fix: Adding structure around the model raised stability or success in two agent systems: RCAgent's full system passed within 15 steps 99.38% vs 86.33% for plain ReAct (invalid actions 7.93% vs 22.82%; swapping in SQL tools gave 65.84% pass and 70.94% invalid), and SWE-agent's linting guard raised SWE-bench Lite success from 15.0% to 18.0% (a small, single-run difference); neither study compares this to prompt changes.

problem: AIOpsLab section 3.6 (raw telemetry via cat overwhelms context, distraction, token exhaustion; failed-case action mix from a figure not checked), Shi et al. (GSM-IC performance dramatically decreased) and Lost in the Middle (GPT-3.5 drop over 20%, below 56.1% closed-book) verified.

Numbers verified (43.3->58.2 OSWorld, 30.3->58.8 WebArena, 93.9% detector; FailFast 66.6->71.8 at 25% FPR vs cold restart 66.8), but cost is lower only versus fixed-interval checking and the large model alone; the cascade costs more than the small model alone ($0.051 vs $0.022 on OSWorld).
fix: A learned stuck or milestone monitor that escalates to a stronger model raises success over the small model alone (OSWorld 43.3% to 58.2%, WebArena 30.3% to 58.8%; held-out stuck-detector accuracy 93.9%) at lower cost than a fixed-interval large-model check ($0.05 vs $0.07 and $0.21 vs $0.24 per task) and than the large model alone, though costing more than the small model alone; FailFast on SWE-bench Verified raised Qwen3.6-27B resolve from 66.6% to 71.8% at 25% FPR with restart plus diff overlay (cold restart 66.8%). Caveats: the first gain mixes detection with a stronger model taking over; the second is one benchmark with open models only.

fix: Patents that cite scientific papers get 49% more 10-year citations and 117% higher odds of being top-5% hits (171% for top 1%) in Ke et al.; among them, citing more recent science adds further impact, but that gain is offset when the cited papers' ages have low variance (Mukherjee et al.: recent and age-varied sources are about 2.2 times as likely to be top 5%).

HINDSIGHT numbers (7.44 vs 7.40, 0.297 vs 0.119, 2.5x, r=-0.29) verified, but Si 2025 does not show novelty rating surviving: AI ideas' novelty scores fell 1.05 points after execution (human -0.01), the human-AI difference at execution is non-significant on novelty simply because the AI advantage vanished.
fix: LLM-rated novelty does not predict real later impact: in HINDSIGHT, LLM-judge scores are equal for grounded and vanilla ideas (7.44 vs 7.40) while matching to future papers shows a 2.5x gap (0.297 vs 0.119), and the HINDSIGHT score correlates -0.29 with LLM-judged novelty. Si et al. 2025 point the same way: AI ideas rated more novel before execution lost 1.05 novelty points and 1.88 effectiveness points after experts ran them, while human ideas lost almost none.

Chen & Zhang (70.6% new at turn 1, 78.3% inherited at turn 3, diversity/novelty peak early near iteration 2) and SciMON (55.6%, 57.8%) numbers verified, but SciMON shows gains still rising at iteration 2, not a sweet spot, and Nova's 3.4x is the framework versus no framework (only 3 rounds run), not growth over rounds; only the no-planning ablation (42.4 to 44.1) is flat.
fix: Iterating recombination appears to have a sweet spot in one study: in Chen and Zhang, diversity and novelty peak near the second iteration while later rounds lock onto the previous version (70.6% new entities at turn 1, 78.3% inherited at turn 3). SciMON's novelty loop still raised novelty on iteration 2 (55.6% of ideas on iteration 1, 57.8% of continuing ideas on iteration 2), and Nova's planned retrieval gives 3.4 times more unique novel ideas than no framework over 3 rounds, with the no-planning ablation flat between rounds 2 and 3 (42.4 to 44.1). All judge novelty with LLMs or embeddings, not outcomes.

problem: Only Weitzman (1998) says the bottleneck is turning ideas into usable form (PDF text not machine-readable here; abstract wording known); Tria 2014 and Pichler 2020 abstracts model rates only and say nothing of a usability bottleneck, and Arthur-Polak 2006 has no evidence line.
fix: Weitzman (1998) models growth as recombination of old ideas, with the supply of possible combinations exploding and the binding limit being the ability to process them into usable form; Tria et al. (2014) and Pichler et al. (2020) model rates of novelty and innovation (Heaps law, network dependencies) and do not address usability. Evidence in this set is about rates, not usefulness.

problem: Numbers confirmed (79%, 71-82%, 19.9%/412 of 2,070), but the 79% comes from 100 queries (Infinity-Chat100) not all 26K prompts, 71-82% is embedding similarity not agreement, and the conclusion that spread must come from different inputs is not tested by either source.
fix: Several LLM samples are not independent: on 100 open-ended queries (50 responses each, top-p 0.9, temperature 1.0) one model gave average pairwise embedding similarity above 0.8 in 79% of cases, and responses from different models had average pairwise similarity of 71% to 82% (Jiang et al. 2025); in Kombine 19.9% (412 of 2,070) of invented concepts reuse two or more properties of another model concept. This suggests that more samples of one prompt or model add little spread; that diversity must come from different inputs is an inference, not a tested result.

problem: Fleming numbers confirmed in full text and Foster 85.8/14.2 found in the arXiv preprint, but the Uzzi paper itself prints both sets: body text says 36.1, 39.8, 49.7% while the Fig. 3 caption says 36.2, 39.9, 49.7%, so the earlier values are not mere transcription slips.

Uzzi et al. print the team shares inconsistently: 36.1, 39.8 and 49.7 percent in the body text and 36.2, 39.9 and 49.7 percent in the Figure 3 caption. Foster et al. report 85.8 vs 14.2 repeat/new (arXiv preprint). Singh-Fleming 2010, Fleming-Sorenson 2001, Katila-Ahuja 2002 and Kaplan-Vakili 2015 are still unread.

fix: Retrieval and recombination pipelines (SciMON, Nova, Deep Ideation, combinatorial creativity framework, Scideator) raise novelty or diversity as scored by their own evaluations: Nova 3.4x unique novel ideas, Deep Ideation +10.25% over the best baseline per domain (10.67% in its abstract versus other methods; five LLM judges), Gu et al. +7-10% similarity to real later papers, Scideator creativity support median 70.5 vs 61.0 (human user study). Most use LLM or embedding judges that K17 says are unreliable; none ran the idea to a real outcome.

problem: Minor: execution-study numbers (4.93 human vs 4.73 AI, p=0.21; drops 1.049/1.760/1.879) confirmed; the math trend is not strictly monotonic (AMC 12 is 54.05%, below AMC 8 at 55.39%) and the abstract says over 100 hours while the AI arm averaged 93.7 hours.

Wenger and Kenett call originality roughly equal but the differences are significant and mixed (LLMs higher on AUT 0.711 vs 0.696 and DAT 0.801 vs 0.753, humans higher on FF 0.603 vs 0.637); NoveltyBench states fewer than 3 distinct responses in 10 for some models (e.g. Claude 3, GPT-4o), not all; the 10.7% human-with-AI story claim has no opened source.
fix: LLMs are individually about as original as people on average but collectively more alike: across 22 LLMs, mean originality was roughly equal (AUT 0.711 vs 0.696 and DAT 0.801 vs 0.753 for LLMs, FF 0.603 vs 0.637 for humans; all differences significant but small) with significantly lower population variability (e.g. AUT 0.459 vs 0.738). Gap search, not opened here: humans with AI ideas write better individual stories but the set is more alike (10.7% lower diversity, search summary only). NoveltyBench reports that models such as Claude 3 and GPT-4o give on average fewer than 3 distinct responses in 10 queries; Artificial Hivemind finds same-model similarity above 0.8 in 79% of cases (100 queries) and 71-82% across models.

The half-ridge result (intermediate prior best on all 20 data sets) is against directed tallying and sign-constrained regression, not TTB and unconstrained regression; TTB appears only in an appendix COR analysis (peak usually in the middle), and the two Parpart lines are one paper while Simsek tests no priors.
fix: Parpart et al. (2018) show that tallying and TTB are limits of Bayesian inference under infinitely strong priors; in simulations on the 20 ABC data sets an intermediate-strength prior that uses all cues (half-ridge) beat directed tallying and sign-constrained regression at every training size, and the COR model with a TTB rule usually peaked at intermediate priors (appendix). Strong bias helps, not simplicity itself; this rests on one paper.

problem: b04 and b05 are the same Hogarth and Karelaia paper (full text could not be opened, only abstracts via search confirm TTB effectiveness with 3-5 binary cues, hybrids better in compensatory worlds, and little advantage over a dominance rule under error); a14 only defines non-compensatory and does not test TTB; the only-with-perfect-order phrasing is not checked against the full text.

The .758/.756/.742 (1.6-point) figures are from one earlier German-cities data set cited by Simsek and Buckmann, not 63 real data sets; across the 63 sets validity ordering is described only as very close to greedy except in a handful, and the paper says continuous cues placed first mask ordering differences (relative accuracy of the orderings drops more in the dichotomized versions), the opposite of validity losing most with continuous cues.
fix: Finding the best cue order for a lexicographic rule is hard to approximate (no efficient algorithm within any constant factor unless P differs from NP; Schmitt and Martignon 2006), and a greedy ordering is proven to do better than take-the-best validity ordering. Empirically (Simsek and Buckmann 2015) greedy is identical or very close to the best order on 63 data sets and validity ordering is very close to greedy except in a handful; on the German cities set fitting accuracy was .758 best, .756 greedy, .742 validity (1.6 points).

problem: r = 0.64 (p = .03, 11 environments), Pohl 89% to 75% and the 64%-96% table range check out, but b10 and b12 are the same Pachur et al. paper and Gigerenzer and Goldstein 2011 (b07/a13) share authors with it (the recognition-heuristic group) and report a different correlation (r = .57 across experiments).

GG96 tallying .656 vs regression .657 is not an out-of-sample test (regression was given all Appendix information, more than any competitor), so it cannot support the out-of-sample wording; Schoenegger numbers (Brier .20 vs .19, p=.85; GPT-4 .15), RRF F0.5 .102 vs .080 and Dawes unit-weight robustness hold, though the ensemble aggregate is a median and Dawes full text could not be fully read.
fix: Equal-weight or unit-weight rules predict nearly as well as fitted weights out of sample in social-science data (Dawes 1979: unit weighting is robust) and, per Czerlinski et al. as summarised by Gigerenzer 2012, on 20 ABC data sets under cross-validation; in the in-sample-favoured GG96 German-cities competition tallying (.656) was level with regression (.657), which had more information. An LLM yes/no checklist counted with unit weights matched or beat elastic-net weights when positives were scarce (RRF, F0.5 .102 vs .080, not separable at founder level). The median of 12 LLMs matched a human crowd (Brier .20 vs .19) but was worse than the best single model (GPT-4, .15).

problem: Minor: FFTrees paper confirms SVM 0.86 vs FFT/RLR/RF 0.83 on ten real data sets (not all small; SVM failed on two); the clinical and legal wins (Green and Mehr, Dhami bail) come from the Gigerenzer and Gaissmaier review, which I only knew from the listed lines and did not re-open.

Numbers check out (36.3 points is the abstract maximum, an o1-preview vs GPT-4o comparison on one task; 17.3 points CI 7.7-25.5 from one pre-registered single-author study), but Tsvilodub et al. and Fan et al. are different experiments (chain length vs answerability, abstention rates only inferred from the abstract), not replications of the accuracy drop, and the effect is absent or reversed in the weakest models.
fix: Longer or forced chain of thought lowers LLM accuracy on some tasks where deliberation also hurts people (Liu et al. 2024: up to 36.3 points lower for o1-preview vs GPT-4o on implicit statistical learning; lower CoT accuracy also on face recognition) and on unanswerable Knightian items (Bogdan 2026, single pre-registered study: 17.3 points, CI 7.7-25.5, strong in mid-to-large models, absent or reversed in the weakest); longer reasoning budgets also lowered accuracy on several task families (Gema et al. 2025). Two other labs report related but different findings: reasoning models write chains at least as long on unanswerable as on answerable items (Tsvilodub et al. 2026) and much longer responses on missing-premise questions (Fan et al. 2025); the 17.3-point size has not been replicated.

problem: Minor: Sprague et al. give symbolic +14.2, math +12.3, logical +6.9, so the claim lists math/symbolic in swapped order; 56.8 vs 56.1, 110 papers, and up to 95% MMLU equals-sign share all confirmed; Liu et al. only supports the CoT-can-hurt side.

Minor: all cited numbers verified (98%, 40% cost at 0.929 vs 0.931 is from the listed lines, UCCI -31% CI 27-35% at micro-F1 0.91, cascade routing up to 8%/12% as AUC gains over cascading/routing); the 30-60% savings range outside the best case is a synthesis (MoT 60%, UCCI 31%) and ignores FrugalGPT HEADLINES at about 80%; the 12-LLM-free MoT accuracy figures were not re-opened beyond the abstract.

Minor: 46.5% (5.3 points above any non-adaptive method) is GPT-3 with GenRead+Contriever whereas the 40% retrieval rate (skip on 60%) is davinci-003 with BM25, so they are separate configurations; correlations about 0.4 and 0.1 confirmed; Ferrando et al. abstract confirms the entity-recognition directions are causal for refusal vs hallucination.

Betas are mislabelled: 0.96 is abstention below answering accuracy, 1.03 is the human comparison, and 1.67 is the question-type by model-type interaction (answer-abstain gap larger in reasoning than instruction models); Fan et al. report longer responses on missing-premise items but abstention rates only inferred from the abstract.
fix: Independent labs see the cost of long reasoning on unanswerable items: reasoning models write chains at least as long on unanswerable as on answerable items (85% posterior probability that they are longer) and abstain credibly worse than they answer (beta 0.96) and worse than humans (beta 1.03), with the answer-abstain gap larger in reasoning than instruction-tuned models (beta 1.67) (Tsvilodub et al. 2026); an efficiency reward raised abstention 14.7% and cut chains 44% on average in fine-tuned 4B/8B models; Fan et al. 2025 independently report much longer responses by reasoning models on missing-premise questions.

fix: LLM uncertainty (first-token probability, choice-order sensitivity) is a real but small difficulty cue: adding it to text features cut test RMSE by about 0.02-0.03 relative to a mean-predicting dummy (Biopsychology .1361 vs .1667; USMLE .2868 vs .3110) but only about 0.01 relative to text-only TF-IDF on Biopsychology (.1479 to .1361); correlation with student answer distributions is weak and differs for right vs wrong answers. A hidden-state probe reaches ROC-AUC 93.09% on ScienceQA for the model's own failures (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) but needs white-box access.

A small engineered feature set can beat 768-dimensional BERT embeddings (RMSE .302 vs .614 in Fulari and Rusert, cited by Peters et al., which attribute it to dimensionality).

Information gain as the test selector is supported in small closed hypothesis sets by separate studies (e.g. Zendo, blicket), not by these sources.

Numbers verified in Vul and Pashler and Steegen et al.; minor: the verified studies used percentage questions only (CIA Factbook), so 'and quantity' is slightly wider than shown.

Numbers match, but 1.1-1.5 is the equivalent number of people for the whole averaged set (lambda 0.11/0.32 is the second guess's worth), and the 'field data say barely better than two different people' clause is not in any opened source (Gomilsek only shows asking someone else wins in all 6 conditions, +8.3 points).
fix: Averaging two guesses from the same person is worth only about 1.1 to 1.3 independent people (Vul and Pashler: lambda 0.11 immediate, 0.32 delayed, i.e. a second guess is worth 11-32% of a second person's guess; 1.04-1.07 in a replication by Hourihan and Benjamin); even an ensemble of five different thinking styles reaches only about 1.5 people (Fujisaki et al. 2025); asking another person beat re-asking oneself in all six conditions of Gomilsek et al. 2024.

problem: Numbers verified; minor: Ross and Vallee-Tourangeau found time spent moving tiles did predict words, and Spiridonov per-problem models show positive effects on problem D in Exp 2 and 3, so 'not reliably' is right but not 'no effect'.

Numbers verified, but the DPO anti-pressure figures are for Llama-3.1-8B on EX-FEVER only (Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma, Qwen3 differ; Qwen3 yielding rose 4.5), the -0.50 is the framing score on SS for Llama-70B (GPT-4o 0.48), and 95% is score 1 (94) plus score 2 (1).
fix: A blanket anti-agreement step can cost accuracy on clean inputs. In ELEPHANT, naive instruction prepending drove Llama-70B's framing-sycophancy score on the SS set to -0.50 (all face-preservation removed, even where affirmation is appropriate; GPT-4o stayed at 0.48); in Llama-3.1-8B on EX-FEVER, DPO anti-pressure cut unsupported yielding by 32.9 points but cut rational updating on real evidence by 48.9-53.7 points (other backbones differ); and a premise-identification prompt scored 1-2 (wrongly challenged) on 95% of true-premise Cancer-Myth questions for gemini-3-flash without RAG.

Numbers (93% of 980 settings; 23 models, 1.6x wall-clock, 3.4x tokens) match the abstracts, but the final sentence 'Only the original debate paper lacked this control' is a sweeping universal no source supports (Du et al. did include a 3-agent majority baseline, just not budget-matched); '9-sample' not on the abstract page.
fix: Debate between copies of one model beats a single agent but not equal-budget voting: self-consistency matched or beat debate in 93 percent of 980 matched settings (5 open models, 4 tasks), and a 23-model study found debate tied or lost to matched-budget sampling/voting at 1.6x wall-clock and 3.4x tokens. The original debate paper (Du et al.) compared only against a 3-agent majority baseline that was not budget-matched; Huang et al. found debate underperforms self-consistency at equal response counts.

problem: Yu (corr 0.45-0.59/0.60, ceiling 1.71-2.21) and Kohli (n_eff 2.18) check out, but 'so a same-model crowd cannot be better' is an inference from a different-model panel on NLI, not shown by any source; Nguyen rho range 0.35-0.77 and 1/rho cap not seen in abstract (full text pending).
fix: Same-model votes are worth about 1.3 to 2.9 independent votes, whatever the sample count. Two independent measurements on small open models agree: correctness correlation 0.45 to 0.60 on GSM8K gives a ceiling of 1.7 to 2.2 effective votes, reached by K=8 to 16 (Yu et al. 2026); error correlation 0.35 to 0.77 across five models and four tasks gives a cap of 1/rho (Nguyen et al. 2026). Nine different frontier models gave only about 2.2 effective votes on NLI (Kohli 2026), which suggests, but does not show, that a same-model crowd is no better.

problem: Minor: 0.46 cap uses the Wald upper bound on the 0.6% disagreement rate (point estimate would be ~0.3); 96-103% of K=32 at 25-44% cost holds across model/task rows.

Taylor 2009 (crows did not avoid trap with hole plus functional trap) and Logan 2014 (95% of objects dropped solid in no-water platform) verified, but Logan et al. only suggest a possible object bias needing further testing, so 'reduces to an object preference' is too strong; Taylor 'used the hole as the cue' is the authors' interpretation.
fix: A failed control narrows the surviving explanation rather than only refuting understanding: crows did not avoid the trap when a bare hole and a functional trap were compared (consistent with using the hole as the cue), and in the no-water platform control 95% of objects crows dropped were solid, which suggests the Aesop solidity result may reflect an object preference rather than understanding of water displacement (a hypothesis needing further testing).

Verified; note Webb et al. 2024 reply argues the permuted-alphabet gap is a counting-cost issue and GPT-4 with code reaches human level, a caveat the claim omits.
