Ellamil 2012 abstract and He et al. 2025 ALE meta-analysis (44 generation, 10 evaluation studies; evaluation: insula, claustrum, MedFG, CG; generation without medial temporal clusters) verified; the meta-analysis is not among the listed evidence lines and the 15-participant figure comes from a table in the review.

Chen et al. 2025 (N=2433, inverted U) verified, but the r range quoted is the intelligence-creativity correlation across six datasets, which runs from -0.01 to 0.39 (0.32, 0.33, 0.39, 0.07, 0.13, -0.01), not 0.07 to 0.39, and the claim does not say which constructs.
fix: The two modes are coupled, not isolated: default and executive networks cooperate during creative thought, and creative ability follows an inverted U of default-executive network switching (N=2433 pooled across 10 samples; the intelligence-creativity correlation in the six datasets that measured both ranged from -0.01 to 0.39). A strict two-module split is a design choice, not a brain fact.

fix: Single-question benchmarks overstate ability: on FANToM (six question types about the same information) models score well on individual question types but far below humans when all must be answered consistently; on BigToM (procedurally generated ToM items with 25 controls) GPT-4 follows human inference patterns but less reliably than humans, and other models struggle.

Numbers match Fix, Wiedenbeck and Scholtz 1993 (20 vs 20; 3.7 vs 1.7, F(1,38)=57.58; 4.0 vs 3.7 n.s.), but it is one study with one 'moderately complex' and one 'very simple' recurring-pattern question, so a general 'only for non-trivial plans' and the label 'complex' are too strong; the review appendix actually shows mixed findings (Davies 1990: plan use may come from design training).
fix: In one study (Fix, Wiedenbeck and Scholtz 1993; 20 novices vs 20 experts), experts labelled a moderately complex recurring plan far better than novices (3.7 vs 1.7 of 4, p=.0001) but did not differ on a very simple plan (4.0 vs 3.7, n.s.); other studies on plan knowledge are mixed.

problem: Scholtz and Wiedenbeck 1992 states Rist 1991b: plan creation for novices, shift to retrieval with experience, even experienced programmers reverting to creation on difficult problems; the support is secondary (a summary of Rist) plus a tiny exploratory study, and Detienne 1995 mostly did not support its own beginner/expert hypothesis.

CodeChain APPS 22.33 to 30.24 and ReGAL +11.5 (LOGO, CodeLlama-13B) vs +1.3 (Date, GPT-3.5) verified, but in the CodeChain ablation (Table 3, CoT + public-test filter) the 30.16 row is centroid whole programs, not random whole programs; the comparison actually shown is centroid sub-modules 35.11 vs centroid whole programs 30.16 and random sub-modules 32.87.
fix: Reusing solved sub-modules or abstractions helps, with more for weaker models: CodeChain APPS pass@1 22.33 to 30.24 (GPT-3.5); ReGAL +11.5 on LOGO for CodeLlama-13B vs +1.3 on Date for GPT-3.5; in the CodeChain ablation, centroid sub-modules (35.11) beat both centroid whole programs (30.16) and random sub-modules (32.87).

CodeRAG-Bench reports ODEX-hard gains of 20.3-40.1 percent RELATIVE (e.g. GPT-3.5-turbo 17.2 to 24.1 with BM25 = +6.9 points = 40.1%), not +20.3 to +40.1 points; DeepSeekCoder-7B no gain on MBPP (60.8 baseline vs 56.4-60.6 with retrieval) is correct; the last sentence about plan libraries is an inference from ReGAL.
fix: Retrieval into the prompt helps most where the model lacks knowledge and little where it already knows: on ODEX-hard (rare libraries) retrieved documents improved results by 20.3 to 40.1 percent relative for most retrievers (GPT-3.5-turbo baseline 17.2, up to 24.1), while DeepSeekCoder-7B did not gain on MBPP (60.8 baseline vs 56.4 to 60.6 with retrieval). With a strong model, a small gain from a plan library on tasks it already solves is expected (ReGAL GPT-3.5 Date +1.3).

problem: NoThinking claim and LiveCodeBench pass@1 exception verified, but the Overthinking paper does not show that more effort lowers agentic scores: o1 high effort is 29.1% at about USD 1,400, single low effort is 21.0% at USD 400, and the 27.3% at 43% lower cost (USD 800) is two low-effort samples with the lowest-overthinking-score selected.
fix: At equal tokens, many cheap samples with a check beat one long thought, except for code at pass@1 (NoThinking: LiveCodeBench pass@1 favors Thinking). Reasoning models already plan inside their thinking, and on SWE-bench Verified selecting the lower-overthinking of two low-effort o1 runs gave 27.3% at USD 800, against 29.1% for one high-effort run at about USD 1,400 (43% less cost; single low effort scored 21.0% at USD 400).

problem: Payoff-minus-cost (EVC) is Shenhav et al.'s theoretical proposal, not a rule shown by the data; Westbrook's results are consistent with it, and the delay-discounting link is modest (R2=0.14, n=33).
fix: Effort-based choice is consistent with a payoff-minus-cost account (EVC theory): in Westbrook et al. 2013 people trade money against n-back load, discounting rises with load, larger offers are discounted less, and effort discounting correlates modestly with delay discounting (B=0.30, P=0.03, R2=0.14, n=33).

problem: Lau 2010 and Alger and Payne 2016 findings were verified only through the Lerner and Gluck review table (secondary); Matorina verified in its preprint.
Evidence line misattributes the 82.5 percent figure to ChatGPT as judge; the 51.3 to 23.8 swing is GPT-4 as judge. The claim itself is unaffected.

Tadros Table 1: SRC is below 0.75 percent rehearsal in three of five columns (e.g. 48.47 vs 79.91) but above it on Inc. CIFAR10 (44.55 vs 39.39) and on the CUB-200 average (63.2/45.4 vs 42.32/51.49), so 'scores below rehearsal' is not general.
fix: In artificial networks, interleaved replay of old items with new ones prevents overwriting, and generative or representation replay beats regularisation: Split MNIST class-IL fine-tune 19.90, EWC 19.90, DGR 91.24, RtF 92.56, upper bound 97.93. Sleep-like replay without stored data (Tadros 2022) raises CUB-200 two-task accuracy from 5/95 to 63.2/45.4, but in its own Table 1 it scores below rehearsal with 0.75% stored data on Inc. MNIST, Fashion MNIST and multi-modal MNIST (e.g. 48.47 vs 79.91), and above it on Inc. CIFAR10 (44.55 vs 39.39).

problem: The R1-32B AIME numbers (55.8 at 12K, 54.9 at 16K; difficulty optima 1.5K and 8K) all come from one arXiv preprint (Zhou 2026, 60 AIME problems, v1) listed twice (c06, c07); the other listed papers (Liu, Sprague) concern chain-of-thought hurting, not token-budget curves.

Self-Refine's roughly 20 percent absolute average gain is real, but it is not specific to 'checkable metrics': its tasks include dialogue, sentiment reversal and constrained generation scored by models or humans, and math reasoning gains were 0 (64.1 to 64.1) without oracle feedback.
fix: Without an external signal, a model critiquing and revising its own answer is flat or worse on reasoning (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after one round; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; Game of 24 5% to 3% with LLM critic). Reported gains come from oracle labels. Self-Refine reports about 20% absolute average gains over seven tasks, but on math reasoning it gained nothing without oracle feedback (64.1 to 64.1), so the effect is task dependent. Gap search (2025 to 2026 models): self-correction gains return when the check is explicit constraints (SAT 34.6 to 65.0 for Mistral Large, 97.0 to 100 for Gemini Pro; right-to-wrong flips up to 13.25 percent on hard reasoning, d16); reasoning models gain only marginally from added correction passes at higher time cost (d17); non-reasoning models fail to fix errors in their own output but fix the same error when shown as external, 64.5 percent blind spot (d15). No matched-token test on open-ended ideas was found.

Dynamic Cheatsheet Table 3 shows Claude 3.5 Haiku gaining +26.7 points on AIME 2024 (10.0 to 36.7), as large as Sonnet's, so gains were not small for Haiku (only GPQA-Diamond and GPT-4o-mini were flat or negative); and ReGAL found the smallest model (CodeLlama-13B) benefited most, the opposite of a gains-shrink-with-weak-models pattern.
fix: Memory gains depend on the base model but do not simply shrink with model size: Dynamic Cheatsheet gains are mixed for GPT-4o-mini (AIME 2024 16.7 to 13.3 under DC-Cu, AIME 2025 10.0 to 16.7 under DC-RS, GPQA-Diamond flat or down) and for Claude 3.5 Haiku are large on AIME (10.0 to 36.7 and 0.0 to 13.3) but flat on GPQA-Diamond except DC-RS (43.4 to 49.0), and minimal or inconsistent for o1 and R1; ReGAL gives its largest gains to the smallest model tested (CodeLlama-13B), though large models also gain; and a memory built by a stronger model does not reliably help a weaker one (Dynamic Cheatsheet). [Gap search: Dynamic Cheatsheet numbers confirmed (30-question AIME sets). Reversal exists: GRASP strong-writer libraries help weaker executors when gated; weak-writer libraries hurt strong ones; 25% of extractor-target pairs are negative in Huang 2026; skill value does not track model size.]

problem: DreamCoder's 3.7 to 79.6 percent includes its recognition network as well as library abstraction, and AWM stores workflows rather than named code primitives; numbers are as stated.

'ReasoningBank reached 46.3 to 56.3' mixes plain ReasoningBank (Claude 46.3) with ReasoningBank plus MaTTS (Gemini-2.5-pro 56.3); plain ReasoningBank spans 46.3 to 53.9. AWM and no-memory figures are exact.
The 2.5x per-query cost saving is stated for about 10 queries per context; the three Lin et al. lines are one paper, so independent support is Lin plus LightMem.

Only ACE contrasts incremental merging with free whole-context rewriting (a single AppWorld case study of context collapse, in a Dynamic Cheatsheet-style rewrite, plus gains over baselines); ExpeL and LightMem are described designs with no head-to-head against free rewrite, so 'works better than free rewrite' rests on one paper.
fix: Incremental edit merging with de-duplication is used in ACE (grow-and-refine: +10.6% agent, +8.6% finance over strong baselines; its context-collapse case study shows free whole-context rewriting destroyed information; dedup threshold effect non-monotone 77.0/73.9/78.6 at 50/70/90%), ExpeL (ADD/EDIT/UPVOTE/DOWNVOTE with removal at zero) and LightMem (append online, merge offline), but only ACE compares against free rewrite.

problem: AWM's gain over whole-example retrieval (Synapse) is on Mind2Web, a web-action task, which contradicts 'but not on action tasks'; the ExpeL split (HotpotQA vs ALFWorld) is the only support for the reasoning versus action contrast.
fix: Abstracting sometimes beats storing whole examples and sometimes does not, depending on the task: AWM beat Synapse's whole-example retrieval on Mind2Web (+5.0 element accuracy, +4.0 step success), and ExpeL insights-only beat retrieval-only on HotpotQA (36% vs 31%) but lost on ALFWorld (50% vs 55%). Mind2Web full-task success stays 1-5%.

A preliminary Lua-function test suggests the collapse depth depends on answer format.

problem: Sweegers 2014, Winocur and Moscovitch 2011, ACE collapse (18,282 to 122 tokens, 66.7 to 57.1 vs 63.7 base) and ExpeL numbers (36/31, 50/55, 37/38) check out, but Schapiro 2017 does not simulate summarising or gist extraction or test its effect on episodic recall; it only shows separate pathways learn regularities and individual episodes.
fix: Keep episodic cases and gist rules as separate stores with separate retrieval: regularity extraction trades detail for gist (Sweegers 2014), the Schapiro 2017 model has separate pathways for regularities and single episodes (it does not test whether summarising harms episode recall), gist is hippocampus-independent while detail is not (Winocur and Moscovitch 2011), and ACE shows full LLM rewriting of a context can destroy information (one case: 18,282 to 122 tokens). [ExpeL numbers rechecked: insights vs retrieve-only HotpotQA 36 vs 31, ALFWorld 50 vs 55, WebShop 37 vs 38. Routing is by the authors' task type; no learned router found.]

problem: All figures check out (HippoRAG +21.3 R@5 on 2Wiki single-step, A-MEM ablation, Stitch 3-4 orders faster, LILO LLM compressor 19.01% valid, similarity vs random mixed), but the headline 'best done with cheap structure, not the model' is wider than the sources: HippoRAG and A-MEM both use an LLM to build their structure, and the claim itself concedes no head-to-head exists.
fix: Overlap finding works better with explicit structure than with an unaided LLM or plain embedding similarity: shared entities (HippoRAG, +21.3 R@5 on 2Wiki single-step, +3 on MuSiQue, below baseline on HotpotQA), linking before editing (A-MEM ablation, though its links use an LLM), and symbolic top-down compression (Stitch, 3-4 orders of magnitude faster than DreamCoder's compressor; an LLM compressor gave valid abstractions only 19.01% of the time in LILO). Caveat: cosine similarity was fooled by shared surface words in LILO and did not reliably beat random example choice. No head-to-head of entity overlap vs embedding vs symbolic compression exists.

problem: Agent KB's +18.7 compares Agent KB at pass@3 (73.9) with the baseline at pass@1 (55.2); like for like it is +6.1 at pass@1 (55.2 to 61.2) and +5.5 at pass@3 (68.5 to 73.9). ExpeL +19 is the full method (retrieval-only is 55 vs ReAct 40, +15). Other figures (Memento +6.7 F1, Sarukkai +16, ReasoningBank +8.3, AWM +12.0, DS-Agent) check out.
fix: Retrieving a few similar solved cases (or distilled strategies) improves LLM agents over no memory in 7 independent agent papers; typical gain is 4 to 19 points on agentic tasks (Memento +6.7 F1 DeepResearcher, ExpeL +19 ALFWorld for the full method and +15 for retrieval-only, Sarukkai +16 ALFWorld, ReasoningBank +8.3 WebArena, AWM +12.0 WebArena, DS-Agent, Agent KB +6.1 GAIA at pass@1 and +5.5 at pass@3 against a matched baseline; its headline +18.7 compares pass@3 with a pass@1 baseline).

problem: Memento's CBR increment on F1 is +3.7 (SimpleQA) to +6.7 (DeepResearcher), with HLE +4.5, so the stated +4.5 to +6.7 leaves out SimpleQA +3.7; planning without CBR (+11.0 to +32.5 F1) and the Dynamic Cheatsheet 23.3 to 36.7 empty-scaffold figures are right.
fix: In Memento, adding CBR gave +3.7 to +6.7 F1 (HLE +4.5, SimpleQA +3.7, DeepResearcher +6.7); planning without CBR gave +11.0 to +32.5 F1 on the same sets. In Dynamic Cheatsheet an empty-memory scaffold already moved Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024 from 23.3 to 36.7 before any cases.

problem: Minor: DS-Agent's 'one case best' is the authors' statement that more cases interfere; OBAM shows the opposite shape for its own region-retrieval (1 case worse than 5, saturating at 5), which the claim already notes.

Minor: 68.80 for CIC-IoT is Xiong's combined (periodic plus history-based) deletion under the coarse judge; history-based alone gave 73.70, periodic alone 78.10, and coarse deletion helped EHRAgent (25.91 to 33.55), so 'noisy deletion judge hurt' is one cherry-picked cell. The 300 are described as correct judge data points.

Minor: the 63.1 vs 80.7 figure is from Shi 2023 irrelevant sentences inserted into math problems (code-davinci-002), applied here by analogy to retrieved cases; Hu 2026 -26.1 is one ALFWorld transfer pair (n=46 hard items).
Minor: all three method comparisons come from one ReasoningBank ablation (WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash), so 'only when' generalises from one benchmark; Synapse also gained slightly (+1.1).
Minor: the ExpeL 59.0 row is the full method (insights plus task-similarity retrieval); the ablation compares retrieval rankings within ExpeL.

Minor: Min 2022 (random labels cost 0-5%, avg 2.6% classification / 1.7% multi-choice) and Agarwal 2024 are about in-context demonstrations on classification/math, so applying them to retrieved agent cases is an inference; KATE shows similar examples still beat random by a wide margin, so priming is only part of the gain.

Minor: Xiong's fixed-memory baseline is a subset of training runs with correct execution, not described as human-curated (only the strict filter is human-evaluated); Aha 1991 IB2 vs IB3 numbers match Table 6.

The +10.9 (DDXPlus) and +1.9 (CaseHOLD) are Self-StreamICL's gains over zero-shot on Claude Sonnet 4 (0.862 vs 0.753; 0.807 vs 0.788), not OBAM's; OBAM's gains over zero-shot are +16.6 and +3.7. Dynamic Cheatsheet figures and Mallen's 5.3-point adaptive-retrieval gain check out.
fix: Memory benefits depend on model strength: Dynamic Cheatsheet gains are large for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o on some tasks, none or harm on others (GPT-4o MMLU-Pro Eng 53.2 to 44.0; Claude 3.5 Haiku AIME 2025 no gain over empty scaffold); smaller models cannot curate memory. Gap search: Mallen 2023 adaptive retrieval (retrieve only below a popularity threshold) beat always retrieving by 5.3 points, and plain retrieve-similar-cases memory (Self-StreamICL in the OBAM paper, Claude Sonnet 4) gains +10.9 over zero-shot on DDXPlus (weak zero-shot, 0.753) but only +1.9 on CaseHOLD (strong, 0.788).

problem: Minor: Reflexion's unit tests for HumanEval/MBPP are self-generated by the model, with execution as the external signal, which is why the false-positive rate matters; Kamoi 2024 was not re-read beyond its stated findings.

Minor: Yasunaga's 'self-generated' exemplars are model-recalled and unverified, while Sarukkai's are environment-verified successful runs, so the two sources show different things; davinci-002 is a tie (48 vs 47) and only davinci-003 clearly favours self-generation (61 vs 57).

Minor: figures match the 2021 lab preprint (depth slope 0.25477 +- 0.06056; mobile 1,000 users slope 0.010814 +- 0.001004; N=30 learning, 30 time pressure) and the published Callaway paper (Exp N = 95, 298, 291, 93, though the published numbering puts 291 in Exp 3 and 93 in Exp 4, the reverse of the evidence line); 'close to a best-first rule whose strategy shifts' compresses the paper's finding that people are close to the optimal metalevel policy and adapt between breadth-first, best-first and depth-first.

Minor: Gentner 1993 Exp 3 (52% vs 7%) and Kubricht 2015 (55/50/81%, chi-square 6.60) match; Catrambone and Holyoak 1989 could not be downloaded (host unreachable), so the 10-30% range was checked only against its abstract (transfer needs comparison of analogues) and the benchmarks restated in Kubricht (about 10% unaided, about 30% with a dissimilar story).

Paper says AnglEBERT k=3 is significant at 95% against both No-RAG and hybrid LegalBERT k=3 (and 90% vs hybrid BERT k=1), not 'only against no-RAG'; other numbers (0.8967, 0.9141, 1.94%, 32 cases, authors attribute high no-RAG score to parametric memory) match.
fix: Retrieval-only case use (CBR-RAG) gives small gains where the base model already has parametric legal knowledge: +1.94% cosine (0.8967 to 0.9141, Mistral-7B), 32 test cases; the best setting is significant at 95% against No-RAG and hybrid LegalBERT k=3, and at 90% against hybrid BERT k=1.

problem: Numbers all match Gentner Rattermann Forbus 1993 (soundness 4.40/2.80/2.74, retrieval .78/.44/.25, r(52)=.15, three-study .78/.53/.52 vs .44/.12/.07); evidence is one paper (plus a same-lab review).

Numbers match Gentner Loewenstein Thompson 2003 (47% vs 6% N=48; 48% vs 19% N=128; 90/70/55/37 face-to-face); the 47% is guided-analogy training, not plain side-by-side comparison, and both sources share authors.
3 of 16 (19%) used the tradeoff principle, 2 before and 1 after a recall question; the 10% Duncker figure is second-hand as stated.

Kapoor (no significant difference, Reflexion/LDB >50% more, LATS >50x), Olausson (marginal or no gain at equal tokens) and Stechly (15 samples ~40%, comparable to all feedback types) all check out; Stechly's 15-sample arm had no feedback and the sound verifier only scored it.
Olausson 33.30% vs 52.60% and Tyen gains (18.04 to 43.92 true location, 5.16 to 21.57 random) and Stechly's null on feedback informativeness all match; 'random 5 to 21' rounds 21.57 down.
Bertsch (51.5 to 4.9 points on Banking-77), Agarwal (MATH500 peak ~125 shots then decline) and OBAM (K1 saturates at 5) all match; the claim already flags the scope limit.
Stevenson et al. table matches (adults .88/.91/.89, children .62/.66/.67, GPT-4o .85/.63/.48, Llama-405B .79/.74/.27 for Latin/Greek/Symbol).

Webb (letter strings OR=1.76, p=6.3e-5), Lewis and Mitchell (humans .753, GPT-3 .488, GPT-3.5 .350, GPT-4 .452 over counterfactual sets; Table 2 text garbled but order consistent) and Hodel and West all agree.

56.75% is the ARC-Potpourri ensemble (TTT+reranking), not ARC-Heavy; on ARC-Potpourri the best single method is 43.00% (transduction TTT+reranking), and on ARC-Heavy the ensemble is 43.25% vs 30.50% best single (induction); the 43.25% in the claim is the ARC-Heavy ensemble, not a best single.
fix: Induction (program) and transduction (direct output) solve different tasks, with solved sets stable across seeds; ensembling beats either: on ARC-Potpourri validation the BARC ensemble reaches 56.75% vs 43.00% for the best single method (transduction with TTT and reranking), and on ARC-Heavy 43.25% vs 30.50% for the best single (induction).

problem: Akyurek: 18.3 to 47.1, 53.0 on BARC base, 61.9 ensemble, 47.5 semi-private; Franzen: 71.6 on public eval with PoE and DFS on a different (NeMo-Minitron-8B) pipeline; paper itself is inconsistent about validation vs public eval naming.

All figures check (MADIL ~7% ArcPrize 2024, CompressARC 20% eval, Icecuber 20% Kaggle 2020 / 17% semi-private, BARC ensemble 56.75%, Akyurek 61.9% which builds on BARC models, PoE 71.6%), but they come from different splits (private, semi-private, public eval) so the comparison is not like for like.
MADIL 57 of 69 (82%), BARC ~9% false positives and CompressARC 20% vs U-Net 0.75% all match; the BARC and U-Net figures do not test length-based selection, which the claim's caveat already says.
MADIL (21 generalisation failures, cause spurious expressions rising with fewer examples and larger expressions), Ferre 2021 (train-test gap 7 to 12 tasks across v2.x), BARC (~9%) all match.

MADIL lists missing conditionals and recursion as a limit and has 21 of 62 search failures needing non-compressive steps; CompressARC Appendix H lists the cannot-do abilities, compiled from observed puzzles (illustrative, not a controlled test).

Numbers match (Icecuber 17.0 to 1.6, o3 medium 53.0 to 3.0, ARChitects 56.0 to 2.5; pooled 2020 entries 49%), but only Icecuber is a brute-force DSL search system; o3 and ARChitects are LLM-based, so the sentence 'search-over-DSL approaches collapse' is wider than the evidence.
fix: On ARC-AGI-2 the 2020 brute-force program-search winner Icecuber fell from 17.0% (ARC-AGI-1 semi-private) to 1.6%, and the LLM-based systems fell as well (o3 medium 53.0% to 3.0%, ARChitects 56.0% to 2.5%); ARC-AGI-2 was designed to be less brute-forcible, and the pooled 2020 Kaggle entries solved 49% of the private ARC-AGI-1 set.

problem: Forbus et al. 2017 gives O(n^2 log n) and the 52 of 56 (93%) figure, but it is a 1990 test (Forbus and Oblinger) of a simple early version of greedy merge, not the current multi-mapping version; the two cited SME sources are the same paper and the SMTB paper does not report it.
fix: SME's greedy merge keeps mapping construction polynomial (O(n^2 log n)); in an early 1990 test of a simple version of greedy merge on 56 analogies, it produced the same best mapping as exhaustive merge in 52 (93%), and failed in 4 where many large kernels conflicted (reported in Forbus et al. 2017).

problem: H-ARC (76.2% train n=784, 64.2% eval n=948, 98.8% coverage) and Johnson 2021 (83.8% on 40 tasks, description length b=-0.17, p=0.03) match; the description-length effect comes from the 2021 paper, not H-ARC.

Moghe and Chin (DeepSeek V3.2, training-pair-score selection ~95% of the 5-candidate ceiling) and Land (167 instances, 22 no correct candidate, 17 correct but not picked) match; Land notes an internal 21/22 inconsistency, and selection there is among all candidates, not only those fitting every training pair.

Land: judge solved 7 more than majority vote, all minority recoveries (computed post hoc on the same pool), 12 and 8 agreeing wrong outputs vs 1 correct; Moghe and Chin dedup by test output; SOAR 9.5 point majority-vote vs oracle gap, all as stated.

SOAR (filter programs whose outputs appear as literals) and Hourglass (anti-patching, no colour special cases in prompts) match, but Moghe and Chin do not require all training pairs exact; they rank by partial training exact-match score (full accuracy is only an exit condition) and dedup by test output.
fix: Guards against fit-but-wrong in LLM programs that are in use (the existence of the guards is established; their effect is not): filter programs whose training outputs appear as literals in the code (SOAR); forbid colour-keyed special cases and if-else patches in repair prompts (Hourglass); rank candidates by training-pair exact-match score and dedup by predicted test output (Moghe and Chin). None is ablated alone, so effect sizes are unknown.

problem: Lopez de Mantaras review (utility problem, Minton, Smyth and Cunningham critical case-base size), Agarwal (MATH500 peak ~125) and OBAM match; Dynamic Cheatsheet text says GPT-4o full-history fell to 6.7 vs 20.0 baseline but its Table 2 shows 13.3, an inconsistency inside the paper.

Mallen 10% (right alone, wrong with retrieval), Hu 2026 Raw memory -26.1 points on ALFWorld baseline-fail instances, Dynamic Cheatsheet GPT-4o MMLU-Pro Engineering 53.2 to 44.0 (DC-Cu is 'cumulative' memory in the paper) and Yoran (random passages cut accuracy by >10 points on average) all match.

Webb numbers (OR=0.37 p=.0003; GPT-3 far p=.065; GPT-4 far two-sided binomial p=.0039) are right, but p=.0039 corresponds to 27 of 36 correct (18 stories x 2 orders; Lewis and Mitchell list Webb's GPT-4 total as 27/36), not 8 of 8 (8/8 two-sided is .0078); also the r=-.032 in Inani et al. is between humans and a BERT sentence-embedding model, not LLM errors.
fix: On the Gentner et al. 1993 story analogies, GPT-3 was worse than students (OR=.37, p=.0003; far analogy not above chance, p=.065), while GPT-4 reached significance on far (27 of 36 comparisons, two-sided binomial p=.0039); GPT-4 is correct more often when the right answer is listed first (Lewis and Mitchell: 1.00 vs .72). Item-level work (Inani et al.) finds a BERT embedding model's item difficulty does not track human difficulty (r=-.03, p=.899).

problem: Lovett and Forbus 2017: 56/60 = 75th percentile (1993 norms), college sample 54/60 = 61st percentile, regressions .63 and .67; the 41st percentile figure belongs to a different (50/60) model.

UoT, BED-LLM, Kobalczyk, Piriyakulkij and Handa mostly show information-driven questioning beating prompted questions, but in these systems the LLM also supplies the answer likelihoods or probabilities that EIG is computed from (BED-LLM uses LLM predictive probabilities; Kobalczyk EIG-logprobs did worse than plain prompting in some models), and the gain is not universal (GPT-4o-mini HumanEval binary +1.9 within noise; BED-LLM below baseline on Qwen-14B Animals).
fix: Choosing questions by an expected-information-gain criterion (with the LLM proposing candidate questions and supplying the answer probabilities the criterion is computed from) usually beats letting the model pick its own question in 20 Questions, diagnosis, code clarification and preference elicitation, but the gain shrinks or disappears for stronger models and depends on how EIG is estimated.

problem: UoT +38.1% (5 datasets, 5 LLMs), BED-LLM +37.4 points (paper's own average; Table 1 rows average closer to 40 by one reading) and Kobalczyk HumanEval/APPS round-4 gains (about +8 to +15 for weaker models) match; the '3 repeats' applies only to UoT's significance test on Llama3 and GPT-4, not all 25 settings.

Kobalczyk GPT-4o-mini gap (79.6 vs 81.5, SE about 2), UoT open-set cells (12.5 to 15.0, 34.2 to 36.9), Hartmann (14B +4.2 and +1.8, BED-LLM 26.4 vs 35.0) and MedClarify (+2.3, +7.8, +4.9) all match, but the budget-control paper says VOI gains are smaller 'in some cells' on GPT-5.4-Mini than Qwen3-32B, not overall, and the Hartmann reward is EIG plus an outcome term.
fix: The gain shrinks or vanishes with stronger models and in open-ended settings: GPT-4o-mini HumanEval binary gap 1.9 points (about 1 standard error); several UoT open-set cells under 3 points; an EIG-plus-outcome-reward-trained questioner gave about x2 on Qwen2.5-7B but +4.2 and +1.8 points on 14B, and inference-time BED-LLM fell below the 14B baseline on Animals (26.4 vs 35.0); MedClarify gained +2.3 on GPT-5.1 versus +7.8 on DeepSeek-R1 and +4.9 on Llama-3.3-70B; the budget-control VOI gain was smaller in some cells on GPT-5.4-Mini than on Qwen3-32B.

problem: Kobalczyk round-10 20Q scores (EIG-uniform best; EIG-logprobs below implicit for GPT-3.5 and Llama3-70B but above for GPT-4o-mini) and BED-LLM GPT-4o Celebrities 86 vs 64 match; the BED-LLM 'Entropy' ablation keeps filtering and swaps EIG for predictive entropy.

Heath et al. concern EVPPI (not EVPI): the 55-minute figure is nested Monte Carlo for a single-parameter EVPPI versus seconds for GP/GAM; the upward-bias remark is about the Strong-Oakley subset method; failure with correlated inputs applies to the restrictive linear/independence shortcuts, GAM is unstable for 6+ parameters and GP slows with more parameters.
fix: Estimating value of information costs compute and is biased: nested Monte Carlo EVPPI took about 55 minutes for one single-parameter estimate versus seconds for GP/GAM regression; nested Monte Carlo EIG estimators are biased for any finite inner sample size (Rainforth); the fast shortcuts are restricted (independence/linearity assumptions deteriorate with correlated inputs, GAM is unstable for larger parameter subsets, GP cost grows with parameters).

problem: Mazzaccara BigBench row (DPO, different-size set): success 17.2 to 31.0, EIG 0.31 to 0.28 as stated; STaR-GATE reports improved elicitation.

Numbers match (Hase Table 4: 0.97 to 0.01, MAE 0.34 to 0.59, on a synthetic-world model; Cohen ICE beats ROME by >10 (GPT-Neo) and 29 (LLaMA); MeLLo 85.5-91.1 on MQuAKE-T holds only for GPT-3.5, GPT-J/Vicuna are much lower).
Ishay and Lee average 54.6 to 78.0 with revisions; Huang Table 3 numbers (GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 at round 2/5 calls; GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8) match.

SEP names the postulates DP1-DP4 (C1-C4 in the original); Booth and Meyer state lexicographic is least and restrained most conservative among admissible operators; the arXiv and JAIR entries are one paper and the two Aravanis entries are one paper.

Only one agent-memory system (Park's Kumiho) is shown rejecting Recovery on purpose, not several 'builders'; Chowdhury adopts AGM-style postulates and disclaims a representation theorem, which fits 'keep the postulates, drop the machinery' but is a single paper.
fix: Belief bases (finite stated lists) with Relevance replace closed sets plus Recovery in practice (SEP); at least one agent-memory system (Kumiho) rejects Recovery on purpose, and a recent agent paper (Chowdhury 2026) keeps AGM-style postulates but claims no representation theorem.

problem: Walsh and Johnson-Laird 17 of 20 (p<.01) and Vasileiou 83.37/85.51/67.16 percent non-minimal (N=62/60/60) verified; Elio and Pelletier verified from abstract/record only (full text not opened).

UoT has only computational-cost mentions (no per-question cost term); Kobalczyk defines U(q)=EIG(q)-c(q) but assumes query cost negligible and selects by estimated EIG; Rainforth frames EIG as information-based utility. The pairing advice is a design suggestion, not sourced.

Kirkpatrick and Sterken: 6 of 8 patterns r<-0.6 between defeasible and deductive accuracy; Leidinger et al.: agreement with generics falls below 50 percent with irrelevant exemplars for Llama-2, Mistral and Mixtral. 'Near-universals' is an interpretation.

bAbI 80.34 to 99.99, MultiLogicNMR 59.0/52.9 to 90.5/81.0 and SMT 35.8/35.0 verified; LOGicalThought +5.5 percent is 'up to', versus the strongest baseline (abstract only); the Yang/Lee and Ishay/Lee overlap is correctly noted.

RaM PDF abstract says 23-45 percent fewer tokens (arXiv abs-page summary showed a different range, likely another version); Adaptive-Consistency average 3.3x fewer samples with under 0.1 percent drop (up to 7.9x); ESC 34-84 percent verified. RaM listed twice (one paper).

Huang oracle table (75.9 to 84.3; 49.0 to 59.0), Olausson (1.05x with 10+1 allocation, 0.97x with 2+10 allocation; human feedback 33.3 to 52.6 percent) and Li 2026 (hints lower correction for GPT-3.5 and Claude, not DeepSeek) all verified.

Mukherjee et al. abstract reports premise-augmented step verification improving error identification by 6 to 16 percent absolute, not 3 to 14 points; other figures (TransCoder 80.4/77.3 to 91.6/88.8, 33.3 to 52.6, 26.8 to 15.5, 29.1 to 12.8, DeFA 48.9-52.7 and 17.2) check out.
fix: Error location is the limit on revision, and real execution output is what supplies it. Unit-test feedback lifted TransCoder 80.4 to 91.6 (Codex) and 77.3 to 88.8 (GPT-4); a human-written diagnosis lifted GPT-4 repair success from 33.3% to 52.6%; model-made hints lowered correction in 2 of 3 models (26.8 to 15.5, 29.1 to 12.8). Locating the faulty step in a long agent trace is hard: 48.9 to 52.7% exact on Who&When, 17.2% on trajectories of 33 to 130 steps; premise links raise step error identification by 6 to 16 points absolute.

problem: Belief-R Llama-3 70B update 10.99 vs maintain 92.09 and DeReLab GPT-5.1 3.5 percent / gap 0.935 / OR 891 / intrusion 0.9 and 0.3 percent verified; 'small models 15 to 36' includes the 70B Llama (15.2) alongside the 8B (36.2); Belief-R 'near 0 to 35' is approximate (some open models reach 44 with PS prompting).
Xie et al. (coherent generated counter-memory accepted, entity-substitution counter-memory resisted) and DeReLab (17 of 19 cells significant) verified.

Xie et al.: models favor parametric memory when both are present, stronger for popular entities, and order-sensitive (Llama2-7B PopQA 33.3 vs 82.8 memorization ratio); counter-evidence alone accepted when coherent. DeReLab only supports the general confirmation-bias point.

Numbers verified (Ma: yielding 17.1-73.6, updating 53.7-64.1, Llama-3.1 EX-FEVER -32.9 vs -48.9/-53.7; Shapira: r=0.87 frontier and 0.90 open, Opus 5 21 vs Sonnet 5 78); but the trade-off is 'often' not always (Ma's orthogonalized steering gave modest selectivity gains, and the -32.9/-48.9..-53.7 figures are one Llama-3.1 EX-FEVER case), and 'discrimination should sit in the scaffold, not the weights' is the researcher's inference, not a finding; the sources call for mitigations that decouple the two behaviors.
fix: Pressure-driven flipping and evidence-driven updating share internal parts, so suppressing one by training or steering often damages the other. In four 3B to 8B models yielding to unsupported pushback was 17.1 to 73.6% and updating on valid evidence 53.7 to 64.1%; in one case (Llama-3.1, EX-FEVER) anti-pressure DPO cut yielding 32.9 points but cut rational updating 48.9 to 53.7 points; the correlation between sycophancy reduction and source-updating reduction was r=0.87 on four frontier 2026 models and 0.90 on open models. Source label and stated reliability change adoption (Claude Opus 5 vs Sonnet 5: 21% vs 78% user-claim adoption). The sources call for mitigations that decouple the two behaviors; placing the discrimination in the scaffold is a design inference, not a finding.

problem: Byrne 96/96/38 and Dieussaert 88/93/60 confirmed in Dietz Saldanha and Kakas; Trehan et al. open-answer MP 100/100/40 (N=10) confirmed; 'answer format and sample drive the size' is an interpretation; Schroyens PMC page not opened.

Knauff: uncertain responses more often cite counterexamples than probabilities; the .187 vs .325 figures are in Schroyens et al. (a raw proportion difference labelled d, many vs few counterexamples), not in Knauff, and are not Cohen's d.

AR-BED shows reasoning lowered final solve rate in every category, but only for one small base model (Gemma-4-E4B); QuestBench's 'not sure' rates (1.4, 4.6, 0.7 percent vs 41.8 true) are for Gemini Flash Thinking, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o in the zero-shot no-CoT setting, not o1-preview, and do not compare reasoning on versus off.
fix: Turning on reasoning in the base model did not make it a better questioner in AR-BED (Gemma-4-E4B base: final 20 Questions solve rate fell in every category with reasoning on). In QuestBench, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o said 'not sure' on only 1.4%, 4.6% and 0.7% of Planning-Q cases (zero-shot, no chain of thought) where the true rate was 41.8%. Evidence is from one small reasoning base model and 2024-25 frontier models; Gemini 2.5 Pro appears only in qualitative traces; no clean test with 2026 frontier reasoning models.

problem: MediQ: 11.3% relative drop BASIC vs Initial and +22.3% from best abstention over BASIC verified in full text; Dong et al. describes inverted-U Fixed Round curves (the arXiv abs page of MediQ alone does not show 11.3).

Qiu et al. (off-the-shelf LLMs fall far short of Bayesian updating), Dong et al. (models reasonably calibrated in animal game, less so in medical diagnosis, argmax-based) and Krishnamurthy et al. (only GPT-4 with CoT and externally summarized history explored well) verified.

Zhang et al.: terminal verifier rejects 61% of oracle-invalid and withholds 17% of correct episodes at under one cent, planning vs release gain flips with liability; Dong et al. Appendix A case study (reward 10 vs reward 1, c=0.05) shows the VoI agent asking longer in the high-stakes task (single qualitative example).

AC 7.9x/under 0.1% (average), ESC -33.8% to -84.2%, CGES 16.0 to 6.7 calls (-58%) at -0.4pp and GPQA failing to save, Certified SC 61-86 of 100 (MATH-500, small Qwen models), CoT-PoT 9.3x and 78.6% in two all verified; the 'none compares to an EVPI/c stop' statement is an absence claim not checkable here.

SEP (Hansson) covers closed belief sets/logical omniscience as an idealisation, the Levi identity, and the need for selection functions or entrenchment; Almeida and Casals survey independently states the same points (Levi identity, logical omniscience, selection function/entrenchment). The five SEP entries are one source.

Kirkpatrick and Sterken (0.99 for aBDRdc/aBDRdd, 0.43-0.54 and -0.05 for others), DeReLab (Gemma-4-31B 0.970 to 0.264 with reversed order) and Jhang (reporting lowers movement significantly in six of seven configurations by 2-5 points) verified.

Zeng and Zhang: error up 46.20 / down 30.28 / unchanged 23.52 percent, anti-anchoring cut prior-directed shift but not error (it raised error; tested on Qwen3-8B only), evidence-validation rule traded coverage for reliability; DERELAB only corroborates anchoring generally (anchoring rates 0.43-0.48 for GPT-5.1 and Qwen3-32B).

Laban et al. (FlipFlop): ten LLMs, seven tasks, flip 46 percent of the time, average accuracy drop 17 percent, verified; BeliefScope corroborates that pressure and evidence both move outputs. The closing sentence is a prescriptive conclusion.

DERELAB (GPT-5-mini C2-eff 95.4 vs C2 acc 20.3) and STALE (Qwen3.5-27B Type I SR 76.0 vs IPA 39.0) verified; 'premise resistance mostly under 5 percent' holds for most systems but not all (Gemini-3.1-pro reaches 30.0 on Type I PR).

DeltaLogic numbers match (Qwen3-1.7B 0.667/0.467/0.600 n=30; Qwen3-4B 0.650/0.450/0.600 n=20; Phi-4-mini 0.950/0.850; the four DeltaLogic entries are one paper); DERELAB (anchoring), STALE (outdated-memory failures) and BeliefShift (models miss legitimate updates) corroborate; ClawArena not opened.

Minor: circumscription gives a disjunction rather than multiple extensions, and Reiter default logic itself has no specificity priority (SEP); claim's 'families agree' is slightly broad but supported by SEP/McCarthy.
Figures are easy-split intrusion rates (GPT-5.1 hard 1.2, Qwen3-32B thinking hard 2.6); DeltaLogic n is only 20-30 episodes per model.

Minor: FlipFlop reports '17%' average accuracy drop (taken as points); Simpson et al. note an April replication drifted (89.7 to 98.5 percent), and the 7-to-4 / 20 false positive result is from a single model and 68 scenarios.
The 'about 60 main schemes' figure is not in the three listed sources (SEP gives 96); it comes from Visser et al. 2021 in another claim. Pinto/Kock caveat that CQs often cannot shift burden.

Minor: tuning claim is a one-sentence remark (results not shown, and the paper elsewhere says no prompt tuning was done); the 67.6 is a manual evaluation of the best submission whose automatic score was 50.0; shared-task overview shares authors with the benchmark paper.

Both numbers match, but the 39.44 percent post-edits were mostly grammatical fixes (verb forms, plurals, double negations), not content repairs; the 68.28 to 72.22 result is one validation ablation where about 75 percent of labels were LLM-made.

LLM F1 0.65 is the best on the 7-scheme EthiX set only (Claude 3.5 few-shot reaches 0.72 on the 4-scheme EthiX4); and on QT30 1.0 is plain RoBERTa while 44.8 is the best of four training variants, so '1.0 to 44.8' is a range across configurations, not a drop.
fix: Scheme classification: trained annotators agree substantially (kappa 0.723 on a 10.2 percent sample for Walton schemes, 0.61 for the full guideline set); the best LLM reaches F1 0.65 on 686 real Kialo arguments over 7 schemes (0.72 on a 4-scheme subset); the same LLMs score 0.98-0.99 on machine-written textbook arguments; and a scheme classifier that scores 99.2 F1 on textbook text gets only 1.0 on real QT30 dialogue, rising to 44.8 with scheme families and dialogue training. Cause to effect and expert opinion are the most misclassified schemes.

problem: Minor: 'does not transfer' is slightly loose, since plain RoBERTa gets 1.0 F1 on QT30 and the best variant (scheme families plus dialogue data) reaches 44.8; 89.1 percent is NLAS-CQ (GPT-generated) while EN 74.8 percent is NLAS-multi, and NLAS-multi Spanish kappa was only 0.22.
Numbers match; GPT-judged MT-Bench with 5 models and ArgMed with 300 items per set; the 'no token-matched best-of-N comparison' part is an absence claim that cannot be checked from these papers.
Minor: Stechly Blocksworld shows LLM critique helping (40 to 55), so 'does not help' holds on most but not all domains; 8-87 is the sound first-error-feedback column.

Huang et al. say debate with 3 responses is slightly BETTER than self-consistency at 3 responses (SC 82.5); debate only falls below SC at equal counts of 6 and 9 (debate 83.2 and 83.0 vs SC 85.3 and 88.2).
fix: At equal calls or tokens, majority voting over samples matches or beats model-run critique and debate, except at large budgets: on GSM8K (GPT-3.5) self-consistency scores 82.5, 85.3 and 88.2 at 3, 6 and 9 responses, debate is only slightly better at 3 responses and clearly below at 6 and 9 (83.2, 83.0); a fine-tuned generative verifier needed about 8x compute to match self-consistency and 128x to gain 3.8 points on MATH; sampling with a sound verifier and no critique text kept most of the gain of critique with a sound verifier.

problem: Actual-persuasiveness half rests on one 2001 experiment (324 readers, one claim about a cultural centre) from the Nijmegen group that also supplied the comparison data for Hornikx 2008; Hornikx concludes expectations are 'generally accurate', so 'only partly match' leans on Hoeken alone.
fix: In one experiment (324 readers, one claim), statistical evidence persuaded more than anecdotal or causal evidence, which were equally unconvincing; lay people rank expected persuasiveness statistical > expert > causal > anecdotal and in a comparison with an earlier study from the same group these expectations were generally accurate, although in the 2001 experiment perceived (causal over anecdotal) and actual persuasiveness did not correspond.

problem: Minor: Lou and Sun test mostly GPT-4/GPT-4o (GPT-3.5 varied), and SynAnchors reports one method (Anti-DP) that lowers Llama anchoring 34.7 to 24.7, so 'fail' means simple prompt strategies.

SACD's own tables show self-help rewriting is no better than (finance 0.1885 vs vanilla 0.1648) or worse than (legal 0.4590 vs 0.3840) plain prompting, and weaker on small models; only GPT-4 BiasBuster and the iterated SACD loop reliably cut bias.
fix: Rewriting the biasing text with a model-run loop cuts measured bias when the cue is planted in the text: the iterated SACD loop beat vanilla, CoT and self-help in every domain by its third round, and one-pass self-help worked on GPT-4 (framing gap -0.405 to -0.010) and gpt-4o but was no better than or worse than vanilla prompting in the finance and legal domains and on small models.

problem: Minor: Huang et al. is the direct evidence (oracle GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CSQA 75.8 to 89.7); the other listed sources are anchoring studies where reflection or self-improving prompts did not help, which is looser support for 'accuracy'.

Minor: Wang et al. report 9.8% and 14.3% accuracy gain in human alignment (not necessarily points); math grading figures are 14/20 to 3/20 on 10 questions with swapped positions; the 2026 gap numbers match Kumar et al. Table 2.

BiasBuster says few-shot 'can lead to failure cases' for some biases and models (Llama-2-7b contrastive admit rates 0.996/1.000), not 'often'; Itzhak et al. only find that same-task examples reduce bias less than format-only examples (they do not show the examples carry the bias), and format few-shot slightly lowered bias in most models.
fix: Few-shot debiasing exemplars can break some models (Llama-2-7b answers collapsing to nearly all-admit or all-reject on several BiasBuster setups), gave no gain for GPT-4 framing, and scored poorly against other methods in SACD; examples taken from the same task reduced bias less than format-only examples in Itzhak et al.

problem: Hagendorff et al.'s 96 percent (GPT-4) is on 50 bespoke, newly written CRT-style tasks per type, not just the famous items, and training exposure is the authors' speculation; the evidence that perturbed items still expose errors is only Binz and Schulz on GPT-3 (adversarial vignettes), not frontier models. The three Hagendorff entries are one paper.
fix: On newly written CRT-style tasks ChatGPT-4 answers 96 percent correctly (ChatGPT-3.5 59, GPT-3 davinci-003 5), which the authors tentatively attribute to training on CRT-like tasks; in older GPT-3, the original CRT items were all answered intuitively wrong and adversarially altered vignettes produced non-human errors (Binz and Schulz), but no source shows perturbed items still trapping frontier models.

problem: Sources show presence of biases, not human-like size: ChatGPT anchoring gap was 85 (20.83 vs 105.97) versus 58 for humans (22.5 vs 80.5), SynAnchors say most LLMs are the same as or worse than humans, and Malberg et al. find some effects (status quo, disposition) opposite to humans; Jones and Steinhardt show accuracy loss from anchoring lines in code, not a human-comparable size.
fix: LLMs show anchoring, framing, availability and related effects on many tasks, including code generation, but the size differs from humans (e.g. GPT-3.5 anchoring gap about 85 vs 58 for humans in one small study) and some biases such as status quo and disposition effect run opposite to the human direction.

problem: Croskerry et al. say awareness 'does not guarantee' debiasing and the field has been gloomy, and list feedback and educational tools, but neither paper tests telling people to be fair or unbiased, nor shows practice with feedback and task redesign 'work better'; Sellier et al. is a primary study (one-shot game training, 29 percent fewer confirming choices), not a secondary source.
fix: Secondary reviews say that raising awareness of bias does not by itself guarantee debiasing, while training with feedback (for example game-based training, which in one field study cut a confirmation-biased choice by 29 percent) and supportive environments are proposed as stronger routes; no source tested 'be fair or unbiased' instructions directly.

problem: The review does not find 'little evidence' of effect: it finds few studies (12 of 52 screened tested retention of at least 14 days, 1 tested far transfer) and most of those reported retained benefit, especially for games over videos; Sellier et al. report transfer (29 percent fewer confirming choices). Willingham is off-topic for debiasing training.
fix: A systematic review of debiasing studies found only 12 of 52 screened studies that tested retention (14 days or more) and just 1 that tested far transfer; most retention studies showed lasting benefit, mainly for game-based training, and the single transfer study (Sellier et al. 2019) found trained participants 29 percent less likely to make the confirmation-biased choice, so evidence is thin rather than negative.

problem: Both usable sources are by Willingham (2007 and 2016) and the 2016 brief repeats the 2007 argument; the third listed source (Sellier et al.) does not address critical-thinking programmes; no effect sizes are given for 'mostly ineffective'.
fix: Willingham (2007, 2016) argues, without citing effect sizes, that critical thinking is not a general skill that transfers across domains, that domain knowledge and practice decide performance, and that the programmes sold after 1983 were not very effective.

problem: Minor: figures are from the Kumar et al. audit (6 judges, 4 datasets); the 7-17 percent replication figure is the paper's range across cells.

Minor: Langley 1977 notes BACON uses a programmer-specified artificial world and cannot handle noise; the 'sufficiency not history' caveat is the claim's own interpretation, not stated in those papers.

Minor: 'recalled, not discovered' is the authors' inference (they write 'suggest'); LLM-SR and LLM-SRBench are the same lab; SR-Scientist's 'nearly 50 percent reached sufficiently small error' is not the same as solved, and it sits in tension with LLM-SRBench calling LSR-Transform hard.

Minor: the 2.1-7.2 vs 10.8-31.5 symbolic accuracy figures all come from one paper (LLM-SRBench, Table 1); LLM-SR also differs from direct prompting by more than the loop (program skeleton, buffer), so it is not a clean loop-only ablation.
Minor: ablation is one problem (Oscillation 2) with one backbone (GPT-3.5); Ma et al. imaginary-law test confirmed in Table 4; both sources are different labs.
Laird text names three types, glossary four; claim lists four, fine. Evidence a01/a02/a19/b06 are the same paper (one source), but the manual independently supports the substate/chunk mechanism.
1986 paper (full text) and Laird 2022 support; Soar Manual notes EBBS (9.6) replaced old chunking for over-specialization, so implicit-generalization is the classic mechanism; minor.

All numbers match Tambe, Newell & Rosenbloom 1990 Table 1 (total speedups 0.99/0.32/0.85/0.25; 25x), but every supporting evidence line is that single paper (the Dynamic Cheatsheet line does not bear on the claim); only one independent source.

Numbers match SkillsBench (87 tasks, 18 configs, 9,396 trajectories, 33.9->50.5) and Xu & Wu (curated +36.0 GPT-5.5, +24.7 DeepSeek). The replication is on a subset of the same benchmark by different authors.

52%/46% are right (Chen et al. 2026, ReasoningBank, position 200 of compound drift), but 29.8%->11.2% is GEPA's clarification rate on BFCL-Miss after the BFCL-Base block (119/400 to 45/400), not a pass/accuracy rate on BFCL-Base, and it is a rewriting-interference result, not a retrieval collision.
fix: Retrieval memories collide: similar queries needing different workflows pull foreign items (at position 200 of a compound stream, 52% of BFCL-Miss and 46% of BFCL-Base episodes retrieve a memory from the opposite workflow); separately, a prompt-rewriting method (GEPA) cut its clarification rate on BFCL-Miss from 29.8% to 11.2% after training on BFCL-Base, losing earlier-learned behaviour.

problem: Kirk et al. 2022 (54%, 30-40%) and Kirk/Wray/Laird 2023 (>70% not viable) verified; both are the same Soar group, so the 'later position paper' is not independent of the first, but the claim itself says so.

ADaPT and GraSP numbers are real, but ADaPT vs Reflexion differs in recursive planner decomposition, not only retry scope (authors only hypothesise the cause), and the GraSP 79.7 is the partial '+Local Repair' ablation row, whereas the matched comparison is full GraSP 80.6 vs global replan 77.4.
fix: Scoped retry did better than whole-trial retry in these comparisons: ADaPT (retries only the failed subtask via recursive decomposition) beat Reflexion 71.6 vs 57.5 (ALFWorld), 44.0 vs 35.0 (WebShop), 52.0 vs 32.0 (TextCraft) with GPT-3.5, though the ADaPT authors only hypothesise that retry scope is the cause; in GraSP, full GraSP with local repair scored 80.6 vs 77.4 with global replanning on ALFWorld.

problem: Both verified (AgentDebugX Who&When strict agent+step 28.8% vs 21.7%, qwen3.5-9b; PALADIN RR 89.68% vs CRITIC 76.34%); note 28.8% is for the authors' own best method on a 9B model, so 'often wrong' is conservative.

Xiong et al. show add-all and the untuned coarse evaluator (C1) widen the gap to error-free memory, but some coarse evaluators (e.g. one fine-tuned on 300 trajectories) improved over time, and the strict-selection result (catching up to and passing error-free after ~2000 executions) is shown for AgentDriver only; the claim is also single-paper (Dynamic Cheatsheet lines only loosely support error clustering).
fix: Memory-addition gate strength matters (Xiong et al. 2025, four agents): add-all and an off-the-shelf LLM-judge (coarse) filter let errors accumulate and widened the gap to an error-free-memory variant, whereas strict (human-grade) selection let AgentDriver close and pass that gap after ~2000 executions; a coarse judge fine-tuned on 300 trajectories also improved over time. Agents copy retrieved records when inputs are similar (experience-following).

problem: Dynamic Cheatsheet (Sonnet AIME24 23.3->50.0 DC vs 26.7 FH; GPT-4o 20.0->6.7 FH) and LEGO-Prover (50.4 vs 47.1, gap widens) verified in the papers; sources are independent.
T&K 1981 text shows N=152 (72%) and N=155 (22% sure-loss option); Data Colada confirms the figures and a replication. Wording note: it is 'sure option', gain vs loss frame.

All figures verified in Kuhberger 2023 and the Many Labs 1 paper (d=1.13 original, Q=37.01 df 35); minor: Many Labs 2 (d=0.40) lies below the stated 0.5-0.6 and is not mentioned, and the 0.44 comes from Pinon & Gambara 2005.

Numbers verified (Pinon & Gambara d=0.260 smallest of risky/attribute/goal; food meta-analysis attitudes 0.82, intentions 0.05 as reported by Kuhberger 2023), but 'smallest framing type in humans' is wider than the sources: Kuhberger reports message framing at only about d=0.10, and Pinon & Gambara compare only three types (1997-2003 studies).
fix: Attribute framing (25% fat versus 75% lean) was the smallest of the three framing types in the Pinon & Gambara (2005) meta-analysis (d=0.26 vs 0.44 for risky and goal framing), and in the food attribute-framing meta-analysis it moved attitudes far more than intentions (d=0.82 vs d=0.05).

problem: Verified (Mandel & Kapler 2018: N=190 d=0.20, N=316 d=0.17 under the stricter frame-consistency coding, between-groups d=0.50 and 0.34); 'within-person consistency' is a loose gloss for the stricter theory-constrained coding, and the two studies use a financial ADP isomorph with 'exactly'.

Kuhberger 2023 (citing Wyszynski & Diederich, Peters & Levin, Best & Charness) and Mandel & Kapler 2018 (CRT, numeracy, AOT, NFC not predictive) support it; 'individual-difference fixes are weak' is an inference but follows.

Numbers match Slovic 1995 (reversals 40-50%, 10% intransitive, 90% procedure-invariance violations, from Tversky, Slovic & Kahneman 1990), but all supporting lines are that one review (a14/a15/a16 are the same paper) and the LessWrong LLM post lines do not bear on the claim; the original 1990 study was not independently opened.

Jones & Steinhardt Table 9 (45.4 vs 74.1, human 28 vs 78) and Suri et al. (ChatGPT 5 vs 4 in 11/11 runs each) verified; note the GPT-3 figures are means over many save probabilities, not only the classic 1/3 setting, and 'base and chat' rests on one GPT-3 and one ChatGPT study.

Jones & Steinhardt (gap near p=1/3, both high above 0.5) and Payne 2025 (sport 85.6%/88.8%, career reversed, abstract math: indifference in 100% of cases for GPT-4o and o3) verified; minor: math test used only two models and at p=0.5 GPT-3 wordings still differed (21.9 vs 46.9).

Verified: Saeedi et al. 57/74/85%, Elkins & Chun mean SVI 0.52, 45.2% high, US OSS 0.81 vs US SOTA 0.36 (OSS/commercial 2.2x), Echterhoff GPT-4 0.375 vs 0.780; minor: arXiv v1 abstract gave 0.53/0.79, and the four results measure different things (framing contradiction, syntactic endorsement gap, admit/reject rate).

Suri et al. 11/11 identical ratings and Elkins & Chun's Wilcoxon p=0.875 are right, but the Elkins appendix does not say the check used 3 models, fragility actually rose 16% (0.67 to 0.80) at T=0 (non-significant), and one rating task plus one non-significant ablation does not show that resampling 'cannot' reveal or fix a frame effect.
fix: In one ChatGPT medicine-rating task, outputs were identical across all 11 runs per frame (5 vs 4), so resampling added no information about the frame effect there; in Elkins & Chun's audit, syntactic fragility did not change significantly when temperature went from 0.7 to 0.0 (mean SVI 0.67 to 0.80, Wilcoxon p=0.875), so it is not simple sampling noise.

problem: Echterhoff Table (GPT-4 -0.405 to -0.010; GPT-3.5 +0.165 to -0.080), RaR (64.95 to 89.77) and S2A (62.8 to 80.3) verified; minor: 'overshot' means sign flip at smaller size, Llama-2-13b barely changed, and RaR/S2A are accuracy studies, not framing studies.

CogBias Table 13 (columns checked by arithmetic: 17.7->24.3 framing, 42.8->21.8 hyperbolic discounting) gives framing +6.6, not +5.8 (that is risk compensation), and hyperbolic discounting -21.0, not -13.4 (that is the halo effect); the other parts (Echterhoff awareness/counterfactual mixed, FRAGILE CoT/instruction/CAA raising flips on 7-8B models, Yechiam) check out.
fix: Generic debiasing instructions and prompt anchors are unreliable: awareness/counterfactual prompts helped some models and hurt others, a debias prompt gave +6.6 points on framing but -21.0 on hyperbolic discounting (CogBias, judgment family), and system prompts or anchors often failed to cut flips. In FRAGILE, CoT, an instruction prompt and CAA steering all raised flips in 7B to 8B models; naming a bias in the prompt can raise it (Yechiam 2026, two models).

problem: CogBias first-option 77.1-79.0% vs 36.8% chance and MathComp (equal cue up to 94%; GPT-4o and Sonnet 3.7 under 55% except Indirect-Equal) check out, but CRTBench's 72.4% (contrapositive) and 84.6% (double negation) are the worst model only (GPT-5.4-mini); other frontier models score about 92-98% on those transformations, so '72% to 85%' is not the range for frontier models.
fix: Option position and cue words are a second source of answer drift that can be larger than judgment biases (CogBias: first-option choice 77-79% vs 37% chance; direction words 'more/less' push answers and free chain of thought reduces the push). With objective answers (MathComp) a cue word pulls errors toward it (equal cue up to 94%); GPT-4o and Sonnet 3.7 stay under 55% drift except for the indirect-equal cue. In CRTBench, logically heavier rewrites hurt more than passive voice (GPT-5.4-mini: contrapositive 72.4%, double negation 84.6%, passive 98.7%; passive 94-100% across models).

problem: Cacioli r=.17 (CI -.29 to .57, n=20), Cao et al. Figure 1 (confidence tracks correctness, reasoning length does not rise) and Finn 2008 (framing moves JOL and restudy choice) check out; the battery authors themselves say the data only 'appear' separable and do not establish independence, which the claim's 'wide CI' flags.

Huang et al. Table 3 (GPT-3.5 CSQA 75.8->38.1->41.8; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5->91.5->89.0; oracle 97.5) verified and Kamoi et al.'s survey agrees; Kamoi allows exceptions for tasks especially suited to self-correction.

Numbers verified (Nelson & Narens Table I: recall .28 vs .10, FOK 5.4 vs 5.2), but the source says FOK misses small amounts of new information from a brief flash, not that it is blind to new information, and Koriat 1997 finds JOLs rely on intrinsic cues like ease while discounting extrinsic ones like repetition (repetition lifted recall more than JOL).
fix: Monitoring cues are inferential, not direct reads: FOK uses acquisition history and partial information (No-Magic Hypothesis), is insensitive to small amounts of new information (a brief answer flash raised recall .28 vs .10 but FOK only 5.4 vs 5.2), and JOLs are built from cues such as item ease (intrinsic cues) and study conditions, with repetition under-weighted relative to its effect on recall.

problem: Kapoor et al. (1,000 graded examples outperform baselines; prompting alone insufficient) and Self-RAG (trained reflection tokens, 7B/13B beat ChatGPT and retrieval baselines) verified; Self-RAG's baselines are retrieval-augmented models rather than prompt-only monitoring methods, so 'prompt-based baselines' fits Kapoor better.

Adaptive-Consistency (up to 7.9x, 3.3x maths, 0.1% drop) and ESC (33.8%-84.2%) verified in the papers, and Meyer et al. reports 4/9 and 2/8 unanimously-supported errors; caveat: the error figures come from a small 100-question workshop study of fixed 3-sample agreement, not from the stopping rules themselves.

Snell et al. (more than 4x vs best-of-N, PaLM 2-S* settings) and Damani et al. (up to 50% less compute or up to 10% better quality) verified; Snell's ~4x holds at lower budgets and shrinks at higher ones, and 'rests on Cao alone' is the writer's inference.

Kalyuga 2007 (existence/title verified via Crossref; content is the standard expertise-reversal review) and Leppink et al. 2011 (interaction F(3,97)=2.762, d=0.96/1.06) verified; note in Leppink the high-prior advantage of arguments over worked examples was not significant (d=0.51), so the 'crossover' is partly a pattern, not a significant reversal.

Only the Kalyuga (2007) abstract/reference list was reachable (full text paywalled; no text on partial vs full reversals) and the Tetzlaff 2025 PDF host (pedocs) refused connection, so Table 3 numbers and the 'partial reversals more common' statement could not be checked; b19 and b20 are also the same Kalyuga paper.

Leppink 2011 verified (crossover, numbers match) but shows a crossover not a graded retention/transfer gradient; Chen thesis host unreachable and its listed finding says the effect reversed for the most knowledgeable group, not 'none'; the retention-only/middle tier is not in any listed finding.
fix: Worked-example benefit shrinks as prior knowledge rises and can reverse for the most knowledgeable learners (e.g., a crossover in first-year statistics, Leppink et al. 2011); a three-step gradient (retention plus transfer / retention only / none) is not supported by the sources checked.

problem: Nievelstein et al. 2013 verified (numbers match; first- and third-year law students both benefited from worked examples) but it covers law only, not art history or literature; the Chen geometry thesis (unreachable) is not an ill-structured domain; 'because students lack the key schema' is interpretation, and the third-year students had much more prior knowledge (d=2.75).
fix: In one study of legal case reasoning (a less structured task), worked examples beat problem solving for both first-year and third-year law students, so no expertise reversal appeared even though third-years had much more prior knowledge; generalisation to art history or literature is not shown.

problem: Minor: the -1.2/-4.1 pp averages in Feng et al. have overlapping CIs and the SkillsBench Claude Code self-generated runs used higher effort than baseline; neither changes the claim.

All numbers come from the single SkillsBench paper (Honda cheat-sheet paper is a different setting and gives no support for the skill-length numbers); comprehensive bucket has only 5 tasks and buckets are observational, not an ablation.

Honda MATH500 numbers (Gemini 1.5 Pro 86.3/82.3/88.0), Agarwal MATH/GPQA decline after 125 shots and Zou harder-tasks-degrade-earlier all match; the 'few shots suffice for strong models' part rests on a GPT-4.1 figure whose values were not read.

All numbers verified in Qiu et al. 2026, but every cited line is the same single preprint (one lab), so the model-strength trend is not independently replicated; 'style change not knowledge-redundant' is the paper's perturbation design, accurately characterised.

Cortex +66.7 vs +5.6 (Haiku 4.5 vs Sonnet 5, CI of the 5.6 spans zero) and Feng rho -0.55/-0.45 over 33 cells verified; the 'no published study found' part is an absence claim that cannot be proven by sources, and Xu&Wu/SkillsBench do not test the split.

Numbers match OpenSkillEval (48%, Opus 4.6 ~20%, 94%) and Liu et al. (Kimi 19.8 vs 21.8, Qwen 19.7 vs 20.5); 'stronger models ignore irrelevant skills better' rests on three models (Opus, Kimi, Qwen), gaps of 0.8 to 2.0 pp with no significance test, and is the authors' interpretation.

Numbers verified in Shang et al. (peak R3, +2 at R5, 72%, +10 over best ungated, 1.7 pp) and Cheng et al. (0.713, 0.775, 0.816), but 'Lessons must be scoped' generalises from one procedurally generated 12-round code-repair benchmark with fixed family conventions (eight streams), and the two results are single preprints from different setups.
fix: In one terminal-task benchmark an unfiltered self-evolving skill pool peaked at round 3 and ended only 2 points above round 1 (a gated pool reached 72%, 10 points above the ungated best), and removing the source skills recovered only 1.7 pp; in a separate procedurally generated code-repair stream, accepted skills applied globally scored 0.713 vs 0.775 for no edits, while the same skills scoped to their originating task family scored 0.816.

problem: All numbers verified in Higham (2002); a14 and b15 are the same paper and Santa and Lamwers (1974) was only checked second-hand through Higham's account, so the claim rests on one paper (single lab).

Smith and Vela (2001) numbers verified (d=.28 +-.05, 93 effects, QT=242.47, reinstatement .23); a12 and b01/b02 are the same paper, and the paper stresses effects are not always modest (18 of 93 exceeded d=.80, interference-reduction d=.68). Murre check not opened.

Smith and Vela (associative .13 vs nonassociative .33, chi2 6.67) and Saufley et al. (21 comparisons, seven courses, none reliable) verified; 'vanish with real-world use' generalises from one university study, and overshadowing/outshining are Smith and Vela's own hypotheses.

Goh and Lu (.37 vs .24, .28 vs .28, .32 vs .25) verified; Poirier et al. (Nairne lab) is independent and consistent but tests response time, not the recall numbers. Interpretive 'drives' is the authors' account; Exp 2 shows match still helped at low overload.
HyDE table, LongMemEval 11.3% (round) with strong-LLM caveat, and Yoon et al. FEVER Recall@5 40.0/23.4/26.8 verified; Weller not opened.
Berglund (96.7/0.1, 0.0, in-context 100/96.67 and footnote) and Allen-Zhu (9.7% to 96.6%) verified; the closing 'long-context retrieved text is untested' is an absence claim.

Liu et al. says 'more than 20%' (the 30-document table shows about 23 pp between first and middle slot, so pp is consistent) and Cuconasu et al. numbers (36-44% vs 28-34%, Qwen 7B 71.73 vs 71.00) verified; Cuconasu itself concludes position bias matters little in real retrieval.

Cuconasu (0.5642 to 0.4068/0.3815/0.3626, +0.08 / +36% from random docs) and Amiraz (6 to 11 points, persists for Llama-3.3-70B, range is across LLMs not 70B alone) match, but Yoran et al. say retrieval caused the error in 73% of 240 manually annotated failures, and separately that in 77% of NQ errors with low-ranked context the wrong entity appeared in the retrieved text; the claim merges these into '73% of retrieval-caused errors copied an entity ... (77%)'.
fix: Retrieved passages that are semantically close to the question but lack the answer cost an LLM reader more than unrelated ones: Llama2-7b 0.5642 gold-only to 0.4068/0.3815/0.3626 with 1/2/4 ADORE distractors, while random passages placed next to the query raised accuracy by up to 0.08 (+36%); hard distractors cost 6 to 11 accuracy points depending on the LLM, and the cost persists for Llama-3.3-70B; in Llama-2-13B, manual review of 240 failures found retrieval caused the error in 73% (65-85% by setting), and with low-ranked context the wrong answer entity appeared in the retrieved text in 77% of NQ errors (37% with random context).

problem: Weller et al. (11 methods, 12 datasets, 24 models, negative correlation, 28 of 28 non-label failures from irrelevant/erroneous added terms) verified; the 28/28 comes from a hand sample of only 30 failures from three datasets, and Yuan et al.'s abstract and the Anthropic post do not bear on the expansion-hurts-strong-retrievers claim. Absence statement about agent notes not checkable.

Yoran NLI filtering (prevents loss, discards relevant passages), Chain-of-Note +7.9 EM at fully noisy retrieval (+2.7 at 0% noise not located in the text read) and Astute RAG (Claude/Gemini) verified in abstracts/text; CoN is a note-writing relevance judgement rather than a pure pre-use filter, and the closing absence claim is not checkable.

Schroeder and Cenkci abstract (58 comparisons, n=2426, g=0.63) and Ginns abstract (50 studies, spatial plus temporal) verified, but the 'pooled size is falling' trend compares Ginns d=0.85 (spatial plus temporal pooled; value from a secondary source) with spatial-only later syntheses (Ginns spatial subset g=0.72 on 37 effects), and the Wang 2016 retention 0.48 / transfer 0.39 figures are not in any listed source and could not be found.
fix: Across meta-analyses, integrated text and picture beat separated text and picture: Ginns (2006) reported a pooled d of about 0.85 on 50 studies combining spatial and temporal contiguity (spatial subset g=0.72 on 37 effects per a German summary), and Schroeder and Cenkci (2018) found g = 0.63 on 58 spatial comparisons (n = 2426), a smaller figure that is not directly comparable because the scope differs; neither abstract reports bias-corrected sizes.

problem: Ginns abstract (50 independent studies, spatial and temporal contiguity) and the Clearing House summary (g=0.72 on 37 effects, 58 = 37 plus new studies) verified; the d=0.85 (CI 0.68-1.02) figure comes from Beege et al. 2019, which I did not open; the claim already marks the spatial-only reading as an inference.

Chen (2016) thesis is behind an SSO login (the trigonometry immediate-vs-delayed interaction could not be checked); only the Cognitive Tutor half was confirmed, second-hand, through Kalyuga's 2010 editorial summary of Salden et al. (adaptive fading won on delayed but not immediate classroom posttest), not the Salden paper itself.

Beege et al. 2019 does print d=0.78 (high complexity) and d=0.28 (p>.05, low), but cites them to Cohen (1988), not Ginns 2006 (it cites Ginns only for the overall d=0.85, CI 0.68-1.02), and I could not find the 0.78/0.28 split in Ginns' abstract or elsewhere; the claim's statement that the pair is 'quoted from Ginns 2006 by Beege' is not what the paper shows. Sweller (1994) supports the interactivity argument but as a theoretical prediction.
fix: Element interactivity is argued to moderate the effect: Beege et al. (2019) write that spatial integration gives high effect sizes (d = 0.78) with complex material and only small non-significant ones (d = 0.28, p > .05) with simple material, but they attribute these figures to Cohen (1988) and their provenance in Ginns (2006) is unverified; Sweller (1994) predicts extraneous load matters mainly when intrinsic load is already high.

problem: Kalyuga, Chandler and Sweller (1999) state the boundary (integration required if sources are unintelligible alone; redundant restatement of a self-contained diagram adds load) and report the text/audio redundancy result (F(2,31)=7.74 and 10.66); but this is the authors' stated condition, tested in small groups (n=11-12), and all supporting items (Kalyuga 1999, Sweller 1994 on Chandler and Sweller 1991) come from one research group, so 'only when' is stronger than the evidence.

GSM-IC (<=18%), GSM-NoOp (up to 65%), Levy (0.92 to 0.68 at 3000 tokens) and GSM-DC (Grok-3-Beta 43% to 19%, step accuracy) verified, but GSM-Plus -2.05% human vs 8.23% GPT-4 is the average performance drop over all eight question-variation types (not irrelevant-text insertion), GPT-4 is not a 'newer' model, GSM-DC reports step accuracy not final accuracy, and Levy's padding is separate from problem text.
fix: Adding irrelevant text to a problem sharply lowers LLM accuracy: on GSM-IC no more than 18% of base problems the baseline solved were solved for all distractor types, GSM-NoOp (one inert clause) drops accuracy by up to 65%, and padding a fixed task with unrelated text lowers average accuracy from 0.92 to 0.68 at 3,000 tokens; in the 2025 GSM-DC benchmark Grok-3-Beta's step accuracy at depth 5 falls from 43% to 19% and GPT-4.1's from 26% to 2% as irrelevant items go from 1 to 15; GSM-Plus (all eight variation types, not only distractors) shows an average drop of 8.23% for GPT-4 vs -2.05% for humans.

problem: Liu et al. (U-shape, GPT-3.5-Turbo >20% drop, worst case below closed-book 56.1%) and Chen et al. (premise order permutation drops accuracy by over 30%) verified; Liu reports 20% without stating points vs relative, and the two effects come from different tasks (document QA vs deductive proofs).
Opened Logic-LM, SatLM, LINC, Faithful CoT; numbers match (SatLM 99.7 vs CoT 80.1 is code-davinci-002, depth-5 ProofWriter, and Logic-LM loses to CoT on PrOntoQA, consistent with 'often').
LINC GPT-4 FOLIO 75.3 vs 72.5, p=0.58, and Logic-LM PrOntoQA 98.79 vs 83.20 all verified.

Task-accuracy deltas -1.7/+0.6/+1.4 in VeriCoT Table 3 are VeriCoT-Base vs the ER baseline after reflection, not vs pre-reflection; pass-rate gains are +7.8 to +15.4 (claim says 8 to 15). All other numbers match.
ProverQA appendix C numbers are right (68.33 to 45.00) but its authors conclude the drop shows models do NOT rely heavily on background knowledge, the opposite of how the claim uses it.
fix: Benchmarks can be partly answerable from world knowledge: JustLogic's prior-knowledge independence test shows FOLIO and LogiQA 2.0 questions are answerable without context, unlike synthetic CLUTRR and ProofWriter. (Contrast: ProverQA's check, removing universal rules from 60 items, dropped GPT-4o CoT from 68.33 to 45.00, which its authors read as showing little reliance on background knowledge.)

problem: JustLogic R1 80.9/o1 72.9/human 73.0/ceiling 100/GPT-4o 65.6, ZebraLogic o1-full X-Large 42.5, Logic-RL Knights and Knaves 0.94/0.81/0.42, FOLIO R1 86.2 all match (o1 is 0.1 below human avg; FOLIO compared across different splits/pipelines).

Evans 1983 numbers all match (n=24, 64, 32). But the opening line is wider than the sources: Lampinen/Dasgupta et al. show humans and models are more accurate when belief agrees with logic (valid-believable, invalid-unbelievable), not simply when the conclusion is believable; invalid-believable is where accuracy drops (92% and 67-72% wrongly accepted).
fix: Models, like people, reason more accurately when the believability of the conclusion agrees with its logical validity, and err when they conflict (belief bias). In people the effect is large (Evans et al. 1983: N=24 Exp 1, percent accepting valid-believable 92, valid-unbelievable 46, invalid-believable 92, invalid-unbelievable 8; Exp 2 N=64: 88/56/72/13; Exp 3 N=32: 91/53/67/6).

problem: Evans 1983 and Trippas et al. 2018 (22 studies, N=993, no unconditional discriminability effect, individual differences mediate) verified.

LogicBench (2404.15522; the other listed source 2401.00757 is LogicAsker, a different paper) gives GPT-4 hypothetical syllogism Yes-class 84.75 (text: about 85), not near 100; modus tollens Yes 59.05 matches. ChatGPT 48.04 / GPT-4 63.98 are propositional-logic average Yes-label accuracy, and 81.88 / 89.58 are the PL average on the multiple-choice task, not a binary-QA average.
fix: On LogicBench propositional logic, GPT-4 reaches about 85% Yes-label accuracy on hypothetical syllogism but about 59% on modus tollens; negation and implicit-premise rules are hard. Yes-label accuracy on binary QA is far below multiple-choice accuracy on the same logic type (PL averages: ChatGPT 48.0 Yes-label vs 81.9 MCQA; GPT-4 64.0 vs 89.6).

problem: LoGiPT parse success 0.33% (CodeLlama-13B-Base, ProofWriter) and ProverQA fine-tune gains 21.4/44.0/34.6 verified; note the ProverQA gains are in-distribution on Llama3.1-8B (fine-tuning on ProofWriter/FOLIO lowered other sets).

Numbers match (music 0.03 active vs 0.25 passive; WM 0.05 vs 0.18; second-order grand mean 0.00 with active controls), but both sources are by the same lab (Sala and Gobet), the 2023 paper re-using their 2019 meta-analytic data; the 332 samples is the whole dataset while the 0.00 grand mean rests on the 142 active-control samples.
fix: One research group (Sala and Gobet) reports that far transfer of trained cognitive skills is near zero when active controls are used: music 0.03 SD vs 0.25 with passive controls, working memory 0.05 vs 0.18; their second-order meta-analysis of active-control studies gives a grand mean of 0.00 (14 meta-analyses, 332 samples overall). Independent labs have not been opened.

problem: Sala and Gobet show effects shrink with active controls in music, WM and chess training, not that 'every' far-transfer effect is partly artefact; chess had only one active-control study and the authors' conclusion is contested; the prompt-control step is a design inference, not a finding.
fix: In cognitive-training meta-analyses (Sala and Gobet), far-transfer effects shrink toward zero when active rather than passive controls are used, which points to passive-control or expectation artefacts in those literatures; by analogy, a scaffold test should include an equal-length placebo prompt.

problem: Wang et al. (text-davinci-002, Table 2): invalid reasoning keeps 39.5/48.5 GSM8K answer accuracy (about 81%), but 9.6 vs 43.9 is intermediate-step recall, not task accuracy (answer accuracy 11.0 vs 48.5); incoherent-only prompts keep about half (23.1 vs 48.5), and Bamboogle drops far less; single model setting. Min et al. (random labels) does not bear on scaffold relevance.
fix: In Wang et al. (InstructGPT, GSM8K), CoT demonstrations with invalid reasoning keep about 80-90% of CoT performance (answer accuracy 39.5 vs 48.5), while relevance-free rationales fall to 11.0 answer accuracy (intermediate-step recall 9.6 vs 43.9); incoherent-only rationales keep about half (23.1). Hence a control prompt should vary relevance and coherence separately from correctness.

problem: GSM-Symbolic Fig 8a (Phi-3-mini -65.7, o1-preview -17.5, o1-mini -29.1) and GSM-IC (fewer than 30% of base problems consistently solved) verified.

Embers numbers are right but they show sensitivity to the probability of the output or input text (GPT-4 word reversal 97% vs 53%, rot-13 21% vs 11%), not pretraining frequency of the task form; the only distinct listed source is this one paper (c25 is blank).
