fix: LLM accuracy on deterministic tasks depends on how probable the text is (Embers of Autoregression, GPT-4): word reversal 97% when the answer is a high-probability sentence vs 53% when low-probability; rot-13 21% for high-probability input vs 11% for low-probability input. The same paper also reports task-frequency effects (common vs rare variants of a task).

problem: DataAlchemy paper (2508.01191) verified: ID 100%, CMP 0.01%, POOD/OOD 0%, LLaMA3-8B CMP 8.52%, small SFT portion generalises quickly; all figures rest on this one paper (other listed sources cover different points and were not needed).

Memory-management paper (add-all vs fixed: 67.53/55.48, 40.11/32.32, 71.50/59.90, plus a fourth agent 16.75/13.05; strict 70.95/51.00/85.40) and Dynamic Cheatsheet (AIME 2024, Claude, FH 26.7 vs DC 50.0) verified; the DC figure is one task and one model, and FH is still slightly above baseline 23.3.

Puranam et al. 2025 verified (humans 6.3/20.3% no hint vs 8.7/37% hint; quoting Gick and Holyoak 29% (8/28) vs 50% (14/28); GPT-4 no-hint precision/recall 0, with-hint recall 1.00, precision 0.50-0.52); Willingham text is a loose second-hand description only. Note GPT-4 'correct-source recall' is not 'solved the problem'.

LLM-SRBench (31.5 / 28.1 best symbolic accuracy), LLM-SR (<20 iterations, lower perplexity on Feynman), NewtonBench Table 17 (2.10/3.61/7.21 to 28.83-35.14) verified; 'much lower' perplexity is just 'lower' in the source.

DiscoveryBench (24.5 Reflexion oracle, best normal 16.3) and DiscoveryWorld (38% easy, 18% challenge, humans 66% on normal/challenge tasks only) verified, but ScienceAgentBench's best is not 32.4%: its abstract reports o1-preview reaching 42.2% (32.4% / 34.3% is the best non-o1 agent).
fix: End-to-end discovery agents are weak: DiscoveryBench best about 25% hypothesis match only with an oracle-feedback Reflexion agent (24.5; best normal agent 16.3); DiscoveryWorld best agent completes 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks versus 66% for up to 11 human scientists on normal and challenge tasks; ScienceAgentBench best 32.4% (34.3% with expert hints) for non-o1 agents, 42.2% with o1-preview at over 10 times the cost.

problem: DiscoveryBench Table (NoDataGuess 0.0/4.7/11.5 vs CodeGen 15.5/16.3/12.1; ratios 0/29/95%), NewtonBench Table 17 and LLM-SRBench verified.

DiscoveryBench Reflexion oracle (max 3 trials) and Co-Scientist 6.14 to 2.38 verified; the Co-Scientist test only covers published (non-novel) ideas, so 'separated known from new' is a slight stretch.

MOOSE-Chem (96.7% top 20%, 83.7% top 4%, GPT-4o, 300-paper corpus) and ResearchBench (45.65% GPT-4o, position bias in ranking) numbers verified, but both come from the same group (Yang, Xie, Gao, Li, Ouyang, Zhou, Cambria at Shanghai AI Lab), ResearchBench extending MOOSE-Chem, so the 'retrieval is strong' pattern is one lab's evidence on its own benchmarks.
fix: Retrieval of the key inspiration is the stronger step for LLMs in one research group's chemistry benchmarks (MOOSE-Chem and its extension ResearchBench, same authors): MOOSE-Chem GPT-4o keeps 83.7% of true inspirations in the top 4% (96.7% in top 20%); ResearchBench final round above 40% (GPT-4o 45.65%); pairwise ranking shows position bias.

problem: Numbers verified (GPT-4o direct 50.0 vs reviewer 56.1; AI Scientist reviewer balanced acc 0.65 vs 0.66, score correlation 0.18 vs 0.14), but the AI Scientist paper itself only says its papers occasionally contain hallucinated plots, wrong comparisons and citation errors, not that they 'carry invented results'; also the 0.65 is the best reviewer configuration (GPT-4o 1-shot with ensembling), other configs 0.52-0.63.
fix: LLM judges of ideas and papers are weak: GPT-4o direct ranking 50.0% balanced accuracy versus human reviewer consistency 56.1%; the AI Scientist's best reviewer configuration matches humans on some metrics (balanced acc 0.65 vs 0.66; score correlation 0.18 vs 0.14; other configurations 0.52-0.63), yet the same paper reports its generated papers occasionally contain hallucinated plots and critical evaluation errors.

problem: Kosmos (79.4% of 102 statements, interpretation/synthesis 57.9%) and AI-Newton (46 mechanics experiments, Newton's second law, energy conservation, gravitation) verified; AI-Newton is a concept-driven system, not an LLM long-run agent, so it is weak support for the 'coherent long agent runs' framing.
LLM-SRBench (GPT-4o vs two authors, 94.6% of 130 = 123, no kappa) and DiscoveryWorld (GPT-4o knowledge grading, human notes graded manually, no agreement reported) verified.

Kosmos 85.5/82.1/57.9 on 102 statements and DiscoveryWorld Reactor Lab regression 0.00 completion in all 9 cells verified, but the Kosmos paper calls its evaluators independent expert scientists; nothing says they are the authors' collaborators (collaborators separately reported the six-month time equivalence).
fix: Interpretation is where discovery agents lose points, in two independent systems: Kosmos 85.5% (data analysis), 82.1% (literature) but 57.9% (synthesis) accuracy on 102 statements judged by expert scientist evaluators the paper calls independent (the authors do not detail how they were chosen); DiscoveryWorld agents have high procedure scores but low completion, and 0.00 completion on Reactor Lab regression in all 9 cells. DiscoveryWorld location of failure is inferred from score columns.

problem: KEKADA technical report (Kulkarni and Simon 1987) verified first-hand: user supplies experiment results and some choices, 'only minor differences' with Krebs is stated without measurement, reconstruction rests on Holmes using notebooks/interviews, Henseleit collaborated; SEP names BACON and KEKADA as heuristic-search programs. The sufficiency-not-necessity point is the researcher's interpretation, which the sources do not contradict.

Ark, Brooks and Eva 2006 (48 students, 12 per group, 42/41 vs 56/53) and Norman and Brooks 1997 (about 30% in dermatology) verified; Norman, Young and Brooks 2007 is a review from the same McMaster group, so the exemplar evidence is essentially one lab, which the claim already flags.

Keemink et al. 2018 (32 students) found a case-based clinical reasoning course raised overall illness-script richness by almost 20%, with relatively more Enabling Conditions and less Fault content; it did not teach enabling conditions specifically. Schmidt and Rikers 2007 abstract says nothing on enabling conditions or first hypotheses; the expert-first-hypothesis point appears only as background citation.
fix: Illness scripts are thought to shift with expertise from Fault (pathophysiology) toward Enabling Conditions (patient features, setting) and Consequences, which are available early and help activate scripts (background in Keemink et al. 2018). A case-based clinical reasoning course raised pre-clinical students' overall script richness by almost 20% (14.47 vs 12.14, n=32) while shifting content toward Enabling Conditions; experts' use of them for first hypotheses was not tested there.

problem: Kanjee et al. (64% in differential, 39% top, n=70), o1-preview paper (78.3%, 52%, n=143; 88.6% vs 72.9% on 70 cases, where that metric is 'exact or very close') and AMIE DDx paper (top-10 59.1% vs 33.6%, 302 cases) verified; the numbers use different scoring rules across studies.

LLM part is supported by one paper only (Schmidgall et al., npj Digit Med/arXiv, listed as b23/b24/c04/d21; the other sources are different multi-agent studies). 'Physician automation bias persists after AI training (-14 points)' appears in none of the opened sources; the only 14.0 is GPT-4's worst false-consensus drop. GPT-4 few-shot mitigation (75.2%) actually exceeded the 72.7% unbiased average, though the authors call gains modest.
fix: In BiasMedQA (1,273 USMLE questions, 7 injected biases, 6 LLMs; Schmidgall et al. 2024), GPT-4 scored 72.7% unbiased and lost about 5% on average with a bias cue (worst case -14.0% for false consensus); prompt-level mitigation (education, one-shot, few-shot) gave only modest, uneven gains per bias and generally did not match unbiased accuracy. (Single-paper evidence; the physician automation-bias claim is unsupported and should be dropped.)

problem: Braitsch (32 models; 212/323 = 65.6%), MedEinst (17 LLMs; paper states stronger models have higher trap rates), MINT (11 LLMs, over 55% in first two turns) and Moell (100 MedQA cases, 7 errors, longer reasoning in wrong answers) all check out. The 'not supported elsewhere (see K32)' part was not checked.

Mandel and Barnes numbers verified (N=1,514, A=0.940, Brier 0.074, eta2 0.758, sensitivity 0.090/0.097, Canadian IAS); the 59% under 6 months / 96% under a year comes from the Tetlock and Mellers reply, not Mandel and Barnes itself. Minor: the 1,514 exclusions are team forecasts and missing data; ambiguous outcomes were dropped earlier.

Tetlock and Mellers (a06/b07 are the same reply) only argue that the analyst questions were short-range and mostly near-certain (59% under 6 months, over half Brier 0 or 0.01); Mandel and Barnes themselves found time frame had no significant effect on discrimination, so stating it as an established question-mix effect is too strong. Paleka (worked example, Brier not comparable across base rates) is verified.
fix: Tetlock and Mellers (2014) argue that the analysts' strong Brier scores partly reflect an easy question mix: short horizons (59% under 6 months) and many near-certain questions (over half scored Brier 0 or 0.01), whereas Tetlock's weak results were mostly long-range; Mandel and Barnes found no significant effect of time frame on discrimination. Raw Brier is not comparable across question sets with different base rates (Paleka et al. 2025).

problem: Mellers 2024 gives training +6-11% per year, teams better each of 4 years, over 50% noise reduction; Mellers 2014 confirms training/teaming/tracking; Satopaa and Ungar abstract supports extremizing (conditions not in abstract); Mandel and Tetlock confirm underconfidence and recalibration helped in IARPA ACE. Caveat: most sources come from the same GJP-linked group (Mellers, Ungar, Tetlock, Baron), Mandel being the independent voice.

Numbers verified (Halawi .179 vs .149 N=914, best baseline .208; Autocast 65% vs 92%, Halawi cites 65.4 vs 92.8; Schoenegger-Park .20 vs .07 N=23, GPT-4 not distinct from .25). But the Halawi 'system' is retrieval-augmented and fine-tuned, and Autocast models are fine-tuned retrieval-based T5/FiD, so they are not 'un-augmented LLM forecasters'; only the .208 baseline and S&P GPT-4 are un-augmented.
fix: LLM forecasters trail the human crowd on real-question sets: Halawi's retrieval-augmented, fine-tuned system scored Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 (N=914 test questions) and its best no-retrieval baseline 0.208; the best Autocast model reached 65% accuracy vs 92% for the crowd; in Schoenegger and Park (2023) GPT-4 scored 0.20 vs crowd 0.07 (N=23 questions, GPT-4 not statistically different from 0.25).

problem: Silicon crowd (12 LLMs, .20 vs .19, p=.850; equivalence non-preregistered; averaging .13/.14 vs updated forecasts, p=.011/.001) and Hsieh et al. (.169 vs .180 agents, .218 vs .210 base GPT-4o, SD .092 vs .150) verified. Minor slip: '0.14-0.17' mixes pre-update (.17) and post-update (.14) GPT-4 scores; 'help agents (SD 0.092)' means lower variance, Brier gain is .169 vs .180.

Pratt et al. (2024): plain prompt outperformed all strategy prompts and the human market baseline; Lu (2025, single author, GMU): narrative prompts worse than direct. Narrative framing is not strictly a 'forecasting strategy' but the wording is acceptable.

Paleka et al.: at least 3.8% of Halawi questions resolved early, search leak example ('jan 6' before 2020), Brier not comparable across base rates (worked example verified). Alur et al. independently document search foreknowledge leakage (about 1.65% of results; 17% of queries in one case) though they find it moves their ForecastBench Brier by under 0.001. Four of the listed sources are the same Paleka paper.

Numbers verified (Schoenegger et al.: best prompts about -0.014 to -0.011, Bayesian Reasoning and Propose-Evaluate-Select significantly worse; Alur et al.: agentic search 0.1140 vs 0.1230 no-news, single forecast 0.1182 vs 10-sample mean 0.1140). But 'only through search, sampling and aggregation' is a universal claim; the sources test prompts and search/aggregation, not other routes, and Halawi's fine-tuning also lowered Brier (.206 to .186).
fix: In the studies read, single-paragraph strategy prompts moved Brier by about 0.01 at best (frequency-based, base-rate-first, chain-of-thought, step-back), Bayesian-reasoning and propose-evaluate-select prompts hurt, and compound prompts gave no robust gain (Schoenegger et al. 2025); the gains from scaffolds came mainly from search (agentic search 0.1140 vs 0.1230 without news), sampling and aggregation (10-sample mean 0.1140 vs single 0.1182; Alur et al. 2025), and fine-tuning in Halawi et al.; no equal-token comparison exists.

problem: Gneiting and Raftery define strictly proper, derive Brier as strictly proper and list zero-one as a point-mass (threshold) rule in Table 1; Hoessly states Brier is strictly proper (Theorem 1 of ref 8). Neither text literally says 'plain accuracy rewards rounding to 0 or 1'; that part is a standard consequence rather than a quoted statement.

Siegert confirms Br = REL - RES + UNC (Murphy 1973) with UNC the Brier of the climatological mean. The decomposition in Siegert is defined for any forecast via the calibration function P(y=1|p); Brocker's 'finite-valued' refers to targets (outcomes), not forecasts. Exactness only for finitely-valued forecasts applies to the empirical (binned) estimators, which neither source states as an 'only' condition.
fix: Mean Brier splits as REL - RES + UNC (Murphy 1973), with UNC = base rate x (1 - base rate), the Brier score of the climatological forecast; a useful forecast has Brier below UNC. The population decomposition holds for general forecasts, but sample estimates are exact only when forecasts take a finite set of repeated values; otherwise binning approximates it.

problem: Siegert (bias-corrected Brier-decomposition estimators have larger variance) and Dimitriadis et al. (binned reliability-diagram estimates: squared bias m(n)^-2 vs variance growing with bin count; CORP MSE compared in Fig. 5) are verified, but neither source analyses ECE, and the CORP MSE comparison is for conditional event probability estimates in reliability diagrams, not for ECE or score-decomposition estimates.
fix: Binned reliability-diagram and Brier-decomposition estimates depend on the bin count and are biased (Dimitriadis et al.; Siegert); bias-corrected decomposition estimators reduce bias but have larger variance (Siegert); in the CORP authors' simulations, the bin-free isotonic (CORP) reliability-diagram estimates had the lowest MSE of the binning variants compared. ECE is not analysed in these sources.

problem: Kadavath et al. Figure 9: RLHF policies miscalibrated, T=2.5 largely fixes it for three evaluations; GPT-4 Technical Report Figure 8: ECE 0.007 pre-trained vs 0.074 post-trained on a subset of MMLU. Minor: GPT-4 figure is a subset of MMLU; Kadavath's RLHF models are Anthropic's small policies, and 'pretrained LLMs well calibrated' holds for larger models (Kadavath shows calibration improves with size).

Xiong et al. state GPT-4 with 93.6% accuracy gets near-optimal ECE 0.064 by assigning 100% confidence to all samples (in the CoT-prompt experiment); the 50% guesser point is arithmetic, not sourced. Tian et al. (listed alongside) do not address gaming of ECE, so the gaming point rests on Xiong alone.

Xiong: GPT-4 vanilla avg AUROC 62.7% over 8 tasks verified; GSM8K 54.8 to 92.7 AUROC verified but it is GPT-3.5 with 5 sampled CoT responses + consistency vs a single response (the claim does not name the model). 'Weakly' is not general: Tian et al. report GPT-4 verbalized AUC .937-.950 on TriviaQA. 'Samples are correlated' is an inference, not in the sources.
fix: On Xiong et al.'s eight tasks GPT-4's vanilla verbalized confidence separates right from wrong only weakly (average AUROC 62.7%, chance 50%), though on easy factual QA such as TriviaQA GPT-4 verbalized confidence reaches AUC about .94 (Tian et al.); sampling 5 responses and measuring agreement raised GPT-3.5's GSM8K AUROC from 54.8% to 92.7%.

problem: Tian et al. gpt-3.5 TriviaQA ECE: 1-stage top-1 .068; 2-stage top-1 .131 and 2-stage CoT .110 (both worse). Slip: .131 is the non-CoT two-stage prompt; the CoT variant is .110. Sarfati et al.: Spearman .90 forced vs free confidence on test and same answer on 67% verified (8B forecaster, one model).

Halawi Table 7 zero-shot Brier for the other models ranges from .219 to .353 (Llama-2-7B .353, Llama-2-70B .283, GPT-3.5-1106 .274), not '.215-.268' (.215 and .268 are single scratchpad cells). GPT-4-1106 .208, S&P GPT-4 .20 vs .25 (t(22)=-1.23, p=.23), Hsieh et al. base-LM ensembles (.218 vs .210; GPT-4 .265, GPT-3.5 .261, Llama3 .256) and Bench to the Future (all no-evidence models better than .25) verified. Also the paper cited as 'Phan' is by Hsieh, Fu and Chen (UC Berkeley).
fix: Zero-shot LLMs without retrieval score close to the 0.25 coin-flip line on forecasting questions (Halawi et al.: GPT-4-1106 .208, other models .215-.353 across zero-shot and scratchpad prompts, many at or worse than .25; GPT-4 .20 not distinguishable from .25 in Schoenegger and Park, N=23; Hsieh et al. base-LM ensembles mostly worse than .25). Bench to the Future finds all no-evidence models better than .25, so the level depends on the question mix.

problem: Halawi (.179 vs .149, difference .03; best baseline .208; base-only .206; ablations .186/.182) and Hsieh et al. (.169 vs .172 on 201 Manifold questions; agent ensemble .169 vs single .180; base-LM ensemble .218 vs .210) verified. Slip: the ReAct paper is by Hsieh, Fu and Chen, not 'Phan'; its .169 does pass the crowd on that small set, as the claim itself notes.

Schoenegger and Park's BMA blend (.13) is better than GPT-4 (.20) but worse than the human crowd (.07), so it does not beat both; Silicon-crowd result is average (.13/.14) vs the models' own updated forecasts (.14/.15), not vs the human crowd; only Halawi (aggregate .146 vs crowd .149 and system .179) shows the average beating both.
fix: Averaging an LLM forecast with the human crowd can beat the LLM alone and sometimes the crowd: Halawi's weighted average of system and crowd scored .146, better than crowd .149 and system .179; in Silicon Crowd, a simple human-machine average (GPT-4 .13, Claude 2 .14) beat the models' own updated forecasts (.14, .15); but in Schoenegger and Park (N=23) the blend (.13) beat GPT-4 (.20) yet not the crowd (.07).

problem: Damani et al. (ECE 0.37 to 0.03 HotpotQA, 0.26 to 0.10 math, in-domain), Turtel et al. (1,265 Polymarket questions, ensemble-7 Brier .190, ECE .062; market .151 so .039 worse) and Leng et al. (CDPO reduces ECE by over 50% vs DPO) verified. Caveats: Leng's method calibrates the reward model's confidence scoring, not a Brier-style reward; 'needs weight updates' is an inference.

Verified: Yoon et al. (confidence often above 85% on incorrect answers, more overconfident with deeper reasoning, introspection helped o3-Mini/R1 but not Claude 3.7 Sonnet), Bench to the Future (Sonnet 4 .1560 vs Thinking .1597, p=.53), KalshiBench (Brier .433 vs .227; 26x tokens, 2M vs 138K), Sarfati (+1.9 pp free vs forced). But the KalshiBench contrast is between two different models (GPT-5.2-XHigh vs Claude Opus 4.5), not a controlled reasoning-effort comparison, so it cannot show reasoning caused the worse Brier.
fix: More reasoning does not help calibration or forecast Brier in the sources read: reasoning models are overconfident (confidence often above 85% on wrong answers) and more so with deeper reasoning (Yoon et al.); thinking mode did not improve Claude Sonnet 4 on pastcasting (.1560 vs .1597, p=.53); introspection helped o3-Mini and R1 but hurt Claude 3.7 Sonnet. KalshiBench found the extended-reasoning GPT-5.2-XHigh (26 times more tokens) had Brier .433 vs .227 for Claude Opus 4.5, though this compares different models; an 8B forecaster's free reasoning added only +1.9 points accuracy over forced answering.

problem: Kapoor (about 1,000 graded examples suffice), Halawi (isotonic/binning no gain; RMS calibration error .42 vs crowd .38), Kotawala (Platt-only REL .0004 vs raw .0357 = 99% reduction; config lists 30% fit / 70% eval split though a table caption says the 30% slice was not used for fitting) and Foresight Arena (n about 0.139/delta^2: 348 for .02, 1,392 for .01 under stated assumptions of base rate .5, |market-forecast| .15, one-sided alpha .05, 80% power) verified. Minor: the Foresight power numbers hold only under those assumptions.

Paleka et al. (date-restricted 'jan 6' search leak; questions resolved early/logically implied), Hambly et al. Bench to the Future (effective sample 178.8 from manual down-weighting of correlated questions) and ForecastBench (evaluates on unresolved questions, so no ground truth exists to leak) verified. Slight inference: ForecastBench 'avoids leaks' is a design property, not an empirical test.

Afifi et al. (n=265: Opus 4.5 soft-Brier .256 vs trained .254; uncertain subset n=104: Opus .281, crowd .232; price worth +.04 to +.075 Brier), KalshiBench (BSS +.057 Claude Opus 4.5 best of five; -.799 GPT-5.2-XHigh) and Ding et al. (agent-market r .97-.99, 104 matches) verified. Caveat: soft-Brier imputes .25 for unanswered questions, which pulls scores toward 0.25; KalshiBench contrast is between different models.

Huang et al. (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8), Tyen et al. (BIG-Bench Mistake, GPT-4 39.80 whole-trace vs 52.87 direct-step) and Kang et al. (over 90% of reflections confirmatory) verified. Slip: 39.8 to 52.9 is a range across prompting methods for locating mistakes (best only 52.87), not an improvement from a fix; Kang's count of 8 models taken from the paper's setup.

Liao et al.: average final accuracy falls 40% (43% on hard questions) when the first step is wrong; Table 1 shows DS-R1-Qwen-7B 94.8 vs 28.5. Kang et al.: reflections after first answer use 16.8% to 47.8% of tokens for only +1.4% to +3.5% accuracy. All on math/science reasoning benchmarks; neither paper tests 'frame choice', so 'frame choice early matters more than review late' is an extrapolation. Minor: tokens range is 16.8-47.8%, not 17-48 exactly (rounding).
fix: In long-CoT reasoning models on math and science benchmarks, the first answer or first step dominates the result: final accuracy falls about 40% on average when the first reasoning step is wrong (DS-R1-Qwen-7B 94.8 vs 28.5 in a perturbation test), and reflection after the first answer adds only 1.4-3.5% accuracy while using 16.8-47.8% of tokens (Liao et al.; Kang et al.).

problem: Lou and Sun (GPT-4o, GPT-4, GPT-3.5 Turbo; hints shift answers; Chain-of-Thought, Thoughts of Principles, Ignoring Anchor Hints and Reflection 'not sufficient'; comprehensive hints from multiple angles needed) and Huang et al. SynAnchors (22-61% of questions anchored; conventional strategies cannot eliminate it, reasoning offers some mitigation) verified. Caveat: Lou and Sun is a small single-author-pair workshop-style study, and 'helps in part' for opposing anchors is a mild reading of 'collect hints from comprehensive angles'.

Huang et al. ICLR 2024 (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 then 41.8, GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 after two rounds) and Kamoi et al. survey (no prior work shows success with prompted-LLM feedback outside exceptionally suited tasks) verified; Tyen/Stechly consistent. Minor: GPT-4 CSQA and HotpotQA changes are small or mixed, so 'often' is fair, not 'always'.

Kamoi et al. (reliable external feedback works; decomposable responses are exceptionally favourable for self-correction; large-scale fine-tuning also works) and Chen et al. Self-Debugging (up to 12% gain with unit tests on TransCoder, 8% on MBPP with execution feedback) verified. Minor: Kamoi lists large-scale fine-tuning as a third route that the claim omits.

The 36% self-critique drop is DeepSeek-R1 only (the largest gap among o1-like models), not a general figure; also the 55% invalid-output figure is the R1-Qwen-1.5B OmniMath cell (51.4% on OlympiadBench).
fix: Error location without ground truth stays hard: the best critic on long reasoning chains reaches F1 40.8 (DeltaBench, GPT-4-turbo), and self-critique is weaker than critique of other models (DeepSeek-R1 shows the largest gap, 36% lower); a plain reasoning-model judge produces invalid output in up to 55% of cases (R1-Qwen-1.5B, OmniMath subset) while a fine-tuned verifier with forced step checks (ThinkPRM) reaches F1 about 86 to 87 on ProcessBench Olympiad/OmniMath subsets.

problem: Chen et al. text says over 92% of cases correct in first round but its Figure 5 shows 89-90% for some model/dataset cells; numbers rest on that one paper, others (AdaptThink, Shojaee) support only the qualitative overthinking claim.

The quoted DEER and Certaindex numbers are right, but 'no accuracy loss' is too strong: answer-convergence paper reports a 0.2% drop on GSM8K/QwQ, and DEER drops on some cells (Qwen3-14B GPQA 60.1 to 57.6, another model GSM8K 96.7 to 96.3).
fix: Stable-answer or transition-point early exit shortens current open reasoning chains with little or no accuracy loss on most benchmarks: DEER (R1-Distill-Qwen-7B AIME24 41.7 to 49.2 with 13,765 to 9,839 tokens; MATH-500 87.4 to 89.8 with 3,858 to 2,143; small drops on some cells of other models), Certaindex up to 50% compute saved at the same accuracy, answer convergence at about 60% of steps (0.2% drop on GSM8K with QwQ-32B). A stable wrong answer is not caught.

problem: Liu et al. say reflection is not positively correlated with accuracy (measured on R1-Zero after RL, not base models); wording slightly looser than source.

Numbers check out (Helms 2008: 4/9 and 5/10 solution-driven projects; Goel & Hancock 2021: 27/74 = 36.5%), but all three sources (Helms et al., Goel & Hancock, Vattam & Goel) come from Goel's Georgia Tech lab, so there is one research group behind the evidence.
fix: Human bio-inspired design starts from either end: problem-driven (reframe the problem in biological terms, then search) or solution-based (start from a biological solution, then look for a problem). Solution-based work is common in the Georgia Tech lab's data (4/9 and 5/10 course projects; 27/74 case studies, 36.5%); independent confirmation from another group is not shown.

problem: Counts verified in Goel & Hancock Table 8 (22/27 = 81.5% vs 14/47 = 29.8%, Fisher p<0.001, using the authors' reclassification; the earlier classification in Table 7 gave 9/10 vs 27/64), but the corroborating Helms 2008 source is the same lab and only a small class sample (100% vs 60%).
fix: Solution-based (source-first) designs were more often multifunctional than problem-driven ones in one meta-analysis of 74 Design Study Library cases (22/27, 81.5% vs 14/47, 29.8%; Fisher p<0.001, authors' reclassified labels); a small earlier class study from the same lab points the same way. Single-lab evidence.

problem: Vattam & Goel 2013 gives 6/9 (Fall 2006) and 4/10 (Fall 2007, not 2008) compound solutions, and Goel & Hancock say compound analogy is rare with solution-based design, but all sources are from the same lab, and the 'in 2008' label is the paper year, not the cohort year.
fix: Compound analogies (several sources combined) were frequent in Georgia Tech bio-inspired design course teams (6/9 in Fall 2006, 4/10 in Fall 2007) and, in the lab's 74-case meta-analysis, are rarer with solution-based design (so associated with problem-driven design). Single-lab evidence.

problem: The bullet-to-'prevent, withstand and heal damage' example is in Helms et al. 2008, but it is a described process step in a class, not evidence that reframing is the step that opens retrieval; Hope et al. 2017 supports only that purpose/mechanism abstraction improves machine retrieval of product analogies.
fix: Reframing the problem in abstract, biology-ready function terms is the second step of the problem-driven bio-inspired design process taught in the Georgia Tech course ('stopping a bullet' became 'prevent, withstand and heal damage'), and separate work on product descriptions finds that purpose/mechanism abstraction improves analogy retrieval; no study isolates reframing as the step that opens retrieval for human designers.

problem: In Dekel et al. Exp 1, 61.9% (13/21) is the surface-schema (and first-order-schema) condition retrieving its matched story and 11.6% is the retrieval rate of that story in other conditions; the higher-order condition retrieved its story 40.9% (9/22) vs 11.9% elsewhere; Exp 2's 37.3% vs 10.8% is the modified higher-order cue condition after a comparison, not unaided retrieval. Puranam et al. is not about retrieval.
fix: After comparing two stories, people retrieved a surface-matched story 61.9% of the time (vs 11.6% in other conditions) but a higher-order (structural) match only 40.9% (vs 11.9%) in Exp 1; in Exp 2 the higher-order condition reached 37.3% vs 10.8% elsewhere (Dekel, Burns and Goldwater, preprint). Without a schema-inducing comparison, retrieval of structural analogues is rare (about 11 to 12%).

problem: All numbers (HR 20.3 to 37, factory 6.3 to 8.7, Gick-Holyoak 29 to 50) come from Puranam et al. alone (the G-H figures are quoted second-hand); Dekel et al. has no hint data; 'modestly' is the paper's relative wording, though HR nearly doubled.

Kulikowski's numbers are right (skeleton AP 0.222 to 0.513 vs abstract with TF-IDF, 18 method families) and BARCODE's 72% vs 36% at top 7 is right (strategy sentences, entire data), but BARCODE compares its whole system against a different baseline system, so it does not isolate a domain-stripped or function-focused representation.
fix: Domain-stripped representations improve cross-domain retrieval in one 18-family benchmark (skeleton fingerprint raised average precision from 0.222 to 0.513 over TF-IDF on abstracts); BARCODE, which retrieves challenge/strategy sentences, got 72% vs 36% strategy precision at top 7 against a different baseline system, which supports sentence-level strategy extraction but is not an ablation of representation.

problem: Jung et al. figures all verified (best of 11 retrievers 0.26, LLM reranker 0.81, fine-tuning up to 0.70, HyDE+BM25 0.16 to 0.44); the retrievers are tested on scientific-paper cross-pollination, not general analogy.

AnaloBench T2 (about random) and StoryAnalogy figures (ChatGPT ~30%, text-davinci-003 37.1%, human 85.7%, chance 25%) check out, but 37.1% is not 'near chance', and the clause that LLMs do better when mapping a given pair is not supported by AnaloBench/StoryAnalogy (Puranam et al. only shows GPT-4 solving strategy problems with a hint).
fix: LLMs are close to random at retrieving analogues from a large story bank (AnaloBench T2, 200+ stories) and weak at StoryAnalogy multiple choice (ChatGPT about 30% and text-davinci-003 37.1% vs human 85.7%, where chance is 25%).

problem: 70.05% (175B, no-source prompt) vs 66.67% human verified in Bhavya et al.; with a source concept given humans beat the 175B model (71.88 vs 53.79), and the 6.7B model reaches 48%, so 'small models mostly fail' fits the 0.3B and 1.3B models best; Ding et al. does not bear on scale.

Ding et al. figures verified (median helpfulness 4/5, observable reformulation changes in 80%, upper bound 25% potentially harmful), but Ma et al. found LLM concepts more feasible/useful and less novel than crowd concepts, with a 'diverse' prompt word helping in one prompt and hurting in another, so 'less diverse unless prompted' is not what the source shows.
fix: LLM analogies as inspiration helped designers on a problem reformulation task (median helpfulness 4/5; observable changes to problem formulations in 80% of cases), with up to 25% of outputs rated potentially harmful (mostly upsetting rather than biased); in a separate study LLM-generated design concepts were rated more feasible and useful but less novel than crowdsourced ones, and prompt wording changed their similarity to the crowd set unpredictably.

problem: BioSpark numbers all verified (novelty 3.9 to 7.1, feasibility 6.8 to 5.7, value 3.8 to 7.0, species 4.6 to 8.2, ideas 5.5 to 10.3, 12 participants), but a feasibility drop alongside much higher value in one small study is not a demonstrated novelty-feasibility cost, and Chan et al. 2011 reports far-field examples raised novelty and quality variability, not lower feasibility.
fix: In one small within-subject study of an LLM-supported bio-inspired design tool (BioSpark, 12 participants, blind expert ratings), novelty rose 3.9 to 7.1 and value 3.8 to 7.0 while feasibility fell 6.8 to 5.7; unique species rose 4.6 to 8.2 and ideas 5.5 to 10.3. Feasibility dipped as novelty rose, but value also rose strongly.

problem: The filter-pass rates and bird share come only from Zhu et al.'s single flying-car case with fine-tuned GPT-3 (Table 5 lists 50% to 84%, not 58-84%; birds >50% of analogues is stated), while BioinspiredLLM (materials Q&A) and the SAPPhIRE RAG tool report nothing on filters, birds or weak structure-level evaluation.
fix: In one flying-car case study with fine-tuned GPT-3 (Zhu et al.), generated bio-inspired concepts passed the automatic relevancy classifiers at roughly 50 to 84% depending on generator and check, and birds made up over 50% of the retrieved analogues; BioinspiredLLM (materials questions) and a RAG tool for SAPPhIRE models show that fine-tuned or retrieval-grounded LLMs can produce usable bio-inspired content, but they were not evaluated at the structure level.

problem: Numbers verified (BARCODE: 40-100 h to hand-describe one organism in the SBF framework, and 3.36% of 3,416 PubMed articles gave design insight, citing Kaiser et al. 2012; Vattam & Goel: about 3 person-hours per relevant article, a rough estimate from one 6-person team), but 40-100 h is the cost of curating a structured database entry, not of looking up biology, and Helms & Goel 2013 contains none of these figures.
fix: Finding and encoding biology is expensive for humans: hand-describing one organism in a structured framework takes 40 to 100 hours (BARCODE paper), only 3.36% of 3,416 heuristically filtered PubMed articles gave design insight (Kaiser et al. 2012, as cited), and one design team spent roughly 3 person-hours of search per relevant article (rough estimate, Vattam and Goel 2013), so automated retrieval has headroom.

problem: TRIZ-GPT numbers verified (recall 0.675 to 0.245 with few-shot, precision 0.259 to 0.333), but AutoTRIZ's 7/10 means 'complete or half match to the textbook's contradiction analysis within the top 3 detections', not 7 of 10 cases fully matched.
fix: TRIZ-style LLM pipelines are only moderately accurate: AutoTRIZ's contradiction detections matched or half-matched the textbook analysis within the top 3 detections in 7 of 10 textbook cases, and TRIZ-GPT few-shot prompting lowered recall (0.675 to 0.245) while raising precision (0.259 to 0.333).

problem: ARCANA figures verified (best model GPT 5.2 51.20% / 48.33% by typo scoring vs human average 68.96% / 58.35%, wide spread: Claude Opus 4.5 8.61%), but ARCANA is whole-benchmark, not 'hard tasks', and neither source compares mapping a given analogy with finding one (ANALOGICAL tests identifying analogous pairs via embeddings and finds harder analogy levels harder).
fix: On the ARCANA far-analogy mapping benchmark the best model (GPT 5.2) scores about 48-51% against human averages of 58-69%, with a large spread between models (Claude Opus 4.5 about 7-9%); this shows far analogical mapping is still unsolved, not that mapping is easier than finding an analogy.

problem: FaulT-Bench (SADE 24%, ReAct 16%, Claude Code 11% over-diagnosis on answered runs; 74% in one agent/vague-ticket cell) and AIOpsLab (only GPT-4-W-SHELL passed the 2 Noop problems, 3 of 4 agents false-positive) check out, but 'has not been tested by anyone' is an unsupported universal negative.
fix: A separate evaluate-after-repair check is needed and the agent must be allowed to conclude 'no fault': on healthy networks agents report a fault in 11-24% of answered runs (FaulT-Bench, standard ticket; up to 74% for one agent with a vague ticket), and 3 of 4 agents did so on AIOpsLab's 2 no-fault problems. We found no study that tests a no-fault exit plus verify gate as a fix.

problem: All figures verified (UoT 43.7 to 67.3 closed-set GPT-4 troubleshooting, +33.8% over CoT-SC and +29.9% over Reflexion; SIA 79.2 vs 75.0; BED-LLM GPT-4o Animals 93 vs Implicit Max. 70 vs Split 83; QuestBench 40-50% on Logic-Q/Planning-Q); the identity of the 43.7 baseline column is unclear from the garbled UoT table.

All figures verified (SADE 0.77 vs 0.55 same-backbone vs ReAct 0.44 in text / 0.40 in abstract and Fig. 1, +21.5 points; Flow-of-Action 64.01 vs 35.50; SIA 79.2 vs 69.0 with overlapping CIs; median input tokens 344k/189k/55k); the SADE paper itself reports two different ReAct F1 values, and SADE and FaulT-Bench share authors but that does not affect this claim.

SADE tokens (344k vs 189k vs 55k median input) and SIA question count (5.2 vs 2.8) verified; Jacovi et al. found strong no-tool baselines competitive with tool-assisted strategies at orders of magnitude more tokens (QA/math tasks, not diagnosis); SADE and SIA are different groups.

GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 (5 self-correction calls) and the Kamoi et al. 'no fair demonstration except tasks where verification is much easier' are verified, but 'gains appear only with an oracle or external feedback' omits that Kamoi et al. also report large-scale fine-tuning enabling self-correction.
fix: Intrinsic self-correction without an external signal does not help and can hurt (GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 after five rounds); gains appear with an oracle, reliable external feedback, or large-scale fine-tuning. Kamoi et al. survey: no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs except in tasks where verification is much easier than generation.

problem: MAST percentages are right (step repetition 15.7, unaware of termination 12.4, wrong assumptions 6.8) and AIOpsLab does show repeated API calls and apologise-retry loops, but no failure mode dominates: reasoning-action mismatch (13.2%) and disobeying task specification (11.8%) are larger than wrong assumptions, and task derailment (7.4%) is larger than 6.8%.
fix: Multi-agent LLM failures are spread over many modes; among the most frequent in MAST are step repetition (15.7 percent), reasoning-action mismatch (13.2), not recognizing task completion (12.4) and disobeying the task specification (11.8), with proceeding on wrong assumptions at 6.8; AIOpsLab shows repeated-call and apologise-retry loops.

problem: Explanation-only 2-3 point gain on Spider holds for Codex (81.3 to 84.1); GPT-3.5 gains 1.1 and GPT-4 0.4, so 'nothing on strong models' is approximate.

The 32.67% leakage and the 12.47 to 3.97% drop come from one agent (SWE-Agent+GPT-4, 251 resolved SWE-bench Full patches) and the drop reflects filtering both leakage and weak-test patches; the claim reads as general.
fix: Passing SWE-bench tests does not show the defect was fixed: PatchDiff re-validation found 7.8% of plausible patches (counted correct) fail the developer-written test suite (Wang et al.), and in a manual audit of 251 SWE-Agent+GPT-4 patches passing SWE-bench Full, 32.67% involved solution leakage and 31.08% passed on weak tests; filtering both dropped that agent's resolution rate from 12.47% to 3.97% (SWE-Bench+).

problem: Sensitivity rises with reasoning depth for only five of eight biases, and awareness prompts gave mixed results (some gain for anchoring in Llama, partial for primacy), not uniformly little.
fix: Telling a model to be aware of bias helps little or inconsistently (Echterhoff et al.: small gains, better for anchoring and primacy in some models, rewriting the prompt works better); models can often recognise a bias without resisting it, and sensitivity rose with Prolog reasoning depth for five of eight biases, up to 49% (Sovrano et al.).

problem: Agent-failure half rests on one small 50-task study (silent semantic failure was 68-80% of failing runs for two of four models).

The opened surveys and design papers (Rissland et al. 2006, Bench-Capon 1997) do show worked examples and one blind expert-graded test (GREBE) and no accuracy figures, but the sources are only a survey and design papers, and factor-based systems such as IBP were evaluated quantitatively elsewhere, so the field-wide claim is wider than the sources.
fix: In the surveys and design papers read (Rissland, Ashley and Branting 2006; Bench-Capon 1997, 1999, 2012), factor-based symbolic legal CBR is illustrated mostly by worked examples, with one small blind expert-graded comparison (GREBE vs law students) and no quantitative accuracy reported.

problem: Two papers only: the best micro-F1 is 28.7 (ReaKase-8B, COLIEE 2022/23) and 25.5 (Sha et al., Indian legal documents, not COLIEE); the paper calls the internal-vs-official gap (MRR 0.97 vs 0.14) a validation mismatch, not leakage.
fix: In two recent studies, legal case retrieval stays hard: ReaKase-8B reaches micro-F1 28.7 on COLIEE 2023 (BM25 21.4) and a four-stage pipeline on an Indian prior-case task reaches 25.5, with lexical BM25 a strong baseline; in the latter, rankers with internal MRR up to 0.97 scored as low as 0.14 on the official evaluation, so internal validation can badly overstate performance.

problem: Savelka et al. F1 .51-.57 is for classifying sentences by value for interpreting a statutory concept (not legal factors), and in Gray et al. human-refined factors did not reliably beat canonical ones for LLM annotation (llama 0.56 vs 0.52 ElasticNet but 0.46 vs 0.61 RF; gpt-4o 0.30 vs 0.32); they only beat LLM-refined factors.
fix: LLM annotation of legal text is mediocre: GPT-4 reached F1 .51 to .57 classifying court-opinion sentences by their value for interpreting a statutory concept (Savelka et al. 2023), and annotating drug-stop cases with canonical factors gave MCC 0.32 (gpt-4o) to 0.52 (llama) with ElasticNet (Gray et al. 2024); human-refined factors beat fully LLM-refined ones but did not reliably beat canonical factors.

problem: Going from about 43% (GPT-4 closed-book) to 17-33% is a relative cut of about 23% to 60%, not 'a third to a half'; the tools are commercial legal RAG products, not generic retrieval.
fix: Commercial legal RAG tools (Lexis+ AI, Westlaw AI-Assisted Research, Ask Practical Law AI) hallucinate 17% to 33% of the time versus about 43% for closed-book GPT-4 (a relative cut of roughly 23% to 60%), so retrieval reduces but does not remove errors; the dangerous residue is a real case cited for a holding it does not contain (misgrounding).

problem: The 45% extra tokens for wrong gpt-5 answers is for legal Task 2 only (4,456 vs 3,081); the 'relative trigger, not absolute cap' conclusion is the researcher's inference.

Only IFPV (listed twice) supports it, on 7 plans from one simulator; Vidra et al. is a synthetic best-response benchmark that does not test static LLM ranking or rule-based checks, and 0.72 to 0.86 is single-step LLM vs the multi-agent planner (MPHA).
fix: In one study (IFPV, 7 candidate plans), an LLM's static ranking of plans disagreed with the ranking from simulation against a fine-tuned world-model adversary, and plans passing a rule-based validator were suppressed by that adversary; its multi-agent planner raised mission success from 0.72 (single-step LLM) to 0.86.

problem: Kambhampati et al. adds the argument but no new numbers; 38.1 is after round 1 (3 calls), 89.0 after round 2 (5 calls).

All numbers come from the Kambhampati/Valmeekam group (the 82%/70% figures are VAL back-prompting results from their earlier paper, cited in the position paper; obfuscated Blocksworld only about 10%); the only outside source (IFPV) does not give these numbers.
fix: One research group (Kambhampati, Valmeekam et al.) reports that about 12% of GPT-4 plans were executable and goal-reaching, and that back-prompting with the external VAL verifier raised LLM accuracy to 82% on Blocksworld and 70% on Logistics (about 10% on obfuscated Mystery Blocksworld); this supports pairing LLM generators with external critics, but is one lab's evidence.

problem: The 38% revision flip is PaLM 2-S* on MATH with a trained revision model (Snell et al.), and the 8-16% flips are on one Yes/No task; wording is slightly wide but numbers match.
'Fixing it is easy' is slightly generous: even with the true location, backtracking cost up to 11 points on originally correct traces.
The 94% obedience is for GPT-4 on graph colouring only.
The 87.3 to 70.3 figure is for a 1.5B distilled model (R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B) on GSM8K.

47.9/29.5/24.8 are one PRM (Math-Shepherd-PRM-7B on GSM8K/MATH/OlympiadBench), not open PRMs generally; Skywork-PRM-7B scores 70.8 on GSM8K, and the PRM average (e.g. 42.1 Skywork, 56.5 PRM800K PRM) is closer to non-reasoning critics.
fix: Reasoning-trained models locate the first wrong step better than most non-reasoning critics and small trained process reward models on ProcessBench (F1 o1-mini 87.9, QwQ-32B-Preview 71.5, GPT-4o 61.9, Llama-3.3-70B 58.0; Math-Shepherd-PRM-7B 47.9/29.5/24.8 on GSM8K/MATH/OlympiadBench), but they still flip correct answers when told to revise (DeepSeek R1 7.9% on a yes/no task).

problem: Debate comparison is GPT-3.5 on GSM8K only; graph-colouring resampling result is GPT-4 on 100 instances.

The 0.60 HELM agreement is for model pairs in general, not specifically different-company pairs; the ambiguous '(corrected, see critique)' remark is fine since Valmeekam's text (38 false positives; 54+7=61 correct) supports 38 of 45 invalid plans accepted, though its Table 2 headers are misaligned.
Kamoi's 16.9 +/- 20.3 is reported as percent higher recall between two prompt types (Type 1 vs Type 2), averaged over 12 LLMs and 3 tasks.
Numbers match Kumar et al. Table 1/2, but plain SFT is not uniformly non-positive: Pair-SFT gave +1.8 (small, vs SCoRe +4.4 called the first significantly positive delta); STaR+ +0.4.
fix: Training (multi-turn RL, SCoRe) gives the first significantly positive intrinsic self-correction on MATH (60.0 -> 64.4, +4.4; correct-to-incorrect flips 15.8% -> 1.4%), whereas prompting and offline SFT variants give negative or small deltas (base -11.2; Self-Refine -1.0; STaR base-data -14.2, STaR+ +0.4; Pair-SFT +1.8). Needs weights, so not a scaffold.

problem: Blavier et al. quote Doireau: self-detected errors are recovered in ~90% of cases, but ~30% is the rate of error detection by a third person (not recovery), so the two are not a like-for-like comparison; the review also notes Doireau's own experiments found the opposite (observers detected mistakes more easily than slips); slips are caught mostly via intention-vs-action mismatch (Sellen action-based), not plan-vs-outcome.
fix: Humans catch slips (execution errors) themselves, mostly through mismatch between intention and the executed action, while diagnosis errors (mistakes) usually need an outside view (Woods; Sellen). Per a review (Blavier et al. 2005) quoting Doireau et al. 1997: self-detected errors are recovered in about 90% of cases, while detection by a third person is infrequent (about 30%); outsiders detect better if they are domain experts, if the error is a mistake, and if detection is close in time to the error.

problem: Perneger 30.6% is the share who correctly placed active error as a hole; 'no measured effect size for agents' is an absence claim not checked exhaustively.

Minor: HF chance baseline is ~0.127 (rounded to 0.12); Weaver does report verifier score correlations (Table 16), only same-family joint miss rates are unmeasured; 'less than Swiss-cheese arithmetic predicts' is an inference.
Self-consistency AUROC 0.823 is for Qwen2.5-3B on MATH-500 only; gap-search statements are absence claims.

Numbers match (He 0.062 vs 0.384; Shirali 0.03-0.09 vs 0.01-0.02), but the headline generalises from one lab task and one petrochemical case to 'classical tools disagree and lack validation'; He did a rough indirect check (21 injuries, Heinrich ratio) so 'not checked' is not strictly true, and Shirali itself describes CREAM vs CREAM-BN as consistent/partly confirmed.
fix: In one university-lab task (23 students, 14 actions) CREAM gave a mean HEP of 0.062 versus 0.384 for SPAR-H (about six-fold), with only a rough indirect check against injury records; in a petrochemical control-room case a Bayesian CREAM variant gave HEPs of 0.03-0.09 vs 0.01-0.02 for basic CREAM, with no comparison to observed errors. Two case studies do not show that classical human-reliability tools generally disagree or lack validation. CREAM control-mode intervals were only seen in secondary sources.

problem: Minor: 0.3% is Direct Prompting/Binary Search all-correct on AgentErrorBench; 'beats unguided retry' rests on the paper's stated comparison with scaling rollouts and unguided self-revision.
Chen reports debugging mostly ends within 3 turns; 'unproven' equal-token edge is an absence claim supported by Olausson (1.05x/0.97x pass@20 at equal samples).

March's finding (slow learning gives higher equilibrium, fast learning reaches equilibrium sooner) is confirmed in Rodan (replicated base model with code March shared) and Chanda et al. (qualitative conformance), but Kavanagh is a historical book chapter that only restates March's result and does not run or reproduce the model.
fix: In a March-type mutual-learning model, slow individual learning keeps diversity and gives a higher final knowledge level, while fast learning reaches equilibrium sooner but lower. Rodan replicated March's base model using code March shared, and Chanda et al. qualitatively reproduced it; Kavanagh only restates March's result.

problem: All turnover/socialisation numbers (peak near 1%, 8% static / 42% dynamic, ambiguity about relative vs absolute, reversal above ~3% / ~10%) are confirmed in Rodan (2005), but that is the only source: the three listed entries include Rodan twice and Kavanagh, which says nothing about turnover; the result is one author's simulation and should be worded as Rodan's finding.

The 'update' that finds processed (importance-weighted) history crucial is Park et al. (2024) as described in Krishnamurthy et al. v3 related work, not Nie et al.; Nie et al. (EVOLvE) show algorithm-guided summary statistics improve performance but raw-history and fine-tuned variants also work, so 'needed' is too strong for Nie.
fix: Krishnamurthy et al. found that only a prompt with a code-summarised history (plus exploration hint and chain of thought) made GPT-4 explore; they note the updated Park et al. (2024) paper finds GPT-4 and GPT-4o succeed with an importance-weighted history and fail without it, which they read as consistent (pre-processing the history is crucial). Nie et al. (EVOLvE) report that algorithm-guided summary statistics help LLM bandit performance (e.g. win rate Flash 27.7 -> 32.2, Pro 45.5 -> 59.6 multi-armed), but not that they are strictly needed; prompts and horizons differ across these works.

problem: Binz & Schulz (GPT-3: no directed exploration, random exploration but not strategic), Nie et al. (Flash: minimal directed exploration via MinFrac) and Zhang et al. (basic LLMs: more random, little directed exploration) agree, but Zhang et al. also find that thinking/reasoning models raise directed exploration to human level (o3-mini above human) in the stationary task, so 'LLMs show little directed exploration' only holds for non-thinking models and fails in the 4-armed task only partly.
fix: Independent groups find little directed exploration (uncertainty bonus) and mostly random exploration in non-reasoning LLMs: GPT-3 on the horizon task (Binz & Schulz), Gemini-1.5 Flash on bandits (EVOLvE), and basic GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-flash and DeepSeek-V3 versus humans (Zhang et al.). Zhang et al. also find that chain-of-thought or reasoning models raise directed exploration to human level (o3-mini high thinking above human) in a stationary two-armed task, though not in a four-armed non-stationary task.

problem: Minor: in the stationary 2-armed task thinking LLMs reached human-like exploration, so 'deficit not removed' holds mainly for the restless 4-armed task.

Minor: AB-MCTS LiveCodeBench edge over sampling/refinement (38.9 vs 37.8) is within the reported spread, and for DeepSeek-V3 standard MCTS scored slightly higher (43.2 vs 43.0); the claim cites GPT-4o only.

Harms et al. (121 people, ages 10-13 vs 18-32) confirm two components and more directed exploration in adults with no age difference in random exploration; Wilson et al. confirm preschoolers show more directed exploration than 7-9 year-olds, but also say it is lower in 7-9 year-olds than adults, so directed exploration is not a simple rise with age (high in preschool, lower in middle childhood, rising again into early 20s), and random exploration decreases from preschool through adulthood.
fix: Human explore-exploit behaviour loads on two components (directed and random exploration; Harms et al., 121 people aged 10-13 and 18-32). Adults showed more directed exploration than early adolescents, with no age difference in random exploration. Across a wider age range the pattern is not monotonic: a review (Wilson et al. 2021) reports preschoolers show more directed exploration than 7-9 year-olds, with horizon-sensitive directed exploration weaker at 10-12 and strongest in the early 20s, and random exploration prevalent in preschoolers and decreasing through adulthood.

problem: Minor: debate-vs-self-consistency row pairing (83.0 vs 88.2 at 9) comes from a jumbled table; 'exploitation trap' is interpretive framing.
Minor: 24-39% is for the three best reasoning models named in the paper (24.2, 27.3, 39.0), not all reasoning models; link to failure is correlational (rho -0.779, 12 models).
Minor: the N=29 human data is Jhaveri et al.'s own small study, not Wason 1960 itself.

Minor: unit-test completion is .60/.64 for ReAct/Hypothesizer but .44 for Plan+Execute; 'failure is in chaining' is the authors' interpretation, not directly tested; ScienceAgentBench 42.2% is o1-preview which exceeds the 32.4% 'best' (the claim notes this).
Minor: SHELDON QNN drop is -0.117 on a 0-1 scale (about 11.7 points), so '6-10 points' is slightly off for that fourth benchmark; the three non-QNN drops are 6.00, 10.00, 9.17.

Numbers confirmed (31.5%/28.1%, data-blind 3.61/2.10/7.21%, 2.5K vs 2M+ iterations), but LLM-SR and LLM-SRBench are the same lab (Shojaee, Reddy et al.), and NewtonBench tests different things; also in LLM-SRBench Appendix F PySR is competitive or better on numeric accuracy (Acc0.1) and only worse on symbolic accuracy, so 'beats search without LLM priors' is not unqualified.

Numbers confirmed (Langley productions 1203/1119/1297/1150/4593; AI Feynman 100/100 vs 71), but 'no noise handling was seen in the sources read' is false: Langley says noise handling is by a tolerance parameter, Kramer et al. say BACON uses a tolerance for noise, and AI Feynman has a section testing dependence on added Gaussian noise.
fix: Classic heuristic data-driven systems rediscover simple laws from clean data: BACON.3 rediscovered five laws (ideal gas, Kepler, Coulomb, Ohm, Galileo) with 1,119-4,593 production firings each, and AI Feynman solved 100/100 Feynman-lecture equations vs 71 for earlier public software. Both address noise only partly: BACON uses a tolerance parameter, and AI Feynman reports how success degrades as Gaussian noise is added.

problem: Minor: ACRE 28% -> 59% is task accuracy for direct IO vs iterative refinement (T=3, N=5) with a symbolic interpreter.

Numbers match (OR 0.885 spanning zero for oracle error, OR 0.016 for bias; WILT best 14/50 = 28%), but oracle error is mistakes by the feedback-giving oracle, not the player misreading outcomes, so it does not show the failure is 'not in reading outcomes'; WILT itself finds models differ in whether they are better at choosing tests or at deducing the rule.
fix: In FalsifyBench, noise in the oracle's feedback does not explain failure (oracle error OR 0.885, interval spans zero), whereas the share of confirming tests strongly predicts it (OR 0.016), so the failure is tied to test choice. WILT reports that models strong in single-turn tests do poorly in the multi-turn game (best 14/50 = 28%), with some models better at choosing tests and others at deducing the rule from them.

problem: Minor: FalsifyBench starts with H strictly inside R, but later guesses can move to other relations (H inside R held in over 50% of turns for most models), so 'the one case' describes the starting condition.
Overall macro 6.0 to 15.0 and micro 72.4 to 77.8 match Shi Table; GSM-NoOp 8-shot claim matches Mirzadeh. (Evidence line a21 cites 2-step macro 8.3 to 20.0, not used in claim.)

Levy et al. 2024 report the opposite: padding from a different source (books) mostly hurts MORE than padding similar to the task. Also Adapala r=0.42/0.35 is residue-condition accuracy degradation vs task-embedding similarity (and the residue decline itself was non-significant, p=.12), not hop-recall drop.
fix: Not all extra text is equally harmful: related-but-wrong passages hurt most (up to -25 percent with one distractor, over -67 percent with several), while random unrelated documents sometimes helped (up to +35 percent, Llama2 on NQ-open). In Levy 2024, unrelated padding (books) mostly hurt more than task-similar padding, so padding similarity has no consistent direction. In Adapala 2025, degradation in the residue condition correlated with distractor-task embedding similarity (r 0.42 Gemini, 0.35 GPT-4o), though the residue decline was not significant overall. Shi 2023: in-topic sentences, overlapping role names and in-range numbers are the hardest distractors in arithmetic reasoning.

problem: In Lindenbauer Table 1 masking cut cost about 51-57% in four of five setups (the 41.5% figure is LLM-Summary on Gemini 2.5 Flash); in Qwen3-32B thinking masking cut only 9.8%. Solve-rate, turns (+15% vs masking, Gemini 2.5 Flash) and ACON 26-54% peak-token figures check out.
fix: Agent loops benefit from trimming history: observation masking (keep last 10 turns) cut cost about 51 to 57% versus the raw agent in 4 of 5 setups (only 9.8% in Qwen3-32B thinking) with solve rate equal within CIs in most setups (Lindenbauer 2025, SWE-bench Verified; Qwen3-Coder 53.4 raw, 54.8 masked, 53.8 summary), and ACON compression cut peak tokens 26-54%. Boundary: Gemini 2.5 Flash with thinking fell from 40.4 raw to 36.4 masked and 31.4 summarised, and summaries lengthened runs (+15% turns vs masking on Gemini 2.5 Flash). Software-engineering tool output only.

problem: Numbers match; 'method gaps smaller than template spread are not interpretable' is the claim-writer's inference from Voronov's finding that selection methods often lose to random once template spread is counted.

CogniLoad does not show accuracy falling as extraneous load rises: it finds task length the dominant stressor (steepest decline N=20 to 50 is a length effect) and a U-shaped response to distractor ratio. Adapala and ToolLoad numbers match.
fix: Cognitive-load-framed LLM benchmarks give mixed support for extraneous load hurting accuracy: Adapala 2025 (Gemini slope -0.003 per percent load, p<0.001; GPT-4o trend p=.07, 32 percent of outputs truncated) and ToolLoad (accuracy decays exponentially with total load, k 0.034 to 0.088, extraneous load degrades like intrinsic load) show declines, while CogniLoad (22 models) finds task length the dominant stressor (steepest decline between N=20 and 50) and a U-shaped, not monotonic, response to distractor ratio. Heterogeneous designs; only 2 of 5 Adapala models informative.

problem: All figures match (Mirzadeh -17.5/-29.1/-32.0; Gema Opus 4 and R1; Cats 4.50 vs 1.50). Minor: the Du 3.8-8.5 point GSM8K drops are from whitespace padding, not a distractor clause.
Numbers match RULER and Dhara; the multi-hop vs single-span contrast compares different datasets (HotpotQA vs SQuAD, n=200), so 'hard multi-step questions' is an interpretation.

KOMBINE 43.4/97.1 and PopBlends 56.7 are right, but PopBlends' 98.3% is the chance that at least one generated scene relates to a strong connecting concept (possibly only one domain), not 98.3% of scenes on-topic; Ge and Parikh show larger LMs give higher precision but do not say the property-finding step is the limiting step.
fix: The weak step in LLM blending appears to be choosing the bridge or shared abstraction, not building the blend. KOMBINE: valid generic space 43.4%, but 97.1% coherent blends once one is valid. PopBlends: connecting concept judged right 56.7% of the time, but given a strong connecting concept at least one generated scene relates to it 98.3% of the time. Ge and Parikh 2021 found larger language models propose better linking properties than smaller ones and than ConceptNet (precision rises with model size).

problem: Si numbers match (5%, 4000 seeds per topic, 5.64 vs 4.84, feasibility n.s.). 'KOMBINE found the same collapse' is loose: KOMBINE reports cross-model repetition (19.9% of concepts, 37.3% on blends), a milder and different measure than Si's 5% non-duplicates.
Lai recruited 29 but the ANOVA dfs (69) imply 24 analysed; all quoted statistics and RTs match.

Per Ritchie, Gibbs raised falsifiability and Harder raised needless complexity/scope (Harder is not a falsifiability critic); Glebkin could not be opened; Turner says blending is more a research-program framework than a theory and that the mental process does not appear algorithmic, not that it lacks a falsifiable hypothesis. a09 and b11 are the same Turner page.
fix: Blending theory is contested as a testable theory: Gibbs (as reported by Ritchie 2004) questions how it could be tested or falsified, Harder objects that it adds needless complexity to simple processes, and Ritchie argues the four-space structure follows from metaphors rather than data and impedes testable hypotheses. Turner (2013) concedes blending theory is more a framework for a research program than a theory, that evidence so far is mostly generalisation over in-sample data tested on out-of-sample data, and that the process itself does not appear to be algorithmic, so computer models are only suggestive.

problem: Numbers match (66%/75%, ICC 0.48, 43.3-53.3 vs 56.1, kappa .43), but Sato 2025 is a tone-modulation study whose only inconsistency is in its own phase-shift analysis, not model ratings of blend quality; KOMBINE itself calls panel ICC fair-to-good and leaderboard ranking stable; the PopBlends kappa is human-annotator reliability.
fix: Model judges give only moderate agreement with humans when scoring blend quality and creativity: the KOMBINE panel agreed with one author 66% overall and 75% when unanimous (ICC 0.48 for blend emergent utility, 0.67 for other blend dimensions, though leaderboard ranking was stable); LLM judges of research ideas reached 43.3 to 53.3% accuracy vs human reviewer consistency of 56.1% (Si et al.). Human annotators on PopBlends connecting concepts also agreed only moderately (kappa .43).

problem: All numbers match (table label offset in extraction aside). Caveat: CCPT Multi-Oracle is an upper bound selected using the metric, not an achievable filter, and 56.7% is the per-concept rate rather than a strict top-1.

VMetaphor numbers (18.9/67.9/69.2, +3.1 to +16.6) match, but 18.9% is the judge's structure-type identification on generated images, and the descriptive prompt details the visual realization rather than naming the structure. IEI measured 11 models (fusion higher precision in 9; its Fig. 5 caption even says the opposite) and only says this mirrors human patterns, with no human replacement-vs-fusion measurement.
fix: In VMetaphor-Bench (11 text-to-image models), images prompted for replacement metaphors were identified as replacement structure only 18.9% of the time versus 67.9% for fusion and 69.2% for juxtaposition; switching from a conceptual to a detailed descriptive prompt raised MCQ accuracy by 3.1 to 16.6 points on the representative models. In the IEI visual-mashup study, 9 of 11 models identified fusion mashups with higher precision than replacement ones, which the authors say mirrors human patterns.

problem: Matsuhira numbers match. Olearo et al.: embedding interpolation (TEXTUAL) was least preferred overall (but not in the Same-class category), and it is the only symmetric method, so order effects and first-concept dominance belong to SWITCH/ALTERNATE/UNET, not to interpolation.
fix: Blend outcome depends on how the inputs are weighted and ordered: interpolating two concept embeddings in Stable Diffusion gave blended depiction 0.621 at the midpoint but 0.389 averaged over all ratios (extremes about 0.14 to 0.26). In Olearo et al. (22 concept pairs, 100 participants), embedding interpolation was the least preferred of four blending methods overall (not for same-class pairs); it is order-symmetric, whereas the switching, alternating and U-Net methods are order-sensitive and often let the first concept dominate.

problem: Only Li et al. and CCPT are listed; neither supports the sentence that embedding models track human plausibility of novel-compound paraphrases less well (older models better), and neither shows LLMs follow humans 'least' on novel combinations. Li et al. found a high GPT-3 match to humans (Exp 1) but no convincing evidence of reasoning beyond lexical items (Exp 3); human CCPT figures 49.2/38.0/81% are right.
fix: Novel combinations are one place where LLM agreement with humans may rest on shallow cues: GPT-3's interpretations of novel noun compounds closely match human patterns (Exp 1), but when nonce words carry the artifact or natural-kind category (Exp 3) there is no convincing evidence it reasons beyond individual lexical items (Li, Carlson and Potts 2022). On CCPT, humans score 49.2 on emergent property induction, 38.0 on noun-phrase completion, and 81% on property-type accuracy.

problem: Binz and Schulz counts verified (128/155, 100/155, 0/155, chi2 13.0). Binz is the only full source (a01, b01, d14 are the same paper); Bilalic 2008 only restates Luchins roughly. The claim already states it is second-hand.

Binz (112/112, 111/112, 79/108, 59/108) and Crooks and McNeil (N=81; 76/22/27/0/12/7 percent; beta -0.15) match; the 1-set-problem condition (22%) is not strictly below the 5-problem one (27%) but the overall trend holds.

Anagram (RT 15.3 vs 13.4 s, accuracy ns) and programming (44% of 39 developers) check out, but none of the listed sources covers the DeCaro maths-equivalence, matchstick or Blech think-aloud statements (Bilalic cites Wiley and Frensch and Sternberg instead).
fix: The effect appears outside water jars: in anagrams a familiar word as the central string slowed solving (RT 15.3 vs 13.4 s, accuracy ns; Ellis and Reingold 2014), in programming about 44% of 39 developers showed a mental set (Sergeyuk et al. 2023), and knowledge acted as a set for baseball experts on misleading remote-associates items (Wiley 1998) and bridge experts adapting to rule changes (Frensch and Sternberg 1989), as cited in Bilalic et al. 2008.

problem: Binz simulation counts (90/84 of 100), ablation conclusion and per-condition beta settings, and Lovett and Anderson R2=.99 (binned; .66 per subject) all match.

Numbers match. 'Help more' is interpretive: MacGyver's self-reflect is itself a reflection prompt, and Huang's results concern self-correction on reasoning benchmarks rather than rigidity; Guan's cue effect is figure-only (stated).

Cheng figures (Table 1: GPT-OSS-20B 58.63 to 20.54, GPT-OSS-120B 61.01 to 48.51, Qwen3-32B 49.70 to 36.90, GPT-5 AIME25 87.50 to 81.73, 10-20% drops) and Weatherhead 85.36% of 567 match; Weatherhead is a different task (test-item writing) pooled into the same claim.

Cheng and Gumaan numbers match, but Bilalic et al. never told the chess players a better solution existed: failing players were just shown a different one-solution position, and the 148 vs 79 s gap was not significant (t(8)=1.67, p=.13).
fix: A rejected route keeps its pull. Explicit error labels and 'do not copy' lines did not restore clean-slate accuracy in reasoning models (Cheng et al. 2026). In small models (135M-1.7B) leaving the failed call in the transcript raised the probability of repeating it from 0.06 to 0.54 over a fixed candidate set; a 'do not repeat' instruction changed nothing; deleting the failed attempt and retrying from a clean context was the worst harness; replacing the verbatim call with a description removed 76% of the inversion (Gumaan 2026). Human parallel: chess players who had failed to find the shorter mate in a first position took about twice as long (148 vs 79 s) to find the optimal solution in a second, one-solution position, though not significantly in the first small study (Bilalic et al. 2008).

problem: Facts match, but Loewe et al. report a positive result (simple networks do show human-like abrupt insight switches, depending on regularised gating and gradient noise), which does not show that network analogues of the set are weak; Gu and Shi found the patch acted as a distractor, with slightly lower final patched accuracy (positive performance deficit), in one CIFAR-100 setting. Gu and Shi entries b27/c23 are the same paper.
fix: Network analogues of the set are limited: in one continual-learning setup (CIFAR-100 with a spurious patch) the networks showed no shortcut-induced rigidity, the patch acting as a distractor rather than a helpful shortcut (Gu and Shi 2025), and networks reproduce the human abrupt insight-like switch only with regularised gating and noise in gradient updates (Loewe et al. 2024). Neither tests LLM agents.

problem: The UCLA host carrying Holyoak and Thagard 1989 and Hummel and Holyoak 1997 was unreachable (timeouts, connection refused), so the ACME 'failed to settle without parameter changes' detail and the LISA simulations could not be checked; Forbus et al. 2017 (opened) only says rival models differ on enforcing systematicity and ACME has drawbacks, and a26 does not bear on the claim.

d=.60 (experiments) / .50 (tests), 57 experiments, 48% vs 16% dyads all verified; the opened meta-analysis text is the 2011 SREE abstract, and its control conditions are 'other instruction' broadly, not only separate study. The 50% vs 19% compares Exp 1B with the baseline of earlier Exp 1A.
Table 2 text extraction misaligns labels but values match; human 0.753 sample counts fine.
Numbers match Webb (p=.0039, .065, OR=.37) and StoryAnalogy (85.7%, ChatGPT 29-36%); science-analogy part is loosely worded.

Salthouse and Pink (2008, nearly 1,000 adults) varied WM-task set size, not Raven item difficulty (and found Gf effects slightly larger at higher set sizes); it does not test the item-wise WM-Raven curve. Unsworth and Engle show a slight decrease, Little 2014 a moderate increase.
fix: Across studies the WM-Raven item correlation does not reliably rise with item difficulty; flat, slightly falling or inverted-U curves are the usual result (Unsworth and Engle 2005 N=160; Smolen and Chuderski 2015 N=347 and 939, overlapping data; Burgoyne 2019; Dokic 2025 N=543 by item difficulty, rule tokens and latent growth models), though Little 2014 found a moderate increase. Salthouse and Pink 2008 (nearly 1,000) varied WM-task set size, not Raven item difficulty, and found Gf effects only slightly larger at higher set sizes. The Dokic review calls the evidence mixed with most studies null; its study count is not stated.

problem: Minor: Frischkorn and Oberauer note decreases at low demand beyond floor/ceiling, but the floor/ceiling inverted-U is Smolen and Chuderski's result as stated.

Numbers match Unsworth and Engle Table 3 and Little 2014 (beta .02, -0.10, Wiley values as cited); Little interprets the small interaction as support for the capacity view, which the claim does not mention.

Salthouse and Pink supports the set-size and trial-order point (latent r .74 and .86, but Gf effects were slightly larger at higher set sizes); Colom 2015 tested RAPM administration time (latent r .74 and .96 by time group, weighted .86), not set size or trials.
fix: The latent WM-Gf correlation is high (.74 to .96 across latent models) and was not reduced by larger set size or later trials in the WM tasks (Salthouse and Pink 2008, nearly 1,000 adults; Gf effects were if anything slightly larger at higher set sizes) or by longer Raven administration time (Colom 2015, weighted r = .86), so strong WM-Gf overlap does not by itself show a load-driven mechanism.

problem: Numbers match (45% drop RC 3 to 9, 24/32/44% explainable variance, fixed-RC larger inputs better on REL-A5/A6; Patil 100% through 12 branches, collapse 20-30); REL-A7 stays unsolvable, a nuance.

All numbers (0.92, 0.56, 0.60, 0.28, 0.25) match Gopnik et al. 2017, but the three human-evidence entries are the same paper, the 4-year-old and adult cells are Lucas et al. 2014 data from the same lab, and the GX-Chen paper only supplies the LLM paradigm; effectively one source.

Matches GX-Chen 2025 (Spearman 0.76 for information gain, deepseek-reasoner at times worse than random, o-mini higher effort lags in 8-object AND) and Samiei 2026 (gpt-5, deepseek-reasoner near-perfect OR, still behind top humans on AND); both papers share authors, and 'explore worse than random' applies to specific models (deepseek-reasoner).

Numbers match the Perspectives paper (GPT-4 75.9, Claude 58.16, adults 95.7); the arXiv v1 lacks GPT-4/Claude figures. 'Match' on imitation is approximate (GPT-4 83.3 vs children 88.4, adults 84.9). All sources share Gopnik's lab apart from Binz and Schulz.

Spearman -0.779 (p=.003, 12 models), OR 0.016, GPT-5.2-Chat 20% vs 50% match FALSIFYBENCH; Jhaveri reports positive I:C-success correlations in thinking and non-thinking Qwen3 variants. Correlational; labs are distinct (Cornell/NYU/Mila vs Trento).

ML1 (62.2% vs 33.5%, chi2=516.41, d=.60, 6344-73=6271) and Rachev (d=.69, N=88,181, 47 countries) check out, but the Many Labs 2 d=0.40 (N=7,228) is the trip/discount-item problem (Tversky and Kahneman 1981 mental accounting), not the Asian disease problem.
fix: Gain vs loss wording of the same Asian disease problem flips majority choice between subjects (72% sure option in gain wording, 22% in loss, 1981). Many Labs 1: 62.2% vs 33.5% sure option, chi2(1)=516.41, N=6,271, d=.60, 36 samples; 47-country COVID survey N=88,181 d=0.69. The replication swing is about 29 points, not 50. (Many Labs 2 d=0.40 concerns a different Tversky and Kahneman 1981 problem, the discounted-item trip, and should not be cited here.)

problem: All d values match (0.31, 0.52, 0.437, 0.56, 0.60, attribute 0.26; 51 studies, 151 estimates, ~13,500), but d of 0.3 to 0.6 is small-to-medium by Cohen's convention, not medium to large; Steiger and Kuhberger's 0.52 is the re-analysis of Kuhberger's data.
fix: Pooled human risky-choice framing effect is small to medium but reliable, not tiny: d 0.31 (Kuhberger 1998), 0.52 after p-curve correction for publication bias (Steiger and Kuhberger 2018), 0.437 (Pinon and Gambara 2005, 51 studies, 151 estimates, about 13,500 subjects), 0.56 (2016 studies), 0.60 (Many Labs 1). Heterogeneity is significant and attribute framing is smaller (0.26).

problem: Pinon and Gambara risky framing d=0.50 between vs 0.18 within (about 64% smaller); Kahneman 2003 and Broniatowski and Reyna support the thoughtfulness point (via LeBoeuf and Shafir).

Zhou et al. 2021 Type 2 57.22% vs 53.63%, N=1119 (df 1113); Type 3 gap 45.8 vs 20.7 points for classic; Broniatowski and Reyna 82/88 (93%); 'favours fuzzy-trace' is the proponents' reading, as the claim notes.

Rachev supports stress and concern raising the framing effect; Best and Charness (18 studies) find the age effect in gain frames driven by small-amount financial AND large-amount mortality scenarios, plus a younger-riskier effect in loss-framed high-amount mortality scenarios, so 'only in gain frame for mortality content' is wrong; 'lives-at-stake strengthens it' is not shown by either paper and the Nakamura foreign-language source could not be opened (page returned only a title).
fix: Context moderates the human effect: higher perceived stress and coronavirus concern went with a larger framing effect in the Disease problem (Rachev 2021, 88,181 participants); in a meta-analysis of 18 studies the age difference in risk taking depended on scenario (gain-framed small-amount financial and large-amount mortality items; loss-framed high-amount mortality items).

problem: Jones and Steinhardt Table 9 gives GPT-3 risky choice of 60.0% (die) vs 11.3% (save) for save probabilities below 0.5; 21.9% is the 0.5 bin and 28/78 are the human 1981 figures. Puutio and Do (27-42% violation range) and Payne (+1.84 max, 5 models) check out.
fix: LLMs reproduce the framing flip: GPT-3 chooses the risky option 60.0% of the time under the die framing vs 11.3% under the save framing for save probabilities below 0.5 (Jones and Steinhardt 2022); four 2025 models show 27-42% framing-violation rates on the Asian disease text (Puutio and Do, preprint); Payne 2025 five frontier models reach a framing effect of up to +1.84 on a 0-2 risk scale in some scenarios (others near zero or negative).

problem: All numbers check (CogBias +5.8 framing with backfires on others, Echterhoff GPT-4 -0.470/-0.410/-0.570 vs -0.405, FRAGILE CoT 28.6 to 57.1, Knipper framing scores for reasoning models); minor: FrameBench frame-robust prompting cut category change from 34.20% to 22.83%, an 11-point drop that is partial rather than none.
Echterhoff Table values (-0.405 to -0.010; GPT-3.5 +0.165 to -0.080; 2.7% framing in GPT-4; Llama-2 1.4%/0%) and DeFrame 92% framing-disparity reduction on BBQ match.

Pooled lambda 1.26 (32 models, 11 studies) is right, but 1.96 is only the strongest human meta-analytic estimate; the paper says 1.26 is compatible with more conservative human estimates (1.07, 1.31), and probability weighting rests on few studies.
fix: LLMs show modest loss aversion on described gambles (pooled lambda 1.26 across 32 models and 11 studies; below the strongest human estimate of 1.96 but compatible with more conservative human estimates of 1.07 and 1.31) and a human-like inverse-S probability weighting (on few studies); replacing numeric probabilities with verbal probability markers shifts LLM choices (Wang et al.).

problem: Payne p-values give o3 significant in 4 of 7 scenarios and Claude-4-Thinking in 6 of 7 (25 iterations per condition, Mann-Whitney); FrameBench GPT-5 33.40% category change and 7.12% same-frame disagreement match (table rows are shifted in the PDF text but the prose agrees). FrameBench is a recommendation task rather than story format.

PAL gives +15 points on GSM8K and +40 on GSM-Hard (larger numbers), supporting the gain-grows-with-difficulty point; Lawsen's function-output result is described as preliminary; Toolformer supports the general direction.

Nye et al. numbers match (8.8 to 20.1 few-shot; 31.8 to 50.7 fine-tuned), but Wei et al. report 46% of 50 incorrect chains (LaMDA 137B, GSM8K) were 'almost correct' with minor mistakes of three kinds (calculator error, symbol mapping error, one missing step); only the calculator errors are fixable by code, so 'slips that code could fix' overreaches.
