fix: A written scratchpad of intermediate steps lets models do multi-step computation they fail at in one pass (polynomial evaluation 8.8 to 20.1 few-shot, 31.8 to 50.7 fine-tuned). In a manual check of 50 wrong chains of thought (LaMDA 137B on GSM8K), 46% were almost correct with minor mistakes (calculator error, symbol-mapping error or one missing step), of which only the calculator errors are the kind code execution would fix.

problem: SWE-agent Table 3 (full file 12.7 vs 100 lines 18.0; iterative 12.0 vs summarized 18.0; full history 15.0 vs last-5 18.0) and Tran and Kiela averages (0.418 vs 0.379, 0.426 vs 0.387) match; at 10000 tokens the single chain's lead over Debate (0.423) and SAS-L (0.424) is only 0.002-0.003; CoThinker 0.95 vs 1.03 only partly traceable in the PDF text.

All Huang et al. numbers match (CSQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; GSM8K GPT-4 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; oracle 89.7); 'must come from environment' is the claim's inference, and Voyager's most important feedback (-73% without) is a GPT-4 self-verification module grounded in game state, so the signal is grounded rather than purely external.

Boldt and Gilbert (hit rate 88.1% vs 82.7%, F(1,361) so N=363), the Gilbert-lab framing paper (loss framing reduces over-offloading) and MeCo (Naive 61.9% vs Always Call 50.0%, Llama-3-8B) match; 'weak gate' is interpretive since the prompted check still beats always-call by about 12 points on a balanced set.

MAST (14 modes, 1600+ traces, +15.6% from a ChatDev verification step), Kim 2026 (260 configs, -39 to -70% planning, 45% ceiling), Tran and Kiela averages, Zhang 2025 (<=15% win rate vs CoT over 36 configs) and CoThinker ablation (style consistent, TMS model-dependent) all match; 'debate rarely beats self-consistency' is supported qualitatively.

Kim 2026 (260 configurations, -39% to -70% on planning, negative returns above about 45% single-agent performance) and Tran and Kiela (single chain better from 1000 thinking tokens on average; Sequential wins only at heavy context degradation, 0.7) match; Zhang 2025 gives supporting but separate evidence.

0.896 is correct, and the arXiv papers support correlation capping the gain (Kohli: 9 judges give about 2 independent votes), but Condorcet's theorem states independence plus p>0.5 as a sufficient condition for majority gain, not 'only if'; the claim's own second sentence concedes correlated voters can still gain.
fix: A majority vote beats a single voter when each voter is right more than half the time and errors are independent (Condorcet: n=3, p=0.8 gives 0.896); with p below 0.5 more voters make it worse. Correlated errors shrink the gain below the independent limit (a 9-judge LLM panel acts like about 2 independent votes, Kohli 2026).

problem: Kim et al. report ~60% agreement when both err on HELM, 0.97 for two Llama siblings, and higher correlation for same provider/architecture and for more accurate models; Goel et al. independently support error overlap rising with capability.
Gain near ceiling is only implicit in sources; hard-item taper appears in Agent Forest's synthetic difficulty scan.

The 25x/no-consistent-gain and 65-87% figures come only from Denisov-Blanch et al. (a18 and a19 are the same paper); other listed sources (Kohli, Shu) only corroborate correlated errors generally and are not truthfulness-benchmark evidence.
fix: A single study (Denisov-Blanch, Kazdan et al. 2026, arXiv 2603.06612) reports that on verifier-absent benchmarks, even at 25x sampling cost, plurality aggregation gave no consistent gain over single samples and often amplified shared misconceptions; on MATH, among plurality-wrong cases the most common wrong answer was 65-87% of wrong responses. Kohli (2026) independently shows correlated errors among LLM judges (n_eff about 2.2 of 9).

problem: Effect-size ranges mix studies (homogeneous d 0.06-0.14 is Study 1; later study homogeneous d 0.01-0.10, heterogeneous 0.26 vs 0.40 in Study 1); meaning unchanged.

Voting beating debate (0.7691 vs 0.7377) is a Qwen2.5-7B result averaged over 7 benchmarks; Smit et al. say debate only 'does not reliably outperform' voting/self-consistency and that tuned MAD (e.g. Multi-Persona) can do better, so a general 'not better than voting' is too strong.
fix: In tested settings, multi-agent debate does not reliably beat simple majority voting: on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, mean accuracy over 7 benchmarks was 0.7691 for majority voting vs 0.7377 for decentralized debate at T=2 (Debate or Vote, 2508.17536), whose martingale analysis says debate alone leaves expected correctness unchanged; Smit et al. (2024) find debate systems do not reliably outperform self-consistency (though tuned variants may), and Wynn et al. (2025) report debate can lower accuracy by flipping correct answers to incorrect.

problem: The '20 of 24 apes' trial-1 figure is in none of the listed evidence; the only matching source (Girndt et al. 2008) reports 'around 80%' of 37 apes solving on trial 1 when they chose where to insert a single tool; the capuchin part is unsupported by the opened sources.
fix: Ape failures on trap tasks are partly caused by tool-use load and action constraints: apes preferred raking over pushing (64.5% vs 18% of pretest strategies, Martin-Ordas et al. 2008), around 80% of 37 apes solved the trap-table on trial 1 when they could choose where to insert a single tool (Girndt et al. 2008), and apes using fingers in a maze outperformed apes using a stick (Voelter and Call 2014).

problem: All four listed lines come from one lab (Voudouris/Crosby/Cheke/Halina group): a16 and c01 are the same 2022 paper, and the 2024 Animal-AI Environment paper is a follow-up by overlapping authors; numbers themselves match (0.6052 vs 0.3412, 0% at L3/6/8/9/10, Dreamer-v3 odds ratio 6.54 vs children 47.2, which are odds of passing vs random, not score multiples).
fix: Reported by a single research group (Voudouris, Crosby et al.): in the Animal-AI Testbed, 52 children aged 6-10 scored higher than 30 AI agents from the 2019 competition (mean 0.605 vs 0.341); on average 0% of the agents passed Levels 3, 6, 8, 9 and 10; and in the group's later paper the odds of passing versus a random agent were 6.5 for Dreamer-v3 and 47 for children.

problem: The pooled letter-string accuracies (humans 0.753; GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452) are averaged over all alphabets including the standard-order one, so they show a human-LLM gap, not the drop itself; the drop for GPT models going from standard to permuted/symbol alphabets (humans staying roughly constant) is in Lewis and Mitchell's per-alphabet figures.
fix: LLM performance drops on counterfactual variants of familiar tasks: in letter-string analogies GPT models fall from the standard alphabet to permuted and symbol alphabets while humans stay roughly constant (pooled over all alphabets, humans 0.753 vs GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452; Lewis and Mitchell 2024), and in Wu et al. 2024 counterfactual performance is above random for most of 11 tasks but lower than default for all. Calling this the LLM version of the cue-removal test is an interpretation.

problem: Both supporting papers (2311.16093 and 2502.15678) are by the same first author and lab (Schulze Buschoff, Schulz); also 'above chance on 2 of 3 tasks' holds only for the largest models (GPT-4, Claude-3 Opus), which the claim does not say. Fine-tuning findings do match.
fix: From one research group (Schulze Buschoff, Schulz et al.): only the largest VLMs (GPT-4, Claude-3 Opus) were above chance in 2 of 3 intuitive-physics/causal domains and none matched humans; fine-tuning on block towers improved in-domain performance (including generalisation to taller and shorter towers) but did not transfer to counterfactual stability judgments.

problem: Jin et al. say fine-tuned models 'drop drastically, by up to 39.29' F1 points on the paraphrased set (and up to 62.30 after variable refactorization); the claim turns the size of the drop into a score ('as low as 39.29').
fix: Pure causal inference from correlation statements (Corr2Cause) is close to random for 17 LLMs (best F1 33.38, BART MNLI; GPT-4 29.08; random uniform 20.38), and fine-tuned models lose drastically on perturbed test sets (F1 drops of up to 39.29 points on the paraphrased set and up to 62.30 after variable refactorization). A structured graph-first prompt lifted Qwen3-32B F1 from 32.71 to 48.26 (Sun et al. 2025).

problem: The LM-agent finding (GX-Chen et al. 2025) and the adult study (Samiei et al. 2026) are by an overlapping team (GX-Chen, Lin, Richards, Precup, Yiu, Gopnik), and c15/c16 are one paper; also 'removes the deficit' and 'only with free interventions' go beyond 'no decrease in conjunctive vs disjunctive' and 'active exploration substantially improves' conjunctive reasoning.
fix: One research group (GX-Chen, Samiei, Gopnik et al.) reports that in blicket-style active causal discovery, LM agents reliably infer disjunctive (OR) rules but systematically fail on equally evidenced conjunctive (AND) rules, with performance declining from 4 to 8 objects; test-time hypothesis sampling showed no conjunctive-vs-disjunctive decrease in the 8-object setting; and in a 2026 adult study active exploration substantially improved conjunctive rule inference (passive observers did worse), though conjunctive rules still needed more tests.

problem: Per-species counts check out (rooks 3/7 and 0 transfers, finches 0 transfers, crows 1/6 first trial and 4 by trial and error, 1 of 8 parrots clear transfer, no dog reached 60%), but the zebra-finch study is a trap-gap task and the parrot study a tray/gap task, not trap-tube work, and the 'no outside lab has reproduced the full Taylor 2009 series' negative is not shown by any listed source.
fix: Outside-lab trap-tube and related trap-task studies find that few animals pass and almost none transfer: 3 of 7 rooks passed the modified trap-tube and 0 passed transfer; Darwin's finches 0 transfers (2 non-tool-using woodpecker finches solved the initial task); hooded crows: 1 of 6 avoided the trap on trial 1 and 4 learned by trial and error; in a related tray/gap task only 1 of 8 macaws and caiques showed clear transfer; zebra finches (N=34) were at chance on a trap-gap transfer test; no pet dog (25) reached 60% correct on the trap tube. We did not find a replication of the full Taylor 2009 series, but that absence is not demonstrated by these sources.

problem: Hennefield's 0.81 (p=.22) is a task-order coefficient, read as 'no transfer'; 11 of 33 experiments in Ghirlanda and Lind rests on a secondary summary; otherwise numbers match.

The 59 vs 52 child counts are not a real disagreement: Voudouris 2022 states 59 children completed all 40 tasks and 52 remained after excluding 7 who failed 2 of 4 Level-1 tasks (44 after the separate outlier rule); Mecattaf cites the pre-exclusion 59.
fix: Mecattaf 2024 gives per-level proportions only (n=12 trials per level, three 2024 models) with no per-task trap-tube result and no scaffold-vs-plain comparison; one in-context example gave mixed changes by model and level. Its child baseline is stated as 59 children, which is the number who completed all 40 tasks in Voudouris 2022; that paper analysed 52 after excluding 7 who failed Level-1 checks (44 after outlier removal in some contrasts).

problem: CheeseBench values are from 15 trials per environment and the authors call them directional/noisy; the 64.5% vs 18% ape figure is a strategy-preference share in a pretest, not accuracy.
All specific numbers come from Huang et al. (four listed lines are the same paper); Kamoi et al. survey independently supports the oracle-label point.

All with/without-execution numbers (72.8 to 80.4-80.6, 77.3 to 88.8-90.4, 61.4 to 57.6, no-execution +1 to +4) come from the single Self-Debug paper (the many listed lines are one paper); LDB (Zhong et al.) is a different method and does not run the no-execution ablation. Numbers themselves match.
fix: In the Self-Debug paper (Chen et al. 2023/24), unit-test execution feedback lifts GPT-4 MBPP from 72.8 to 80.4-80.6 and TransCoder from 77.3 to 88.8-90.4, whereas without code execution gains shrink to about +1 to +4 (GPT-4 MBPP 76.0-76.4, TransCoder 78.2-78.4) and Codex MBPP with simple feedback falls from 61.4 to 57.6; this is a single study, loosely corroborated by LDB, which also builds on runtime execution.

problem: Agentless text states 90.0% file-level match and 23.67% resolved for StarShip (the '79.0% in its table' could not be tied to that row); the -4.45 to +0.40 pass@1 range is real (17 of 18 settings negative, none significant after Holm) but comes from mini-swe-agent with GPT-5.6 Luna / DeepSeek-v4 Flash / Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, and the paper does not show that the benefit 'shrinks as agents get better'.
fix: Repair benefit depends on correct location and diagnosis: in agentic pipelines the correct-location rate tracks solve rate, but file-level location alone is not enough (Agentless reports OpenCSG StarShip at 90.0% file-level match yet only 23.67% resolved on SWE-bench Lite). A 2026 study of mini-swe-agent with three recent LLMs found that adding fault-localization output changed pass@1 by -4.45 to +0.40 points (negative in 17 of 18 settings, none significant after Holm correction), so predicted locations did not reliably help such agents.

problem: 60.8-69.1% spans two scaffolds (SWE-Agent up to 69.1, OpenHands from 60.8); 35-40% of Verified failures still miss the file, so 'file-level not the bottleneck' is a majority statement.

Beller et al.'s 91%, 13.7% and 51.9% match, but they measure IDE-debugger use by Eclipse/IntelliJ developers (13.7% is time in debugger intervals, 132 of 458 users ever used the debugger), not all debugging; Alaboudi and LaToza find debugging episodes take about 48% of live-streamed session time, so 'debugging is 13.7% of IDE time' and 'mostly not done with debugger tools' are wider than the data.
fix: Debugging is frequent and uneven (about once every 8 minutes of programming, 13-95% of session time per session; Alaboudi and LaToza 2021), while in Java IDEs (Eclipse/IntelliJ, Beller et al. 2018) developers did not start the debugger in 91% of sessions, time in debugger intervals was 13.7% of active IDE time, and reading preceded 51.9% of debug intervals.

problem: 'About 90 percent' is 100-9.3 = at least one false insight across up to six primed lures, taken from a citation of an earlier FIAT study within Grimmer et al. 2022; Danek & Wiley used 35 analysed magic tricks.
Figures are from one paper (d'Aliberti and Horta Ribeiro; Qwen2.5-1.5B, association not causal); Wu et al. (8.3% Aha, no reliable gain in VLMs) independently supports rarity and lack of benefit.

Every figure (+8.41 pp, 50,574 vs 23,500, +0.45, +0.01) is from one paper (d'Aliberti and Horta Ribeiro 2026; a29 and c06 are the same paper) on Qwen2.5-1.5B; the other listed papers (entropy-based stopping etc.) test different interventions and do not replicate it. Numbers themselves match.
fix: One study (d'Aliberti and Horta Ribeiro 2026, Qwen2.5-1.5B) finds that externally triggered reconsideration at high token entropy raises MATH-500 accuracy from 32.21% to 40.62% (+8.41 pp; 50,574 wrong-to-right vs 23,500 right-to-wrong flips) while model-chosen shifts do not help, with near-zero effect on crosswords (+0.45 pp) and Rush Hour (+0.01 pp); not independently replicated.

problem: 64.5% and the Wait reduction (89.3%, accuracy +156.0%) come only from Self-Correction Bench (14 models); Kim et al. 2026 independently supports only that a doubt cue like 'Wait' recovers failed trajectories.

Kadavath shows calibration on multiple-choice/true-false and P(True) on open-ended self-samples; 'task-dependent' is an interpretation (the paper notes weaker OOD calibration), and Ji-An et al. concerns monitoring internal activations rather than P(True).
The 323%/within-15% comparison is for the murders item only; on other Lorenz items median and geometric mean were far off too (e.g. rapes -55%/-61%), which supports 'no universal rule'.

SP percentages (21.3/24.2/22.2) were verified only through secondary coverage (Wikipedia, MIT press), not the Nature full text; Douven's 0.241 vs 0.313 is on the 94-item clean subset with aggregators trained on the other 160 items; SP is a human-crowd result.

I reproduced the beta-binomial ceilings independently (0.887 at rho=0.1, 0.805 at rho=0.2 for p=0.69); beta=0.052 on MATH-500 rests on only 17 all-wrong events (CP 0.030-0.081); Kaniovski and Zaigraev was read only via search snippets, and the exchangeable beta-binomial model is an assumption.

Numbers match (+24.2 pp, 0.0 pp same-source, -11.2 pp; win rates 0.810/0.496/0.179), but Shu's own post-mortem says the different-model vs same-source contrast confounds provenance with verifier strength (role-reversed different-model verifier hurt), and Maryanskyy's judge-selection 0.810 falls to 0.611 or 0.500 when judges are decoupled from the generators, so 'a verifier from a different build' is not what the sources show.
fix: Spending extra tokens on a strong, accurate selector or verifier can beat more same-source votes: in Shu (2026, MATH-500, n=570, k=7) a strong different-model verifier gained +24.2 pp on pivotal items versus 0.0 pp for an extra same-source draw, but a role-reversed verifier lost 11.2 pp, so verifier strength rather than a different build is the active ingredient; in Maryanskyy et al. judge selection reached a 0.810 win rate vs 0.496 for voting and 0.179 for synthesis, which fell to about 0.50-0.61 with decoupled judges.

problem: Within-question discrimination 52.2% to 62.3% and the 7.9x / under 0.1% adaptive-stopping figures match, but the ~40% sample saving is only for the best confidence method P(True) (41% at budget 5, 46% at 10); other methods cut 10-31%, and 7.9x is the best case on one dataset (3.3x on average).
fix: Own-confidence signals are weak truth signals but useful for saving samples. Within-question discrimination was 52.2% to 62.3% (chance 50%); confidence-weighted voting with the best signal (P(True)) cut samples by 41% to 46% (other confidence signals 10% to 31%); adaptive stopping cut the sample budget by 3.3x on average and up to 7.9x with an average accuracy drop below 0.1%. All on checkable-answer tasks, and agreement cannot detect a shared error.

problem: a13 and b10 are the same Akam 2015 paper (one source); c24 is Morris & Cushman 2019, an independent second source; chunk-mimics-MF holds only under specific reward-representation conditions.
Bracketed '2026 sample n=140' has no listed evidence line and was not checked; core numbers (d=0.35 N=839; Exp1 d=0.47 N=98; replication d=0.29; Exp2 d=-0.04) match.
'Thinkless similar' is vague (Thinkless cuts long-chain use 50-90% but with accuracy drops, e.g. AIME); 39/901 tokens is a single worked example (Fig 2), 1,953% is for the 2+3 question.

All numbers match He & Feng Table 1, but the +1.02 is the learned IDPR gate, not a confidence-only gate (low avg log-prob +0.32, low logit gap -0.06); the He & Feng figures come from one preprint listed four times.
fix: Gates give small gains: a learned fast-answer controller (IDPR, using confidence, logit margin and cost features) that sends 8.20% of items to slow reasoning lifts accuracy from 47.90 to 48.92 (+1.02) vs 46.76 for random routing at the same slow-call rate, while simple confidence-only selection gives +0.32 (avg log-prob) and -0.06 (logit gap); cost-aware utility of every routed method stays below always-fast (IDPR 0.4731 vs 0.4789). A separate router LLM misjudges the target model's difficulty (Thinkless, AIME). Single-paper preprint evidence for the gate numbers.

problem: Mean w range 0.40-0.65 comes from the pooled Exp 1 (.65) vs Exp 2 (.40) means; the 'no sample combines story instructions with payoff-gap design' part is an absence claim not checkable from sources.

Descriptions of He&Feng (equal slow-call count, all routed utilities 0.4517-0.4731 below 0.4789), RaM (VOC reward trained by expert iteration) and ITP (budget curve) match; the 'no LLM study' part is an absence claim that sources cannot establish.
Snell R=0.16 low-inference-load and 14x-model comparison, Paglieri 38,836/11,511=3.4x with 0.349 vs 0.379, and Yue Llama2-13B no-saving all match; 'no LLM study' part is an absence claim.
Wu 2024 tested GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude, PaLM-2 (not only GPT-class); GSM-NoOp Phi-3-mini is 'over 65%'; 'no study tests an agent's own cached solution' is an absence claim.
Snell says difficulty estimation 'incurs additional computation cost' that can be subsumed in the inference run (claim's 'non-trivial' is slightly stronger); all other numbers match.
'No predictive rule was found' is an absence statement; the rest matches Paglieri App C.5 and ITP (ScienceWorld-type longer-horizon environments favor larger lookahead).

Newbury & Monaghan 2019 found no overall sleep effect but moderated effects (list length, recall>recognition); Lutz et al. (J Sleep Res 2026) is an adapted, not direct, replication of their 2017 protocol (N=16, 12 at one year, 2 excluded from sleep analyses) and tests visual gist, not word-list DRM.
fix: The DRM meta-analysis (Newbury & Monaghan 2019) found no overall effect of sleep on accurate or false memory, with sleep effects only emerging with moderators such as shorter lists and recall rather than recognition tests; an adapted follow-up of the authors' own 2017 visual-gist protocol (Lutz et al. 2026, N=16) found no gist difference between sleep and wake, so these two sources do not show a reliable sleep effect on DRM gist.

problem: Numbers match Tadros 2022 (CIFAR-10 19.01 to 44.55; CUB-200 new-task 95.41 to 45.4), but the 2026 follow-up (A. Bazhenov, Delanois, Krishnan) shares Krishnan with Tadros et al. and builds directly on that SRC method, so all evidence is one group's work; a22 a19 a20 c17 are the same paper.
fix: Sleep-like replay (SRC) in small neural nets restores old tasks after sequential training in the Bazhenov/Krishnan group's studies (CIFAR-10 19.01 to 44.55 in Tadros et al. 2022), with a cost to the newest task (CUB-200 second task 95.41 to 45.4) and, in the same group's 2026 follow-up, reduced recovery as more tasks pile up before sleep (on CIFAR-10 the drop saturates after 3 tasks); no independent replication is cited.

problem: All numbers match; effect sizes differ greatly (-29 points RecMem vs -2.1 F1 All-Mem, no CIs) and the 'raw tier' removal also removes the faithful-detail layer, so 'protects against abstraction loss' is an interpretation.

Retraction notice of Stanyer et al. 2022 was first published online 16 June 2025 (it sits in the Feb 2026 issue, vol 35 no 1), not 'in 2026'; all other numbers (g=0.25 p=0.07 10 studies 177; g=0.68; N=27; N=34; N=20) match.
fix: Acoustic slow-wave stimulation evidence is weaker than the original papers suggested: the 2021 meta-analysis found g = 0.25 (p = 0.07, 10 studies, 177 people); the 2022 meta-analysis that reported g = 0.68 in under-35s was retracted (notice online June 2025, in the February 2026 issue) for using SE as SD and wrong sample sizes; closed-loop stimulation was null for memory in chronic insomnia (N 27) and at home (N 34, authors flag low power); and a tDCS plus CLAS study (N 20) was null overall, with a memory decrement only in an exploratory high-fluid-intelligence subgroup.

problem: Dayan 1993 formula did not extract as text from the PDF; SR definition, TD learning, latent learning and policy-dependence/staleness confirmed via Dayan's text and Russek et al. 2017.

Both the human result (Momennejad et al. 2017, N=88, policy resembles transition revaluation and differs from reward revaluation, p=.0043 / .5771) and the simulation (Russek et al. 2017) come from the same research group (Momennejad, Russek, Botvinick, Daw, Gershman are on both); the Dyna repair is simulation-only, and b03's cited 'Carvalho 2024 review' URL is actually the Momennejad paper.
fix: Policy revaluation (a changed distal reward that flips the best earlier action) is hard for humans (Momennejad et al. 2017, N=88: switching 0.50 vs 0.66 for reward revaluation, similar to transition revaluation 0.47) and for SR-TD without replay in simulation; in simulation (same research group, Russek et al. 2017) SR-Dyna or Dyna-Q with enough replay repairs it. No independent lab replicates either part.

problem: Akam et al. 2015 show model-free strategies can look model-based (the opposite artefact: false MB signatures), so they do not support 'apparent model-free influence is an artefact'; only Feher da Silva & Hare 2020 supports the false-hybrid / mostly-MB claim, and it is one lab's single study (spaceship N=21, magic carpet N=24).
fix: Two-step task signatures are ambiguous in both directions: model-free strategies can mimic model-based behaviour (Akam et al. 2015, simulations), and pure model-based agents with a wrong task model are labelled hybrid (median w 0.36 or 0.80 vs 0.94 for a correct model); with a detailed story and comprehension checks, humans in one study (Feher da Silva & Hare 2020, N=21 and N=24) were mostly model-based (median w 0.78-0.79).

problem: RAP's 6-step LLaMA-33B result (0.26-0.42) is still at or below GPT-4 CoT (0.40) at the low setting; WebDreamer 23.6 is below tree search (26.2); claim compares to the stated baselines only.
Predictive-map-like is the authors' 'resembles predictive representation learning' qualitative claim, not a tested equivalence.

R1 Table 15: distilled models gain 10.3 to 29.6 points at cons@64 on AIME 2024 (Distill-Llama-8B 50.4 to 80.0 is +29.6), not 10-28; other numbers (56.5 to 74.4; 60.1 to 78.0; More Agents GSM8K 12-24 points) match.
fix: Majority vote over 5-40 sampled CoT paths raises accuracy on math and reasoning for capable models; e.g. PaLM-540B GSM8K 56.5 -> 74.4, code-davinci-002 60.1 -> 78.0, More Agents GSM8K +12 to +24 points, and R1-distilled models gain 10 to 30 points on AIME 2024 at cons@64 (Distill-Qwen-14B +10.3 to Distill-Llama-8B +29.6).

problem: Slight blending across papers: GPQA ~2 pp loss is ESC -2.0 and CGES-LNS -2.3 (budget 16); '2-5x on average' is a loose summary of Bo-infinity 2x-5x and Adaptive-Consistency 3.3x average.
All numbers match; but CISC and CGES are efficiency gains at equal accuracy (not accuracy gains over plain vote) and Soft-SC +4.2% is for CodeLlama-34B on agent tasks, so 'beats plain vote' is loose.

Numbers match Brown et al. 2024, but 'only closed by an automatic verifier' is stronger than the paper (it says coverage turns into accuracy where verifiers exist and warns that even unit-test verifiers are imperfect, Sec 4.2); five of six evidence lines are the same paper, with Cobbe 2021 not bearing on the voting result.
fix: In Large Language Monkeys (Brown et al. 2024), coverage keeps rising with sampling while voting and reward-model selection plateau near 100 samples (Llama-3-8B-Instruct MATH: coverage 82.9 to 98.44% from 100 to 10,000 samples; majority vote or reward model 40.50 to 41.41%); in domains with automatic verifiers (tests, proof checkers) coverage translates into accuracy (SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2 15.9% to 56% at 250 samples), though the authors note even such verifiers are imperfect. Single-paper evidence.

problem: gpt-4.1 vs mini 'no accuracy advantage' (0.48 each) comes from Ding's own K=20, 48-case re-run; the single-author preprint flags a possible model-snapshot confound.
TT-SC AUROC 0.836 vs 0.655 and Pause-and-Reflect 90.1% at under 5% abstention vs 82% match; 200 calibration items and small open models only.

Mirzaei 2026 is a single small preprint (150 questions per setting, Qwen2.5 only); Wang et al. 2024 supports the direction (budget-matched CoT+SC matches or beats debate/Reflexion) but was read at abstract level only.
Minor: majority 70% vs 83.3% is a 32B-solver AIME2025 result, a different setting from gpt-oss-120b; 'wrong answer is the mode' is the authors' framing, not a measured number.
Self-critique lowered Game of 24 and coloring, but Blocksworld rose 40 to 55, so the claim holds only for the two domains it names.
Numbers match Huang Tables 2-3, Stechly, SCoRe; 'not yet measured with 2025-26 reasoning models' is an absence claim not checkable here; SCoRe is Google DeepMind like Huang, though different authors.

Numbers match Kirk et al. Table 2 (STARS 77.5/94.4/92.9 vs TBP 52.5/66.7/35.7; over 70% unviable in one task), but both supporting papers are the same Soar group (Kirk, Wray, Laird) and the evidence is one simulation study, one run per condition; Zhu and Simmons does not test this.
fix: In one Soar-group simulation study, checking LLM-proposed goals with agent analysis and repair (STARS) beat template-based prompting: 77.5/94.4/92.9% vs 52.5/66.7/35.7% task completion on three tasks; over 70% of raw responses were not viable in one task. Single lab, single study.

problem: Numbers check out (ExpeL 40.0 to 59.0; task-similarity 59.0 vs random 42.5; Voyager; AWM +12.0 pts), but no source tests the 'only where a cheap executable check exists' condition, and ExpeL stores text insights and trajectories, not compiled rules or code.
fix: Reusing experience from earlier episodes helps in Voyager (verified code skills), AWM (workflows from successful trajectories), ExpeL (text insights plus retrieved successes; ALFWorld 40.0 to 59.0, task-similarity retrieval 59.0 vs random 42.5) and bootstrapped agents; Voyager's ablations show self-verification matters most, which suggests (not shown) that a cheap executable check is needed. Payback at equal total tokens is unmeasured; Laird 1986 chunking data unread.

problem: Numbers match (R2 0.98/0.98/0.96; 1,596 participants, 108 concepts, 88%), but the two papers share authors Tenenbaum and Goodman and the same Bayesian-grammar program, and the Berkeley and gwern PDFs are one paper; the conference escholarship version could not be opened (journal version used).
fix: Two papers from the Tenenbaum and Goodman group (Goodman et al. 2008; Piantadosi et al. 2016) find that Bayesian inference over short logical formulas with a simplicity prior fits human rule-learning data well (R2=0.98 on the Medin and Schaffer structure; 88% of held-out variance on 108 concepts). No independent lab is cited.

problem: Goodman et al. fit one-formula-per-person sampling to 36 patterns at R2=0.85 in the journal version (0.83 could not be confirmed from the conference version); that fit shows the model is consistent with, not proof of, one rule at a time, and Piantadosi gives only raster plots.
fix: A model in which each person holds one formula sampled from the posterior explains R2=0.85 of the variance in 36 individual generalization patterns (Goodman et al. 2008), and raster plots of single participants (Piantadosi et al. 2016) are consistent with sharp switching between rules; this fits, but does not prove, the one-rule-at-a-time view. Both sources overlap in authors.

problem: Minor slips: MiniARC task accuracy IO 13.8 vs best refinement 14.6 is not a loss (the loss is raw accuracy 33.1 vs 18.7 and small budgets 3.8-9.2); SOAR paper says much larger non-reasoning models; equal-token absence claim not checkable.
Minor: MiniARC refinement raw range 5.9-12.8 omits the T=3,N=5 value 18.7; 'free router' is the researcher's inference; ensemble 56.75% is stated in the text though the table is garbled.
Minor: the 85-93 range mixes task accuracy (85.0 in Fig 3) with raw accuracy (93.3); GPT-4 comparison is from a figure.
Minor: Greenblatt's 50% is on a 100-task public test subset and the 42% is the ARC Prize report figure for the public eval; Lee K=128 to 256 baseline 54.4 to 55.0 matches.
Minor: the MiniSCAN T=3,N=1 over N=5 finding is a footnote about one setting in Qiu et al. (task accuracy table shows N=5 higher on the main row).

Numbers match (83.8% on 40 tasks, 95 participants; ConceptARC humans 91% vs Kaggle program 52% and GPT-4 25%, the latter cited via Mitchell et al.; 56.75% vs 60.2%), but 56.75% vs 60.2% is near parity on ARC validation, so 'much better' holds only for ConceptARC and for GPT-4/program solvers; Moskvichev and Mitchell are the same group.
fix: Humans beat machines on ARC-type induction by a wide margin on ConceptARC (humans about 91% vs GPT-4 25% and the best Kaggle program 52%; per-task human accuracy 83.8% over 40 ARC tasks, N=95), but the best 2024 AI ensemble on ARC validation (56.75%) comes close to average human accuracy (60.2%), though still far below the best humans (97.8%).

problem: Minor: random-alphabet figure is mean 43.6 with SD 6 over 5 alphabets (reported 44+-6), not 44-46; 13/50 to 23/50 and 85 match.

One-shot numbers match SOAR (GPT-4.1 8.00, Claude-4-Sonnet 20.75, o3-mini 38.25), but 'all of the benefit' is too strong: sampling alone helps (14B 1.0 to 5.63) and Hypothesis Search shows program format alone lifts ARC 17 to 23; the survey does not isolate this.
fix: One-shot program writing is weak even for strong non-reasoning models (GPT-4.1 8.00%, Claude-4-Sonnet 20.75%, o3-mini 38.25% on ARC-test); most of the gain comes from sampling many programs and refining them with execution feedback (e.g. 14B: 1.0 one-shot, 5.63 with 6k samples, 14.25 with sampling plus refinement), though writing programs instead of grids helps somewhat on its own.

problem: Minor: Luo says finite-answer topics show slower growth (not strictly flat); the 0.0% collapse is for any dedup method, so memory type is not isolated.

The 10-16 points is LLMs' advantage on association and analogy over blending (59.0, 53.4 vs 43.4), not over humans; against 75 humans LLMs lead by about 37, 20 and 31 points (59.0 vs 22.1, 53.4 vs 32.9, 43.4 vs 12.8).
fix: KOMBINE: LLMs are 10-16 points better at association and analogy than at blending, and score well above 75 humans on every task (valid association 59.0% vs 22.1%, analogy 53.4% vs 32.9%, blend 43.4% vs 12.8%), yet 19.9% (412/2,070) of invented concepts reuse a property another model invented; adding an explanation step improved text-to-image mashups (mean rank 1.98 vs 2.40, Peng et al.).

problem: Minor: AlphaEvolve 52 of 54 is 38 matched plus 14 surpassed (2 fell behind); the Sodarace 1,728 is the size of the niche map; 'supporting exploratory creativity' is interpretation.

Wikipedia is a derivative source (the Dechter-Pearl point lives there); the primary check is Hart et al. 1968 pp.104-105 viewed as page images: Lemma 2 and Theorem 2 assume consistency and delta graphs, Theorem 3 handles ties. 'LLM scores have no lower-bound guarantee' is the researcher's inference.

Table cells match (GSM8K 74.5 vs 78.8/80.8, MATH 46.8 vs 49.1 and 54.3 vs 55.4, MBPP 75.0 vs 77.0; RAP random-reward 24.34 vs 22.90/22.67), but those numbers give Q* gains of 1.1 to 6.3 points (GSM8K PRM+QVM +6.3), not 'only 1 to 4'.
fix: A learned scorer beats prompting the model to score itself (TS-LLM; Q* real table cells: GSM8K best-of-N(QVM) 74.5 vs Q* 78.8 and 80.8, MATH 46.8 vs 49.1 and 54.3 vs 55.4, MBPP 75.0 vs 77.0). Small models' self-reward is near random (RAP with random reward on LLaMA2-7B GSM8K: 24.34 vs 22.67 to 22.90). Q* gains over best-of-N are about 1 to 6 points.

problem: Numbers match (RAP LLaMA-33B 6-step CoT 0.00 vs RAP(20) 0.42, GPT-4 CoT 0.40; LATS no-LM-heuristic 0.37 vs 0.63), but neither paper compares search gains across base-model strength, so 'gain shrinks for strong base models' is an inference from comparing RAP on a 33B model with GPT-4 CoT.
fix: Model value plus search helps: RAP lifts LLaMA-33B on 6-step Blocksworld from 0.00 (CoT) to 0.42, matching GPT-4 CoT at 0.40; removing the LM heuristic from LATS drops HotPotQA EM from 0.63 to 0.37. Whether the gain shrinks for stronger base models was not tested in these papers.

problem: Minor: heuristic selection samples several heuristics per domain and picks the best on training tasks; Tuisov et al. (400 tasks, 20 domains) is a separate smaller replication in the same direction.
Minor: 93.7% is the optimal-solution rate (solved 95.5-96.0); the 26.8% is average shorter search dynamics of the final model.
Minor: the 352 vs 372 nodes and 34 vs 27 path length are the Aisle map only; the other maps show 133 vs 145 and 197.67 vs 210 nodes.

Minor: Wilt and Ruml's tested explanations (percent error, h-h* correlation) are rejected on the paper's domain set, and 'Hanoi 29.47 vs inverse tiles 29.49' in the notes is a mix-up of unit tiles; the claim's wording is unaffected.
Minor: Snell says beam search over-optimizes on easy bins 1-2 at higher budgets (not strictly 'hurts' at all budgets).

Lightman (78.2/72.4/69.6) and the 0.4-1.7 step-scorer gap match, but in ReST-MCTS Table 3 Math-Shepherd beats SC by only 3.2 (GSM8K) and 2.2 (MATH500); the ReST-MCTS value model beats SC by 3.6 and 3.9.
fix: Step-level (process) scorers beat outcome scorers and majority voting: MATH best-of-1860 PRM 78.2, ORM 72.4, majority 69.6; at 256 outputs (Mistral-7B MetaMATH) the ReST-MCTS value model beats self-consistency by 3.6 (GSM8K) and 3.9 (MATH500) points and Math-Shepherd by 3.2 and 2.2. Gaps among step scorers are small (0.4 to 1.7).

problem: Minor: 'GPT-4 near random on TheoremQA' is shown only graphically; the 18.55% false positive belongs to Blocksworld and 0.5% to Mystery Blocksworld, consistent with the stated range.

Minor: the Adaptive-Consistency 7.9x / under 0.1% figure is from Aggarwal et al. (arXiv 2305.11860, abstract), not from the ESC paper listed as its source; rStar-Math shows saturation or slow gain at 64 trajectories on MATH, AIME, Olympiad Bench but not College Math.
Voyager 19 is the Diamond Pickaxe task only (with-library 18-21 vs without 26-36); minor.

Union numbers are right but unions pool many methods and cutoffs, and the LeanPremise union with MePo (37.6) is only 0.3 above the neural multi-size accumulation (37.3); 'far more' mostly reflects extra attempts.
The 56% figure is DeepMath's 'at least 56% with perfect selection' (56.2% = theorems with a known ATP proof); Flyspeck 50% uses HOL Light proof dependencies; minor labelling.
Thor 39.0 is the LM alone and Thor+Sledgehammer 57.0; fine.

All three supporting lines (a21, c13, b15) are the same LeanDojo paper; the numbers (51.2 to 26.3, R@10 38.4 to 27.6, GPT-4 29.0 to 7.4) are correct but rest on one source; LEGO-Prover and Rango listed here say nothing about unseen premises.

The LeanPremise ablation is mislabelled: on Mathlib-valid (medium baseline recall@32 71.9) naive data extraction costs 5.1 points (66.8), removing negatives costs 12.4 (59.5), and removing the loss mask costs only 2.3 (69.6).
fix: Negative mining and hard negatives matter: DeepMath mining raised proved theorems 61.3 to 66.4 percent (union over cutoffs); LeanDojo in-file negatives are worth 2.7 R@1 and 5.3 R@10; in LeanPremise, removing sampled negatives costs 12.4 points recall@32 (71.9 to 59.5), naive data extraction costs 5.1 (to 66.8), and removing the loss mask costs 2.3 (to 69.6).

problem: Headline 'small, noisy gains' ignores that the same sources report large gains from structure (FormulaNet 83 to 90.3 percent; Lean GNN R@10 39.6 to 50.0, R@1 +34 percent relative); only single-graph ablations move R@10 by about 1 point, and those ablated runs scored higher than the no-ablation run.
fix: Structure gives uneven gains, and names carry much of the signal: on HolStep names alone give 81.5% at zero graph steps vs 90.3% full; adding a GNN raises ReProver-style Lean retrieval R@10 from 39.6 to 50.0, yet ablating the context or premise graph individually moves R@10 by only about 1 point (ablated runs even scored above the no-ablation run); the CSLibPremiseBench structure reranker adds +0.0175 MRR over BM25 but not over BM25+symbol (+0.0037, CI crosses zero); in Rango, BM25 over proof states proved 46% more theorems than CodeBERT dense retrieval.

problem: LeanPremise recall differs from Yang 2023 because the ground-truth premise definition differs (premises of the whole proof vs the next tactic), not an 'upper-bound definition'; the upper-bound footnote concerns the random-forest baseline; this point is also about metric definitions, not offline-vs-prover mismatch.
fix: Offline metrics may not predict prover success: XGBoost looked better on similarity metrics but worse on ATP success (0.31 vs 0.40 for the NMT model); labels from ATP proofs vs human proofs differ (Magnushammer human-only labels 54.0 vs augmented 56.3); and LeanPremise recall numbers are not comparable with Yang 2023 because ground-truth premises are defined over the whole proof rather than the next tactic.

problem: ReasonIR does charge the rewriting cost: it estimates test-time FLOPs for rewriting and reranking scenarios (200x less than Rank1-32B), and Rank1 studies test-time compute, so 'not charged in these papers' is false.
fix: Reasoning-style retrieval (LLM rewrites query, sketches, judges candidates) beats fixed-embedding retrieval on informal-to-formal queries: group recall@10 46.1 vs 38.0 vs 9.3. Outside formal maths, BRIGHT shows the same: BM25 14.5 to 27.0 nDCG@10 with GPT-4 reasoning-step queries. The BRIGHT and LeanSearch numbers do not charge the extra LLM reasoning tokens against a budget; ReasonIR does estimate that compute.

problem: MizAR gains shrink each round (+3.0, +2.4, +1.2, +0.7, +0.3 points) and the prover set and time limits change between rounds; 'keeps adding gains' is true but with diminishing returns.
Cuconasu text says 'peaks of 0.24 (-25%)'; the table shows about -24% relative (Llama2, near setting), and -67% matches Llama2 mid at 18 distractors; fine.
'Substitutes' is slightly stronger than Rango's 'captures a significant amount of the information'.
Stated directly by Salge et al. (one source); Garg et al. only supports it indirectly (empowerment used as an auxiliary exploration bonus in goal-conditioned RL).

Massari et al. found the empowerment-inspired agent significantly faster than the A2C baseline in MultiRoom-N3-S4 (p<0.001) and KeyCorridor-S3R1 (p=0.041); it was not significantly different only in DoorKey-8x8 (and the text describes three environments, not four).
fix: In deep RL, empowerment bonuses give mixed exploration gains: in sparse-reward MiniGrid worlds an empowerment-inspired bonus beat the A2C baseline significantly in two of three environments (MultiRoom, KeyCorridor) but not in DoorKey-8x8, where only the curiosity agent was faster after outlier removal; the offline empowerment bonus beat CRL on 5 OGBench tasks and was on par elsewhere; best-of-N gains are small and task-dependent; and with PPO pretraining shows no clear improvement.

problem: The paper's abstract says +37.4 pp, but the Table 1 means (70.7 vs 30.3) differ by 40.4 pp, so the claim's two figures contradict each other; also the 'GPT-4o-mini vs GPT-3.5' boundary comes from HumanEval/APPS clarifying questions (Kobalczyk et al.), not from 20 Questions, and BED-LLM's own gains do not shrink for stronger models (GPT-4o 45 to 93 on Animals).
fix: Choosing questions by explicit expected information gain computed by code over sampled hypotheses roughly doubles 20 Questions success versus prompting (BED-LLM: +37.4 pp on average per the paper, never decreasing across 6 LLMs; Table 1 means over the 18 cells are 70.7% vs 30.3% prompt-only, a 40.4 pp gap, with 11 of 18 cells more than doubling). Boundary from other tasks: on HumanEval clarifying questions the EIG gain is +14.8 pts for GPT-3.5 but +1.9 for GPT-4o-mini, and GPT-5 does not significantly benefit from Bayesian question selection in Battleship.

problem: The BSC rank-equivalence is the claim's own derivation (it follows from eq. 4 since EIG is monotone in |p-0.5|), not a statement in the paper.
BED-LLM only says Prompt-Only is a stronger baseline on the film task and BED-LLM still helps; 'shrinks' is an inference with no per-turn numbers; OPEN (c18) does not address it.
'Many LMs' rests on two named models (Llama-4-Scout 18.5%, GPT-4o 14.6% redundant questions); GPT-4 about 1/3 is from Zhang et al. 2024.

ASIG is trained separately at each size; the paper reports a smaller gain at 14B (+4.2 animals, +1.8 plants points vs more than doubling at 7B) and says it transfers well to MediQ at 7B, so 'transfer across model size is weak' misstates it.
fix: Training can internalise EIG-based questioning (DPO on EIG-labelled pairs raises Llama-2-7B success from 56.7 to 68.9 on INLG; RL with an EIG reward more than doubles 7B success on 20 Questions), but the benefit shrinks at larger scale: the 14B model improves by only +4.2 (animals) and +1.8 (plants) points.

problem: c14 and b16 are the same paper (Kobalczyk et al.), but CuriosiTree and the preference-inference paper are independent.
Table 1 means recomputed from the 18 cells: ICL Beliefs 26.8, Prompt-Only 30.3.

Sources support the problem/solution/outcome core (Aamodt-Plaza, Memento (s,a,r), Hatalis (P,S,O,M)), but the explanation-of-why is only in Aamodt-Plaza/Kolodner (Memento and Hatalis tuples hold no explanation), and the (Q,S,E,A) tuple appears in none of the listed sources.
fix: A case worth storing carries problem description, solution and outcome (including failures); classic CBR (Kolodner, Aamodt-Plaza) can also store an explanation of why the solution works or failed, but the LLM-agent tuples (Memento state,action,reward; Hatalis P,S,O,M with metadata) hold only the problem-solution-outcome core and no explanation.

problem: Only Kolodner and ReasoningBank carry the claim; the other ReasoningBank entries are the same paper.
Most evidence entries are the same Xiong et al. paper, but MINJA and AgentPoison independently support the follow-the-retrieved-record effect.

Numbers are right (55.48 vs 67.53, strict 70.95), but Kolodner and Aha IB3 do not give 'the same' rule: Kolodner admits a case only if it adds capability or efficiency, IB3 drops stored instances with poor classification records as a noise filter.
fix: Admission control matters: adding every run gave worse results than a small fixed memory when the filter is weak (RegAgent add-all 55.48 vs fixed 67.53); a strict filter reached 70.95. Kolodner (admit a case only if it adds capability or efficiency) and Aha IB3 (drop instances with poor success records as a noise filter) point the same way, though they are different rules.

problem: Slight softening needed: history-based deletion did not help RegAgent even with the strict evaluator (70.95 to 66.58); gains were on EHRAgent, AgentDriver and CIC-IoT. Second source (Aha IB3) is only analogous.

Numbers are correct (49.7 to 55.1; 39.0 to 42.2; Refine removal -6.06), but the paper measures task success rising with more trials when memory is present, not memory quality directly, and the Agent KB Refine ablation says nothing about repeated trials.
fix: With memory, more trials per task raise success (ReasoningBank MaTTS parallel k=1 49.7 to k=5 55.1; without memory 39.0 to 42.2, not monotone). Separately, Agent KB shows that removing its Refine/adapt step gives the largest drop (61.21 to 55.15 pass@1 on GAIA).

problem: MINJA, AgentPoison and Xiong numbers check out, but merge-and-dedupe is only asserted by ACE's authors as a 'first line of defense' (ACE tolerated harmful reflections but its dedup threshold study did not test mitigation), and benign density lowered ASR on EHR/MIMIC (68.9 to 31.1) but barely on Webshop.
fix: Misleading cases are followed by GPT-4-class models: MINJA injection above 95 percent, attack success above 70 percent in half the configurations; AgentPoison about 80 percent attack success with poison below 0.1 percent. Measured mitigations: more benign records in memory (lowered MINJA attack success on EHR, little effect on Webshop), strict admission, and utility-based deletion (Xiong et al.); ACE's merge-and-dedupe is proposed by its authors as a defense but was not measured as one.

problem: Abreu et al. show the three formulas reduce to different trade-offs of a11 and a10 (not mathematical near-equivalence) and report Ochiai consistently beating Tarantula and Jaccard on Siemens; Pearson's 2% is of non-defect variation only, and the 0.0025 EXAM spread holds for DStar/Ochiai/Barinel/Tarantula (Op2 is 0.0071 above DStar).
fix: Formula choice matters little on real faults: Tarantula, Jaccard and Ochiai all rank blocks by a trade-off between failed-run hits (a11) and passed-run hits (a10), though Ochiai beat Tarantula on the Siemens set; on 395 Defects4J faults the formula explains at most 2% of the non-defect variation in EXAM, mean EXAM of DStar, Ochiai, Barinel and Tarantula lies within about 0.0025, and on Python bugs Ochiai/Tarantula rank correlations with DStar are 0.99 and 0.94.

problem: SemLoc entries are one paper; independent support is only Abreu et al. 2006 for the structural causes, which matches.
Minor: LLM4FL Top-1 is 326 in text/table 3 and 327 in a later table; an LLM-only arm without a classical shortlist was not tested in FlexFL (Agent4SR alone, 232, is the nearest).

19 (statement level, DeepFL tie handling) and 80 (method level; AgentFL 157 = 77 more than Ochiai; SieveFL table) check out, but the '101 of 501 in Order Matters' figure is in none of the listed sources, the cause (granularity and tie rules) is inferred, and 'no paper compares ... on fresh bugs' is an unsupported negative.
fix: Cross-paper SBFL baselines differ by granularity: Ochiai Top-1 on Defects4J v1.2 (395 bugs) is 19 at statement level with DeepFL tie handling (LLMAO Table 2) and 80 at method level (AgentFL, as 157 minus 77, and the SieveFL table); the gap fits the different units and tie rules rather than an error.

problem: Numbers match (50.0 vs 82.0 on SemBugs; FuseFL TestRes 187, baseline 150, SusScore 169), but no ablation isolates the failing-test output: the 82.0% LLM also received SSA form and passing tests.
fix: Adding test information helps an LLM far more than the function alone: on SemBugs an LLM given the function, SSA form, passing and failing tests with errors (no coverage) reached 82.0% Acc@1 vs 50.0% for the function alone; in FuseFL the test-results prompt gave the largest single-prompt Top-1 (187 vs 150 baseline, SusScore alone 169).

problem: Exp 1 numbers (4.40/2.80/2.74, N=30) and Webb N=54 check out, but in Exp 2 object similarity did raise soundness (main effect F(1,19)=7.01, p<.02; literal 4.50 > analogy 4.09, surface 3.40 > first-order-only 2.88), though the relational effect was far larger (F=85.78).
fix: Soundness ratings of a match follow shared relational (higher-order) structure much more than shared objects: Exp 1 analogy 4.40 vs surface 2.80 vs first-order-only 2.74 (N=30); in Exp 2 the relational effect (F(1,19)=85.78) dwarfed a smaller object effect (F(1,19)=7.01, p<.02). Humans in the LLM story test also pick the causal-structure story (N=54), using the same Gentner et al. materials.

problem: Only Colhoun & Gentner opened (Lee & Holyoak page blocked 403, N=42/60 not checked): they reproduced the dissociation for the single effect-inference rating (N=70 = 36+34, replicating L&H 2008b Exp 1) but showed it disappears when overall inductive strength over all candidate inferences is measured, so 'stable' is too strong.
fix: Lee and Holyoak's dissociation (removing a shared preventive cause lowers similarity but raises the rated effect inference; reported N=42 and N=60, not re-checked) was reproduced by Colhoun and Gentner (N=70) for the single effect inference, but their Study 1B found overall inductive strength over all candidate inferences follows similarity, so the pattern depends on how inferential strength is measured.

problem: ARN numbers match (far 39.6 vs 94.1; GPT-4 far-near 29.1, far-far 57.1; GPT-3 far p=.065), but across models near analogies were 75.0% vs 97.9% for humans, so only GPT-4 (94.0/92.5) was close to people on near analogies; 'LLMs about as well as people' is too wide.
fix: Only the strongest model (GPT-4, 94.0 and 92.5 on near analogies) came close to people on near analogies, while the model average was 75.0% vs 97.9% for humans; on far analogies models averaged 39.6% (below the 50% chance line) vs 94.1% for humans, and GPT-4 scored 57.1% far-far and 29.1% far-near. GPT-3 was not above chance on far story analogies (p=.065) in Webb et al., while GPT-4 was in an initial test.

problem: GSM8K 75.0 to 77.8 and MATH 33.0 to 37.3 (GPT-3.5-turbo) are right but are gains over 5-shot CoT, and 'modest' does not hold across models (text-davinci-003 50 to 61, PaLM2 60.8 to 81.7 on GSM8K); small models (curie-001, davinci-001) did gain nothing; Thought Propagation does not bear on the numbers.
fix: Self-generated analogical prompting helps strong base models and not small ones (text-curie-001 about 2-3%, davinci-001 no gain over 5-shot CoT): over 5-shot CoT it gives GSM8K 75.0 to 77.8 and MATH 33.0 to 37.3 for GPT-3.5-turbo (modest), but larger gains for text-davinci-003 (50 to 61) and PaLM2 (60.8 to 81.7). No structure-mapping score is used.

problem: Sultan & Shahaf figures check out (top-3 precision 0.87 and 0.94; top-1 0.82 vs 0.48 on ProPara), but 37.7 is the gap between humans and the best LLM, not the best LLM's accuracy (humans 85.7%; text-davinci-003 about 37.1%).
fix: Text-to-mapping pipelines can recover systematic mappings: top-3 precision 0.87 (ProPara) and 0.94 (psychology stories); question-form relations beat verb-only 0.82 vs 0.48 (ProPara top-1 precision). Yet LLMs are weak at story analogy identification: humans score 85.7% on StoryAnalogy multiple choice and the best LLM falls short of humans by 37.7 points (text-davinci-003 averaged 37.1%).

problem: SBERT 77.9% on near analogies (ARN) is right, but the authors of the children's-analogy paper attribute GPT-4 solving over 70% from the C term only to likely data contamination (footnote 1), not association; their association finding is about GPT-3, XLM-V and others scoring lower once association is controlled.
fix: Many LLM analogy successes are reachable by association or shortcuts: embedding similarity alone gets 77.9% on near analogies in ARN, and on children's verbal analogies most correct LLM answers were reachable by association with the C term (accuracy fell 1 to 2 age-years when controlled); GPT-4 solved over 70% from the C term alone, which the authors attribute to likely data contamination.

problem: Content is accurate (suboptimal for all large n, not all n; SafeBayes eta about 0.4 repairs the regression case), but all listed sources are Grunwald's own group (Grunwald-Langford, Grunwald-van Ommen, Grunwald-Roos review) and the review merely summarises the other two; there is no independent replication in the evidence.
Voita and Titov use control tasks (random tags per word type) and show larger model code, which supports but is not the same experiment as Blier and Ollivier's MNIST fake labels.

Numbers check out (MADIL 69 fit, 57 correct, 82%, 59 vs Icecuber 117 under the all-test criterion that also counts two tasks with a non-fitting model; CompressARC 20.0/18.5%, 76K, 138 h, about 20.7 min), but MADIL is described as efficient (80% of solutions within 20 s, 'greater efficiency'), so 'slow' applies only to CompressARC; 'stricter' count is a mislabel.
fix: Pure MDL learners on ARC are verified but weak: MADIL fits 69 of 400 evaluation tasks and 57 are correct (82% generalisation, 180 s budget per task but 80% of solutions within 20 s; 59 correct under the all-test criterion vs Icecuber 117), while CompressARC gets 20.0% pass@2 on the 400 evaluation tasks (18.5% pass@1) with 76K parameters and no pretraining, at about 20.7 GPU-minutes per puzzle on an RTX 4070 (138 h total). Both generate their own candidates; neither was tested as a ranker of LLM-proposed programs in these papers.

problem: Information Capacity follow-up (56 models) is a different measure and only loosely supports; the claim rests on Huang et al.
The 1000x upper end is not a stated figure (papers give 6-60x, 35-118x, weeks vs minutes/hours; Heath 2017 reports 8.4 s vs 2.4 days); the 6% max difference is in Heath 2021 as stated.

Sadatsafavi shows EVSI/EVPI zero only at thresholds 0.05 and 0.10; at 0.01 EVPI was 0.00037 (EVSI nonzero, not given), so 'at others 0' is wrong. 81% is computed (0.00101/0.00125), not stated. Pei 2023 supports threshold dependence (EVSI 0 at WTP 3000, nonzero near 780).
fix: EVSI is zero when current evidence already settles the decision, and its value depends on the decision threshold. In the Sadatsafavi 2024 validation case study, at the 0.02 threshold EVSI was 0.00101 at N=1000 (about 81% of EVPI 0.00125), while EVPI, and so EVSI, was 0 at thresholds 0.05 and 0.10 (EVPI was 0.00037 at 0.01). In Pei 2023, EVSI was 0 at WTP 3000/YLS and nonzero near 780/YLS.

problem: Only Sadatsafavi (one case study) shows the steep rise and plateau toward EVPI; Fleischhacker 2023 does not report a plateau (it gives closed forms and an optimal sample size).
fix: In one external-validation case study (Sadatsafavi 2024), EVSI rose steeply for small samples and plateaued toward EVPI, with little gain beyond N=4,000; generality is not shown by the other listed source.

problem: Abstract says 3 of 6 inclusion options (12 designs) had cost exceeding benefit and 12 designs had benefits exceeding costs; 'negative net benefit' is the paper's cost-exceeds-benefit wording.

Neither the Wikipedia EVSI page nor Fleischhacker 2023 contains the binary sensitivity/specificity formula or the example; I checked the algebra myself and the formula and the four example values (0, 0.100, 0.200, 0.400) are correct, so it is the agent's own derivation, not a sourced claim.
fix: Label as the agent's own derivation (not sourced): for B=C=1, sens=spec=0.9, EVSI = p*0.9 - (1-p)*0.1 gives 0, 0.100, 0.200, 0.400 at p=0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50, and EVSI <= EVPI = p*B.

problem: UoT 38.1% is a relative success-rate gain over direct prompting averaged over 5 datasets; the three results come from different games/models, as the claim lists.

The 0.618 to 0.029 ECE is from Ding et al. (verbalized confidence + isotonic regression on PopQA), a different paper and setting from Dong's VoI belief calibration; the two are combined in one sentence.
'Beat' means improved over (6/10 absolute, 7/10 AUC), not necessarily significantly; OPEN's human study shows it beating LM-based elicitation.
All BACON primary papers are by Langley's group (one lab), which is fine for a claim about BACON itself; BACON.4 is named only implicitly via BACON.5's Snell/Black laws.

Sources show BACON laws were rediscoveries with programmer-specified attributes and (BACON.1) no noise handling, with only a tolerance parameter later; none discusses AM, hand-prepared data, or the absence of success rates (absence claim not verifiable from these), and BACON.5 explicitly states it deals with noise.
fix: BACON demonstrations were rediscoveries of known laws: BACON.1 used programmer-specified attributes and laws and could not handle noise, and later versions handled noise only via a tolerance parameter. The listed sources do not discuss AM's evaluation or whether success rates were reported.

problem: All usable evidence lines are the one LLM-SRBench paper (a15, c05, c06 share the same URL; b25 is an internal reading note with no source). Numbers match Table 1/Table 3 (LaSR Acc0.1 45.94-50.45 vs SA 5.41-12.61 on LSR-Transform; PySR SA 0 on chemistry/biology/material science), but this is one benchmark by one group.
fix: In the LLM-SRBench paper (Shojaee et al. 2025, single source), numeric accuracy and exact-form recovery diverge: on LSR-Transform LaSR reached 45.94-50.45% Acc0.1 but only 5.41-12.61% symbolic accuracy, and PySR had 0% symbolic accuracy on the chemistry, biology and material-science sets while matching or beating LLM methods on Acc0.1 in places.

problem: All numeric details are from LLM-SR (one paper; 4 of 6 lines duplicate it); the broader 'beats LLM-only' role-split claim is independently supported by the separate SGA paper (Ma et al.).

Every usable evidence line is the one DiscoveryBench paper (c28 is an internal reading note); its text supports the findings (ReAct and DataVoyager do not improve CodeGen, Reflexion with oracle score helps, best 25%, biology 0%), but 'in LLM data-driven discovery benchmarks' (plural) generalises from one benchmark.
fix: In DiscoveryBench (Majumder et al. 2024, single benchmark), ReAct and planning with a self-critic (DataVoyager) did not improve on the simple CodeGen agent, while Reflexion with an oracle score signal improved it; the best non-oracle agent scored about 25% overall and 0% in biology.

problem: FunSearch not opened by researcher or me (claim says so); 'earlier 49 over general fields' is paraphrased from 'rank less than 49 over any field of characteristic 0 was open'.
ShinkaEvolve ablations are on circle packing (and other tasks per 'across all tasks'); depth-over-breadth in Eureka is specific to its ablation, framed here as a general rule.

Median is 5 references per paper in Beel (abstract says citations); the 70%/AUC 0.65 reviewer figures and under-15-dollar cost are the AI Scientist authors' own claims; 'reviewer calibration differing by backbone' is from Lu et al.'s thresholding note (Sonnet needs threshold 8).

Kramer et al. 2023 has no Langley co-author (listing says 'Kramer, Langley et al.'); it supports only 'integrating both is rare'. 'Most work is batch' rests on Langley 2024 (a position paper about data mining and individual discovery components); WorldCoder and Qiu are not about this.

NewtonBench 12-16% drop is for GPT-5-mini only and is a drop in accuracy (symbolic) with RMSLE 'relatively stable' across noise levels; Snell's PRM point is beam search degrading on easy questions with signs of PRM exploitation.

The 0.20 pooled slope is specifically for the N=1-sample studies (Figure 2 Panel A), and per-N slopes at 3 and 5 are not below 1 (0.98, 1.06), so the 0.52-1.06 range includes no-underinference cases. 8:4 .7 vs .97 is Edwards via Wikipedia (secondary); 0.231/(0.231+0.008)=0.967 checks.

Benjamin 2019 says Kahneman-Tversky found complete base-rate neglect in some experiments and only partial neglect in others (Koehler 1996); the cited engineer-lawyer example (ratio 1.2 vs Bayes 5.4; Dick case 50% in both groups) is near-complete neglect, so 'usually partially' is not supported by the example. Numbers 5.4 and 1.2 match; Benjamin's text labels the groups the other way round (55% for the 30-engineer group). Wikipedia gives no figures.
fix: People under-use base rates: in the Kahneman-Tversky engineer-lawyer task (30 vs 70 percent engineers) mean judgments were about 50 vs 55 percent, an odds ratio of about 1.2 against the Bayesian 5.4, which is near-complete neglect (complete for an uninformative description); some other experiments find partial use of base rates (Koehler 1996, via Benjamin 2019).

problem: Over-50% figure is violation rate over 30 Dutch-book scenarios in Filbry et al. (cross-conversation), dropping markedly within one dialogue; Falck shows martingale violations; stronger/tool-equipped models do better, consistent with 'without tools'.

Only Zhang et al. (arXiv 2512.18489, a single short preprint) finds a discounted filter (gamma below 1, e.g. 0.88 for Llama-3.1-8B) fits better than exact Bayes; Gupta et al. conclude LLMs broadly follow Bayesian posterior updates, with deviations mainly from miscalibrated priors, so the sources point in partly different directions. Gupta supports wrong priors and non-instruct models failing to converge to an explicit stated bias.
fix: In one preprint (Zhang et al. 2025, discounted Bayesian filters) in-context belief updates in changing environments were better described by an exponential forgetting filter with gamma below 1 than by exact Bayes, whereas Gupta et al. 2025 (static coin flips) found updates broadly Bayesian with deviations mainly from miscalibrated priors, and non-instruct models failed to converge to a priors stated explicitly in the prompt.

problem: Interpretive framing ('non-evidential priors'); Zhao's 54.3 to 93.4 is the SST-2 range across training-example permutations; Zheng's 67.2 to 60.9 and 53.1 to 68.2 match the abstract/Table 1.

Tian: verbalized confidence beats token probabilities for RLHF models; Kadavath: calibration on multiple choice depends on lettered-option format and 'none of the above' harms accuracy/calibration. Kadavath's models are pre-RLHF-era, so the two findings come from different model types.
Arora et al. state explicitly that non-Bayesian laws fit equally well so they do not claim LLMs are Bayesian; Xie et al. prove their result only in an HMM toy setting.

'Semi-decidable' and the checker conclusion are not stated in the fetched pages (they give completeness, compactness, the 1936 undecidability result and Cook 1971 NP-completeness); semi-decidability follows from completeness plus undecidability and is standard.

Multi-LogiEval figures are 6-model averages (propositional 85.42 to 42.96, first-order 83.21 to 32.96); ProverQA GPT-4o CoT 94.2/79.4/50.0 match the table; ProverQA is a different paper by different authors.
Paper says accuracy decrease 'up to 20-30%' for GPT-4-turbo and PaLM 2-L (claim drops 'up to'); Gemini 1.0 Pro and GPT-3.5-turbo 'more than 40%' on its example; units are accuracy drops in points.
Table 5 values match; 'execution accuracy' is used as the proxy for semantic correctness; Logic-LM independently shows executable-rate far above accuracy on FOLIO.

The 'about 54% pooled correct' is Yang & Johnson-Laird Exp 1 correct rate over ALL quantified illusions (possibility 23%, impossibility 67%), not illusions of impossibility alone; other numbers (15/91 N=20, 19/95, 6/83 N=80 r=.87) check out.
fix: Illusory inferences are systematic: confident, uniform errors on problems where reasoning from true cases only gives a wrong answer. Found with propositional, embedded-disjunction, quantified, modal and conditional problems. Human rates from originals: modal 15% correct vs 91% on controls (N=20), embedded disjunctions 19% vs 95%, conditionals 6% vs 83% (N=80, Spanish lab, r=.87, only partly independent of the Johnson-Laird network). Illusions of impossibility are weaker than illusions of possibility (quantified problems, Yang & Johnson-Laird: 67% vs 23% correct; 54% pooled over both kinds). LLMs also produce the predicted fallacies on disjunction problems (d01, d02), though those tests are by a rival theory's authors and have no matched controls. Gap pass: an independent lab (Sable-Meyer & Mascarenhas 2021, N=64 and 70 analysed) found the disjunction illusion again with controls at 87%/26% and 90%/20% accepted, and showed it is triggered by knowledge links, not only word overlap (d24).

problem: Cited confidence values match Goldvarg and Johnson-Laird, Espino et al. and Khemlani and Johnson-Laird; JL&S 1999 not opened; note Yang and Johnson-Laird found a small reliable confidence gap (.13), and 4 of 5 sources are one lab.

Numbers match (80/21, 92/51, 98/72/8), but every source is a Johnson-Laird-lab paper (Bucciarelli, Khemlani, Goodwin, all co-authored by the theory's author); no outside lab replicates the model-count effect, and the relational 98/72/8 is cited from earlier work.

In Bucciarelli and Johnson-Laird, no-valid-conclusion items (50%, 41% in Exp 2) are harder than one-model items (80%) but easier than multiple-model items (21%), so it is not 'the hard case' for humans; the LLM part (rarely say 'nothing follows', ICL does not fix it) is supported by Eisape et al. and Bertolazzi et al.
fix: 'Nothing follows' is a hard case for humans and a very hard one for LLMs. Humans do worse on no-valid-conclusion items (50% in Exp 1) than on one-model items (80%), though better than on multiple-model items (21%) (Bucciarelli & Johnson-Laird); LLMs rarely produce it (PaLM 2, Pythia, LLaMA) and drift to form-based (atmosphere) answers; in-context examples did not fix it for the open models.

problem: Numbers verified (5.6 vs 1.1 unbiased, 56% violations N=39, 53% vs 8% cited second-hand from Girotto and Gonzalez), but both papers are Johnson-Laird-lab work testing his own theory; the Bayesian rescue figure is only a citation; the notes' 'r=.76' is actually R2.

51/21 and 74/92 match Johnson-Laird 2010 (a self-review of one cited study); but the 228 experiments show people select instances, counterexamples or both (not simply 'default confirming'), and the feedback switch comes from the repeated selection task, not the 228-study meta-analysis; both sources are model-theory authors' work.
fix: In Wason selection tasks people select instances of the hypothesis, its potential counterexamples, or both, depending on content and instructions (meta-analysis of 228 experiments, Ragni & Kola 2018); with feedback in the repeated selection task they switched from instances to potential counterexamples. When judging given conclusions, counterexample use was higher and correct rejection lower for conclusions merely consistent with the premises than for inconsistent ones (use 51% vs 21%; correct rejection 74% vs 92%; Johnson-Laird 2010, citing one study).

problem: Mondorf and Plank (31.7% Llama-2-70B sound, symbolic strategy only occasional) and Eisape et al. (NVC accuracy near 0%) match; note Zephyr-7B uses the symbolic strategy most often among tested models, and the closing design inference is the notes' own.

Chen et al. say permuting premise order 'can cause' a drop of over 30% (a maximum, not a drop shown for each listed model); the 14%, 7% and +4% figures (11 LLMs), and the 13-22% moral-judgment order effects match their abstracts.
fix: Premise order and counterfactual content hurt LLM deduction. Permuting premise order can cause accuracy drops of over 30% (Chen et al. 2024; models tested include GPT-4-turbo, GPT-3.5, PaLM 2-L, Gemini 1.0 Pro). Premises that contradict world knowledge cost an average 14% across 11 models; a flag-and-reason prompt cut the gap to 7% and raised overall accuracy 4%. Note the Johnson-Laird view predicts order effects (model construction is serial) and belief effects (believable conclusions stop search), but neither paper tests it. Gap pass: no 2025-26 premise-order measurement on frontier or reasoning models for deduction was found; d26 is training-based on 7B-70B models and d27 shows order effects of 13-22% in frontier models on moral judgments only.

problem: Numbers match (Dong et al. 47.27->56.64, 77.39->80.01, 111 and 51 tasks; Jha et al. 19/20 vs 2/20), but Dong's feedback was only 'your answer is not correct' (no counterexample), and the Jha figures are GPT-4 baseline success by problem size, not a measured effect of counterexample feedback, so 'counterexample feedback helps but is weak' is not shown.
fix: An external checker telling ChatGPT that its answer is wrong (no counterexample content) improved it only slowly: gpt-3.5 rose from 47.27% to 56.64% and gpt-4o from 77.39% to 80.01% on 256 syllogism satisfiability tasks over up to 10 rounds, with 111 and 51 tasks never solved (Dong et al.). Separately, in blocks-world planning GPT-4 alone solved 19/20 problems at 3 blocks and 2/20 at 10 blocks, and Jha et al. use solver counterexamples in an LLM loop, but that paper's baseline numbers here do not measure how much counterexample feedback helps.

problem: Oaksford and Chater 1994 and Sperber et al. 1995 (independent labs) support the 4% and ~10% logical rates; the 46%/33% modal figures come from Johnson-Laird and Wason (1970), quoted second-hand, while the 34-task pooled counts support the general pattern.

Klayman and Ha (positive test strategy as general default heuristic; fails when H lies inside T) and Wason 1960 (29 subjects, 6 correct first time) match; the conditions for soundness rest on the single Klayman and Ha paper.
Jhaveri et al. (6% to 78%, eleven LLMs, I:C correlates with success) and Bertolazzi et al. (12 LLMs, Spearman -0.779, p=0.003) match; two independent groups.

Numbers match, but the general claim is too strong: in FalsifyBench the smallest reasoning models (GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%) did worse than all instruction-tuned models; Jhaveri's Gemini-2.5-Pro vs small non-thinking comparison confounds scale (thinking helped Qwen3 but without a consistent rise in disconfirming tests); and on WILT the best model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, 14/50) is not a reasoning model, with o1-mini 13 and o1-preview 12.
fix: Larger reasoning (thinking) models generally do better at rule discovery and falsify more: GPT-5.2-Chat 75 percent and GPT-OSS-120B 68 percent vs 33 to 41 percent for instruction-tuned models (FalsifyBench), although the smallest reasoning models (GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%) did worse than all instruction-tuned ones; Gemini-2.5-Pro (thinking) 0.73 vs 0.06 to 0.33 for small non-thinking models (Jhaveri, confounded with scale). On WILT no model solves more than 14 of 50 and the best (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) is not a reasoning model.

problem: Dasgupta et al. (z>2.2 for Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5, humans; marginal 1.78) and Seals and Shalin (chance 1/6, mostly 0.06-0.29) match, but Seals and Shalin found that social content does benefit LLMs (significant social-rule by content interaction; realistic social > realistic non-social), only less than in humans (about 30% vs about 70%), so 'weak or absent' overstates.
fix: LLMs show the human content effect on the Wason task: realistic rules beat arbitrary ones (Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5 and humans, all z>2.2; only marginal for PaLM 2-M and Flan-PaLM 2). Small open models mostly fail the standard form (0.06 to 0.29, chance 1/6). In one study the social-rule advantage in LLMs was real but much smaller than in humans (about 30% vs about 70% solved).

problem: Numbers check (Maegherman n=27: 22.2% correct, 40.7% confirming only; maths majors and mathematicians under 50% in Dasgupta et al.; Swann and Giuliano F(1,47)=4.161), but the judges' task was a leaves-and-pot variation, not the abstract task, with n=27 and the thesis itself calls 22% a relatively good result against the typical under 10%.
fix: Confirmatory choices remain common in trained people: in a small survey (n=27) of Dutch judges on a Wason variant, 40.7% chose only the confirming option and 22.2% gave the correct confirming-plus-falsifying pair (the thesis reads this as relatively good versus the typical under 10%); undergraduate maths majors and academic mathematicians scored under 50% on the arbitrary abstract task (Dasgupta et al., citing others); and in social interviews people favour confirmatory questions, especially when certain (Swann and Giuliano).

problem: Parab et al. (4.3% of semantically wrong hypotheses yielded a program passing the training examples, 5,500 trials GPT-4o) and Moghe and Chin (N=1 never above 45.5%, N=5 57.5% pass@2, refinement only -0.75pp) match; Chari and Pattanaik's EIG result is about a support mismatch with the generator, so the EIG sentence is the notes' inference, and Parab also finds the summarizer step loses about a quarter of correct hypotheses.

Cosmides et al. 2010 ('only 5-30%' on indicative rules, 65-80% on social contracts) and Klauer et al. 2007 ('typically fewer than 10%' P and not-Q) support it; the 5-30% range is Cosmides' summary, not a pooled meta-analysis, and Fiddick and Cosmides sources share a lab.

Fiddick 2003 (realistic rules failed to replicate Wason and Shapiro; Manktelow and Evans 1979), Cosmides et al. 2010 and Kroger et al. 1993 (permission 47% vs arbitrary 5% only with violation-checking plus explicit negatives) support it; Fiddick and Cosmides are the same theoretical camp, while Kroger/Cheng/Holyoak and Sperber/Girotto are independent rivals.

Cosmides 2010 (64/46/26 additive factors, 5-30% indicative), Cosmides 1989 pages via 2010 summary, and Gigerenzer and Hug (n=93, 94% vs 44%) match; minor slip: Cosmides' familiar descriptive control was 46%/38%, just above the stated 45% top of the control range; the claim already flags that 65-80 is one lab's spread.

Sperber and Girotto 2002 Exp 2 (N=120, 33%/43% vs 10%/0% P and not-Q) and Gigerenzer and Hug 1992 (perspective flips P and not-Q 75% to not-P and Q 61%) match; independent labs; note Sperber and Girotto's cheater cells were below Fiddick et al.'s original (33% vs 66% failed replication).

Lampinen et al. (Wason z>2.2, NLI no effect with ceiling, item-level t(832)=3.49, t(345)=4.98) and Ando et al. NeuBAROCO (GPT-3.5 31.37% inconsistent vs 61.05% symbolic) match; the NLI null is partly due to ceiling effects, and the claim omits that stronger models show little belief effect (see K12).

Lampinen et al. (Chinchilla 5-shot Wason content effects exaggerated), Bertolazzi et al. 2025 (CE 0.348 to 0.096; 0.213 to 0.014 with CoT) and Bertolazzi et al. 2024 (LLaMA-3 8B 70.74 to 52.59, LLaMA-2-inst 7B 32.22 to 19.26) match; 'ICL often cut accuracy' rests on other sources I did not open.

Cosine 0.48-0.64 vs 0.10-0.17, debias vector CE 0.348 to 0.072, and K-CAST up to 15% absolute match, but 'not reachable by a text scaffold' is contradicted by the same Bertolazzi et al. paper, where chain-of-thought alone cut CE 0.348 to 0.096 and 0.213 to 0.014; also the two Bertolazzi entries are versions of one paper.
fix: Validity and plausibility are linearly encoded and aligned inside open models (cosine 0.48 to 0.64 vs 0.10 to 0.17 for controls); a debias vector cut CE from 0.348 to 0.072 and conditional activation steering (K-CAST) gave up to 15 points absolute on models that static steering could not fix. Chain-of-thought prompting alone also cut CE substantially in strong open models (0.348 to 0.096), so text prompting reaches part of the effect, while steering offers a further internal lever.

problem: GSM-Symbolic found accuracy falls when numbers (or names plus numbers) change, but changing names alone leaves GSM8K performance near the name-changed distribution (only extra variance); the 65% figure is a maximum and Wu et al. report 'substantial and consistent' degradation over 11 tasks (not verified per task).
fix: Models are brittle to surface content beyond logic tasks: changing numerical values lowers GSM accuracy (changing names alone mainly adds variance), adding one irrelevant but plausible clause drops accuracy by up to 65 percent (GSM-NoOp), and on counterfactual variants of 11 tasks performance degrades substantially and consistently relative to the default versions (Wu et al.).

problem: Ahn and Graham (n=22; control P and not-Q .18), Macchi et al. (control 4%/10%; Necessarily 66%/77%) and Kroger et al. (47% vs 5%) match; minor slip: n=130 is Macchi's Exp 1 control sample, the 'necessarily' groups are smaller (N=82 combined), and Ahn and Graham's 50% is a mean over three explicated conditions rather than the same measure as the control's 18% P and not-Q.

FOLIO 93.8 vs 74.1 (81 items), Symbolic Tree ChatGPT 71.8 vs 53.7, and Phi-3-mini over 65% NoOp drop all match; slip: the 65% drop is for the irrelevant clause (NoOp), not for name or number swaps, and name-only swaps do not clearly lower accuracy.

Eisape et al. (about 75% vs about 50%, near 0% on 'nothing follows', 30 samples at temp 0.5, binary discrimination markedly higher on those items) and Bertolazzi et al. (pretrained LLaMA/Pythia rarely say 'nothing follows') match; the 'does this conclusion follow' wording is the notes' description of Eisape's binary-validity method.

Wu et al. (93.8 vs 74.1 on 81 FOLIO items; consistent drops on 11 tasks), Tang et al. (70.1 vs 71.8), and Saparov and He (true ontology allows skipping hops) match; Kim et al. only report 'evidence of partial contamination' from extra attention heads, so 'inject world knowledge' is stated more firmly than the paper; 'so it was using memory' is Tang's inference.

Ozeki et al. (87/90 = 96.67%, 77.78 to 83.33; GPT-3.5 58.89 to 52.22/54.44), FregeLogic (Z3 74.7%, invalid 97.6, valid 52.2), LINC (syntax errors 38/24/13%) and Kartac et al.
