(95.83 vs 84.17, +11.7) all match; the closing 'weak link depends on size and data' is the notes' synthesis, and the Z3 figure comes from one SemEval system paper.

Kim et al. (recovery fails on belief-inconsistent data, 'suggesting' extra heads), Bertolazzi et al. (cosine 0.48-0.64 vs 0.10-0.17, alignment tracks content effect) and Valentino et al. (up to 15% absolute with K-CAST) match; hedged wording in Kim is firmer in the claim, Kim and Valentino share authors (Valentino, Freitas), and the claim is a three-paper synthesis with each finding resting on one paper.

Minor: the Maverick 3.83 to 10.11 and simple-CoT 5.24 figures come from the Phase 1 prompt comparison on a 200-sample inner subset (5.24 averaged over 3 models), not from the final SemEval ensemble; Tang numbers are only a pattern.
Lampinen Appx B.2 says PaLM 2-L scored over 75% in every Wason condition WITHOUT the prior correction (raw likelihood), not with prior-corrected scoring as the claim says; the other parts check out.
fix: Scoring method, answer format and run-to-run noise can swamp the content effect in measurements, so absolute numbers in this field are fragile. Lampinen: raw-likelihood scoring with an instruction prompt made several models answer 'valid' to everything on syllogisms, and on Wason, scoring without the prior correction gave PaLM 2-L over 75 percent in every condition (including arbitrary and nonsense) although Chinchilla got worse. Eisape: generative vs binary format changed 'nothing follows' accuracy from near 0 to 'markedly higher'. Macmillan-Scott: ten runs per prompt gave highly inconsistent answers. Poddar used adaptive majority voting. The direction of the content effect is broadly stable across scoring choices; the size is not.

problem: Stupple and Ball cells verified, but the aggregate 80% vs 33% comes only from a Wikipedia summary and is contradicted by the primary paper: Evans, Barston and Pollard (1983) Exp 1 shows believable 92% (valid) and 92% (invalid) vs unbelievable 46% and 8% (mean 92 vs 27), Exp 2 86/62/66/13, Exp 3 91/53/67/6.
fix: Believable conclusions are accepted far more often than unbelievable ones, and the pull is strongest on invalid arguments (accepting believable-invalid is the dominant error). Evans et al. (1983) Exp 1 (N=24) had valid-believable 92%, valid-unbelievable 46%, invalid-believable 92%, invalid-unbelievable 8% accepted; Stupple and Ball (2008, N=48) accepted 71% vs 36% of invalid believable vs unbelievable conclusions (figure AB-BC) and 61% vs 25% (figure BA-CB).

problem: Trippas 2014 (title is actually 'Fluency and belief bias in deductive reasoning: new indices for old effects', effect sizes are omega2), Markovits 2017 and Pennycook 2013 numbers verified; the analytic-disposition link is only indirect and the older-adults point rests on a secondary thesis with no numbers.

Claim rests on one paper (Lampinen et al., listed several times); its numbers check out, but high sensitivity/low specificity applies only to GPT-3.5 and larger PaLM 2, and Chinchilla and PaLM 2-M showed no significant validity x believability interaction. Ozeki et al. GPT-3.5/GPT-4 numbers also verified.

Bertolazzi numbers (30.31, 0.83, 82.97, 96.25) and Noe et al. figures verified; note the claim understates Bertolazzi, who say models overcame content-effect biases only in the SFT setting (while cautioning it may be pattern matching).

Numbers verified in Akinfaderin and Diallo (98% invalid, 52.2% valid, 11 wrong flips all rejecting valid, 8 unbelievable), but this is one system in one paper (listed twice); LINC (Olausson) does not show an invalid lean, and the 11 wrong flips are Z3 overrides in the tiebreaker setup, not Z3 alone.
fix: In the FregeLogic SemEval 2026 system (one paper), a Z3 solver run on LLM-extracted logical forms leaned toward 'invalid': Z3 alone was 97.6% right on invalid items but 52.2% on valid items because extraction mistakes break valid chains; as a tiebreaker on 3-2 ensemble splits all 11 of its wrong overrides rejected valid syllogisms, 8 of them with unbelievable content.

problem: Read Evans, Barston and Pollard (1983) PDF myself: Exp 1 92/46/92/8, Exp 2 86/62/66/13 (A-C 88/56/72/13), Exp 3 91/53/67/6 and the 92/27, 87/48, 97/43 correct rates all match; Macchi and Trippas agree.

Pennycook 2016 (64.9% vs 4.8%, N=372) and Travers 2016 (36/58/6, N=131) verified; Raoelison and De Neys 94.9% is the heuristic share of initial responses in an appendix whose denominator (wrong responses) is not explicit.

Bouwmeester RRR numbers verified (ITT -0.37 points, N=3,596, 21 labs), but the disfluent-font replications have no listed source, the compliant-only analysis still showed +10.37 points, and Rand 2014 (original lab) found positive effects; time pressure also manipulates intuition rather than switching on analytic mode.
fix: A preregistered 21-lab replication of the time-pressure cooperation effect (Bouwmeester et al. 2017, N=3,596) found about zero effect under intent-to-treat analysis (-0.37 percentage points vs 8.6 in the original data), while the original-style compliant-only analysis still showed +10.37 points (15.31 originally); the authors read this as consistent with selection bias and no causal effect of time pressure. The disfluent-font replication claim has no opened source.

problem: Sprague (14.2 symbolic, 12.3 math, 6.9 logic; 56.9 vs 45.5; 56.8 vs 56.1) and Hagendorff (davinci-003 CRT correct 5% to 28%) verified; the claim lists the gains in the order math, symbolic, logic whereas the paper gives symbolic 14.2, math 12.3.

Liu et al. numbers (87.5 to 64.4, o1-preview 57.7 vs 94.0, six models worse on faces, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 65.9 vs 67.7 on grammar) and Gema et al. distractor failure mode verified; Liu et al. is listed three times but is one paper, and Gema is independent.

Hagendorff, Ma et al., Phantom Recall and Malek et al. verified; slip: Malek's text says gaps of 9.1 (o3) to 54 (G1.5) points but its Table 1 implies 13.4 and 61.9, so the claim repeats an internally inconsistent figure.
Sprague (Plan + Tool Solver beats CoT and Plan + CoT Solver on average, on the formal tasks) and Yao (Game of 24 4% to 74%) verified; Sprague appears twice but is one paper.

Findings match Hayes, Stephens, Ngo and Dunn (2018) (capacity x validity chi2 28.30, speeded validity effect .11 vs .25, no speed x belief effect, concurrent load little effect), but three of the listed sources are that same paper and the others (Hayes et al. 2014 review, Trippas fluency study) do not test capacity or speeding on belief, so the claim rests on one study (N=122).

Itzhak et al. support that instruction tuning and RLHF mostly raise belief-bias scores and that task few-shot lowers but does not remove it, but Lampinen et al. found instruction-tuned models showed no consistent difference from base models and say a simple instruction substantially cut bias in NLI, so 'a plain instruction is a modest remedy' is unsupported and the instruction-tuning claim is contested.
fix: In Itzhak et al. (2024), instruction-tuned and RLHF models (Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct, GPT-3.5, GPT-4) mostly showed higher belief-bias scores than their pretrained counterparts, and few-shot examples from the same task lowered it noticeably but left substantial bias; Lampinen et al. (2024) found no consistent content-effect difference between instruction-tuned and base PaLM/GPT models, and found that on syllogisms 5-shot examples only slightly weakened the effect while a simple instruction substantially cut bias only on the natural language inference task.

problem: Logic-LM (18.4% over CoT, PrOntoQA 98.79 vs 83.20, depth gaps 7.1 to 39.4, exe rates 79.9 and 32.6) and LINC (75.3 vs 72.5, p=0.58; 5.3 vs 18.8 premises) verified; 'LINC and SatLM agree' is loose since LINC only ties CoT on FOLIO.

Wang et al. abstract (17% direct, 30% LLM summaries on 100 ARC problems) and Parab et al. (generator 46.4%, implementor 61.2%) verified; note the generator/implementor figures are from 100 list functions, not ARC, and the Wang abstract does not name GPT-4.

Poddar (99.2 precision/42.8 recall for Qwen3-Next 80B Thinking; 61.0/93.1 for Gemma 3 27B; 76 valid of 160) and Lampinen raw-likelihood bias verified; I recomputed d' as 2.56 and 1.39, matching the rough figures (these are derived, not reported).

LINC (57% vs 41% Uncertain, precision 93% vs 81%, lower recall) and SatLM (abstains on UNSAT/AMBIG) verified; LINC attributes the extra 'Uncertain' mainly to lossy translation to FOL, and the design advice in the last sentence is the researcher's inference, not a source finding.

Numbers check out (Markovits 2015: 30 of 107 statistical; de Chantal 2020: 45/31/24% of 139; Gratton and Markovits 2021: 36.2/37.4/26.4% of 2,122) but every source is from Markovits' own lab using the same diagnostic, and two listed entries are the same 2021 paper, so no independent replication is shown.

Numbers verified (Markovits 2015 Study 1 F=15.29, Study 2 probability ratings .789/.775 vs .763/.762; Brisson and Markovits 2020 strategy x validity F=10.5), but no opened source tests non-sequiturs or invalid syllogisms, probability-rating equality is shown in two studies (Brisson Study 3 had counterexample reasoners rating higher overall, 77.0 vs 68.3), and all sources come from the Markovits lab.
fix: In Markovits-lab studies, the strategy gap appears on the uncertain conditional inferences (AC and DA) and when people are asked about logical validity; on MP and MT, and when asked for explicit probability or likelihood ratings, the interaction with strategy is absent (Markovits et al. 2015 Studies 1-2; Brisson and Markovits 2020 Studies 1 and 3). Modus ponens diverges when premise strength is stated (Statistical accept more) or disabling conditions are many (opposite pattern), so the strategies are processing styles rather than degrees of logic (Markovits et al. 2017, abstract only).

problem: Numbers verified (.76 vs .32 conflict-item accuracy in de Chantal et al. 2020; belief effect 2.47 vs 1.47 of 4 in Markovits et al. 2017), but both papers and the review are by the Markovits group using the same strategy diagnostic, so the finding has no independent-lab replication.

Direction is confirmed in Markovits (2024) review (time constraint gives many more Statistical patterns; Counterexample reasoners stay stable; confidence predicts keeping a strategy) but every source is the Markovits group, and the 2013 original (sample sizes, the claim that statistical answers carry lower confidence) was only seen second-hand or as an abstract, so there is no independent support.
Markovits, Lortie Forgues and Brunet (2010) (87.1% vs 38.6%, scaled condition F=23.63 frequency effect) and Geiger and Oberauer (2007) (frequency not number of disablers) verified in the PDFs.

Numbers verified (PHM r(318)=.90 over 320 points; NeuBAROCO atmosphere GPT-3.5 39.42%, BART 0.96%, RoBERTa 0%-ish; Eisape LMs rarely say nothing follows; Hasan 9 of 29), but no source says the Markovits 'statistical strategy' is modelled by PHM min/attachment heuristics (that link is the researcher's inference), and Hasan's abstract says 9 of 29 exceed random chance rather than a 'Yes/No competence floor'.
fix: The Probability Heuristics Model (min and attachment heuristics) fits human syllogism answers closely (r(318)=.90 over 320 data points), and language models show a similar form-heuristic signature: they almost never answer 'nothing follows' (accuracy near 0% on those items), and on NeuBAROCO atmosphere items (answer is neutral) GPT-3.5 got 39.42% and RoBERTa and BART about 0 to 1%; across 29 models only 9 exceeded random chance on probability-operator inferences. Whether PHM models the Markovits statistical strategy is a hypothesis, not a source finding.

problem: REFUTE (<9%), Drucker and Mahowald (69% to 17-30%) and Zouak et al. (0.27 to 0.00, 97.7% of 177) all verified; scope notes: the 0.27 to 0.00 collapse is counterexample-only SFT on Qwen3-4B (not 'always disprove' in general), the 97.7% is the authors' own audit of their own verifiers, and the three results come from different domains (algorithms, concept definitions, algebra conjectures).

Effect sizes verified (Beghin and Markovits 2022 partial eta2 .036 and .038; Gratton and Markovits 2021 interaction .004), but all sources (contingency, belief revision, social reasoning, base rates, denominator neglect) are from Markovits and Thompson's group using the same strategy diagnostic, so generalisation is shown by one lab.

Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) verified (Kendall W .86, .64, .45; entropy vs accuracy r=-.52; 90% vs 1%), but the six data sets are US and Italian samples (N=156 total) largely from the Johnson-Laird circle, and the other listed entries are the same paper or only Eisape's qualitative LM comparison.

Heit and Rotello Exp 1 (.89/.22 vs .93/.55, d' 1.68 vs 0.93, via the authors' 2012 chapter) and Lassiter and Goodman 2012 (necessary .82/.41, plausible .94/.82, d' 1.15 vs 0.63; 507 recruited, 485 analysed, 10,185 judgments) verified; slip: Lassiter's valid acceptance differs by 12 points (.82 vs .94), so 'similar' is loose, though the false-alarm shift (.41 vs .82) is far larger.

The 80%/20% figures come from one study (Johnson-Laird and Steedman 1978, cited as 'e.g., around 80%' in Khemlani and Johnson-Laird 2012); Eisape et al. corroborate the order-of-terms effect only qualitatively, and the other K&JL entries are the same paper.
Minor: PaLM 2 claim from Eisape (largest model 'somewhat lower' than second largest); LLaMA-3 70B numbers (58.89 valid base; 54.44 valid and 32.50 invalid instruct) match Bertolazzi Table 1.

Byrne cells (MP 96/96/38, AC 71->13) match two secondary sources; Dieussaert MP 88/93/60 appears only in the v1 of arXiv 2002.10149 (not the latest version). Byrne and Dieussaert numbers are secondary, via logic-programming papers.

Graded effect rests on one paper (De Neys et al. 2003, listed twice); Neth and Beller (1999) does not vary counterexample number; and the DA result is only non-significant when comparing 1 to 4 alternatives (Rao R p<.15), while any alternatives (vs none) lowered AC and DA.
fix: Suppression is graded in the number of counterexamples in De Neys et al. (2003): MP and MT fall with number of disablers and AC falls with number of alternatives; among 1 to 4 presented alternatives the extra effect on DA was not significant (p<.15), and presenting disablers raised AC. Single-study result.

problem: Ordering MT < disjunctive < MP (all p<.001), MT hardest, and Evans 2007 high-ability MT trend and Holliday overgeneralization all check out; the exact soft-accuracy means .59/.54/.31 could not be located in the arXiv text (probably only in a figure).
Evans 2007 numbers (MT 35 vs 61) match, but Ye et al. report degradation for all models with GPT-4 staying above chance, so 'collapse' is too strong for LLMs in general.
fix: Negation changes conditional inference rates (Evans et al. 2007: for 'if not-p then q', MT is endorsed 35% vs 61% for 'if p then q'), and step-by-step LLMs degrade when a predicate is replaced by its lexical negation (Ye et al. 2023: all models degrade, many fall toward chance, GPT-4 stays above chance).

problem: Minor slips: the 98.6 lower bound is gpt-oss-20b (98.56); GPT-5 variants and Qwen3-32B span 98.84 to 99.72; BIS Reasoning is a Japanese-language dataset; 'medium effort' does not apply to Qwen3-32B (thinking on/off).
Minor: 95.83 is the validation score (test 95.29); in the Kartac paper only 2 of 21 validation errors are clear parse errors, most are wrong gold labels and logic-type ambiguity.
Meta-analysis 4% to 24% is quoted by Weber et al. from McDowell and Jacobs (2017), not opened directly; 46% is under half-correct, so 'most still fail' is true but only just (50% in short menu).

Heit (2000) notes diversity is the least robust effect and that Itzaj later showed diversity in a corn-cob context, so 'boundaries' are context-dependent; Kemp and Tenenbaum and Heit corroborate the core effects.

The 13/16 and 14/16 figures come from two small studies by one lab (Wu and Gentner 1998, 16 undergraduates each, fictional animals) pitting a shared causal antecedent against a shared attribute; Kemp and Tenenbaum give only a modelling argument, so 'similarity alone is the wrong default' is wider than the data.
fix: In Wu and Gentner (1998), with fictional animals, 13 of 16 and 14 of 16 undergraduates (two experiments) predominantly preferred an inference based on a shared causal antecedent over one based on a shared attribute; Kemp and Tenenbaum argue theoretically that the best induction model depends on the property and context.

problem: Minor: the 'plateau after about 2 rounds' result is on a 40-task ARC subset (Wang et al.), with GPT-4; Qiu et al. report refinement hurts only on MiniARC while helping on the other three datasets.

Only one source supports the claim (Greenblatt's blog post, one author, not peer-reviewed); the +3 per doubling is measured on the V2 prompt without revision, while the 50% result also uses revision and prompt tweaks (about 100,000 V2 samples would be needed for 50% without them).

Li et al. report about 9% of samples that fit the training examples are false positives (not 9% of tasks), and the 28.7% (640 of 2,228 problem instances = 1,114 functions x 2 versions) is a share of all problems, i.e. 42.5% of the 1,506 that fit the examples, so the two rates are not like-for-like.
fix: Programs that fit the training examples still fail the test: about 9% of train-fitting samples are false positives in Li et al. (2024) on ARC, while for o3-mini's first attempt on the Li and Ellis (2025) benchmark 640 of 2,228 problem instances (1,114 functions in two versions; 28.7% of all, 42.5% of the 1,506 that pass the 10 examples) pass the examples but fail the differential-testing oracle.

problem: Minor: in the d17 table .753 is self-consistency (best-of-N is .819, weighted voting .817), but the 0 to 4 point GSM8K gap (BFS .824, MCTS .838 to .854 vs .817) still holds; the Blocksworld 0.00 to 0.42 is LLaMA-33B CoT vs RAP (GPT-4 CoT gets 0.40).
Minor: 51.6 is RAP(10) with aggregation; RAP(10) alone is 48.6 (vs CoT+SC(10) 46.8); GSM8K 86 vs 90 and StrategyQA 82 vs 83 match ToT Table B (100 random items, GPT-4).

Generation-bottleneck numbers (64% vs 31%) and LATS 0.37 vs 0.63 (HotPotQA) are correct, but in the Stanford student project the fine-tuned value function shrank the BFS-1 vs BFS-5 gap from about 48 to about 16 points (BFS-1 18.18 to 47.47, BFS-5 66.66 vs 63.63), which is not 'nearly closes'; it is also a small (~99 problem) course project.
fix: On Game of 24, generation, not evaluation, is the bottleneck (GPT-4 generate + GPT-3.5 evaluate 64%; reverse 31%); in a small open-model re-run (Stanford course project, about 99 problems) a fine-tuned value function raised BFS-1 from 18.2% to 47.5% and cut the BFS-1 vs BFS-5 gap from about 48 to about 16 points; LATS on HotPotQA drops from 0.63 to 0.37 without the LM value heuristic.

problem: All numbers check out, but the verifier-works half (82% Blocksworld, graph coloring 1/100 vs 16%) comes from the Kambhampati group only (Valmeekam, Stechly; the 82% is quoted second-hand in the 2402.01817 position paper from Valmeekam et al. 2023c); only the GSM8K self-correction result (Huang et al., 75.9 to 74.7) is from an independent lab, and Stechly found sampling alone matched the verifier gain.

Numbers check out (1361/1361, 1.2 to 2.8 tries, GPT-4o 2.0 to 5.8 and mini 4.8 to 10.0 calls, $14,000 and $16,000 estimates), but the two papers are from the same IBM group (Katz, Kokel, Srinivas, Sohrabi; the second is an explicit follow-up), and the costs are estimates from token counts; the crossword run also assumed candidate answers were given.
Minor: the cost claim is a single-domain (calendar scheduling) example and the LLM-Modulo loop is the Kambhampati group's own system; the log-linear fit is described as 'often' log-linear.

Sprague et al. give the average CoT gains as symbolic 14.2, math 12.3, logical 6.9; the claim lists math, symbolic, logic in that order with 14.2 / 12.3 / 6.9, swapping the math and symbolic labels. The other figures (56.8 vs 56.1, Blocksworld findings of Stechly et al.) are correct.
fix: Step-by-step text helps mostly on symbolic, math and logical tasks (average CoT gain 14.2 / 12.3 / 6.9 points respectively) and barely elsewhere (56.8 vs 56.1); CoT gains on Blocksworld come from prompts matched to the problem class and shrink as instances grow past the examples. A symbolic solver or tool beats CoT on symbolic work.

problem: Numbers check out (79.7 vs 19.9/13.0 min, 24 of 41 failed in two hours, 16:1 and 2:1 recapped), but both opened sources are by Kotovsky (with Simon and Fallside) and recap the Hayes/Simon/Kotovsky programme; no independent lab confirms the legality-testing-cost explanation.

F(1,53)=2.12 (21 vs 31 moves), 13% and balls-out-of-boxes heuristic check out in Kotovsky and Simon, but Jarusek and Pelanek show shortest-path length is a strong predictor for Rush Hour (Spearman 0.90) and weak only for Sokoban (0.41) and Replacement (0.21), so 'do not set difficulty' is too general.
fix: In the Chinese Ring Puzzle (linear space), starting 21 vs 31 moves from the goal gave no reliable solving-time difference (F(1,53)=2.12, p<.2), solvers show long unproductive stretches then a fast final run, and a misleading progress heuristic (balls out of boxes) traps them; across transport puzzles, solution length predicts human difficulty well for Rush Hour (Spearman 0.90) but poorly for Sokoban (0.41) and the Replacement puzzle (0.21).

problem: Simon (1975) supports multiple strategies (goal recursion, perceptual, move-pattern/rote) and that behaviour diversity hides under one label, but his rote strategy fails to transfer to a different disk count (not 'when rules change'), and 'people do not start with goal recursion' rests on Anderson and Douglass, whose PDF could not be reached, so it is unverified.
fix: Several different strategies (goal recursion, perceptual, rote move pattern) solve the same Tower of Hanoi problem (Simon 1975); a rote strategy memorised for four disks does not transfer to five, and correct solutions can hide very different strategies.

problem: The MATER 20-to-2 branching and k*b^(L/k) waypoint figures are confirmed in Simon (1972); the Planning GPS and hand-written difference-table half could not be checked (AI Magazine article PDF unreachable, 1959 RAND report is an image scan), and every cited source is Newell/Simon work or a retrospective on it, so there is no independent lab.

Minor: Snell et al. say compute-optimal allocation 'nearly outperforms' best-of-N with up to 4x less compute in the low-budget regime only; Wu et al. compare REBASE with sampling (not beam search) and show 'comparable' on levels 1-2 and a significant gain on levels 3-5.

Norvig (PAIP ch. 4) supports clobbered-sibling, Sussman anomaly, taxi case, protected goals and achieve-all; interleaving as the fix comes from Wikipedia's Sussman anomaly entry; both are secondary or textbook sources, and the taxi case is Norvig's own toy example.

All three sources (PlanBench 2023, o1 PlanBench 2024, LLM-Modulo position paper) come from the same Kambhampati/Valmeekam lab and reuse its benchmark; the quoted numbers (206/600, 4.3%, 2%, 97.8%, 52.8%, 23.63%) do check out.

Only Sel et al. (AoT+) supports the claim (its other listed entries are the same paper); the second distinct source (MEDAKA) actually reports state hallucination and drift persisting in AoT+ traces. The 70.0 vs 71.0 Game of 24 numbers and memoization argument do check out in AoT+.

Lovett and Anderson find group-level near-matching but many individuals overmatch (some select the better strategy almost exclusively), and Rieskamp's reanalysis shows slow adaptation after environment switches (only 27% moved to a compensatory strategy), so 'in proportion to learned success rates' is too strong.
fix: People's strategy choices track learned success rates, at group level close to probability matching in the Building Sticks Task, though many individuals overmatch (choose the better strategy more often than its success rate); simple reinforcement (SSL) and Bayesian success-estimate (ACT-R) models fit the choices, with adaptation to environment changes sometimes slow.

problem: Evidence is from numerical domains (fractions, numerosity); the Siegler theory entry is the same Fazio paper, so two independent sources.

Slip: ZebraLogic merge gains for Phi-4 are +0.6 to +1.0 (vote+verifier 28.3 vs 27.3), so 'under 1 point' should read 'about 1 point or less'; Select-then-Solve text says self-routing average 48.4% while its table row shows 46.7.
Note the Illusion of Thinking collapse in effort has been disputed as a token-limit artifact by later commentary, but the paper does report it.

Numbers check out (74.7%/87.5% Self-Discover, 4,371 MicroDYN students, 7/12/27% Plan-and-Solve); 'execution errors dominate' rests on one PaLM-2L MATH analysis and the claim itself notes the error mix varies by method.

The 'neither necessary nor sufficient' statement is the editorial's summary of Molnar and Csapo 2018, and Wu and Molnar 2022 is the same lab, so these are effectively one source; only Schoppek and Fischer 2017 is independent and it supports the claim only partly (VOTAT did not mediate transfer, knowledge-control r about .35-.41).

The scaffold-alone drop (87.3% to 77.3%) is not statistically significant (Fisher p=0.077) and is explained by exposure to a structural trap, and the hypothesis-sampling fix is said to remove the disjunctive bias in the 8-object setting rather than the gap generally; the Lampinen Wason source is unrelated.
fix: LLM agents explore hidden-rule (Blicket) tasks poorly and prefer OR over AND rules; sampling many distinct hypotheses and choosing actions that eliminate them removes the OR bias at high sample counts in the 8-object setting, while in a rule-switch Blicket variant a typed scaffold alone scored numerically lower than base (77.3% vs 87.3%, not significant, p=0.077) and the scaffold plus a monitor scored 89.1% (p=0.015 vs scaffold alone).

problem: Numbers verified (53.1/50.3/47.6, 26% gap recovery, 17.1pp, 7.0k vs 14.0k tokens); the final sentence about a single lucky run is the researcher's inference (paper notes single-seed runs but argues the variation is complementarity, not noise).

Numbers match (Vending-Bench breakdowns not tied to context fill; Haiku 4.5 about 40 idle days of 90; Tailorshop 305k vs 138k with gpt-5.5 at no reasoning); the Dorner analogy is the researcher's interpretation, and the 138k human figure is a control-group mean from a different study sample than the 50 single-seed AI runs.

LIMBO and MemCon numbers check out (LIMBO says comparable or better accuracy, not equal; MemCon 2.6-4.2 points and 10.9-24.1% cost reductions are framework averages), but neither source says anything about LLMs failing to explore in-context from raw history or that only GPT-4 with CoT and external statistics worked.
fix: A persistent per-task-type record of what worked helps agents when a small outside controller reads it (LIMBO bandit: comparable or better accuracy than the strongest fixed baseline at up to 83% lower inference cost, 53% on average; MemCon bandit on GPT-4.1-mini: +2.6 to +4.2 points over G-Memory on the six-benchmark mean, with 10.9-24.1% lower token cost depending on framework). No test of the LLM reading its own strategy-success table was found.

problem: Rhodes and Tauber report g=0.93 (4,554 participants, 112 effect sizes) and g=0.08 (3,807, 98), but call the memory benefit 'modest but reliable' rather than absent, and it includes the Dunlosky and Nelson studies; cue-dependence (1992) was not opened.

Numbers match, but both studies test self-assessed IQ only (not skills in general), and the large-sample paper reports a statistically significant, minimal Dunning-Kruger effect (quadratic dR2=.011, p<.001) rather than a purely linear relation.
fix: For self-assessed intelligence, the Dunning-Kruger quartile pattern is mostly a statistical artefact (better-than-average effect plus regression to the mean; N=929 shows an essentially linear relation), and in a large representative sample (N=13,977) the extra low-ability miscalibration is statistically significant but very small (quadratic dR2=.011).

problem: Thompson et al. support FOR being driven by answer fluency and predicting thinking time and answer changes, but Gangemi et al. only show (via post-hoc questionnaire, N=145 and 148) that people giving the wrong intuitive bat-and-ball answer report more unease; they do not show FOE predicts a second look or answer change, or that it is fast or conflict-driven.
fix: Feeling of rightness is a cheap signal driven by answer fluency that predicts thinking time and answer changes (Thompson et al. 2013); a feeling of error (self-reported unease) accompanies wrong intuitive answers on the bat-and-ball problem (Gangemi et al. 2015), but its role in triggering a second look is not shown.

problem: All numbers come from one paper (Xiong et al.) listed five times; independent corroboration comes only from Pawitan and Holmes (models giving 100 to every answer), so the claim stands on two sources.

Xiong 5-dataset average 56.4 to 73.0 compares Top-K M=1 with Prompt M=5 (different configurations); Kuhn's 'distinct answers' count is of semantically distinct answers, not raw strings; limits from the audit papers (0.62-0.78, 0.20-0.59) were not opened.

All supporting numbers (ECE 0.140/0.050, 0.256/0.065, 0.451/0.203, TruthfulQA AUC 0.455-0.551) check out in Tian et al., but every supporting entry is that single paper and the second source (Kadavath et al.) concerns temperature recalibration of pretrained and RLHF models, not verbalised vs token-probability calibration.

Kapoor et al. support ~1,000 graded examples sufficing and gains slowing after ~5,000, and Steyvers et al. independently show fine-tuning beats the untuned model; the 'no-training constraint' and 'recalibration map allowed' sentences are project policy, not literature claims.

All numbers check out (72.9% vs 50%; 34.2% vs 9.6%; Kimi K2 23.3% accuracy at 95.7% confidence; r=0.94 vs 0.48), but Michael et al. show confidence does respond to difficulty (hard-easy effect, underconfidence on easy items), only less than accuracy does, so 'regardless of evidence or difficulty' is too strong.
fix: Models are on average overconfident and their confidence responds less to evidence and difficulty than accuracy does: in debates both sides start at about 73% confidence (rational 50%) and raise it; on the hardest question set confidence was 34% against 9.6% accuracy; one model had 23.3% accuracy at 95.7% confidence. Reasoning models track actual probability better (r=.94 vs .48 for other models).

problem: The cascade gains in ConfTuner come from routing low-confidence answers to a stronger model (GPT-4o), not purely from self-revision; the Huang CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 figure is right.

The 4-of-12 (ECE), 9-of-12 (AUROC) and 0.072 figures appear only in v3 of Kim and Kang; the current version (v4) uses five models and 20 settings and reports the better signal flipping in 8 settings under each metric; the metacognitive-efficiency correlations (-0.80 TriviaQA, +0.00 NQ) match the current version.
fix: Reported LLM calibration numbers are unstable across protocol details: changing the context in which the token score is read flips which of verbalized or token confidence looks better in 8 of 20 settings under both ECE and AUROC (Kim and Kang, current version; an earlier version reported 4 of 12 under ECE and 9 of 12 under AUROC and a 0.072 shift from alias vs canonical answer); metacognitive efficiency correlates with accuracy -0.80 on TriviaQA and 0.00 on Natural Questions.

problem: Kadavath says models are 'somewhat better' at predicting their own P(IK) than another model's; Kapoor et al. found a different model (Mistral) predicting LLaMA-2 correctness better than LLaMA-2 itself, which qualifies the first clause.

Numbers match (0.56 to 0.80 at 100-500 tokens, 0.88 peak, reader 0.841 vs R1 0.851, Qwen3 0.650 to 0.807); 'discriminates only when real reasoning came first' and 'mostly summarises the trace' are interpretive glosses; the Yoon Qwen3 Thinking row equals the QwQ row in the paper's table.

In Knoblich 1999 Exp 3 the 61% to 100% rise is the regular-first group going from regular Type C (Block 1) to tautological Type C (Block 2), not an effect of tautology-first exposure on regular C; the rate effect of prior tautology exposure on regular C could not be ascertained (ceiling), only solution times show it (U=8, p<.001); all evidence is one paper (Miller et al. 2025 paywalled, 403).
fix: In Knoblich et al. (1999) Exp 3 (N=34), tautological Type C was solved by 100% in Block 1 versus 61% for regular Type C (p<.001), and prior exposure to the tautological form shortened regular Type C solution times (p<.001) while Type D initial rate was unaffected (61% vs 69%, p=.64); Type D times also improved after exposure (p<.01), so the separation of constraint relaxation from chunk decomposition is supported for initial rates and only partly for times; this rests on one experiment from one lab.

problem: Minor: the 2001 eye-tracking study labels differ (its Problem C is a tight-chunk problem, so it does not test tautology), and the Knoblich lab papers (1999, 2001, Oellinger 2006) count as one lab; only Spiridonov 2025 is independent, so 'several labs' is really two.

Li et al. (2024) recalibrate each slice from k unlabeled examples (labelled data is needed only once, to train the recalibrator), so 'need labelled runs from the target slice' is not what the source shows; the k=5 to 20 result is target-precision success (0.81 at k=5), not an ECE gain.
fix: Calibration maps should be per task type, not global. Per-slice few-shot recalibration beat global temperature scaling in every setting tested (MMLU ECE 0.063 to 0.053 at PaLM2-L; 0.109 to 0.074 at LLaMA-65B) using only k=5 to 20 unlabeled examples from the target slice, although the recalibrator is trained once on labelled data from many slices; an agent calibrator learned on one domain transferred only partly (about 500 labelled trajectories per dataset). How many held-out items a counting-table map needs without training is not measured.

problem: Minor: the 54.8 to 92.7 GSM8K AUROC figures are GPT-3.5 (Table 3: CoT M=1 vs Self-Random M=5 with consistency), not GPT-4; claim does not name a model there.
Xu et al. 2024 supports every part of the claim; the second listed source (Huang et al. 2024) does not measure self-bias, so the claim rests on one paper.

Table 1 of Li et al. reports accuracy in percent, so the changes are percentage points (GPT-4 0.00 on MATH/GSM8K/CSQA; GPT-3.5 StrategyQA -0.19 points), meaning weaker models also lose almost nothing; 'weaker models lose more' is only relative, and the final sentence on correlated samples is not from the sources.
fix: Stopping sampling when answers agree (early-stopping self-consistency) cut samples by 33.8% (MATH) to 84.2% (Coin Flip) with accuracy changes of at most about 0.2 percentage points in the reported cases (GPT-4: 0.00 on MATH, GSM8K, CSQA and -0.02 on Last Letters; GPT-3.5 StrategyQA -0.19 points); Llama-2 7B lost slightly more (-0.14 points on StrategyQA and Coin Flip), so weaker models lose a little more but still very little.

problem: Adaptive-RAG Table 1 (GPT-3.5) gives single-step time 1.00; the 0.86 is the Mallen adaptive-retrieval row, and the time column is relative to single-step (no-retrieval 0.71), so the units are not ambiguous.
fix: Always-retrieve and always-multi-step pipelines waste compute; routing by question complexity matched multi-step quality at lower cost (Adaptive-RAG GPT-3.5 F1 50.91 vs 50.87 for multi-step IRCoT, relative time 1.46 vs 3.33, where single-step is 1.00 and Mallen adaptive retrieval 0.86), but a large gap to the oracle router remains (F1 62.80); the classifier is only 54.52% accurate.

problem: Minor: s1 Table reports 57.6 at the best setting (abstract says 57%); 'not uncertainty-gated' is the note's interpretation.
Minor: the learned-vs-random MATH gap ranges about 2.6 to 4.5 points across models and budgets, so '3 to 4' is a rounding of that range.

Zollo (ECE 0.268, AUROC 0.635, 36 pairs) and Cao (Sonnet 4.6 numbers) check out, but Gemma 4's passing joint ECE 0.044 belongs to a joint signal whose AUROC is 0.699 (passes); the 0.534 AUROC is its FOK signal, whose ECE is 0.466 (fails), so no single near-uninformative signal passes on ECE.
fix: Raw verbalized confidence from open reasoning models is not good enough to drive control without recalibration: mean ECE 0.268 and AUROC 0.635 over 36 model-dataset pairs, against Cao's bar of ECE at most 0.15 and AUROC at least 0.60. Cao's Sonnet 4.6 numbers (JOL AUROC 0.745, FOK 0.612) are model-specific, and ECE and AUROC must be checked separately: Gemma 4 passes the joint ECE row (0.044) while its FOK AUROC fails (0.534) and its FOK ECE is 0.466.

problem: AgentAbstain reports post-hoc abstention (acting irreversibly and then claiming to abstain) in only 2.6% of abstain runs (about 10% for GPT-5.1/5.2), so 'often' is too strong; also the 53% to 91% threshold span is the GPT-5 pair only (other models exceed 91%, up to over 100%).
fix: When errors have explicit costs, models do not hold a stable act-or-escalate stance: implicit escalation thresholds differ widely, for example 53% (GPT-5-mini) to 91% (GPT-5-nano) accuracy within the GPT-5 family, and are not predicted by scale; in an agent benchmark abstention is largely independent of solving ability (best of 17 models 59.5% paired accuracy), and a minority of failures (post-hoc abstention, 2.6% of abstain runs overall, about 10% for GPT-5.1) come after an irreversible step. This supports a code-level cost threshold placed before irreversible actions.

problem: Minor: the value bias holds for long fixations only (short fixations show none), and the rising fixation duration over time held for problems B and C (no interaction).
Minor: Spiridonov et al. found a few exceptions (VR interactive sticks about +6 points, and interactivity helped problem A while hurting B and C), which fits 'not reliably'.

Minor: the false hints in Ammalainen and Moroshkina were unreportable (flashed) words and the effect is small; 'fixation' is the note's interpretation, and the nine-dot comparison is dot-turn vs non-dot-turn training (N=64).
Minor: NazoNazo 17.6% is the reasoning-model average on the 120-item subset (non-reasoning 7.6%), and BrainTeaser 53/63% is the best model (ChatGPT) on its two subtasks.

Mizumoto et al. call verification failure a distinctive failure mode that is only 5.23% to 39.34% of incorrect answers (4 models with usable logs), so most wrong answers do not contain the gold answer and it is not shown to be the main failure; the o1-like 70% figure (Wang et al.) is from math/science sets, not riddles.
fix: A distinctive reasoning-model failure on insight-like riddles is verification failure: a correct candidate appears in the thought log but is not endorsed (5.2% to 39.3% of wrong answers across four models with usable logs). Outside riddles, more than 70% of wrong o1-like responses on math and science sets contain at least one correct thought (Wang et al.), and hidden states encode intermediate-answer correctness (ROC-AUC above 0.7 in-distribution, Zhang et al.), so models may know more than they endorse.

problem: Minor: the 'Oh!' evidence is a qualitative thought-log observation in Mizumoto v1 (Claude Opus 4 and Grok 4 only, absent from the later arXiv version I opened); d'Aliberti's own shift annotation shows shifted traces were better in crosswords.

Kang et al. supports every part (over 90% confirmatory reflections, wrong-to-right mostly under 2%, 24.5% fewer tokens within a 2.9% accuracy drop); d'Aliberti and Ribeiro is only indirectly related, so the claim rests on one paper.

Minor: step-back alone on TimeQA is 41.5 to 66.0 (+24.5; the paper's 27% includes retrieval), physics and chemistry gains are +6.8 and +10.9, and structure-matched examples (RISCORE) were tested on multiple-choice riddles with smaller gains.

Numbers check out (six-coin 10/48 vs ten-coin 36/48 within 5 min, z=2.67, p=.008; partial-ring 4/27 vs straight-line 11/27, chi2=4.52; Ormerod et al. 2002 abstract confirms the eight-coin effect), but all three sources are the same Lancaster group (Ormerod, Chronicle, MacGregor), so the generalisation rests on one lab.

Sources report minimal or modest (non-significant) gains from visual or 'go outside' hints rather than none, and large gains came from combined aids and training (Kershaw and Ohlsson; Chein et al. got 46% with training plus a partial-solution hint), not from partial-solution hints alone.
fix: Hints that only say to go outside the box, or give visual cues, give little or no gain on the nine-dot problem (base rate under 5% in a few minutes; shading cue minimal gain, verbal plus visual hints slight gain). Large gains came only when aids addressing several difficulties were combined, for example training plus a hint that gives away part of the solution (46% solved in Chein et al.).

problem: Jones (2003) found that all 30 solvers had an impasse (fixation time at or above personal mean plus 2 SD on some move) somewhere before the taxi move, only 5 immediately before, and all 7 non-solvers also had at least one impasse; it did not show that the longest fixation precedes the key move in every solver (only that the taxi move had longer average fixation than the 3 moves before and after, p<.01). Fedor et al. (2017) do name inactivity and repeated attempts as behavioural correlates of impasse.
fix: Impasse is observable in behaviour: in a car-park insight problem (Jones 2003, N=37 analysable) all 30 solvers showed an impasse, defined as a move fixation time at or above that person's mean plus 2 SD, before the key taxi move (5 immediately before it), and fixation time on the taxi move was longer than on the three moves before and after it; non-solvers also had impasses. A neural model paper (Fedor et al. 2017) cites inactivity and repeated attempts as behavioural correlates of impasse.

problem: Wang et al. (2026): 7 of 11 deployments follow the reporting duty (93.2-100%) and 4 only 0.6-10.1%, but the 90.6-99.4% pre-action and 5.8-11.5% mid-task figures are for just gpt-4.1 and gpt-5.5; other compliant deployments (gemini-3.8-flash, gpt-6-astra, claude-opus-5) hold 74-100% mid-task and fail instead at completion (48-64%), so the mid-task failure is not general.
fix: Wang et al. (2026, tau2-bench telecom): 7 of 11 models follow a progress-reporting duty on 93.2-100% of checkpoints and 4 on only 0.6-10.1%; for gpt-4.1 and gpt-5.5 reports are correct at 90.6-99.4% of pre-action checkpoints and 87.3-88.9% after completion but only 5.8-11.5% mid-task, while several newer models are accurate mid-task (74-100%) and weak at completion (48-64%), so the weak stage varies by model.

problem: Li et al. check out (verbal confidence AUROC 0.85 at completion, none above 0.60 at 50% progress), but in d'Aliberti and Ribeiro the pooled OR 0.77 (CI 0.58-1.02, p=0.070, N=723,200) is the association between entropy and whether a shift occurs, not entropy predicting when a shift helps.
fix: Uncertainty signals (verbal confidence, perplexity, entropy, consistency) predict failure well only at the end of a long-horizon agent trajectory (verbal confidence mean AUROC 0.85 at completion over 15 model-benchmark pairs) and poorly mid-way (no signal above mean AUROC 0.60 at 50% progress). In reasoning traces, token entropy was only weakly and inconsistently associated with whether a spontaneous shift occurs (pooled OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.02, p=0.070, N=723,200; positive in crosswords, negative in math).

problem: Minor: N=723,200 is the Qwen2.5-1.5B all-domain count in the paper's own table (7.65%, 3.95 vs 20.42), so the 'pooled over all models' label for 2.57 vs 16.44 is doubtful (the paper's text is itself ambiguous), and GPT-4o was tested for shift rate (0.88-2.21%), so 'no closed frontier model tested' is not fully right.
Minor: the Pipis loop figures (76% vs 37%) are at low temperature for Qwen-1.5B vs Qwen-32B and do not themselves show loops mark failure; 225% and 418% are averages over o1-like models.

Minor: the +5.0 pp (PMCoder) and ALFWorld +40 pp come from whole systems, not stuck rules alone (plan-only 148.7 and memory-only 150.7 vs both 167.3 resolved), which the claim already states; vendor docs confirmed to give thresholds with no ablation or false-positive data.
Minor: in Snell et al. it is beam search, not best-of-N, that over-optimises on easy questions (best-of-N does not), and the 400-completion peak is Cobbe's 6B verifier only.
Optimal-K 'about 3 or fewer' is Fig 13 (Llama 3.1 8B fitted model); empirical cost-ratio-4 case is K about 5; both are in the paper and match.
Verified Huang et al. Tables 2-3 (75.9->74.7, oracle 84.3, GPT-4 95.5->89.0) and Stechly et al. graph coloring; independent authors.

Huang et al. Table 2: GPT-3.5 GSM8K with oracle stop is 84.3, not 95.5 (95.5 is GPT-4 standard prompting); CSQA 38.1 is round 1 (41.8 after round 2). Kang et al. numbers (90% confirmatory, <2%, 1.4-3.5, 16.8-47.8%) check out.
fix: Reflection or a forced re-check after the first answer mostly confirms it. In 8 reasoning models on 5 maths sets over 90% of reflections are confirmatory, wrong-to-right is under about 2%, first-candidate accuracy is within 1.4-3.5 points of final, and reflections take 16.8-47.8% of tokens. Without an outside label, prompted self-correction lowers accuracy (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after one round, 41.8 after two); with an oracle stop it raises it (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3; GPT-4 95.5 to 97.5). The paired right-to-wrong rate for a forced Wait is still unreported.

problem: The 32.2->40.6 math gain (d'Aliberti Table 5, probably Qwen2.5-1.5B) is for a reconsideration cue appended to all prompts, not only high-entropy ones (entropy gating is a separate appendix analysis with larger gains); shifts are 'strongly harmful' on math and only 'mildly harmful' on crosswords. 6.31%, 85-95%, AUC>0.7 and >0.9 on AIME at 32B are confirmed.
fix: Spontaneous self-verification by RL-trained reasoning models rarely finds errors. Mid-trace shifts occur in 6.31% of traces and are harmful on math (strongly) and mildly so on crosswords; about 85 to 95% of rechecks in Qwen3-8B are confirmatory; but appending a forced reconsideration cue to every prompt lifted math accuracy from 32.2% to 40.6% (small Qwen2.5 model), with gains larger on high-entropy instances. Hidden states carry a correctness signal (probe ROC-AUC above 0.7, above 0.9 on AIME for the 32B distill) that the model does not use.

problem: Lightman numbers (78.2/72.4/69.6; 72.9/63.8/61.3 on 234) and Uesato 12.4->3.4-5.5 trace error match; slip: 22.3 vs 23.5 is process- vs outcome-supervised final-answer error without RMs, not with vs without RM feedback.

All numbers check out, but the poor-generalisation evidence (ProcessBench F1s and the 56.5 vs 28.9 / 64.9 vs 64.3 comparison) comes only from two papers by the same Qwen Team; the third source (Math-Shepherd) is the model being criticised, not independent evidence.
fix: Open PRMs trained on automatic (Monte Carlo) step labels generalise poorly to hard problems and lose to prompted strong models as step critics, per the Qwen team's ProcessBench and PRM-lessons papers (single lab, not independently replicated): ProcessBench F1 (GSM8K/MATH/Olympiad) Math-Shepherd-PRM-7B 47.9/29.5/24.8 vs GPT-4o 79.2/63.6/51.4 vs o1-mini 93.2/88.9/87.2; a PRM800K human-label model averages 56.5 vs 28.9 for MC Math-Shepherd labels, while best-of-8 hides the gap (64.9 vs 64.3).

problem: Zheng et al. Table 2/3 numbers (65.0/46.2/23.8; 91.3/91.3/8.7 of 23) and Shi et al. quality-gap and judge-level variation verified; independent labs.
CodeT 47.0->65.8, Konstantinou et al. 2026 (14% vs 25%, -13.2%, CoT/CoVe no better) and Stroebl readability finding all verified; the 'errors correlate' inference is supported by the 2026 paper.

Huang et al. (450 iterations, 77.9 in attack table, generative more vulnerable) and Helff et al. (458 vs 40; gpt-5-mini 0 to 84) verified; the 77.9 table label is garbled in text extraction but plausible.

Both papers report the stated figures (TrACE 33/39/55/65% fewer calls, n=50/n=30, 3B; PETS GPQA 75%/55%); caveat only: TrACE is a single-author small test where SC barely beats greedy on MiniHouse, so 'matched' is weak evidence.

ReASC numbers and DSC Table 4 (ASC +74%, ESC +3%) verified, but Manvi et al. give no comparison against a fixed best-of-4 in the text; they report 1.2 samples capturing 74% of the 16-sample Best-of-N gain.
fix: Savings quoted against 40 or 512 samples shrink against a realistic small baseline and when input tokens are counted. Against 16 samples ESC saves 44.6% / 15.4% / 4.4% (GSM8K / MATH500 / Omni-Math) for Llama-3.2-3B and 71.4% / 56.6% (GSM8K / MATH500) for Gemma-3-27B. With the prompt re-sent per round, ASC costs 74% more and ESC 3% more than SC-40 on Mistral-7B GSM8K. Adaptive resampling with a self-evaluation head reaches about 74% of the 16-sample Best-of-N gain with 1.2 samples on average (Manvi et al.).

problem: Aggarwal (2.9-3.8x, Vicuna 1.9x, GPT-3.5 4.4x), Li et al. ESC, ReASC 4.4-71.4% vs k=16, and DSC Table 4 (+74%, +3%) all verified; 2x-5x is a slightly generous summary for ESC MATH (-33.8%, about 1.5x).
GSM8K -80.1%, Coin Flip -84.2%, MATH -33.8% (GPT-4), Boolean Expressions 7.9x, and ReASC MATH500 offline accept ratio 7.2% (Llama-3.2-3B) all found in the papers.

Chen et al. (1,953% more tokens on 2+3; first round correct in over 92% cases using under 60% of tokens) and DEER abstract (19.1-80.1% shorter chains, accuracy +0.3 to +5.0) verified; independent groups.

Brown et al. (98.44 vs 41.41; 11.3% flaky; CodeContests false negatives) verified; BATS self-verify early stop vs full run is 18.7 vs 24.6 on BrowseComp (5.9 points), so '6-8 points' is slightly generous for that cell.
Laird 2022 glossary lists four as state no-change, operator no-change, tie, conflict (no constraint-failure); only the Soar manual lists tie, conflict, constraint-failure, no-change.
fix: The count of impasse types is not canonical: Laird 2022 main text says 3 (state no-change, operator tie/conflict, operator no-change); the Laird 2022 glossary says 4 (state no-change, operator no-change, tie, conflict); the Soar manual impasse-types list also says 4 (tie, conflict, constraint-failure, no-change), and splitting no-change in the manual's list gives 5. Constraint-failure is absent from both the main text and glossary of Laird 2022.

problem: Huang Table 3 (75.9->74.7, 75.8->41.8, 26.0->25.0) verified; NL2GenSym ablation (critic removal biggest drop) and STARS analyse-and-repair paper exist and support the grounded-check statement.

Missing-premise paper (2x-4x more tokens, low abstain rates) and underthinking paper (wrong answers switch thoughts more) verified; 'unreliable stuck signal' and design recommendation are the note-writer's inference, and the 3,000 vs 1,000 token figures could only be partly read from the figure.
Laird-Rosenbloom-Newell 1984 Table 1 (1731/485/7) and Doorenbos-Tambe-Newell 1992 footnote (4 decision cycles) verified; claim itself discloses same-group weak independence.

Laird 1984 Tic-Tac-Toe example (A-C,E,I,G,F tested, D and H not), Soar manual causes list, and Taatgen-Lee ACT-R passage all verified; slight stretch: the manual allows local negations by default and only offers an option to reject them.

Kim-Rosenbloom Table 1 (1.42/0.46/0.34) and Magic Square (over eight million tokens, out of memory) verified; Tambe abstract confirms expensive-chunk slowdown and restricting expressiveness; 'partial matches' is tokens; Minton link is unsourced background.
ASI Table (32.6/39.0/36.4/40.1; 15.6% vs 31.4%), Xiong Table (38.50 vs 16.75 vs 13.05), and Voyager self-verification ablation (-73% items) all verified; independent groups.

Xiong Table, SkillsBench v1 Table 5 (+18.6 vs +5.9; later v4 revises these to +19.0/+10.1), 34,198-skill pool, Dynamic Cheatsheet FH (26.7 vs 23.3; 6.7 vs 20.0), ACE collapse (18,282->122, 66.7->57.1) and Memp over-retrieval all verified.

Voyager transfer table (AutoGPT with library 1/3, 1/3, 2/3, 0/3 vs 0/3), SkillsBench v1 (Haiku 4.5 27.7 vs Opus 4.5 22.0), ASI p=0.1673, LATM Table 2 (5 of 6 about on par), Memp +5% and 1.6 steps all verified.
LATM Table 3 (GPT-3.5 0/5 on hard tasks, tools only fit training cases), Dynamic Cheatsheet smaller-model drawbacks, and Buffer of Thoughts limitation passage all verified; independent groups.
Reiter 1987 Theorem 4.4 and Corollary 4.5 read directly; theorem is stated for conflict sets (Corollary 4.5 for minimal conflict sets); Greiner correction and Rodler consistent.

Greiner et al. confirm HS-tree pruning loses diagnoses with non-minimal conflicts and give the HS-DAG fix; Reiter's remark (3) says no edge is marked redundant with minimal conflicts; DynamicHS (Rodler) labels nodes with minimal conflicts only; the 'still unseen' part is a negative statement I could not check.

Roos (1993) gives O(n^2) worst case (linear for low connectivity) via focusing heuristics but never says 'tree-structured'; BARINEL O(N*M+M log M) and HTC-BDD exhausting 32 GB are verified, as is SNIPER hitting 32 GB on TCAS.
fix: Full model-based diagnosis does not scale to software; cheaper approximations (spectrum-based BARINEL O(N*M+M log M); Roos's focusing heuristics O(n^2) worst case, linear for low connectivity; BDD hitting sets that often run out of 32 GB) trade completeness for speed.

problem: BARINEL wasted effort 1.2/2.4/4.8 for 1/2/4 faults on print_tokens verified in Abreu et al.; Peischl-style VHDL paper shows 25 single vs 66 dual-fault diagnoses for one bug; 'explodes' and 'ranking is required' are mild interpretation.

arXiv 1207.5879 and 1408.2048 are the same paper (Hay, Russell, Tolpin, Shimony, Selecting Computations) and the MITECS overview is by Russell, a co-author; Theorem 7 and the myopic-stops-too-early point are verified in that single source.
fix: The ideal rule from rational metareasoning (stop when no available computation has expected value above its cost) is intractable in general. Per Hay, Russell, Tolpin and Shimony (2012; a single source), cheap myopic or blinkered approximations exist, and the optimal policy computes whenever the myopic one does (Theorem 7), so myopic rules often stop too early where one step is worth zero but several together pay.

problem: Reiter PDF is a scanned image and could not be read in full; its no-probabilities scope was checked only via abstract and secondary commentary; GDE entropy rule confirmed in Siddiqi and Huang.

All numbers check against BED-LLM Table 1 (CoT 39.5 vs 70.7 mean, Llama-3.3-70B Animals 40=40, Things GPT-4o 49 vs 40), but both BED-LLM entries are one paper and the Zhang et al. paper never tests chain-of-thought question selection, so there is only one supporting source.

BED-LLM Table 1 confirms ICL Beliefs 18 vs 88 for Animals GPT-4o-mini; the only other source (Kobalczyk et al.) tests log-prob versus uniform weights, not filtering of hypotheses against history, so the filtering claim rests on one paper.

HumanEval gaps verified (GPT-3.5 binary 70.8 to 85.6, GPT-4o-mini 79.6 to 81.5, open 75.9 to 85.0 vs 83.5 to 83.8), but BED-LLM says its film-preference result is still a boost over Prompt-Only with sizes only in plots, and the ASIG MediQ figures were not shown on the abstract page (authors describe transfer as positive).
fix: Gains from computed-EIG question choice shrink as the base model gets stronger: on HumanEval after 4 questions the gain is about 15 points for GPT-3.5 (binary) but about 2 for GPT-4o-mini; in BED-LLM preference elicitation Prompt-Only is a stronger baseline than in 20 Questions and BED-LLM still gives a boost, with the size shown only in plots.

problem: Zhang et al. Table numbers verified (GPT-4 0.31/0.50, Human 0.24/0.31); all specific numbers come from one paper, QuestBench only corroborates the general weakness.

Golovin and Krause's (ln Q+1)^2 bound for self-certifying instances and the open single-log question are confirmed in the paper, but every supporting entry is the same paper and the de Kleer 1991 entry says nothing about the guarantee.
AbstentionBench 24% figure was checked only through search snippet of the abstract; Guess My City rates (0.19-0.36) and QuestBench BFS depth-10 99.8% verified.

Schoenfeld reports 'little empirical evidence' and only relatively small correlations rather than 'small gains' from taught heuristics; Hembree abstract verified via Crossref (487 reports, grade pattern, diagrams largest gain).
Numbers verified, but Tyen et al. report that with the true error location 18 to 44 percent of originally wrong traces become correct, which is not 'most' wrong traces.
fix: On non-reasoning models of 2023-24, a model checking its own reasoning without outside information does not help and can hurt: GSM8K GPT-4 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0 over two self-correction rounds, GPT-3.5 75.9 to 74.7; pointing to the first wrong step is hard (best overall 52.87%, GPT-4) and gets worse with more calls per trace (more false alarms). Telling the model the true error location lets it fix a substantial minority of wrong traces (+18 to +44 percent of wrong traces corrected, depending on task), but a random location breaks 7 to 16 percent of right traces.

problem: All numbers verified (TTS 60.0 to 73.3, 3.3 to 23.3; DIV-SE 15/23 to 97, GPT-3.5 Blocksworld no gain, LLaMA-2 ZS-CoT 31.32 to 32.00), but 'gains shrink as the base model gets stronger' holds only within TTS and is contradicted at the weak end by DIV-SE, where weaker models gain nothing.
fix: Spreading attempts over several distinct named approaches beats spending the same calls on one prompt, on non-reasoning models: TTS-Uniform (strategy list then equal sampling) lifts GPT-4.1-mini AIME 2024 Acc@32 from 60.0 (self-consistency) to 73.3 and GPT-4o-mini AIME 2025 from 3.3 to 23.3 at the same sample count; DIV-SE (5 approach prompts) lifts GPT-4 Graph Coloring from 15 (CoT) and 23 (SC-10) to 97, with gains vanishing on GPT-3.5 planning and LLaMA-2 zero-shot where the model cannot follow the approach. Both use majority vote, not a verifier. In TTS the gain is smaller for the stronger GPT-4.1-mini than for GPT-4o-mini, but DIV-SE needs a model strong enough to follow the approach prompts.

problem: The '2 to 4 times longer' multiplier is not stated in the Fan et al. abstract; it is inferred from the length table (roughly 2.6x to 4.4x), a minor slip.

The 24 percent token saving belongs to the probe paper (Zhang et al.), not DEER, and DEER's abstract reports an average CoT length cut of 19.1 to 80.1 percent with accuracy up 0.3 to 5.0 percent; probe AUC figures (above 0.7, above 0.9 for R1-Distill-Qwen-32B on AIME) are confirmed.
fix: A small probe on hidden states predicts whether an intermediate answer is correct (ROC-AUC above 0.7, above 0.9 for R1-Distill-Qwen-32B on AIME) and, used as an early-exit rule, cuts inference tokens by about 24 percent without losing accuracy; the training-free confidence-based early exit DEER cuts CoT length by an average of 19.1 to 80.1 percent across 11 models while improving accuracy by 0.3 to 5.0 percent. Two independent groups. Both need model internals or an answer-probing call.

problem: Mehle 3.43 vs 3.36 and Elstein 'three to five' verified; HyGene capacity 2 vs 4 is a simulation parameter in Sprenger et al., not an observed count.

Sprenger et al. numbers verified (261.8 to 271.5 is about 3.7 percent, text says about 10; mediation shown in Experiment 3), but the other source (Thomas, Dougherty, Buttaccio 2014) is a review by the same research group whose abstract does not state the finding, so there is effectively one source.

Numbers verified (Handler et al.: about 70 to 48 percent, 55-81 percent spread, Grok 3 accuracy cost; Bedi et al. JAMA Netw Open drops 8.8 to 38.2, reasoning models least), but both papers come from the same Stanford group (Suhana Bedi and Nigam Shah authors on both), so the 'second source' is not independent.
The 78.3 vs 52 percent figures come from a single model (o1-preview), so 'LLMs' is slightly wider than the evidence; gap 23.0 points (66.6 vs 43.6) verified.

Numbers check out (Bedi: 8.82 to 38.24 point drops on 68 items; Handler: ~70% false action), but Bedi 2025 and Handler 2026 share authors Bedi and Shah (same Stanford group, Handler is a follow-up), and two of the three listed Handler entries are the same paper, so 'reliably' rests on one lab.

Samples are tiny (30 protocols; 2 technicians x 40 trials) and split-half is not absent: Rasmussen and Jensen report about 20% of 75 check measurements and some topographic search fields chosen by split-half; 'trained rule, not natural' is an inference, not a finding.
fix: In two small studies of electronics troubleshooting (Rasmussen and Jensen 1974: 30 protocols; Burroughs 1979: two TV technicians, 40 trials), skilled troubleshooters usually opened with a functional search, ran many cheap good/bad checks, and localised by anchoring on a hunch; strict half-split was occasional (about 20% of check measurements in Rasmussen and Jensen) or absent (0 of 40 trials in Burroughs), while instructors report teaching it as a named strategy.

problem: ChatGPT numbers check (7.24 vs 3.5, 56.67%, 39.44%), but 'best split in a minority of turns' rests on two Qwen3 models picking the best of their own considered candidates (19-36%); ChatGPT in fact used halving questions more often than optimal (73.77% vs 57.14%).
fix: Unaided LLMs choose poor tests in some settings: ChatGPT in 8-candidate 20 Questions needed 7.24 questions vs 3.5 for the optimal questioner, kept asking after one candidate remained in 56.67% of games, and 39.44% of its second-turn questions had zero information gain; two Qwen3 models chose the highest-information question among their own considered candidates in only 19-36% of turns.

problem: Minor: in UoT the LLM still simulates answers and partitions candidates, so scoring is only partly in code.
Design conclusion (ledger in code) is inference; the 6.4 vs 7.24 and contradictory-question numbers (13.50 to 8.42) match, though trivial questions did not fall (25.15 to 26.78).
Numbers check, but 'more steps are not better' is too general: AIOpsLab shows ReAct and FLASH improved with more steps (FLASH peaked at 59.32% at a 20-step limit); only weak agents plateaued.
fix: More steps are not better for weak models: in Cloud-OpsBench the weakest models used 14-16 steps (about 3x the 5-6 of strong models) with repeated calls and low accuracy, GPT-3.5 in AIOpsLab gained nothing but token cost beyond 5 steps, and AR-Bench shows diminishing returns (+7.7% process score in rounds 5-10, +2.5% in rounds 20-25); stronger agents such as FLASH and ReAct did improve with larger step limits.

problem: Alaboudi and LaToza is a small null result (25 participants, p=0.41/0.13/0.67), not proof of no effect, and Parnin and Orso found a ranked suspiciousness list did help on the easy task for high performers.
fix: In a small study (25 participants), offering potential fault locations (where, not why) gave no significant gain in correct hypotheses (p=0.41, 0.13) or fix rate (p=0.67); Parnin and Orso likewise found a ranked suspicious-statement list helped only on the easy task and only for high performers.

problem: Numbers match AutoSD (73% vs 63%, DONE +12.4 vs -11 points); 'must' generalises from one ablation of one system, with LDB only indirectly supporting.
Olausson et al. studies self-repair with test feedback, not purely intrinsic correction, so it only loosely supports; the Huang numbers (75.8 to 38.1) and oracle-label point are correct.
Minor: debug(5) beat debug-from-start only for the two strongest models; for Claude 3.7 the 37.2/48.4/52.1 figures are exact.
Minor: Arafa et al. is self-rated 'harder or equal' (30 of 32 forms) plus longer locating time, with 14 students.

TRAJEVAL's 56.9% is the weighted average across all seven models on SWE-agent (Verified, 1,607 failures), not 'strong models'; for the five strong models the Edit-Quality share is 64-69%. Other numbers (Chen 61.9/69.2%, 52.0%, ~65%, 39.7%/22.6%, 18.6%) check out.
fix: Debug loops repair small slips (missing WHERE, DISTINCT, wrong JOIN; 62-69% output mismatch), while unresolved agent runs are dominated by wrong or over-narrow implementations (52%) and flawed reasoning (about 65%). Loops fix near-misses, not wrong designs. TRAJEVAL (16,758 trajectories, 7 models): on SWE-agent Verified, 56.9% of failures across all models (64-69% for the five stronger models) reach and edit the right function and still fail (Edit-Quality bucket); of those, overwriting a correct edit (coherence collapse) is 39.7% (22.6% of all failures) and a wrong branch point 18.6%.

problem: Reflexion and PatchDiff numbers match; note the SWE-bench figures concern benchmark (developer-written) tests being incomplete, not self-generated tests, so they only loosely support the headline.

SWE-agent ablation numbers all check out (18.0, 11.0, 2.67, +3.0, 14.3, 12.7), but AutoCodeRover (19.0% vs SWE-agent 18.0%, different setups) does not isolate an interface effect, and CodeAct reports a 'up to 20%' action-format effect only in its abstract.
fix: Tool and interface design changes results at fixed model. SWE-agent GPT-4 Turbo on Lite: 18.0 vs shell-only 11.0 vs RAG 2.67; linting-guarded edits +3.0; 100-line viewer beats 30-line (14.3) and full file (12.7). CodeAct (up to 20% higher success from executable-code actions across 17 LLMs, per its abstract) points the same way, while AutoCodeRover (19.0% on Lite) does not isolate an interface effect. Lite has 300 items, so single ablations carry about 2 points of noise.

problem: Numbers all check; note the 12.47 to 3.97 drop is SWE-agent+GPT-4 only, and lower scores on SWE-bench-Live/Pro could partly reflect task difficulty rather than inflation alone.
Minor: R1-Distill-Llama-70B blind spot is -0.031 and -0.05 on two sets but +0.113 on SCLI5, which the claim omits; 'moot' is an inference.
Minor: DEI paper quotes the union (oracle) as 54.3% for the 10-agent group (53.3% at 9 agents), not exactly 'about 53%', and the 34.3% headline and union come from different group sizes.
Spider paper says improvement after one turn is 'within 0.1%' (claim says under 0.1%), trivial.
Minor: arXiv 2602.02416 is titled 'Structure Enables Effective Self-Localization of Errors in LLMs' not the title the notes give; Table 1 numbers match.

The 72-81% right-file rate is for failed runs on SWE-Bench Lite only (3 agents); on Verified it is 59-67%, and 56.9% is the weighted average over 7 models (strong models range 64.7-69.1%), not only strong ones.
fix: For strong models, failures are mostly not localisation. In SWE-agent on SWE-bench Verified, 56.9% of failures (weighted over 7 models; 64.7-69.1% for the five capable models, GPT-5 68.1%) reach and edit the right locations yet produce a wrong patch; a separate study finds failed runs still hit the gold file in 72-81% of cases on SWE-Bench Lite (59-67% on Verified). The largest single sub-type is coherence collapse (overwriting or thrashing a correct edit, 22.6% of all failures); an edit-commit checkpoint recovered all 5 bit-identical-to-gold cases (existence proof only). Wrong branch point is about 10.6% of all failures.

problem: Minor: Pro's 43.6% (Sonnet 4.5) and 17.8% (Opus 4.1) are best scores of different model sets (same-model GPT-5 41.8 vs 15.7), and Pro's held-out set results are not released, only commercial.
Minor: 98.7% is a Codenames clue revision rate for Claude Haiku 4.5 (not all answers), and the 44-task/no-reframing result is from 11 participants on structure tasks only.
Minor: the 'shared reasoning process, different knowledge base' sentence is Rankin et al. restating Klein et al. 2007 second-hand, and Pontis is only 5 experts vs 6 novices.

Minor: Pontis says 'more than two activities occurred simultaneously' made decomposition hard (it does not mention coder disagreement stats); the evidence note b01 saying all frame activities were seen contradicts a02 (3 unobserved), but the claim does not use it.

Accuracy numbers match (76.8 vs 60.1 p=.004; 22.7 vs 16.7 p=.080), but 'no gain in calibration' holds only overall (p=.19): on easier cases the reflection group was better calibrated (p=.016); the residents availability-bias clause has no source among those listed and JAMA 2010 says reflection 'tended to counter' the bias, not removed it.
fix: A prompted step to question the first diagnosis raised accuracy in dermatology students on easier cases (76.8% vs 60.1%, p=.004), with a smaller non-significant effect on harder cases (22.7% vs 16.7%, p=.080), and no overall change in confidence or calibration (calibration p=.19; on easier cases calibration was better in the reflection group, p=.016). In internal-medicine residents, structured reflection tended to counter an availability-bias deficit (Mamede 2010). Gap 3 note: no LLM study splits the question-first-answer gain by item difficulty; the nearest (Stav 2026) found gain unrelated to baseline accuracy (rho 0.05) and related to verifiability (rho 0.65).

problem: Minor: GPT-4 CommonSenseQA barely moved (82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0) and the 98.7% figure is Haiku 4.5's Codenames revision rate; all quoted numbers match Tables 2 and 3 of Huang et al., CRITIC, Stechly and Stav.
CRITIC with tool did not beat no-tool in every row: text-davinci-003 SVAMP is a tie (80.7 vs 80.7); other QA and GSM8k/TabMWP rows do favour the tool (e.g. ChatGPT HotpotQA F1 52.9 vs 46.1).
fix: A model-only check is weak and an outside signal is strong. Tool-based critique beat or matched no-tool critique in every CRITIC QA and math row (one exact tie: text-davinci-003 SVAMP, 80.7 both); a model-only check on graph coloring accepted only 2 of 100 optimal colorings, and in 39 of 40 cases where the generator had produced an optimal coloring the verifier hallucinated same-colour adjacent pairs. For 2026 models the gain from a no-tool revision correlates with verifiability (rho 0.65), not with baseline accuracy (rho 0.05).

problem: Minor: FalsifyBench 68-75% are only the top two reasoning models (GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%), and the SIA ablation is a single small-sample agent (100 scored cases).

Minor: Lou and Sun tested only GPT-4 and GPT-4o on 62 questions; Kraishan's delta +0.031 is reasoning vs sibling non-reasoning model across 4 families, and the restate-the-anchor effect (p=.057) was not significant.

Minor: Shi et al. tested distractor sentences in math word problems on GPT-3.5-era models, not anchoring, so 'partly help' is evidence about irrelevant context in general; Lou and Sun tested only GPT-4/GPT-4o.

Minor: narrative-closure evidence is a small sample (72 responses, 24 prompts, 3 models) from a different task and population than the medical false-action results; 'default' is the authors' 87.5% not-open figure (40% narrative closure).

Minor: 'about 70%' is the mean false-action rate on no-correct-option medical MCQs (range 55-81% by model), and the 41% abstain vs 90% act figure is one scenario (S3) for the aggregate, not best agent.

Minor: the 0.78 vs 0.40 no-clarification gap is from only 18 goal variants, late-is-worse-than-never applies to deferral past mid-trajectory, and the 26.7 to 57.4 figure is Llama-3.3-70B only on an abstention-only WebShop subset.

Minor: Snowball's 15-20% is the share of the full-to-sharded drop mitigated (GPT-4o and 4o-mini, four tasks) and MINT's 24.2% is the average accuracy drop from early answering in a medical benchmark, not the same measure as Laban's 39%.
Minor: recovery counts (7 of 8, 1 of 14) rest on very small per-model denominators in one clinical study; 'recaps recover only part' is strictly snowball (15-20%); recap on last turn did better.

Minor: the N=50 Whitesmith figure could not be verified (second-hand, as the claim itself says); Karvetski and Mandel report ACH sometimes produced worse performance (Mandel 2018), not merely null; Lehner's N=24 null is on projection error only.
Minor: Trickett is 3 scientists in two datasets and Meister 11 pre-service teachers, so 'people' is a broad generalisation; the 7.6 vs 1.5 figure is astronomy only (physics 3.0 vs 1.25).
Al Essa et al. report accuracy 0.110 (early) vs 0.168 (late) but the pairwise contrast between early and late distractors was not significant; only reading time per word fell for early distractors.
fix: Salient distracting findings placed at the start or at the end of a case both cut medical students' diagnostic accuracy (0.269 to 0.110 and 0.168); the accuracy difference between early and late was not significant, but only early distractors shortened reading time per word, which the authors read as premature closure (single study, 58 students).

problem: Minor: Kan et al. found full elimination in their direct+alternative condition (score equal to baseline) and Mickelberg found full discounting of person misinformation in 2 of 3 experiments, so 'rarely remove it fully' holds for the literature as the authors frame it, not for every condition; Chan et al. meta-analysis not opened.

All four supporting lines are the same Xie et al. 2024 paper (arXiv 2305.13300) and the fifth, a survey, gives no numbers; the numbers themselves (GPT-4 about 80% memorization on most popular questions, order sensitivity, coherent single-source counter-evidence accepted) do match the paper.

Shapira et al. report that anti-sycophancy prompts/steering lowered adoption of the source's claim along with the user's and that the two drops correlate (Pearson 0.87), not that useful and harmful updating fell by about the same amount; also the COMPARE prompt cut adoption more than VERIFY only for search and sub-agent (code: 31.2 vs 30.4, no accuracy loss).
fix: Models weigh in-context claims by how credible the source looks (adoption rose with stated source accuracy 20/50/90%), not by whether the claim is true. Anti-sycophancy prompts and steering lowered adoption of a credible source's claim together with adoption of the user's, with the two drops correlated (Pearson 0.87 across frontier models), so useful updating falls along with harmful. An explicit authority-limiting frame cut misleading-clue flips from 49.8% (TOOL) to 19.1% (TOOL+ANTIDOTE), cross-model mean on high-prior cases with no tool executed. For tool outputs, mean adoption of corrupted returns was 68.0% (search), 40.1% (sub-agent), 35.5% (code); a verify-by-tool-call prompt cut adoption modestly with little loss on correct returns, and a compare-with-prior-knowledge prompt cut adoption more for search and sub-agent tools but lowered accuracy on correct returns there.

problem: Minor: both checked from PubMed abstracts only (as the claim states); the two figures use different denominators (subjects vs incidents), as the claim says.
